article_title: DaisyQuest (Early Childhood Education)
citation: DaisyQuest for Preschool Children. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Story-framed mastery-based computer activities with reward clues
description: DaisyQuest organizes phonological awareness practice as levels embedded in a fairy-tale narrative, where mastering each level yields clues advancing the story. The report states: "As children master each level of instructional activities, they are rewarded with clues that eventually lead them to discover where Daisy is hiding." The same structure recurs in Daisy's Castle, where completing levels yields clues to lost eggs, and "DaisyQuest uses story lines and colorful graphics to engage children in the learning process."
requirements: Instructional activities organized into mastery levels with an overarching narrative providing reward clues
target_learners: Preschool through second grade children
target_learning_goals: Phonological awareness skills practiced through game-like mastery levels
examples: DaisyQuest's search for the dragon Daisy and Daisy's Castle's search for Daisy's lost eggs both link activity levels to narrative clues
key_sources: DaisyQuest for Preschool Children. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc

article_title: STEMscopes Math
citation: STEMscopes Math Evidence Summary. (2024).
title: 5E+IA instructional model with Concrete-Representational-Abstract progression
description: The program's organizing instructional pattern is the 5E+IA model: "Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate, plus Intervention and Acceleration pathways." It structures whole-group instruction, small-group differentiation, and blended learning, and follows a "Concrete-Representational-Abstract progression" that sequences mathematical representations from concrete materials to abstract symbols, with digital tools such as virtual manipulatives and PhET simulations integrated.
requirements: Digital access devices for teachers and students to use the integrated digital tools
target_learners: K–Algebra 1 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics concept and skill development across representational levels
examples: The curriculum embeds Intervention and Acceleration pathways alongside the five E phases
key_sources: STEMscopes Math Evidence Summary. (2024). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/stemscopes-math-2/

article_title: STEMscopes Science
citation: STEMscopes evidence rating summary. (2024). Evidence rating: promising. https://www.stemscopes.com
title: 5E-based inquiry curriculum design with embedded formative assessment
description: The curriculum is organized around the 5E instructional model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate), pairing hands-on, inquiry-based investigations with real-world problem solving and embedded formative assessments. The article states the program is "grounded in the 5E instructional model" and is "designed to promote student engagement through interactive investigations, real-world problem solving, and embedded formative assessments."
requirements: Digital and print resources plus hands-on materials to support science instruction
constraints: Aligned to state standards, as evaluated in a Grade 5 science context
target_learners: Elementary science students
target_learning_goals: Science conceptual understanding and engagement through inquiry
examples: STEMscopes implements this pattern with interactive investigations and embedded formative assessments across digital, print, and hands-on materials.
key_sources: STEMscopes evidence rating summary. (2024). Evidence rating: promising. https://www.stemscopes.com

article_title: Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI)
citation: Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) program evidence summary. (2024). Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Four types of peer collaboration embedded in a reading intervention
description: STARI was designed to promote social interactions that foster student engagement, structuring peer collaboration in four recurring formats across its units. The program "uses four types of peer collaboration: partner-assisted fluency practice, reciprocal teaching of comprehension strategies, partner reading and responding to novels and nonfiction texts, and peer debate, in which teams gather text evidence and build arguments." Peer contexts also push students to articulate personal stances on texts and compare them with partners or classmates.
requirements: Trained teachers able to facilitate discussion and build a strong classroom culture
constraints: Implemented within the STARI curriculum's thematic units for struggling middle school readers
target_learners: middle school students who struggle with reading
target_learning_goals: fluency
comprehension strategies
argumentation from text evidence
engagement
examples: Peer debate teams gather text evidence and build arguments; partners read and respond to novels and nonfiction texts
key_sources: Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) program evidence summary. (2024). Evidence for ESSA. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/strategic-adolescent-reading-intervention-stari/

article_title: Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI)
citation: Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) program evidence summary. (2024). Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Staff STARI with trained teachers who facilitate discussion and build classroom culture, not necessarily reading specialists
description: STARI is a teacher-led program whose success depends on the teacher's facilitation rather than on specialist credentials. "STARI is a teacher-led program, and the program’s success relies on the teacher’s ability to facilitate discussion and build a strong classroom culture." Because the curriculum is clearly laid out and professional learning is comprehensive, teachers from a variety of backgrounds have demonstrated success, and a licensed reading specialist is not necessary.
requirements: Teachers trained to implement STARI, able to facilitate discussion and build a strong classroom culture
constraints: A licensed reading specialist is not necessary; success depends on facilitation ability
target_learners: middle school students who struggle with reading
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension and component reading skills
examples: Certified teachers recruited from participating schools received training during a 3-day summer institute and feedback from literacy coaches throughout the intervention
key_sources: Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) program evidence summary. (2024). Evidence for ESSA. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/strategic-adolescent-reading-intervention-stari/

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Use concrete models strategically and remove them as soon as students can work without them
description: JUMP Math uses "a range of models (concrete materials, tables, diagrams) ... strategically to help students grasp abstract concepts but the models are removed as soon as students are able to work without these supports." The principle is deliberate, temporary scaffolding: models support abstraction but are faded promptly rather than retained.
requirements: Concrete materials, tables, or diagrams available to support abstract concepts
target_learners: K to 8 students
target_learning_goals: grasping abstract math concepts
examples: The program's practice of removing models as soon as students can work without supports.
key_sources: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/jump-math/

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Streamline student materials and reserve lesson detail for teacher guides to protect working memory
description: JUMP Math has no student textbooks; students complete work in "practice and assessment guides that are streamlined to limit extraneous information and contain only the essential language." Lesson details are reserved for teachers' guides "so that teachers can control the timing and amount of information the students receive so as not to overwhelm student working memory."
requirements: Detailed teachers guides separate from streamlined student guides
target_learners: K to 8 students
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous load while learning math concepts
examples: Smart board materials are not required but many teachers choose to use them.
key_sources: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/jump-math/

article_title: Understanding the Capacity of State Apprenticeship Systems: Apprenticeship Evidence-Building Portfolio
citation: Alicia Harrington, Ryan Ruggiero, Samina Sattar, Lauren Eyster. (2022). Understanding the Capacity of State Apprenticeship Systems: Apprenticeship Evidence-Building Portfolio. Urban Institute. https://www.urban.org
title: Eight-characteristic framework of state apprenticeship system capacity
description: The report organizes state apprenticeship system capacity around an enumerated set of characteristics, spanning program registration, employer recruitment, apprentice diversity, rural and opioid-related expansion, financial incentives, costs and federal grants, COVID-19 impacts, and data infrastructure. The report states it covers "variation of systems across states in key characteristics" and lists them as topics for the series. The framework structures both this overview and the later state interviews.
requirements: Requires scanned apprenticeship data, literature, and recent studies to populate the characteristics
constraints: Applies to United States state-level Registered Apprenticeship systems
target_learners: apprentices in Registered Apprenticeship programs
state apprenticeship system staff
target_learning_goals: understanding and expanding state Registered Apprenticeship systems
examples: The report lists characteristics including "strategies for recruiting employers" and "the role of financial incentives in expanding apprenticeship"
key_sources: Alicia Harrington, Ryan Ruggiero, Samina Sattar, Lauren Eyster. (2022). Understanding the Capacity of State Apprenticeship Systems: Apprenticeship Evidence-Building Portfolio. Urban Institute. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/understanding-the-capacity-of-state-apprenticeship-systems-apprenticeship-evidence-building

article_title: Research Review: Data-Driven Decision Making in Education Agencies. Data Driven, not Data Drowning
citation: Mid-Atlantic Regional Educational Laboratory. (2018). Research Review: Data-Driven Decision Making in Education Agencies. Data Driven, not Data Drowning. Washington, DC: Mid-Atlantic Regional Educational Laboratory. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Start data-use design from who will access, analyze, or review the data and for what purpose
description: The review recommends that meaningful use of data in education agencies begin by identifying the decision makers and the decisions the data will serve. It states that "Meaningful use of data begins with who will access, analyze, or review the data and for what purpose," and that data must be "relevant and diagnostic for each decision maker and decision." The principle directs agencies to design data use around specific users and purposes rather than around data availability alone.
requirements: Data must be relevant and diagnostic for each decision maker and decision, as the review states.
target_learners: education agency decision makers
target_learning_goals: effective use of data for educational decision making
examples: The review frames its guidance for education agencies around identifying who will access, analyze, or review data and for what purpose before data use efforts begin.
key_sources: Mid-Atlantic Regional Educational Laboratory. (2018). Research Review: Data-Driven Decision Making in Education Agencies. Data Driven, not Data Drowning. Washington, DC: Mid-Atlantic Regional Educational Laboratory. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/research-review-data-driven-decision-making-in-education-agencies-data-driven-not-data-drowning

article_title: The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Kristin Hallgren. (2015). The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making. Issue Brief, Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Develop a teacher of record definition that reflects all professionals and educational settings
description: The brief recommends that states adopting teacher of record definitions craft a definition that covers every professional contributing to instruction and every educational arrangement, citing co-teaching as an example. A definition limited to traditional single-teacher classrooms would misattribute students in shared-instruction settings. The brief pairs this with implementing the definition through a roster verification system so teacher-student data links are valid.
requirements: The definition must reflect all professionals and educational settings, such as co-teaching.
target_learners: K-12 students in state accountability systems
target_learning_goals: Valid attribution of student achievement growth to teachers of record
examples: The brief's key findings list: 'Develop a definition that reflects all professionals and educational settings (for example, co-teaching).'
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Kristin Hallgren. (2015). The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making. Issue Brief, Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-importance-of-a-teacher-of-record-definition-and-roster-verification-for-highstakes-decision

article_title: Early Education Essentials
citation: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. Chicago, IL: The Ounce of Prevention Fund and the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research.
title: Strong instructional leadership: purpose-driven vision, relational trust, and protected collaboration
description: When Effective Instructional Leaders is strong, leaders hold a vision "rooted in developmental science and developmentally appropriate practice," view teachers as professional educators, build relational trust with staff, maneuver around incompatible mandates by reframing them toward shared purpose, and cultivate family partnerships. Weak programs instead show compliance-driven visions, micromanagement, and transactional leadership, as contrasted in the report's Table 1.
requirements: Leaders need knowledge of child development and early childhood instructional practices to ground the vision
constraints: Leaders in strong sites still face frequent central/grantee office mandates, some incompatible with their vision, which they must reframe
target_learners: preschool children and the teachers, staff, and families surrounding them
target_learning_goals: consistent, developmentally appropriate early learning and staff capacity for improvement
examples: One leader protected the first two days of the school year for collaboration and split another day across the year for professional learning groups
A leader scheduled around staff family commitments, asking whether a 5:30pm finish was too late for a staff member's husband's birthday
key_sources: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. Chicago, IL: The Ounce of Prevention Fund and the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/early-education-essentials-illustrations-strong-organizational-practices-programs

article_title: Early Education Essentials
citation: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. Chicago, IL: The Ounce of Prevention Fund and the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research.
title: Strong collaborative teachers: protected, structured, data-driven peer collaboration
description: When Collaborative Teachers is strong, leaders ensure teachers have "routine protected time, weekly and monthly" to meet, with collaboration that is structured by goals, data, and protocols focused on real problems of practice. Teachers observe each other's classrooms, bring up problems of practice, and share innovations; weak programs show individual accountability, minimal feedback, and no routine peer observation (Table 2).
requirements: Leaders must allocate and protect collaboration time and facilitate it with clear purpose and structured processes
constraints: Teachers reported struggles using collaboration time productively and that the work demands being highly multitask oriented
target_learners: preschool teaching teams, including special education and dual-language learner contexts
target_learning_goals: meeting diverse learning needs of young children and continuous improvement of teaching practice
examples: A teaching team met weekly to discuss individual children and set goals across social-emotional, cognitive, language, and literacy areas
Peer learning groups broke out during staff meetings several times a quarter to visit each other's classrooms
key_sources: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. Chicago, IL: The Ounce of Prevention Fund and the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/early-education-essentials-illustrations-strong-organizational-practices-programs

article_title: Early Education Essentials
citation: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. Chicago, IL: The Ounce of Prevention Fund and the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research.
title: Strong involved families: welcoming routines, multi-channel communication, and partnership in learning
description: When Involved Families is strong, staff treat partnerships with families as critical to teaching effectiveness: families are welcomed "in every part of the building throughout the day," staff "use multiple, ongoing strategies to build relationships and communicate with families," and teachers partner with families to extend learning at home. Weak programs limit family engagement to funder requirements, homework folders without context, and inconsistent formal communication.
requirements: Staff must treat engaging and partnering with families as a critical part of the job, equally as important as work directly with children
target_learners: preschool children and their families, including grandparents and extended family
target_learning_goals: family understanding of children's development and extension of learning opportunities at home
examples: Leaders and staff greeted families and children by name at drop-off and pick-up, and families walked all the way to classrooms
Classroom webpages posted photos of units and home-connection suggestions alongside newsletters
key_sources: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. article_title: The Development of Racial/Ethnic and Socioeconomic Achievement Gaps During the School Years
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, Elizabeth Gershoff, Katherine Paschall. (2018). The development of racial/ethnic and socioeconomic achievement gaps during the school years. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 57, 62-73. https://www.journals.elsevier.com/journal-of-applied-developmental-psychology
title: Study race and poverty in interaction when measuring achievement gaps
description: The article concludes that achievement-gap measurement should treat race/ethnicity and poverty jointly rather than separately, because their association with math and reading achievement varies together across development. The results "highlight the importance of studying race and poverty in interaction when measuring achievement gaps." The authors support this with TVEM estimates showing that gaps among poverty groups differ by race/ethnicity and widen at specific ages.
requirements: Longitudinal achievement data spanning school entry through middle school, analyzed with a method such as TVEM that estimates associations across continuous age
constraints: Findings are based on two large longitudinal data sets covering ages 5 to 15 in math and reading achievement; the abstract does not report effects outside this range or domain
target_learners: students from age 5 to age 15 in U.S. schools
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
reading achievement
examples: The study modeled developmental trends in achievement gaps between poverty and race/ethnicity groups from school entry to middle school using two large longitudinal data sets
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, Elizabeth Gershoff, Katherine Paschall. (2018). The development of racial/ethnic and socioeconomic achievement gaps during the school years. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 57, 62-73. https://www.journals.elsevier.com/journal-of-applied-developmental-psychology

article_title: The IEP Project: A Strength-based, Whole Learner Teacher Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2023, February). The IEP project: A strength-based, whole learner teacher guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/169
title: Write IEPs and teacher reports through a strength-based, whole learner lens so student strengths are used to address growth areas
description: This principle holds that IEP reporting should begin from what students can do, seen through a whole learner lens, rather than from a deficit inventory. The guide states that "A goal of this guidebook is to see student strengths through a whole learner lens and write IEPs that reflect strengths to be used to address growth areas." It frames deficit-based approaches as surfacing only struggles, especially harmful for students with learning disabilities facing stigma.
requirements: A shared understanding of the student's strengths among stakeholders, situated within the student's context
constraints: Designed for PreK-12 public education IEP processes
target_learners: PreK-12 students with learning disabilities and other IEP-eligible students
target_learning_goals: Academic growth in literacy and math
Social-emotional learning and behavior
examples: The guide's sample response bank describes Antonio, who struggles to read with fluency and accuracy but has strong listening comprehension and extensive vocabulary, with decoding instruction and text-to-speech kept on two tracks
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2023, February). The IEP project: A strength-based, whole learner teacher guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/169

article_title: Equity in the Driver’s Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education
citation: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Begin R&D agenda-setting from districts' specific equity challenges rather than from the research literature
description: The article recommends structuring agenda-setting so that practical field perspectives drive the framing of research questions. 'We intentionally structured the day to begin with the specific equity challenges that the invited district teams were facing, rather than starting from a research perspective,' based on the hunch that this would yield questions relevant and usable in practice. Research is then consulted in service of those challenges, with district teams first sharing what they found most useful in topic overviews and what else they would need to know.
requirements: Access to district teams who can articulate authentic equity challenges with supporting data and artifacts
Topic overviews prepared in advance so participants enter discussions with working knowledge
constraints: The authors note that published research 'often does not provide a meaningful starting point for action' on its own and must be mediated by practitioners' local knowledge
target_learners: K-12 students in participating districts, with attention to students at the margins
target_learning_goals: Producing R&D agendas that address schools' most pressing equity-related needs
examples: District teams shared viewpoints on topic overviews before researchers added additional findings, flipping the traditional dynamic in which researchers kick off such dialogue
key_sources: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/1185beda-6355-47f0-b3f2-980f6541172b

article_title: Fostering Market Effciency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement
citation: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768
title: Districts should use structured pilots for discovery and evaluation of ed-tech products
description: The report recommends that districts and providers would benefit substantially from guidelines for conducting formal pilots to facilitate discovery and evaluation. Pilots that are structured and rigorous generate evidence about product efficacy that is useful locally and to other districts considering the same products. Effective strategies are needed for matching products to teachers, funding pilots, collecting qualitative and quantitative data, and analyzing results.
requirements: Strategies for matching products to be piloted to teachers based on interest and instructional needs
Funding for pilots
Collection of both qualitative and quantitative data on implementation, satisfaction, and educational outcomes
constraints: Informal pilots (demos, brief try-outs, committee reviews) may yield questionable conclusions about product quality
target_learners: K-12 school district administrators and ed-tech providers
target_learning_goals: Evaluating ed-tech product quality and effectiveness for selection decisions
examples: District participants overall reported a moderate-to-extensive reliance on pilot tryouts (mostly informal demos and field tests) within the district for ed-tech procurement.
key_sources: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768

article_title: Fostering Market Effciency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement
citation: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768
title: Districts should create guidelines for structuring instructional needs assessments
description: The report recommends districts would likely benefit from the creation of guidelines and models for structuring instructional needs assessments to ensure that selections and acquisitions are linked directly to priority areas. Districts should also more integrally involve end-users in defining needs more specifically and operationally, and should obtain guidelines for matching instructional design features of ed-tech products to needs assessments.
requirements: Guidelines and models for structuring instructional needs assessments
Greater involvement of end-users (teachers and principals) in defining needs specifically and operationally
constraints: Current needs assessments are most frequently surface in nature and do not identify specific types of support and product attributes
target_learners: K-12 school district administrators, curriculum directors, and technology directors
target_learning_goals: Linking ed-tech selection and acquisition directly to priority instructional areas
examples: The report recommends involving end-users in defining needs operationally, such as 'To teach problem-based learning more effectively in STEM classes.'
key_sources: Morrison, J. R., Ross, S. M., Corcoran, R. P., & Reid, A. J. (2014). Fostering Market Efficiency in K-12 Ed-tech Procurement. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563768

article_title: Accelerating Change: How Education Technology Developers Can Jump-Start a New Adult Education Market
citation: DeSchryver, David A., with Deirdre Dlugoleski. (2015). Accelerating Change: How education technology developers can jump-start a new adult education market. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Adult ed-tech should enable stackable, portable micro-credentials and employer-connected accelerated learning
description: The report recommends that adult ed-tech developers use micro-credentials and digital badges to "breathe life into the policy objectives of “stackable credentials” and “portable credentials" emphasized under WIOA. Stackable credentials accumulate over time to build qualifications; portable credentials are recognized in other settings such as educational institutions, industries, or employers. It also recommends accelerated learning models (e.g., coding bootcamps) that give students "just enough training to get started in a new career" and connect them with partner companies for employment, extending these to low-skilled adults.
requirements: Credentials must be recognized and accepted as verifying qualifications in other settings such as educational institutions, other industries, or employing companies
constraints: The report notes accelerated learning programs currently work outside traditional workforce and higher education models, and connections to adult learning programs are only beginning
target_learners: Adult learners seeking better jobs or career advancement, including low-skilled adults
target_learning_goals: Occupational and workforce skills
Recognized, portable qualifications
examples: Digital Promise is building a coalition to develop a micro-credential system for K-12 educators; General Assembly and Flatiron are creating bridge programs and partnerships to put adult learners on track for accelerated programs
key_sources: DeSchryver, David A., with Deirdre Dlugoleski. (2015). Accelerating Change: How education technology developers can jump-start a new adult education market. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/29f39d7d-87f2-4e1e-920e-0c1ce86035cc

article_title: A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education
citation: Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2024). A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Student Voice and Leadership tenet: students as prioritized collaborators in education R&D
description: The Student Voice and Leadership tenet holds that "students are collaborators and their perspectives are prioritized in the creation of solutions to educational challenges." Four R&D principles operationalize this: center the voices and leadership of students proximate to the challenge, commit to disrupting power dynamics, co-create engaging student-friendly structures and processes with students, and value and validate student lived experience in problem definition and solution design. The work starts with teaching adults that students can and should lead R&D efforts to dismantle inequities, rather than involving students later to advance adult perspectives.
requirements: Adults must learn to listen and champion students' rightful place in R&D with actions signaling the primacy of student voice
Structures and processes must be accessible and designed for student-first engagement
Students' choices must carry greater weight in decision-making processes
target_learners: students proximate to educational challenges, especially from historically marginalized communities
target_learning_goals: student agency
student engagement
equitable solution design
examples: Bristol Township students received weighted votes on solutions and PD design; Sunnyside student interns conducted research and designed three solutions for writing engagement
key_sources: Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2024). A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/73f2e0fa-dca8-4cd0-a8da-eb18b59453c4

article_title: Teacher Learner Connect Project
citation: Iwatani, E., Simmons, C., & Bustillos, A. (2023). Adolescent Development Convening: Extended Learning Support Final Report Narrative (Teacher Learner Connect project). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Put student voice at the center of assessment decisions because students' experiences are rarely considered in assessment decision-making
description: The report's collaborators repeatedly affirmed the importance of student voice: "Any time there's an opportunity to give students a voice, that is powerful. Their experiences are not considered in so much of the decision making around assessment." The project treated listening to students as valuable in itself and as a route to reevaluating how students are assessed, with district leaders expressing interest in pursuing this collaboratively.
requirements: Opportunities and structures for students to share their perspectives, such as the TLC conversations
Willingness of educators and district leaders to act on what students share
constraints: Educators' control is limited to classroom assessments versus standardized assessments outside their control
target_learners: adolescent students in secondary classrooms
target_learning_goals: assessment practices that support exploration and healthy risk-taking
student agency and belonging
examples: One education leader began raising new questions about how the district and schools are assessing and including student voice after participating in the study.
key_sources: Iwatani, E., Simmons, C., & Bustillos, A. (2023). Adolescent Development Convening: Extended Learning Support Final Report Narrative (Teacher Learner Connect project). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/b675c423-a956-4e86-a124-89962f8ef1d6

article_title: Nico & Nor Teacher Flyer
citation: Early Science with Nico and Nor®. (2022). WGBH Educational Foundation. https://www.wgbh.org
title: Use digital tools to strengthen, not replace, hands-on exploration in early science learning
description: The program's design principle is that technology should augment physical investigation: it "leverages digital tools with unique affordances for STEM learning to strengthen (not replace) hands-on exploration". In practice, apps gave children opportunities not possible in class and let them easily practice what they learned in hands-on activities, while games and journals supported observation, testing, and data practices across school and home.
requirements: Digital tools paired with hands-on investigations rather than substituting for them
target_learners: preschool children
target_learning_goals: science phenomena observation
science practices
STEM learning across domains

title: Blueprint for Statewide Pathways Scaling (five-component theory of action)
description: The report's central framework is a theory of action for scaling career pathways statewide, consisting of "three critical layers": state-level actors, models, and policy/funding mechanisms; regional-level district cohorts, pathways design, and partnerships; and measurable outcomes across education and economic systems. article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis
citation: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm
title: Design elements for STEM PLCs: time and pacing, subject composition, protocols, and facilitation with administrator support and trust
description: The synthesis identifies recurring design considerations for STEM PLCs drawn across its knowledge sources. Designers must attend to "many aspects related to time and pacing", wisely factoring the relationship between desired PLC purposes and available conditions into decisions about how much and how often to meet. Group composition matters: "Comprising PLCs with teachers from multiple subjects (even limited to mathematics and science) can limit the depth or effectiveness of work on content knowledge or PCK." Protocols for group functioning and for examining student work are important but must be monitored, and facilitation, administrator support and trust-building are described as crucial.
requirements: Having facilitation, administrator support and trust-building are crucial; facilitators require professional development because facilitating adult learning is different than facilitating student learning.
Protocols for STEM PLC group functioning and for examining students' work should be built in, with design and use carefully considered and monitored.
constraints: Multi-subject composition, even limited to mathematics and science, can limit the depth or effectiveness of work on content knowledge or PCK.
The protocol can become the end instead of the means if not monitored.
Public discussion of content knowledge and PCK might be very foreign and threatening given the historical practice of teaching in isolation.
target_learners: K-12 STEM teachers in inservice PLCs
target_learning_goals: STEM content knowledge
pedagogical content knowledge (PCK)
collaborative examination of student work
examples: The reviewed lesson study articles ranged from one partial cycle in one semester to multiple cycles across two years, illustrating why level of effort must be factored into design decisions.
key_sources: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis
citation: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm
title: Taxonomy of studied STEM PLC models: lesson study, university course plus follow-up, collaborative action research, grade-level or department meetings, and discussion groups
description: The synthesis categorizes the PLC phenomena investigated in the reviewed research into face-to-face inservice modes — lesson study, university course plus follow-up, collaborative action research or collaborative inquiry groups, grade-level or department meetings, and discussion groups — plus separately tabled online PLC experiences and preservice PLC experiences. It reports that "The most common kind of PLC was variations of lesson study, but there was a wide range of phenomena among this group", with a full Japanese cycle involving joint planning, teaching, group revision and debrief, re-teaching and a final debrief, though most studied cycles omitted the revise and re-teach stages. The taxonomy exists because of great confusion in the literature about what a PLC is.
requirements: Readers need the level of effort — meeting frequency, duration, and time span — to accurately deliberate the findings' applicability, but many articles only state that groups met regularly or often.
constraints: Online and preservice phenomena are termed PLC experiences rather than PLCs because their informality, loose structure, or time constraints limit them from being fully conceived PLCs.
Only eight studies investigated online PLC experiences and only eight strongly focused on preservice teachers.
target_learners: K-12 inservice STEM teachers
preservice STEM teachers
target_learning_goals: collaborative improvement of STEM teaching practice
joint investigation of content and instructional practices
examples: The lesson study category spans one cycle in one semester, two cycles in one semester, one multi-lesson-unit cycle in one year, two stages over two years, and multiple cycles over one or two years.
key_sources: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching
citation: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf
title: Design and implementation principles of effective STEM learning teams
description: The synthesis identifies key design and implementation features shared by STEM learning teams that met high research standards: "shared goals and values, leadership support, issues of time and pacing, focus on student data and work products, collective responsibility for student achievement, good facilitation, and building trust." Teams should identify a STEM learning challenge, keep a steady focus on improving student learning, meet on common regular time, examine student data and work with common rubrics and protocols, and hold mutual accountability for student achievement. A single school subject focus is also identified as easing deep content engagement.
requirements: Teams need support of principals and administrators, including dedicated space and time to meet
Teachers need common time to meet on a regular and sustained basis
Teams should examine student data and work using common rubrics and protocols
constraints: It can take more than a few weeks or months for an unfamiliar team to open up about deeper aspects of STEM teaching
Cross-content teams need additional time and more complex strategies to engage meaningfully in subject content and pedagogy
U.S. school structure emphasizes individual teacher performance over teamwork, and pressure for rapid outcomes can trump the time and trust needed
target_learners: K-12 STEM teachers, including prospective teachers
target_learning_goals: Improving STEM teaching practice and student STEM learning
examples: The expert panel ranked shared values and goals as the most important factor
The report notes Shanghai middle school mathematics teachers each belong to two math learning teams
key_sources: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf

article_title: Design Principles for Schools: Putting the Science of Learning and Development into Action
citation: Learning Policy Institute & Turnaround for Children. (2021). Design principles for schools: Putting the science of learning and development into action. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Organize schools through structures and practices that build positive developmental relationships
description: The report recommends that schools be deliberately organized so educators can form continuous, secure relationships with students, collaborate with colleagues and families, and build community. It states that "Schools can be organized to foster positive developmental relationships through structures and practices that allow for effective caring and the building of community". Named structures include small learning communities, advisory systems, looping, home visits, staff collaboration time, and shared decision-making; practices include trust-building behaviors and pedagogies that develop deep knowledge of students and their cultural contexts.
requirements: Structures that enable continuous, secure relationships and allow teachers to know children well, plus opportunities among adults for collaboration toward shared goals
target_learners: k-12 students
target_learning_goals: student agency and self-direction
motivation and self-efficacy
sense of being known and valued at school
examples: Gateway Middle School in San Francisco uses student-led conferences in which students present their work and goals to families; the profiled school reports a 98% graduation rate and 96% college matriculation since 1998
key_sources: Learning Policy Institute & Turnaround for Children. (2021). Design principles for schools: Putting the science of learning and development into action. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

article_title: Magnet Schools and Metropolitan Civil Rights Planning: A Strategy to Revitalize and Stabilize Distressed Communities
citation: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312
title: Stable Metropolitan Racial Integration framework for affirmatively furthering fair housing
description: A proposed classification system that divides metropolitan areas into three community types — areas of minority concentration, racially mixed areas, and predominantly white areas — and sets different fair housing requirements for each. The report states: "The proposed Stable Metropolitan Racial Integration system divides metropolitan areas into three types of communities." Under the framework, magnet schools are encouraged in areas of minority concentration to reintegrate and revitalize them, encouraged in racially mixed areas to preserve integration, and discouraged or disallowed in predominantly white areas.
requirements: Jurisdictions conducting AFFH planning would be encouraged or required to consider magnet school creation consistent with their neighborhood classification
constraints: The report notes a centralized HUD taxonomy could elide regional distinctions, and classifying communities entirely on economic characteristics while omitting racial demographics is inadvisable
target_learners: K-12 students in metropolitan school districts
target_learning_goals: Racial and socioeconomic integration of schools
Access to high-quality integrated education
examples: HUD or entitlement jurisdictions could determine classification criteria during AFFH rulemaking or Consolidated Plan processes

article_title: State Approaches to Developing Educational Leaders
citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Statewide induction support for early-career leaders via mentoring, coaching, and cohort learning
description: Ten states operate initiatives specifically targeting early-career leaders, six focused exclusively on induction into the principalship and four covering other roles such as the assistant principalship. Programs pair new leaders with experienced mentors (e.g., Idaho's twice-monthly calls and two site visits per quarter), provide cohort-based seminars and coaching (Hawaii's 2-year New Principal Academy), and build networks. The report notes 23 states required early-career principal induction as of 2021, and that state programs can supplement or substitute where districts provide none.
requirements: Mentors matched in a similar role or with relevant leadership experience
Structured contact frequency such as regular coaching calls, site visits, or monthly seminars
constraints: In states without induction requirements, participation in these state initiatives is voluntary; the report does not evaluate the outcomes of the described programs
target_learners: Early-career principals
First- and second-year assistant principals
Newly appointed district leaders
target_learning_goals: Acclimating to new leadership roles
Building policy knowledge and professional networks
Coping with role-related stress
examples: The Kansas Educational Leadership Institute served 132 principals and assistant principals, 38 superintendents and assistant superintendents, and 16 special education leaders in 2022–23, with completers earning credits toward license renewal
key_sources: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572

article_title: Funding Student Needs: A Review of State Funding Policies for English Learners and Students from Low-Income Backgrounds
citation: Griffith, M., & Burns, D. (2025). Funding student needs: A review of state funding policies for English learners and students from low-income backgrounds. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/471.440
title: Taxonomy of state K–12 funding formula models: student-based, resource-based, hybrid, and unique systems
description: The report organizes state school funding systems into a taxonomy of models. "Student-based systems (36 states, including the district of Columbia) provide a base amount of money for each student, with additional weights or funds for specific student groups, such as English learners or students from low-income backgrounds." Resource-based systems (nine states) set amounts based on staffing positions via student-to-position ratios; four states use hybrid systems combining facets of both, and two states (Vermont and Wisconsin) have unique systems. This taxonomy frames the report's comparison of how states allocate supplemental EL and at-risk funding.
requirements: Understanding supplemental funding requires knowing both the extra weight and the state's base funding amount, which varies widely
constraints: Some states using student-based formulas do not have a set base funding amount, making analysis of additional funding difficult
target_learners: K–12 public school students, particularly English learners and students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Equitable allocation of educational resources to support student learning needs
examples: Colorado's 2023–24 student-based formula provided a base of $8,076 with an additional 0.08 weight for English learners, translating into an additional $646 per EL student
key_sources: Griffith, M., & Burns, D. (2025). Funding student needs: A review of state funding policies for English learners and students from low-income backgrounds. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/471.440

article_title: Standards-Based Education Reforms: Looking Back to Look Forward
citation: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623
title: Sticky reforms share new structures, powerful constituencies, and easily accessible evidence of compliance
description: The paper proposes a three-part pattern for judging whether an education reform will persist: new organizational or physical structures, powerful constituencies created by the reform, and easily accessible evidence of compliance. It illustrates the pattern with the Advanced Placement program, which "has caused changes in organizational structure in the form of separate courses," created constituencies among colleges accepting AP credit, and is easily monitored through national standardized tests. Classroom pedagogy reforms, by contrast, are hard to monitor and lack constituencies, so they rarely last.
requirements: Reforms must create structures, constituencies, or monitorable compliance evidence to persist
constraints: Practices within the classroom are difficult to monitor and to change, so pedagogy-focused reforms are unlikely to last without teacher support
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. public schools
target_learning_goals: Sustained implementation of standards-aligned instruction
examples: The Advanced Placement program persists since the mid-1950s because it meets all three stickiness criteria
key_sources: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623

article_title: Does Teaching Experience Increase Teacher Effectiveness? A Review of the Research
citation: Kini, T., & Podolsky, A. (2016). Does Teaching Experience Increase Teacher Effectiveness? A Review of the Research. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/our-work/publications-resources/does-teaching-experience-increase-teacher-effectiveness-review-research
title: Increase stability in teacher job assignments so teachers can refine instruction at a given grade level and subject
description: The review recommends that administrators and policymakers "Increase stability in teacher job assignments so that teachers can refine their instruction at a given grade level and subject," because its review shows repeated experience teaching the same grade level or subject is associated with more rapid improvement in effectiveness. It pairs this with recommendations to build collegial working conditions and to distribute experienced teachers more equitably across schools.
requirements: Teachers must be assigned to and retained in a consistent grade level and subject so repeated experience can accumulate.
constraints: The recommendation rests on the review's synthesis of observational studies using fixed-effects methods, not on an experimental test of assignment stability.
target_learners: K-12 public school students in the United States
target_learning_goals: Improved student achievement through faster growth of teacher effectiveness
examples: The review's policy recommendations section advises increasing stability in teacher job assignments, creating strong collegial relationships among staff, and strengthening equitable distribution of more experienced teachers.
key_sources: Kini, T., & Podolsky, A. (2016). Does Teaching Experience Increase Teacher Effectiveness? A Review of the Research. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/our-work/publications-resources/does-teaching-experience-increase-teacher-effectiveness-review-research

article_title: Learning from Young People about How Safe and Supportive Conditions at Home Can Inform School Climate
citation: Mosley, J., & Valdez, A. (2022). Learning from young people about how safe and supportive conditions at home can inform school climate. Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd. https://SELcenter.WestEd.org
title: Student voice as a continuum from adult-run feedback activities to student-led action
description: The brief organizes student voice as forms ranging "from adult-run activities, such as soliciting student feedback on a lesson, to adult-supported activities, such as training students to research a problem that affects them through youth participatory action research, to more student-led forms of action, such as student advisory groups and student organizing." All forms involve taking notice of and acting on what students say about school from their point of view. The framework positions students as experts of their own experiences and essential partners in their education.
requirements: Adults take notice and act on what students say about school from their point of view
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those marginalized by the education system
target_learning_goals: School climate improvement; student leadership and co-creation of learning environments
examples: The brief cites youth participatory action research, student advisory groups, and student organizing as progressively more student-led forms
key_sources: Mosley, J., & Valdez, A. (2022). Learning from young people about how safe and supportive conditions at home can inform school climate. Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621228

article_title: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems
citation: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems. (2022). Education Trust, Education Reform Now, and FutureEd. https://www.edtrust.org/
title: Statewide intensive tutoring programs with dedicated funding and vetted vendor hubs (Accelerate, TN ALL Corps, Vetted Texas Tutor Corps)
description: The brief profiles named statewide tutoring systems built with relief funds: Louisiana's Accelerate program (part of $90 million in academic and social-emotional recovery spending, with a year-long math and ELA tutoring curriculum developed with the teacher-leader community and a vendor guide of state-approved private providers); Tennessee's TN ALL Corps (an estimated $200 million initiative under the Learning Loss Remediation and Student Acceleration Act, with matching grants to LEAs); and Texas's Vetted Texas Tutor Corps, which "provides districts free access to instructional materials for tutoring" and TEA-subsidized tutor training with ongoing technical assistance via Regional Education Service Centers.
requirements: District participation criteria such as Tennessee's requirement that about 500 intervention schools have fully implemented tutoring programs to receive state funding starting fall 2022
Trained tutors and, in Louisiana, use of formative assessment data to inform sessions
constraints: Colorado's CDE has not stated how much of its $58 million set-aside it plans to spend on tutoring and has made no indication it plans structured professional development
Tennessee's math resources are optional for participating districts
target_learners: K-12 students statewide with unfinished learning
Students in districts approved for matching-grant participation
target_learning_goals: Accelerating literacy and math learning through intensive tutoring integrated with state recovery strategies
examples: Louisiana works closely with a cohort of eight LEAs providing extra implementation support while WestEd studies the process and outcomes
New Mexico committed $22 million to targeted intensive tutoring programs and $40 million to a teacher-pipeline program providing tutors

article_title: How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: States should set equity-centered discipline goals, publish disaggregated discipline data, and promote positive approaches such as restorative justice
description: The brief argues harmful discipline and dress codes damage students' SEAD and disproportionately exclude students of color and students with disabilities. It recommends states "adopt more positive approaches to discipline, such as restorative justice, which empowers students to build, maintain, and repair relationships and resolve conflicts," set goals to reduce disparities, and make discipline data publicly transparent.
requirements: Clear state goals to reduce disparities and overuses in discipline
Publicly transparent discipline data
constraints: Many of these policy areas are led at the local level; states influence districts through goals, guidance, and funding rather than direct control
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to learning opportunities free from exclusionary discipline
examples: Texas limits out-of-school suspensions for students below third grade to offenses involving weapons or drugs and publicly reports district-level discipline data disaggregated by race
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628037

article_title: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://EdTrust.org
title: States should set equity-centered discipline goals, transparent data, and positive approaches such as restorative justice
description: The brief argues that harmful discipline practices and dress codes damage students' social, emotional, and academic development, and that students of color and students with disabilities are disproportionately excluded from school. It recommends that "States can influence district and school disciplinary actions by setting clear goals to reduce disparities and overuses in discipline, ensuring a strong set of data is publicly transparent, and adopting more positive approaches to discipline, such as restorative justice." Washington's bright spots include banning corporal punishment, zero-tolerance policies, exclusionary discipline for young learners and minor offenses, and discriminatory hair and grooming codes.
requirements: Guidance and funding for restorative discipline policies, professional development in positive discipline practices, and state agency staff to support districts with technical assistance
constraints: Washington still needs equity-centered goals to decrease exclusionary discipline and reduce disparities, and discipline data disaggregated beyond race and gender
target_learners: P-12 students, especially students of color and students with disabilities who are disproportionately excluded
target_learning_goals: Opportunities to learn and develop holistically without exclusionary discipline
examples: Washington bans corporal punishment and harmful practices including zero-tolerance policies and discriminatory hair and grooming codes
key_sources: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630072

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: State certification processes for community schools: Florida's UCF Community Partnership Schools and Georgia's Whole Child Model School certification
description: Two states support community schools through university- or state-led certification. Florida funds a certification process administered by the University of Central Florida's Center for Community Schools, with $7.1 million in state funding in fiscal year 2022 serving 36 schools; certification rests on 12 standards in the UCF-Certified Community Partnership Schools Fundamental Practices 3.0 and a partnership of a nonprofit, a university or college, a school district, and a health care provider. Georgia's Department of Education created a Whole Child Model School certification process whose "overarching goal ... is to help community schools develop and independently sustain a whole child education model," combining the four community schools pillars with five whole child tenets.
requirements: Florida schools submit quarterly progress reports and complete a self-study reviewed by four to six external reviewers including site visits; Georgia participating schools must employ a whole child coordinator and establish a collaborative leadership team with a needs-assessment-based improvement plan.
constraints: Georgia participation is voluntary with no direct state funding for pilot schools; certification lasts 3 years with recertification contingent on growth in at least one whole child area. Florida grants step down after certification as schools blend and braid funding.
target_learners: Students in participating Florida and Georgia community schools
target_learning_goals: Whole child education, sustainability of community school models, and nonacademic barrier reduction
examples: Florida planning grants are awarded up to $80,000 with a 25% community contribution match; implementation grants typically range from $150,000 to $200,000 per year for the first 5 years.
key_sources: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402

article_title: Cultivating Relationships in Secondary Schools: Structures That Matter
citation: Hernández, L., & Darling-Hammond, L. (with Nielsen, N.). (2024). Cultivating relationships in secondary schools: Structures that matter. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/cultivating-relationships-secondary-schools-brief
title: Pair relationship-building structures with trustful, empowering, reciprocal, and culturally responsive interactions, because structures alone do not guarantee success
description: The brief's central caution is that 'School structures can create opportunities for relationships to develop, but those structures are only as powerful as the interactions within them.' Schools should therefore ensure that student–practitioner interactions are trustful, empowering, reciprocal, and culturally responsive for every student; only then can the promise of positive relationships be fully realized. Day-to-day practices are treated in the companion brief on classroom practices.

Schools must attend to the nature of relationships, not only the existence of structures
constraints: The principle is stated for relationship-centered structures generally; the brief directs readers to its companion brief for the classroom practices involved
target_learners: secondary school students
secondary school educators and staff
target_learning_goals: realizing the learning and well-being benefits of positive relationships
development of trustful, reciprocal student–adult connections
examples: The brief pairs each structure section with classroom-practice guidance deferred to its companion brief, Cultivating Relationships in Secondary Classrooms: Practices That Matter
key_sources: Hernández, L., & Darling-Hammond, L. (with Nielsen, N.). (2024). Cultivating relationships in secondary schools: Structures that matter. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/cultivating-relationships-secondary-schools-brief

article_title: Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice
citation: Kristen Hengtgen and William Rodick. (2025). Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Empower students as climate actors through agency, mentorship, and community-partnered learning opportunities
description: The report's first principle holds that students' school experiences should prepare them to be future leaders and "support them to act now on the issues they care about most." It argues the antidote to climate anxiety is empowerment, and that schools enable youth empowerment by listening to students and providing opportunities for action. Recommended system-level changes include professional development building mentorship and leadership into school routines, funding professional learning communities that engage students as researchers, and partnerships with universities and climate-focused organizations.
requirements: Professional development for school leaders and teachers to build mentorship and leadership opportunities into regular school practices
Partnerships with universities, climate-focused organizations, and community groups developing research and civic engagement skills
constraints: Children cannot bear the full responsibility of solving a problem they did not create, per the report
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color and students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Climate literacy
civic engagement and agency on climate issues
examples: The Tucson Unified School District's 2024 climate action plan was written and researched by the youth-led Arizona Youth Climate Coalition; the Climate READY dual-enrollment program had students generate a community resilience plan presented to local government, and an evaluation found participants improved environmental literacy and felt more prepared, confident, and capable of communicating about climate change.
key_sources: Kristen Hengtgen and William Rodick. (2025). Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED674764

article_title: Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future
citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: Provide strong coaching and continuous support to teacher candidates in alternative certification programs
description: The report states that "Strong coaching and support are essential ingredients for alternative programs to be successful," according to program administrators and teacher candidates. Support appears as intensive summer institutes, classroom observations, frequent professional development throughout the year, on-site coaching when the program is housed in the school building, and intentional candidate placement in supportive buildings. Because alternative-route candidates often work as teachers of record while training, the report says any certification training program should offer robust support and continuous feedback loops.
requirements: Robust support and continuous feedback loops for teachers-in-training
Support mechanisms such as summer institutes, observations, and professional development sessions
target_learners: Alternative-route teacher candidates, including teachers of record early in training
target_learning_goals: Deliver quality instruction and complete certification
examples: EDI is housed directly in the school building for on-site coaching; DPSCD places candidates only with principals committed to the support model.

article_title: Toward Agent-based Educational Science: Rethinking Educational Research in the Age of AI
citation: Zhang, Y., Jiang, J. & Tang, X. (2026). Toward Agent-Based Educational Science: Rethinking Educational Research in the Age of AI. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 113. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10209-5
title: Student Development Agents: computational agents generating developmental features under counterfactual educational environments
description: Student Development Agents are the article's concrete instantiation of AES: "computational agents designed to generate developmental features under counterfactual educational environments." They serve as simulated learners whose developmental trajectories can be examined in silico, allowing educational innovations to be evaluated before large-scale implementation. The article presents them as enabled by recent advances in generative artificial intelligence.

constraints: The article presents them as a concrete instantiation of a proposed agenda, not as a validated system
target_learners: simulated learners representing students in educational environments
target_learning_goals: generating developmental features under counterfactual educational environments

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: Follow GenAI-enabled adaptive pretesting with structured spaced retrieval practice rather than learner-directed AI study to preserve gains
description: The article concludes that adaptive pretesting elevates initial understanding but that "sustained learning depends on how subsequent AI-supported practice is structured." When pretesting is followed by retrieval-based practice — especially adaptive retrieval — gains in retention and engagement persist; when followed only by learner-directed AI interaction, benefits may attenuate. AI access should be structured to elicit retrieval rather than enable passive review.
requirements: AI-supported practice sessions held constant in number and timing across learners, with interaction structure designed to elicit retrieval attempts
constraints: Evidence comes from a single instructional context (one applied statistics course and topic); the article calls for replication across domains and task types
target_learners: undergraduate students learning applied analytical content with GenAI support
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and near-transfer of concepts after AI-assisted pretesting
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to adaptive spaced retrieval, fixed spaced retrieval, or learner-directed AI study after a common adaptive pretesting and instruction phase, with the same posttest at semester's end

description: The article recommends that institutions treat Stage 2 (Informed Use) as the minimum acceptable level and Stage 3 (Critical Evaluation) as the aspirational target for most degree programs, with Stage 4 reserved for advanced students. Stage 2 means graduates "understand how AI works at a functional level, use AI tools responsibly, and recognize when human judgment is required." The continuum should be interpreted within disciplinary contexts.

article_title: The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices
citation: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215
title: AIED research should standardize reporting of computational and environmental costs of LLM and ML usage
description: The article argues that awareness of environmental issues should become standardized in AIED through norms for reporting specifics of LLM usage in papers. It presents three recommendations: use CodeCarbon to measure and report carbon intensity for any AIED system run on local or cloud hardware; use the TerraFlops wrapper for ML tasks to report carbon emissions alongside accuracy with PUE-equivalent and composite metrics; and use theoretical FLOP estimations for proprietary LLMs. Making the environmental footprint of LLMs more visible would let the community set standards for sustainable educational AI research.
requirements: Community adoption of shared reporting norms and tools
Tools such as CodeCarbon and TerraFlops tested for non-expert usability
constraints: The current framework does not consider the water consumption of cloud-based GPUs, which has a very significant detrimental effect on some communities
PUE-equivalent baselines could be refined for consumer-grade versus cloud-based GPUs
target_learners: AIED researchers and conference organizers
target_learning_goals: Accountability and transparency regarding the environmental impact of AI in education
examples: The authors report their own paper's sustainability metrics (total corrected carbon intensity, total computational cost, training efficiency) immediately before the introduction as an example of how these metrics could be reported, and suggest future AIED conferences could require sustainability reporting as a condition of submission, similar to anonymity requirements

citation: Udeshi, T., Khazenzon, A., Khan, K., Breen, N., Corwin, R., DiGiano, C., Weatherholtz, K., Zaluski, M. (2026). Methodologies for Improving the Quality of AI Tutoring in K-12 Education. https://sites.google.com/khanacademy.org/aied2026supplementalmaterial/home
title: Anticipate student adaptation when tightening guardrails against answer giveaway
description: Because some students try to cheat by coaxing the AI tutor into giving away the answer, improvements in the answer-giveaway metric erode over time: "This results in a seesawing giving-away-answer metric, where we eventually lose some (but not all) the gains after the change is put into production." Practitioners should therefore treat answer-giveaway gains as provisional and continue monitoring after launch.

constraints: Gains on this metric are partially lost as students find new ways to coax the answer out of the tutor

citation: Özgür Tutal. (2026). Artificial intelligence assisted design of a novel cooperative learning technique for higher education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-50770-1
title: Structure cooperative learning so that group work embeds the five essential elements rather than merely placing students in groups
description: The article argues that effective cooperative learning depends on intentional structuring, not group formation alone. It states that "merely placing students in groups does not guarantee effective cooperation or learning" and that without structuring, group work "may devolve into unproductive or even counterproductive interactions." The five elements—positive interdependence, individual accountability, face-to-face promotive interaction, interpersonal and small group social skills, and group processing—guided both the design of CCCT and its evaluation rubric.
requirements: Careful planning, clear expectations, and ongoing support so that students engage in meaningful and productive collaboration
constraints: Stated for cooperative learning generally; the article notes that without built-in inclusion mechanisms some students, such as shy students, non-native speakers, or students with learning disabilities, may be marginalized or disengaged

target_learning_goals: meaningful collaboration, individual accountability, and productive peer interaction
examples: CCCT operationalized the elements through assigned roles ensuring individual accountability and positive interdependence, face-to-face collaboration during constellation creation, and a closing reflection and group processing activity.
