citation: M. Said Doğru & Emily K. Faulconer. (2026). ChatGPT as a Virtual Laboratory Teaching Assistant in Undergraduate Biology. Research in Science Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11165-025-10271-z
title: Sociotechnical Systems Theory frames ChatGPT as a technical support provider interlinked with the social context of the laboratory course
description: The article applies Sociotechnical Systems (STS) Theory, which "gives a systems thinking perspective to an entity where people (with their effectiveness and abilities) work towards goals by following specific processes and using technology." In this framing, ChatGPT is a technical component interlinked with the social components (students, instructors, TAs), supporting laboratory engagement through collaborative questioning and increasing participation in active learning, but not directly managing laboratory experiments. The framework positions ChatGPT as "a technical support provider but not as the primary executor of experimental processes."
requirements: Students should receive instruction on using the technology tool based on its functionality, accuracy, reliability, and user interface.
constraints: The degree of integration and scaffolding of ChatGPT into the existing laboratory course structure is a contextual factor; institutional policies and culture related to AI use can influence the relationships.
target_learners: undergraduate biology laboratory students
target_learning_goals: laboratory concept understanding
active learning through collaborative questioning
examples: The study used the STS framework to explore how students and instructors interact with ChatGPT as a virtual TA in an introductory biology laboratory course.

Studios can link multiple boards, educators manage classes and invitations, learners contribute to boards, and researcher access supports class analytics and export within role boundaries.

article_title: Artificial intelligence perceptions and career anxiety among health sciences students
citation: Dağ, E., Nal, M., Topuz, İ., Kılınç, H., Demir, Y. & Bektaş, G. (2026). Artificial intelligence perceptions and career anxiety among health sciences students. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-42030-z
title: AI anxiety as a perception-driven appraisal mechanism within the Stress and Coping framework
description: The article frames students' AI anxiety using Lazarus and Folkman's process/interaction model, in which "stress stems not so much from the external threat itself, but rather from the individual's perception of how risky the threat is". AI anxiety is conceptualised as a perception-driven mechanism that converts technological change into career-related stress: students appraise AI as a threat to expected employability (primary appraisal) and judge their coping resources, such as AI literacy and self-efficacy, insufficient (secondary appraisal). The study's main contribution is classifying AI anxiety as a multidimensional stress response specific to the job search process rather than a general fear of technology.
requirements: The framework applies to populations who have not yet entered the labour market, whose assessment is gain- or failure-focused rather than loss-focused
constraints: The article distinguishes students' employability-threat appraisal from working adults' job-loss appraisal; workplace job-insecurity inferences should not be drawn from student findings
target_learners: University health sciences students preparing to enter the labour market
target_learning_goals: Understanding AI-related career stress and employability perceptions
examples: The study interprets its regression findings as showing AI is appraised as a threat because students believe they lack the knowledge, skills and resources to meet AI-related demands

citation: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196
title: Combine structured prompt templates with a pre-constructed robot function library to improve LLM instruction-parsing reliability
description: The principle is to send user instructions to the LLM through a structured prompt template and to execute LLM output against a pre-constructed library of robot action functions, so that natural language is converted into reliable, executable control code. The article reports that "The integration of structured prompts and a pre-constructed function library improves parsing reliability and system responsiveness." This pairing is how EduSim-LLM converts free-form instructions into sequential Python calls in CoppeliaSim.

non-expert robot users

article_title: CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity
citation: Hornung, I., Marasinghe Arachchige, D., Kumarage, T., Agrawal, G., Deng, Y., Chen, Y.-C., & Liu, H. (2026). CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07965
title: Structured autonomy: bounding generative agent behavior through layered pedagogical and domain constraints
description: CyberAGENTS is a layered, ontology-guided multi-agent framework for gamified cybersecurity learning built on the principle of structured autonomy. The article states it "enables structured autonomy through ontology-guided validation, schema-governed behavioral control, and competency-based progression." Three layers regulate the system: a competency graph initializes gameplay, behavioral schemas bound each agent's instructional role, and a cybersecurity ontology validates all generated content before display. The design principle is that "generative flexibility should be bounded through structured autonomy rather than eliminated through static scripting."

Behavioral schemas encoding operational modes, trigger conditions, progression logic, and evaluation criteria for each agent
A domain ontology defining valid entity types and permissible relations for pre-display validation
constraints: Evaluated only in cybersecurity education at novice difficulty with short 5-15 minute sessions
The authors state the small-scale deployment and preliminary ablation limit broader claims about long-term learning outcomes
target_learners: Undergraduate cybersecurity students
target_learning_goals: Cybersecurity reasoning about attacks, defenses, vulnerabilities, and tools
Sustained engagement and iterative skill-building in practice-driven technical domains
examples: Deployed as a live web-based system with React frontend, Python Flask backend, and Llama-based models served through the Together AI API

article_title: CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity
citation: Hornung, I., Marasinghe Arachchige, D., Kumarage, T., Agrawal, G., Deng, Y., Chen, Y.-C., & Liu, H. (2026). CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07965

citation: Bi T, Araily S, Lyu A and Xiu S (2026) Research on the optimization of the training system of university faculty development centers in the context of GenAI: a comparative analysis based on Chinese and Kazakhstani universities. Front. Psychol. 17:1890508. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1890508
title: Faculty development centers should build GenAI readiness by having faculty work on their own course artifacts under a structured prompt-task cycle
description: The article's practical lesson is that "faculty development centers can support prompt design, critical judgement, instructional design, and assessment capacity by asking faculty to work on their owncourseartifactsunderastructuredprompt-taskcycle". The cycle runs prompt formulation, generated-output review, course-material revision, and written reflection, organized around course-material preparation, learning-task design, assessment revision, and AI-use rule explanation. It outperformed conventional GenAI-focused faculty development (function introduction, teaching-case explanation, general application advice) on all seven readiness dimensions at post-test.

citation: Ariyan Hossain, Kazi Kamruzzaman Rabbi, Farig Sadeque, S M Taiabul Haque. (2026). Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15914
title: Stereotype Congruence Rate (SCR): a free-text occupational stereotyping metric grounded in BLS labor-market gender distributions
description: SCR is a complementary bias metric the article introduces because existing benchmarks "probe model-internal associations via templated inputs and cover only broad occupational categories", which does not suit free-text career recommendations. It is defined as "the proportion of essays in which the recommended occupation matches the biography subject's gender stereotype", with occupations labeled via BLS CPSAAT11 workforce gender shares (over 60% one gender = stereotyped; otherwise neutral). Neutral occupations count in the denominator but not as matches, making the metric conservative.
requirements: Requires extracted occupation strings matchable to BLS CPSAAT11 categories (fuzzy matching threshold ≥85 with manual resolution) and population-level occupational gender distribution data
constraints: The article notes US occupational norms were used because locally grounded labor-market gender data were not publicly accessible in the study's deployment country
target_learners: undergraduate students writing career-plan essays
target_learning_goals: career planning and occupational attribution in AI-assisted writing
examples: Applied to the 123-participant experiment's essays, SCR was 0.714 in the biased condition, 0.450 in control, and 0.390 in neutral; sensitivity analyses at 55% and 65% thresholds preserved the ordering

citation: Ugwuanyi, K., Mair, C., Dovchin, S., Erdocia, I., Kuteeva, M., & Airemionkhale, E. (2025). Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes. https://scholar.google.com
title: The standardisation paradox: GenAI makes English simultaneously more homogeneous and more heterogeneous
description: The standardisation paradox is contributor Christian Mair's account of GenAI's dual effect on English: "LLMs confront us with a standardisation paradox, with English becoming more homogeneous and more heterogeneous at the same time". On the homogeneous side, only one dominant written standard (US English) prevails in LLM output, marginalising even British English. On the heterogeneous side, prompting for a Nigerian or Jamaican English version of an American English text yields output full of Nigerian Pidgin or Jamaican Creole, opening space for hybridised forms rather than handbook-described national standards.
requirements: Interpretation of LLM output requires distinguishing national standard varieties from creole and pidgin varieties
constraints: The article leaves open whether the notion of national standard varieties needs revision or whether LLM training data are biassed against them
target_learners: Scholars of World Englishes, linguistics students, academic writers
target_learning_goals: Understanding how GenAI reshapes norms of written English in scholarly communication
examples: Prompting for Nigerian or Jamaican English versions of an American English text producing Pidgin/Creole-heavy output instead of the national standards described in handbooks

description: Students lead in AI use and should be positioned as genuine participants in shaping change, not recipients of it. The article states: "AI-driven institutional change should position students not simply as the recipients of reform but as genuine participants in shaping it". Change efforts should surface students' current practices and goals and redirect student energy toward productive and critical use rather than prohibiting or ignoring existing patterns; a structured early-course survey of student AI use is a useful entry point.

article_title: Academic integrity in the age of generative AI: A scoping review of research on higher education student voices
citation: Ji Ying. (2026). Academic Integrity in the Age of Generative AI: a Scoping Review of Research on Higher Education Student Voices. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09752-1
title: Students as active ethical agents navigating an ethical grey zone in GenAI use
description: The review's organizing framework positions higher education students not as passive recipients of GenAI technology or institutional policies, nor as culprits who breach integrity without ethical constraints, but as active agents who interpret, adapt, and shape the ethical contours of GenAI use. Drawing on Bandura's notion of ethical agency, it frames students as navigating the 'grey areas' of academic integrity through personal ethical frameworks and reasoning, exercising agency via human-AI collaboration, de facto policymaking, strategic calibration, and resistance to over-reliance. The framework underpins the review's call for students to be treated as partners in developing policies.
requirements: Recognition of student voice as moral-ethical agents with their own moral-ethical awareness and judgement that need to be highlighted and heard.
constraints: The framework is synthesised from studies the review notes are largely single-context, self-reported, and cross-sectional, limiting generalisability.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: ethical reasoning and agency in GenAI use
academic integrity
examples: The review synthesises 38 empirical studies thematically, including Bearman et al.'s (2026) 'coming from me' imperative on intellectual ownership.
UK students in O'Dea et al.'s (2025) study described exploring where the ethical boundaries might sit.

description: The article's design implication is that prompting functions as instructional scaffolding embedded in the interaction process, directing attention, supporting organization, and encouraging reflective evaluation. description: The article's second lesson: "No single signal reliably captures difficulty." Silence, wrong answers, and verbalized uncertainty each miss cases the others catch, and the authors report that fusing them "produced far more humane behavior than any one alone." Struggle detection in adaptive learning systems should therefore combine temporal, behavioral, and linguistic signals.

title: StatBot: a RAG-enhanced GPT-4 chatbot deployed as a voluntary virtual teaching assistant for graduate statistics courses
description: StatBot is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbot built on GPT-4 that served as a virtual teaching assistant in three graduate statistics courses. As the article describes it, "StatBot was developed based on the GPT-4 large language model within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to support instructional interactions in the introductory statistics course." It retrieves from a curated corpus of lecture transcriptions, slides, textbooks, assignments, examinations, answer keys, and Q&A archives via vector-based semantic similarity, then applies a post-generation guardrail module that refines tone and pedagogical alignment, outputs "answer not found" when retrieval is insufficient, and appends source-based citations. It was integrated with the LINE messaging platform via Azure services and use was encouraged but not mandatory.

Deployment infrastructure (Azure Bot Service, OpenAI Service, Blob Storage, Key Vault, App Service) for real-time messaging integration

If retrieved source content is deemed insufficient, the system outputs "answer not found" rather than answering

target_learning_goals: statistics content mastery
self-directed problem-solving during a semester-long data analytics project

citation: Kaushik Dutta. (2026). From Precision Medicine to Precision Education: A Vision for AI-Powered Student Digital Twins, Preventive Student Success, and Career-Aligned Academic Pathways. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06322
title: Student Digital Twin: a continuously updated learner model built for counterfactual simulation, not dashboard display
description: A Student Digital Twin is defined as "a continuously evolving model of an individual learner's academic performance, learning behavior, career interests, degree progression, financial circumstances, co-curricular engagement, and workforce preparedness." Its purpose is "to simulate": answering counterfactual questions such as what happens if a gateway course is repeated with tutoring, or if the student changes majors. The paper specifies three design properties: fidelity matched to purpose, calibration of predicted probabilities to observed rates, and validation of simulated causal claims against real outcomes. It cautions the twin "is not the person" and should be a decision aid, not an oracle.

Validation of simulated intervention effects against experimental or quasi-experimental evidence
Fidelity matched to the decision at hand
constraints: The model omits context, motivation, relationships, and circumstance that no data stream captures
Education digital twin literature is described as still young and partly aspirational
target_learners: higher education students
working and returning learners
target_learning_goals: advising decisions about pathways and interventions
early risk identification
examples: The paper proposes advising moves from retrospective consultation toward future-state simulation, with advisor and student examining plausible futures together

article_title: Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education
citation: Sun Y., Liao Y. & Ma X. (2026). Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00459-9
title: StructRAG: a pattern-aware framework combining visual parsing with pattern-level structural reasoning for diagram interpretation
description: StructRAG is a four-component framework for interpreting engineering diagrams in AI tutoring systems. It converts a student-uploaded diagram image into a graph representation, retrieves structurally similar templates from a curated library, constructs pattern-aware prompts, and uses GPT-4 to reason about structural completeness. As printed, "StructRAG is composed of four main components: (1) Diagram-to-Graph Conversion, (2) Structural Pattern Retrieval, (3) Pattern-Aware Prompt Construction, and (4) LLM-Guided Structural Reasoning and Correction." The core idea is shifting "from surface-level recognition to pattern-level validation", so missing connections can be inferred from structural logic rather than pixel-perfect recognition.
requirements: Requires a curated library of abstract graph templates built independently of the evaluation questions
Requires OCR-based visual recognition plus classical computer vision line and contour extraction to produce an initial graph and an uncertain-edge set
constraints: When both the connection trace and one of its endpoints are absent, the visual module may still produce an incomplete graph
Dense mesh diagrams may contain crossings that cannot be reliably distinguished from actual junctions
target_learners: STEM students in electrical engineering, computer science, and systems engineering
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of structural engineering diagrams such as circuit schematics and network topologies
Structure-aware feedback and automated grading of diagram-based assessment
examples: The framework was evaluated on 1,650 STEM questions, achieving 89.3% question-level accuracy and 93.0% edge-level F1

citation: Sun Y., Liao Y. & Ma X. (2026). Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00459-9
title: 1,650-question STEM diagram dataset collected via campus-wide submission campaign
description: The evaluation dataset was built from a campus-wide question submission campaign launched in April 2024, spanning four months, which received 2,047 unique submissions from STEM faculty and students. Twelve experienced STEM educators independently reviewed the submissions, removing duplicates and trivial or invalid entries such as diagrams with fewer than 8 nodes and edges. "After applying these ﬁlters, a total of 1,650 valid and structurally meaningful questions were retained for further experimentation." The questions span electrical engineering, computer science, and systems analysis, with star, ring, chain/bus, bridge/mesh, tree, hybrid, and layered topologies. A data-separation audit confirmed no overlap with the template library.
requirements: Submissions were required to include at least one diagram image with a minimum combined count of 8 nodes and edges
constraints: The full dataset cannot be publicly released because it contains university teaching and assessment materials; it may be provided upon reasonable request subject to institutional approval

citation: I Putu Yoga Laksana, Ni Made Ratminingsih, Made Hery Santosa & I Putu Indra Kusuma. (2026). The authors deployed a web application replicating ChatGPT's core functionalities and logged interactions while students worked on Python programming assignments. It contains 2,214 conversations from 203 students totaling 16,851 utterances, plus 924 graded assignment submissions, all annotated with dialogue act labels and filtered for PII.

Participants knew conversations were recorded, so behaviors may have been altered by the Hawthorne Effect

description: Student_100 is a dataset the authors built from the online programming platform PTA for evaluating student simulation. It contains 100 students, each with 50 well-annotated task-solving records: 40 past learning records and 10 simulation records, each including a Python programming task, the student's solving behavior with error analysis, and the student-written code. Records were restricted to those completed within a week to keep cognitive states stable, and 10 trained annotators added task descriptions and behavior evaluations. title: Student development agent framework: learning environment, endowment dimensions, developmental dimensions, actions, behaviors, and history
description: The article defines a design framework whose input includes "the learning environment, the endowment dimensions of students, the developmental dimensions of students, the actions defining how student agents can interact with the given learning environment," and whose output is simulated learning behaviors and changes in developmental dimensions. Developmental dimensions serve as "both outcomes for one period and inputs for the next period," enabling iterative simulation, while history records past trajectories. This framework targets prospective evaluation of AIED innovations without exposing real students.

article_title: Multimodal Dialogue in STEM Education
citation: Akshay Syal, Lawrence Swaminathan Xavier Prince, Evin Gultepe, Nik Bear Brown, Srinivas Sridhar. (2026). A Dialogue-Based Framework for Correcting Multimodal Errors in AI-Assisted STEM Education.
title: Structured multimodal dialogue functions as a scaffolding strategy that decomposes visually integrated tasks into sequenced steps before problem-solving
description: The article frames its intervention as an instructional design principle: "the structured multimodal dialogue developed in this study functions as a scaffolding strategy that decomposes a complex, visually integrated task into discrete, sequenced steps." Drawing on cognitive load management, the dialogue first elicits an explicit visual description, corrects misidentified elements, and only then prompts problem-solving, mirroring pedagogical scaffolding used in human tutoring. The authors position it as "a replicable instructional pattern" adoptable without model changes.
requirements: Corrections in the intermediate step must be restricted to observable visual properties of the source image, without hints regarding underlying physics principles or formulas.
constraints: The intervention was tested on each strategy independently rather than in combination, and problems requiring graphical outputs were excluded.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students using AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: reliable AI-assisted problem-solving on image-rich STEM content
examples: The three-step dialogue asked models to describe the figure, received researcher correction of misidentified visual elements such as a force vector direction or a graph intercept value, and then prompted problem-solving.

article_title: StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
citation: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048
title: StanBKT: an open-source Python package for Bayesian estimation of BKT models in Stan
description: StanBKT is an open-source Python package for estimating classical BKT models and several extensions using Bayesian inference in Stan. It provides a unified interface for model specification, parameter estimation, and posterior analysis, including filtered and smoothed latent-state estimation, posterior predictive prediction, visualization utilities, and diagnostics such as ESS, MCSE, and R-hat. Source code is public on GitHub, installable via pip, with online documentation and worked examples.
requirements: A compatible C++ toolchain is required because Stan models are transpiled to C++ and compiled before execution
target_learners: students working in intelligent tutoring systems whose response sequences are modeled
target_learning_goals: estimating mastery, learning, forgetting, guessing, and slipping parameters from student interaction data
examples: The package fits models through a three-stage workflow of model specification, parameter estimation, and analysis, demonstrated in a worked example with simulated data for 100 students and 30 problems

article_title: 'It''s OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing'
citation: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090
title: Taxonomy of 23 student rationalizations for AI use in six classes
description: The article presents a taxonomy of 23 distinct moral justifications, termed Rationalizations (R1–R23), that students use to justify AI use in writing assignments, grouped into six Rationalization Classes: victimless behavior, minimal AI contribution, ex ante contribution, post hoc contribution, responsibility denial, and perceived benefit. Definitions were developed inductively from participant accounts through thematic analysis of interviews, chat logs, and course documents, with representative participant quotes for each rationalization. The taxonomy classifies the justifications rather than the AI-use practices themselves, so the same practice can be justified through different rationalizations.
requirements: The taxonomy was built from semi-structured interview excerpts in which participants described or justified their AI use, consolidated from 46 subcodes through team consensus.
constraints: The article notes space limits prevented in-depth description of every rationalization, and the sample comprised students who self-reported at least sometimes using AI for writing.
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI for academic writing
target_learning_goals: moral sense-making about acceptable AI assistance in academic writing
examples: Class examples include R3 Busywork (AI acceptable for low-value assignments), R6 My Ideas (core ideas originated with the student), R12 My Style (output sounding like the student makes it theirs), R13 Normalization, and R19 Time Economy.

article_title: Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages
citation: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278
title: Structural Silence: four interlocking infrastructure failures that systematically exclude a language from AI
description: Structural silence is the article's explanatory framework: "the systematic exclusion of a language from AI infrastructure not through explicit policy but through the accumulated weight of design decisions that were never made with that language in mind." It organizes four interlocking failures—web presence gap, training token deficit, tokenization penalty, and connectivity exclusion—that intensify one another over time. Bengali, with roughly 285 million speakers, classical recognition, and an active NLP research community, serves as the case demonstrating that uneven performance reflects infrastructure-level resource distribution rather than model quality alone.
requirements: Each failure compounds the others, so the framework requires analysis at corpus, tokenizer, benchmark, and deployment layers together
constraints: The article's contribution is explicitly explanatory and diagnostic rather than a new benchmark or empirical dataset
Evidence is drawn from published benchmarks, public indicators, and educational theory rather than newly collected learner data
target_learners: Bengali-speaking learners in low-connectivity environments
Speakers of underrepresented languages
target_learning_goals: Access to AI-assisted educational support (debugging help, concept explanation, feedback) in one's native language
examples: The paper consolidates Sangraha/Common Corpus token counts, BenLLM-Eval results, BBS ICT survey figures, and Cognitive Load Theory findings into one account of why Bengali AI support is uneven

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: StudentSimEval: a standardized per-student simulator benchmark over 60 students in chess, L2 writing, and math with released code
description: StudentSimEval is a standardized evaluation protocol spanning 60 students across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. It "turns public learner corpora into a fixed per-student record schema with per-student train/held-out splits, and scores every method on two metrics, behavioral fidelity (F) and guidance responsiveness (R)". Because every method is fit on the same per-student records and scored on the same held-out records, simulators from any family are directly comparable; the authors release the construction pipeline, per-student splits, and evaluation code so others can score new methods and extend the benchmark.
requirements: Evaluation uses frozen per-student held-out sets scored identically for every method, with per-student evaluation records disjoint from training data.
constraints: The multi-turn corpora are real-teacher-annotated for L2 but LLM-tutor-generated under fixed style templates for chess and math, where the LLM determines only the wording of guidance.
target_learners: real human students: 30 chess players, 15 L2 English learners, 15 math students
target_learning_goals: measuring behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness of student simulators
examples: Chess records come from the Lichess May 2025 database, L2 essays from the EFCAMDAT corpus, and math from a foundational-assistance corpus of annotated open-ended problems.

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: Two-stage pooled-then-specialized training: pretrain a domain base simulator on pooled student data, then specialize one adapter per student
description: StudentSim overcomes sparse per-student data with a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 trains one domain-specific base simulator on records pooled across all students, learning "common mistake patterns, the response format expected in the domain, and the pathway from natural-language tutor guidance to a changed response". Stage 2 initializes from that base and adapts it to one specific student using only that student's own recorded responses and tutor-guidance interactions, producing one LoRA adapter per student on a shared Qwen3-4B-Instruct backbone.
requirements: Stage 1 must supply what is shared across students and cannot be learned reliably from one student's sparse data alone; Stage 2 then supplies what is specific to each individual.
constraints: Per-student data is sparse: a learner in the L2 corpus writes three essays at the median, and more than two thirds write five or fewer; training one simulator end-to-end per student from such records would overfit.
target_learners: individual learners with sparse recorded interaction data in chess, L2 writing, or math
target_learning_goals: simulating an individual student's baseline responses and their revision after tutor guidance
examples: In chess, the article reports that performance drops when pooled records are replaced with repeated records from one student, supporting the pooled stage.

citation: Curtis Northcutt, Inaara Hasmani, Kevin Feng, Trevor Khangi, Andreas Plesner, Jonas Mueller. (2026). StudentBench: AI and human tutoring yield equivalent GRE learning gains. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28470
title: StudentBench platform and open dataset for evaluating AI tutoring by real student learning gains
description: StudentBench is "a suite of AI teaching evaluations and a public platform that enables large-scale data collection with over 175,000 student–AI messages". It runs randomized pre/post learning-gain studies comparing AI tutors, human tutors, and control, and produces five leaderboards covering lesson planning, practice-problem creation, conversational pedagogy, cost, and engagement. article_title: Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering -Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI-
citation: Riichiro Mizoguchi, Tomoki Aburatani, Kento Koike, Machi Shimmei. (2026). Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering —Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI—. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05545
title: Structural-gap-driven metacognitive support: treat the gap between subjective intention and objective structure as the engine of metacognition
description: This principle holds that the dissonance between a user's subjective intention toward an artifact and its structural reality, computed from objective indicators, should be treated "not as a defect to be removed but the occasion that makes the user ask anew what they had misjudged." The support system externalizes quantitative structural parameters, forces them into confrontation with subjective self-assessment, and recirculates the resulting gap as a constraint on the next act of construction. The authors contrast this with standard methods whose criteria are given from outside and whose evaluation results never flow back as constraints.
requirements: Objective structural indicators computable by the AI with practically acceptable accuracy
Domain-specific structural-complexity parameters definable by hand for each target domain
constraints: The approach presupposes users with minimum domain knowledge; complete novices are out of scope
Whether presenting the structural gap significantly improves evaluative judgment awaits quantitative evaluation
target_learners: Researchers
Learners engaged in problem posing and reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: Evaluative judgment
Metacognitive monitoring of one's own constructions
examples: Vibe Compiler detects unfilled slots via type checks and returns probing questions rather than corrections
The learner-layer example contrasts a problem poser rating a one-step problem as fairly difficult with the problem's actual structure

citation: Mathias Mejeh, Yvonne M. Fromm (2026). Fostering self-regulated learning through adaptive learning technology: A differentiated perspective on the role of feedback. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102394

It "comprises four components aiming to assist students' SRL: an automated feedback system, a digital dashboard, personalized SRL strategies, and a planning tool." When a pre- or post-task self-report fell below a threshold, the system recommended an SRL strategy video; the dashboard visualized weekly responses as individualized progress curves and functioned as an indirect informational feedback source encouraging autonomous adjustment.

citation: Kirschner, P; Sweller, John; Clark, Robert. (2006). Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work: An analysis of the failure of constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching. Journal Article. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/50516
title: Design instruction with a strong emphasis on guidance of the student learning process, especially for novices
description: The article recommends that instruction place "a strong emphasis on guidance of the student learning process," because minimally guided approaches are less effective and less efficient given human cognitive architecture. Guidance is most critical for learners without high prior knowledge, since sufficiently knowledgeable learners can supply their own internal guidance. This principle follows from the article's synthesis of half-century empirical evidence and cognitive load reasoning.

article_title: Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning.
citation: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S. (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(3), 900-908. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000001
title: Strategy-choice account: solving a mathematics problem requires discriminating problem kinds and associating each kind with a strategy, and interleaved practice trains this choice
description: The article proposes that a mathematics problem's solution has two steps: choosing a strategy and executing it. In its formal terms, "the choice of an appropriate strategy requires students to both discriminate between different kinds of problems ... and associate each kind of problem with an appropriate strategy". Blocked practice removes the need for choice because students know the strategy before reading the problem, whereas interleaved practice forces strategy choice on the basis of the problem itself, as tests do. The authors argue this, plus the inherent spacing interleaving guarantees, explains its benefits.
requirements: Assignments must juxtapose different kinds of problems so that students must select a strategy from the problem features rather than from lesson context
constraints: Blocked practice is not to be avoided entirely; a small block immediately after introducing a skill may help students focus on execution of the strategy
target_learners: seventh-grade mathematics students
mathematics students at elementary, middle school, and college levels
target_learning_goals: choosing an appropriate solution strategy for mathematics problems
retention of mathematics skills
key_sources: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S. (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(3), 900-908. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000001

article_title: Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications
citation: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://www.springer-ny.com
title: Stochastic approximation paradigm: recursive stochastic difference equations with small step sizes
description: The book's organizing framework is the stochastic approximation paradigm, in which "a stochastic diﬀerence equation such asθn+1 = θn +ϵnYn" is iterated, where θn is a parameter estimate, Yn is a random variable derived from noise-corrupted observations, and the step size is small and may go to zero. One "recursively adjusts the parameter so that some goal is met asymptotically." The book concerns the qualitative and asymptotic properties of such recursive algorithms across their diverse application forms, including constrained variants where iterates are projected back to a set if they leave it.
requirements: A goal to be met asymptotically through recursive parameter adjustment based on noisy observations
constraints: In applications where the optimal value changes with time, step size is kept strictly away from zero rather than sent to zero
target_learners: Graduate students and researchers in applied probability, optimization, and adaptive systems
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying recursive stochastic algorithms for root finding, function minimization, and on-line optimization under noise
examples: Root finding for an unknown function via noisy measurements, recursive Monte Carlo minimization, and parameter adjustment for drug dosage level estimation

article_title: Fostering self-monitoring of university students by means of a standardized learning journal—a longitudinal study with process analyses
citation: Fabriz, S., Dignath-van Ewijk, C., Poarch, G., Büttner, G. (2014). Fostering self-monitoring of university students by means of a standardized learning journal—a longitudinal study with process analyses. Eur J Psychol Educ, 29, 239–255. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10212-013-0196-z
title: Standardized learning journal (structured learning diary) for fostering self-monitoring in university courses
description: A standardized learning journal (structured learning diary) is a self-monitoring tool that university students keep over the course of a semester to record and regulate their learning behavior. The study embedded it in four courses, in some cases combined with a weekly course intervention on self-regulated learning, and evaluated it with pre–post measures and process analyses of the diary data.
requirements: Structured diary format so entries are comparable across students and time points
Sustained use over the study period to yield process data
constraints: Used alone it did not improve self-regulation and decreased motivation
Effects were studied in university courses with pre–post and process measures
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: self-monitoring of learning behavior
self-regulated learning
examples: Students in two of four courses kept the structured learning diary, with or without the additional weekly self-regulated learning course
key_sources: Fabriz, S., Dignath-van Ewijk, C., Poarch, G., Büttner, G. (2014). Fostering self-monitoring of university students by means of a standardized learning journal—a longitudinal study with process analyses. Eur J Psychol Educ, 29, 239–255. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10212-013-0196-z

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: Engagement as a continuum from outreach to shared leadership
description: The article conceptualizes stakeholder engagement not as a dichotomy but as "a continuum ranging from academic-driven research to equitable shared decision making". It aligns three frameworks: an NIH continuum from outreach (researchers provide information) to shared leadership (final decision making at the community level); Key and colleagues' range from community informed to community driven; and the IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation from inform to empower. The article draws one implication: "the choice of participation level is closely tied to the impact research will have in real world settings".
requirements: Deliberate choices about the desired level of participation at each stage
constraints: Terms and definitions differ across the three frameworks, though the implications are the same
target_learners: Community-engaged researchers
Community partners
target_learning_goals: Assessing and selecting appropriate levels of community engagement in research
examples: Community Advisory Boards tend to operate on the involve level; training neighborhood residents as co-researchers exemplifies the collaborate level
key_sources: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244

article_title: Fitting in or Feeling Excluded: The Experiences of High School Students with Visual Impairments
citation: Jessup, G; Bundy, AC; Broom, A; Hancock, N. (2018). Fitting in or feeling excluded: The experiences of high school students with visual impairments. https://doi.org/10.1177/0145482X1811200305
title: School staff should ensure adolescents with visual impairments can participate in lessons and facilitate opportunities to reciprocate with peers
description: The article recommends that school staff act on the social dimensions of students' everyday school experience: "The social impact of doing nothing at school provides an imperative for staff members to ensure that adolescents with visual impairments can participate in lessons." Because few school interactions involved giving help, staff may also need to facilitate opportunities for these students to reciprocate with peers. The principle rests on the study's findings about fitting in, acceptance, and interaction patterns at school.
requirements: Staff awareness of students' in-the-moment social experience at school, including participation in lessons and help exchange with peers
constraints: The authors note adolescents may need to lean on their families for assistance with valued out-of-home activities until they can participate independently
target_learners: High school students with visual impairments (blind or low vision)
target_learning_goals: Social participation and inclusion at school; reciprocal peer interaction
examples: Twelve visually impaired high school students completed the same in-the-moment survey seven times daily for seven consecutive days, comparing experiences across home, school, and other contexts
key_sources: Jessup, G; Bundy, AC; Broom, A; Hancock, N. (2018). Fitting in or feeling excluded: The experiences of high school students with visual impairments. https://doi.org/10.1177/0145482X1811200305

article_title: Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory
citation: Robert Kail and Lynda K. Hall. (2001). Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory. Memory & Cognition, 29(1), 1-9. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421/29/1
title: Embedded-processes account in which STM is activated long-term memory and WM adds controlled attention
description: The article frames its predictions with theories (Cowan 1988, 1995; Engle, Kane, & Tuholski 1999) in which STM is information in long-term memory activated above threshold, and WM includes STM plus attentional processes. As the article puts it, "WM includesSTM as well as the at-tentionalprocesses used to keep some STM contentsin an activatedstate." Engle and colleagues' version defines WM as a system of active long-term memory traces, activation-maintaining processes, and controlled attention. This framework yields the two predictions the studies test: STM tasks should correlate with but load separately from WM tasks, and WM should predict higher-order cognition better.
requirements: Tasks must tap the hypothesized elements: simple span tasks for active memory traces and complex span tasks for traces plus controlled processing
constraints: No tasks are pure measures of STM or WM; tasks often share other processes such as encoding perceptual information, which inflates cross-construct correlations
target_learners: elementary school children aged 7 to 13
target_learning_goals: understanding the relation between memory storage and controlled attention in cognition and reading
examples: The studies administered digit, letter, and word span as STM tasks and reading, listening, and least number span as WM tasks to test the framework's predictions
key_sources: Robert Kail and Lynda K. Hall. (2001). Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory. Memory & Cognition, 29(1), 1-9. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421/29/1

article_title: Social Class is Dead. Long Live Social Class! Stereotype Threat among Low Socioeconomic Status Individuals
citation: Spencer, B; Castano, E (2007). Social class is dead, long live social class! Stereotype threat among low-socioeconomic individuals. Social Justice Research. https://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s11211-007-0047-7
title: Stereotype threat: stigmatized-group members underperform for fear of confirming a negative ingroup stereotype
description: Stereotype threat is the mechanism by which "members of a stigmatized group perform poorly on a task because they fear confirming a negative stereotype that is associated with their ingroup." The article applies this mechanism to socioeconomic status, treating low-SES students as a stigmatized group whose test performance can be depressed when SES-related threat is made salient or when a test is framed as diagnostic of intelligence. It uses the construct to interpret the performance and self-confidence differences observed across its four experimental threat conditions.
requirements: A negative stereotype associated with the individual's ingroup must be relevant to the task being performed
constraints: The article applies the mechanism to socioeconomic status among American students in standardized testing contexts
target_learners: low-socioeconomic status American students
target_learning_goals: standardized test performance
academic self-confidence
examples: Participants were placed in one of four conditions that varied in level of ''threat'' related to socioeconomic status.
key_sources: Spencer, B; Castano, E (2007). Social class is dead, long live social class! Stereotype threat among low-socioeconomic individuals. Social Justice Research. https://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s11211-007-0047-7

article_title: Improving Stealth Assessment in Game-based Learning with LSTM-based Analytics
citation: Akram, B., Mott, B., Min, W., Boyer, K. E., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2017). Improving Stealth Assessment in Game-based Learning with LSTM-based Analytics. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Improving+Stealth+Assessment+in+Game-based+Learning+with+LSTM-based+Analytics
title: Strategy-based temporal analytics framework for stealth assessment using LSTM evidence models
description: A stealth assessment framework that derives temporal evidence from students' dynamic in-game strategy use rather than only from ECD evidence modeling. Student flip sequences are encoded as n-grams, clustered per task with EM clustering to yield strategy labels, and sequences of strategy cluster memberships across consecutive tasks are fed to an LSTM evidence model that predicts post-test performance. The article states the approach "does not require a labor -intensive process of labeling data" because strategies are discovered unsupervised from log data.
requirements: Learning environments in which students solve problems by performing sequences of actions from a limited pool of available actions, so that behavior traces can be encoded as n-gram flip sequences and clustered
constraints: The article states the approach "is not appropriate for analyzing ill -defined problems where players are not bound to certain actions"
target_learners: middle school students (ages 11-13) learning computational thinking
target_learning_goals: computational thinking, including binary representation, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking
examples: Applied to 11 binary representation tasks in the ENGAGE game's Digital World level, using data from 168 middle school students in four public middle school classrooms
key_sources: Akram, B., Mott, B., Min, W., Boyer, K. E., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2017). Improving Stealth Assessment in Game-based Learning with LSTM-based Analytics. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Improving+Stealth+Assessment+in+Game-based+Learning+with+LSTM-based+Analytics

article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Stealth assessment: embedding skill measurement invisibly in game play so that player choices supply the assessment data
description: Stealth assessment is an approach in which measurement of a skill is woven into gameplay so that students' ordinary choices generate the assessment data without them knowing they are being assessed. The article describes it as assessments "woven directly and invisibly into the fabric" of the game, with "players' choices during gameplay provide the data needed for assessment." Zoo U applies this by logging dialogue choices, clicks, and time on and off task to compute social skills performance indices, reducing observer reactivity compared with naturalistic observation.
requirements: Extensive logging of player actions (clicks, dialogue choices, timing) so behaviors relevant to the target skill can be scored automatically
constraints: The article notes a key challenge was determining the appropriate level of difficulty to garner enough student variability in responses to develop useful performance indices
target_learners: third- and fourth-grade elementary school students
target_learning_goals: social skills competencies: emotion regulation, impulse control, communication, empathy, cooperation, and initiation
examples: Zoo U scenes present social problems (e.g., feeding the elephant before recess) where impulsive clicks on distractor crates lower the impulse control score
key_sources: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791

article_title: Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education
citation: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485
title: Staff development for attribute assessment must address underlying conceptions and traditions, not just provide technique toolkits
description: The paper argues that 'toolkits' of practical techniques for teaching and assessing graduate attributes are of limited benefit unless related to underlying assumptions about the purpose and focus of assessment. Staff development must also engage long-standing disciplinary traditions and 'signature' pedagogies and assessments, which can produce inertia or resistance to the assessment innovation needed. Assessment design should be justified through understanding of task dimensions such as authenticity and clarity of criteria-attribute relationships.
requirements: Staff development must address conceptions of teaching and learning as well as techniques
constraints: Traditional methods do not always have the capacity for adaptation to the assessment of graduate attributes
target_learners: university academics and teachers
target_learning_goals: valid assessment design for graduate attributes
examples: The paper lists task dimensions including authenticity to practices of a discourse community, authenticity of task conditions, clarity of criteria-attribute relationships, and student involvement fostering metacognitive abilities
key_sources: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485

article_title: The Effects of Game and Student Characteristics on Persistence in Educational Games: A Hierarchical Linear Modeling Approach
citation: Rahimi, S., Shute, V., & Zhang, Q. (2021). The effects of game and student characteristics on persistence in educational games: A hierarchical linear modeling approach. International Journal of Technology in Education and Science (IJTES), 5(2), 141-165. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijtes.118
title: Stealth assessment of persistence via in-game time-on-task measures
description: Stealth assessment embeds evidence-centered-design models into digital games, collecting log-file performance data as learners play and using statistical methods such as Bayes nets to make real-time inferences about hard-to-measure competencies. In this study, persistence was operationalized as time spent on ultimately unsolved problems plus time above the per-problem average on solved problems, yielding 3,803 data points from 137 students. The authors state that "stealth assessment (Shute, 2011) uses technology-rich environments (e.g., digital games) as vehicles for assessment." Prior work validated such in-game measures against external performance-based measures.
requirements: Log files capturing timestamps of gameplay events per problem
A defined operationalization of persistence (time on unsolved problems and above-average time on solved problems)
constraints: The authors caution that persistence is different from the difficulty of game problems, since harder problems can simply take more time; their measure included unsolved and above-average-time solved problems to partially separate the two
target_learners: Eighth and ninth grade students (grades 7-10 are the game's target population)
target_learning_goals: Persistence as a 21st-century skill
examples: The study parsed Physics Playground log files, coding trophy = none for unsolved problems and selecting solved problems whose solution time exceeded the per-problem average
key_sources: Rahimi, S., Shute, V., & Zhang, Q. (2021). The effects of game and student characteristics on persistence in educational games: A hierarchical linear modeling approach. International Journal of Technology in Education and Science (IJTES), 5(2), 141-165. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijtes.118

article_title: Formative and stealth assessment
citation: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25
title: Stealth assessment: formative assessment seamlessly woven into immersive learning environments
description: Stealth assessment is "an evidence-based approach to assessment where the tasks that students are engaged with are highly interactive and immersive, such as within video games." Performance data is "continuously gathered during the course of playing/learning" and inferences about competency states are stored in a dynamic learner model. The approach aims to support learning, maintain flow, reduce test anxiety without sacrificing validity and reliability, and "blur the distinction between assessment and learning." It relies on automated scoring and machine-based reasoning to infer competencies across a network of skills.
requirements: Evidence-centered assessment design to structure claims and evidence
Formative assessment and feedback mechanisms to support learning
Automated scoring and machine-based reasoning to infer competency values
constraints: Developing the evidence model is difficult when students collaborate on quests, since individual actions and thinking are hard to trace in a combined effort
Scoring qualitative products such as essays and discussions retains high subjectivity even with comprehensive rubrics
target_learners: K-12 students in game-based or computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: Content and key competencies such as creative problem solving
examples: The chapter illustrates stealth assessment in the commercial game Oblivion, inferring creative problem solving from quest actions via Bayesian networks
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25

article_title: Stealth assessment of creativity in a physics video game
citation: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940
title: Stealth assessment: invisible assessment woven into gameplay
description: Stealth assessment involves designing, developing, and weaving assessments directly and invisibly into the fabric of complex learning environments, particularly video games. Evidence for targeted skills comes from players' interactions with the game itself (the processes of play), with inferences about competency states stored in a dynamic learner model in real time. This contrasts with singular outcome measures typical of educational environments. Real-time estimates can drive adaptivity (e.g., adjusting task difficulty) and timely individualized feedback while maintaining flow.
requirements: A well-designed game environment producing rich sequences of player actions that serve as evidence sources
A psychometric model (e.g., Bayesian network) to accumulate evidence into competency estimates
constraints: Requires identifying level-specific in-game behaviors and scoring rules, which the authors note can be tricky depending on the nature of a given level
target_learners: students in game-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: 21st-century competencies such as creativity, problem solving, and physics understanding
examples: Prior stealth assessments have measured problem solving, mathematics, computational thinking, physics, social skills, and conscientiousness in various games
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940

article_title: Young Children's Interpretation of Multidigit Number Names: From Emerging Competence to Mastery
citation: Mix, Kelly S., Prather, Richard W., Smith, Linda B., & Stockton, Jerri DaSha. (2014). Young Children's Interpretation of Multidigit Number Names: From Emerging Competence to Mastery. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12197
title: Statistical learning account of emerging place value knowledge
description: The article proposes that children acquire partial understanding of multidigit numerals through statistical learning, "the idea that learners actively make sense of the perceptual stream by tabulating the statistical patterns in it." Because multidigit numerals are ubiquitous in children's environments (room numbers, calendars, price tags), children detect regularities such as two-digit names containing /ee/ and use them, together with single-digit number meanings, to make educated guesses about numeral identity and magnitude. This bootstrapping occurs before formal schooling and parallels statistical learning in language acquisition.
requirements: Exposure to written and spoken multidigit numbers in everyday environments
Prior knowledge of single-digit number meanings
constraints: The correlation between number names and digit strings is imperfect and breaks down for longer number names
The study does not identify the origins of this knowledge or the experiences it depends on
target_learners: Preschool children aged 3 to 7 years
target_learning_goals: Interpreting written multidigit numerals and spoken number names
examples: Children hearing numbers named while seeing them in print on calendars, elevators, and room numbers could detect that thirty-four maps onto XX rather than X
key_sources: Mix, Kelly S., Prather, Richard W., Smith, Linda B., & Stockton, Jerri DaSha. (2014). Young Children's Interpretation of Multidigit Number Names: From Emerging Competence to Mastery. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12197

article_title: A burden for the boys: Evidence of stereotype threat in boys' reading performance
citation: Pascal Pansu, Isabelle Régner, Sylvain Max, Pascale Colé, John B. Nezlek, Pascal Huguet. (2016). A burden for the boys: Evidence of stereotype threat in boys' reading performance. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 65, pp.26-30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2016.02.008
title: Stereotype threat account of the gender gap favoring girls in reading
description: The article extends stereotype threat theory to reading, assuming that boys are negatively stereotyped in this domain. It proposes that situational threat — a test framed as diagnostic of reading ability — depresses boys' performance and thereby contributes to the well-known gender gap favoring girls in reading. The experiment supports the account conditionally: the predicted reversal appeared only among highly-identified students, and the authors present the findings as offering another explanation for the gap.
requirements: A domain in which one gender group is negatively stereotyped (here, boys in reading)
A performance situation that can be framed as diagnostic of ability versus low-stakes
constraints: The pattern was obtained only among highly-identified students
Evidence comes from one experiment with eighty third-grade students
target_learners: elementary school students (3rd grade)
target_learning_goals: reading performance on standardized-style tests
examples: Eighty third-graders took a reading test framed either as diagnostic of reading abilities or as a game
key_sources: Pascal Pansu, Isabelle Régner, Sylvain Max, Pascale Colé, John B. Nezlek, Pascal Huguet. (2016). A burden for the boys: Evidence of stereotype threat in boys' reading performance. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 65, pp.26-30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2016.02.008

article_title: Latinos’ Changing Ethnic Group Representation From Elementary to Middle School: Perceived Belonging and Academic Achievement
citation: Morales-Chicas Jessica, Graham Sandra. (2017). Latinos’ Changing Ethnic Group Representation From Elementary to Middle School: Perceived Belonging and Academic Achievement. Journal of Research on Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1111/jora.12292
title: Stage–environment fit extended to ethnic minority youth: mismatch between same-ethnic representation across the middle school transition and adolescents' developmental needs
description: Stage–environment fit theory holds that "the middle school transition can be especially challenging because of the mismatch between the developmental needs of early adolescents and the school environment to which they are transitioning." The article extends this framework to ethnic minority youth by proposing ethnic incongruence — a decline in same-ethnic peers from elementary to middle school — as a specific mismatch, since same-ethnic group esteem and belonging grow in early adolescence and Latinos tend to be more collectivistic. The framework predicts poorer adjustment when fewer same-ethnic peers accompany the transition, and treats school-level diversity as a dimension that can buffer developmental mismatch.
requirements: Applies during school transitions where ethnic representation changes between departing and receiving schools, at a developmental period when same-ethnic peer preference heightens
constraints: The article notes the theory "has rarely addressed mismatches that might be particularly challenging for ethnic minority youth"; the extension is tested cross-sectionally at one time point only
target_learners: Latino early adolescents transitioning from elementary to middle school
target_learning_goals: School belonging
Academic achievement (GPA)
examples: The study measured representation change by subtracting each student's elementary-school Latino proportion from the middle-school proportion, and Simpson's diversity index at the school level, then tested the cross-level interaction.
key_sources: Morales-Chicas Jessica, Graham Sandra. (2017). Latinos’ Changing Ethnic Group Representation From Elementary to Middle School: Perceived Belonging and Academic Achievement. Journal of Research on Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1111/jora.12292

article_title: What you say, and how you say it: Preschoolers' growth in vocabulary and communication skills differentially predict kindergarten academic achievement and self‐regulation
citation: Ramsook K. Ashana, Welsh Janet A., Bierman Karen L. (2020). What you say, and how you say it: Preschoolers' growth in vocabulary and communication skills differentially predict kindergarten academic achievement and self‐regulation. Social Development, 29(3), 783–800. https://doi.org/10.1111/sode.12425
title: Two-dimension account of early language: structural language (vocabulary) versus social communication (pragmatic) skills as distinct contributors to school functioning
description: The article distinguishes structural linguistic competencies such as vocabulary from "competency in using language effectively in social contexts, referred to as social communication or pragmatic language skills". Social communication covers using language to initiate interactions, settle disagreements, express ideas clearly, and understand spoken instructions. The study treats these as moderately correlated yet distinct dimensions that differentially predict academic achievement and self-regulation, with social communication uniquely predicting self-regulation.
requirements: Assessment must capture both dimensions separately; the study used an expressive vocabulary test and an 11-item teacher-rated Social Communication Scale
constraints: The social communication measure relied on teacher ratings relative to age norms, with somewhat low inter-rater reliability; mechanisms linking it to self-regulation are not well understood
target_learners: preschool children from low-income families enrolled in Head Start programs
target_learning_goals: language development
self-regulation
school readiness
examples: The study measured vocabulary with the EOWPVT and social communication with the Welsh, Nelson, & REDI Social Communication Scale across three waves
key_sources: Ramsook K. Ashana, Welsh Janet A., Bierman Karen L. (2020). What you say, and how you say it: Preschoolers' growth in vocabulary and communication skills differentially predict kindergarten academic achievement and self‐regulation. Social Development, 29(3), 783–800. https://doi.org/10.1111/sode.12425

article_title: Epistemic Curiosity and Situational Interest: Distant Cousins or Identical Twins?
citation: Henk G. Schmidt & Jerome I. Rotgans. (2021). Epistemic Curiosity and Situational Interest: Distant Cousins or Identical Twins?. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09539-9
title: State epistemic curiosity measure developed via content analysis of published questionnaires
description: A newly constructed multi-item state epistemic curiosity scale built from a content analysis of epistemic curiosity questionnaires published between 1975 and 2019. The article states "we decided to create a multi-item 'state'epistemic curiosity measure based on a content analysis of the epistemic curiosity questionnaires published between 1975 and 2019". Items such as "I am really curious to know more about this topic" were scored on a 5-point Likert scale, and the measure showed high construct reliability (H = .92 in Study 1). It was used in both studies to measure momentary curiosity about the physics of heat.
requirements: Items must be scored on a 5-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)
The scale targets a state rather than trait form of curiosity, administered in response to a specific topic
constraints: The authors acknowledge the new scale may have been "less successful than hoped for" because no state epistemic curiosity scale previously existed
A reviewer suggested the two scales show semantic overlap, which the authors dispute
target_learners: secondary-school students
target_learning_goals: measuring momentary epistemic curiosity about a topic to be studied
examples: In Study 1 the measure achieved H = .92; in Study 2 its four administrations achieved H between .94 and .95
key_sources: Henk G. Schmidt & Jerome I. Rotgans. (2021). Epistemic Curiosity and Situational Interest: Distant Cousins or Identical Twins?. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09539-9

article_title: The effects of readers’ goals on inference generation and memory for texts
citation: P. van den Broek, R. F. Lorch, Jr., T. Linderholm, & M. Gustafson. (2001). The effects of readers' goals on inference generation and memory for texts. Memory & Cognition, 29(8), 1081-1087. https://link.springer.com/journal/13414
title: Standards of coherence as the mechanism by which reading goals shape inference generation and memory
description: The article proposes that as readers proceed through a text they maintain "standards of coherence that act as criteria for comprehension," which "dictate the inferential activities in which the readers engage at each point during reading." A reading goal prompts the reader to select particular standards, operationalizing the goal; a strict standard yields coherence-producing inferences at a cost of greater effort, while a relaxed standard yields less effortful reading but a less coherent representation. The framework integrates bottom-up and top-down accounts of inference generation and connects goal-based reading theories to computational models of text comprehension.
requirements: A reading goal that the reader translates into relevant standards of coherence
constraints: The article states none of the existing reading models provides details on how goals influence the standards readers employ
target_learners: college students reading expository text
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
construction of coherent memory representations of text
examples: Study-goal readers employed stringent standards focused on intratextual relations, generating explanatory and predictive inferences, paraphrases, and repetitions; entertainment-goal readers adopted a relaxed standard, generating associations and evaluations connected to personal experience
key_sources: P. van den Broek, R. F. Lorch, Jr., T. Linderholm, & M. Gustafson. (2001). The effects of readers' goals on inference generation and memory for texts. Memory & Cognition, 29(8), 1081-1087. https://link.springer.com/journal/13414

article_title: Processing Speed is Impaired in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder, and Relates to Social Communication Abilities
citation: Haigh Sarah M., Walsh Jennifer A., Mazefsky Carla A., Minshew Nancy J., Eack Shaun M. (2018). Processing Speed is Impaired in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder, and Relates to Social Communication Abilities. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-018-3515-z
title: Use standardized measures of processing speed when assessing processing speed in ASD
description: The article recommends that assessments of processing speed in ASD rely on standardized tests rather than ad hoc or inspection-time tasks, because inspection tasks may produce ceiling effects and fail to detect clinically meaningful deficits. The authors state that their findings "advocate for the use of standardized measures of processing speed to ensure that the test is sensitive enough to detect clinically-related deficits." Standardized MATRICS battery measures revealed large deficits that inspection-time methods had missed in prior studies.
requirements: Assessments must use standardized, validated processing speed tests with adequate sensitivity rather than inspection-time or ad hoc tasks.
constraints: The deficit found may reflect perceptual and/or motor output demands shared by the standardized tests themselves.
target_learners: Adults with autism spectrum disorder without intellectual disability
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of information processing speed as a target for cognitive intervention
examples: The study administered three standardized MATRICS subtests (Trail Making Test A, Symbol Coding, Category Fluency) and found significant deficits on all of them, whereas prior inspection-time studies had concluded processing speed was intact.
key_sources: Haigh Sarah M., Walsh Jennifer A., Mazefsky Carla A., Minshew Nancy J., Eack Shaun M. (2018). Processing Speed is Impaired in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder, and Relates to Social Communication Abilities. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-018-3515-z

article_title: Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System
citation: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016
title: Statistical learning account of spelling development
description: The review's organizing framework is statistical learning, defined as "the process whereby organisms pick up patterns by observing and internalizing the relative frequency with which objects and events occur and co-occur". On this account, children first learn salient graphic characteristics of print implicitly, then apply the same mechanisms to phoneme-spelling links, including context-conditioned and morphological patterns. Learning is shaped by the statistics of the writing children see, including their own names, and spelling learning in turn reshapes children's ideas about language.
requirements: Sufficient exposure to examples of writing in the child's environment, since the account holds that children learn letter and digram frequencies from the print around them.
constraints: The review states people are not ideal statistical learners: context conditioning is learned slowly, adults underuse context relative to its strength in the vocabulary, and the account's role in nonalphabetic systems needs further work.
target_learners: preschool and school-age children learning alphabetic writing systems
target_learning_goals: spelling development
implicit knowledge of orthographic patterns
examples: The review interprets prephonological spellers' language-specific letter and digram use, own-name letter use, and the gradual emergence of context sensitivity as manifestations of statistical learning.
key_sources: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016

article_title: The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics
citation: Ayush Gupta, David Hammer, Edward F. Redish. (2008). The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/hlns20
