title: Static Ontologies (SO) framework: ontological categories are distinct, stable, and constraining
description: The SO framework, advanced by Chi, Slotta, and colleagues, holds that entities and science concepts belong to a single hierarchical ontological category (matter, processes, mental states) whose trees do not share attributes. The article summarizes its core: "ontological categories are distinct, stable, and constraining", so novices' difficulties with heat, light, current, and diffusion arise from mis-categorizing processes as matter. Conceptual change is re-assignment across trees, and predicates serve as empirical markers of categorization.
requirements: Empirical evidence for categorization is taken from the verbal predicates participants use to describe concepts
constraints: The article contests this framework, arguing it mischaracterizes everyday, expert, and novice reasoning
target_learners: novice physics students
target_learning_goals: understanding of physics concepts such as heat, light, electric current, and diffusion
key_sources: Ayush Gupta, David Hammer, Edward F. Redish. (2008). The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/hlns20

article_title: Guiding group cognition in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2010). Guiding group cognition in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9091-7
title: Stahl's framework of major influences on group cognition in CSCL
description: The article presents a visualization of "major categories of these influences" on collaborative learning, placing at the center "the dialogical interaction through which individual participants form into a collective knowledge-building agency." Sequential interaction weaves individual Bakhtinian voices into group meaning making, whose shared meanings are embodied in team knowledge artifacts and produce team outcomes driven by the team's task. Surrounding influences include individual resources and experiences, the culture of the discourse community, interaction context, and technology and media.
requirements: Analysis of group cognition must treat the group level of description rather than only individual preconditions
constraints: Individual background, perspectives and abilities are preconditions of collaboration and are of interest to education and psychology in general, but not specifically CSCL's concerns
target_learners: small collaborative learning groups
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
group problem solving
examples: Figure 1 diagrams influences including individual voices, task, technology and media, interaction context, culture of discourse community, team knowledge artifacts, and team outcomes around sequential team interaction
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2010). Guiding group cognition in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9091-7

article_title: Scaffolding of small groups’ metacognitive activities with an avatar
citation: Molenaar, I., Chiu, M. M., Sleegers, P., & van Boxtel, C. (2011). Scaffolding of small groups' metacognitive activities with an avatar. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 601-624. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9130-z
title: Structuring versus problematizing as two scaffolding mechanisms
description: The article adopts Reiser's distinction between two mechanisms by which scaffolding affects learning. "Structuring simplifies the learning assignment by reducing its complexity, clarifying the underlying components and supporting performance", for example by showing an exemplary plan, while problematizing increases complexity by posing questions that elicit learners' own strategies and metacognitive activities. The study instantiates these as two avatar scaffold conditions and finds they foster qualitatively different student interactions.
requirements: Scaffolds must be context-suitable and delivered at the point in the learning process where the metacognitive activity is typically executed
constraints: Structuring scaffolds encourage attention to the scaffold's information but do not invite students to construct their own metacognitive activities
target_learners: elementary school students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge and domain knowledge during collaborative inquiry
examples: The avatar David showed an exemplary mind-map plan in the structuring condition and asked "How are you going to make a mind map?" in the problematizing condition.
key_sources: Molenaar, I., Chiu, M. M., Sleegers, P., & van Boxtel, C. (2011). Scaffolding of small groups' metacognitive activities with an avatar. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 601-624. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9130-z

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: Study knowledge, roles, space, and time through detailed analysis of situated interaction rather than assuming their characteristics
description: The editorial's closing design recommendation for CSCL research: computer-supported collaborative learning opens a multi-dimensional shared world in an evolving, co-created context, where "Knowledge, roles, space, and time are not simple givens whose characteristics can be assumed". Each must be studied in each case through detailed analysis of the situated interaction. The editorial adds that many research questions can still be rigorously pursued within established perspectives, and the journal welcomes both kinds of studies.
requirements: Detailed analysis of situated interaction in each specific CSCL case
constraints: Not every paper needs to address these theoretical frontiers; traditional frameworks remain appropriate for many questions
target_learners: CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing CSCL studies that capture characteristic phenomena of computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The four ijCSCL case studies each propose intriguing extensions to theories important to CSCL, such as distributed cognition, discourse analysis, tacit knowledge, activity theory, and temporal analysis.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0

article_title: The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies
citation: Diana Laurillard. (2009). The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL), 4, pp.5-20. https://hal.science/hal-00592750
title: Start technology-enhanced learning design from the requirements of education — learners' and teachers' needs — rather than from the technology
description: The article argues that exploiting collaborative technologies for learning requires beginning with educational requirements rather than with the affordances of the technology. As the abstract puts it, "To get the best from them for education we need to start with the requirements of education, in terms of both learners and teachers needs." The principle directs designers to derive technology use from what learners and teachers need, instead of adapting teaching to whatever a new tool happens to offer.
requirements: Designers must identify learners' and teachers' needs before selecting or adapting a technology for learning.
constraints: The article notes that technologies themselves are rarely designed with teaching and learning in mind, so educational requirements must be imposed on them rather than assumed of them.
target_learners: learners using collaborative technologies
target_learning_goals: genuinely enhanced learning experiences through technology-supported collaboration
examples: The paper's own approach: building what is known about what it takes to learn into a pedagogical framework used to challenge digital technologies.
key_sources: Diana Laurillard. (2009). The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL), 4, pp.5-20. https://hal.science/hal-00592750

article_title: Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
citation: Eddy Y.C. Lee, Carol K.K. Chan, & Jan van Aalst. (2006). Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-6844-4
title: Turn over epistemic agency to students so assessment doubles as scaffolding for collaborative inquiry
description: The article's key design principle is that "The key design principle involved turning over epistemic agency to students"; students themselves identify knowledge-building episodes in the computer discourse, guided by knowledge-building principles used as criteria. This makes assessment dual-purpose: it both measures and fosters inquiry, since "Assessment should be designed as a tool that both measures and fosters deeper inquiry and collaboration." The portfolio-plus-principles condition, which most embodied this agency, produced deeper inquiry and understanding than comparison classes.
requirements: Students need a shared discourse database whose notes they can revisit, select, and analyze
Assessment tasks must be embedded in the instructional process, with principles provided as selection and writing scaffolds
constraints: Effectiveness was examined against Knowledge Forum-only and portfolio-only conditions in quasi-experimental classroom settings; conditio nal complexity is acknowledged by the authors
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
deeper inquiry
conceptual understanding
examples: Students in the portfolio-and-principles class selected note clusters illustrating five principles and wrote explanations and essays based on their portfolios
key_sources: Eddy Y.C. Lee, Carol K.K. Chan, & Jan van Aalst. (2006). Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-8997-6

article_title: Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment
citation: Xintian Tu, Joshua Danish, Megan Humburg, Mengxi Zhou, Nitasha Mathayas, Noel Enyedy, Tessaly Jen. (2023). Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 18:231–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09395-z
title: Three embodied communicative acts — showing particle behavior, guiding peers' movement, and responding to suggestions — support collective and individual functions in MR learning
description: Through embodied interaction analysis of the STEP classroom video, the authors grouped students' embodied moves into three communicative acts: using gestures to demonstrate what they knew about particle behavior, giving direction to peers' movement, and following or responding to others' suggestions (including mimicking movements such as the "jellyfish" motion). The iterative analytic sequence shown in the video data determined the acts and their functions, which the authors tabulate with both collective functions (e.g., repair, guiding collective work) and individual functions (e.g., representing one's own ideas, experiencing relative speed and distance). One demonstration episode in which a group came to be recognized as a liquid shows all three acts overlapping.
requirements: A collaborative mixed-reality environment with a shared collective goal in which movement is tracked and displayed, so that communicative acts can be observed and coordinated.
constraints: The acts were identified within the STEP particle curriculum's whole-class embodied activities, debriefings, and interviews with young children; the authors present representative clips rather than claiming exhaustive coverage.
target_learners: elementary school students (first and second grade)
target_learning_goals: communicating and collectively constructing understanding of particle behavior and states of matter
examples: In a day-3 episode, Lily gestured distance, directed peers with 'Stay away back', and the group's coordinated walking and spacing was finally recognized as a liquid by the simulation's state meter.
key_sources: Xintian Tu, Joshua Danish, Megan Humburg, Mengxi Zhou, Nitasha Mathayas, Noel Enyedy, Tessaly Jen. (2023). Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 18:231–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09395-z

article_title: Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment
citation: Xintian Tu, Joshua Danish, Megan Humburg, Mengxi Zhou, Nitasha Mathayas, Noel Enyedy, Tessaly Jen. (2023). Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 18:231–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09395-z
title: STEP mixed-reality platform: whole-body particle simulation with person tracking and a projected state meter
description: STEP (Science through Technology Enhanced Play) is a mixed-reality environment in which students' tracked movements appear as colored circles representing particles in a projected simulation, with color-coded lines linking nearest neighbors and linked bar graphs displaying the proportion of particles in each state. Technically, "the STEP platform utilizes the Open PTrack person tracking system to monitor student movement via Kinect cameras," feeding a JavaScript web application whose display is projected on a shared classroom screen. Students collectively adjust speed and distance to be recognized as a solid, liquid, or gas, supporting exploration of states of matter and micro–macro connections.
requirements: A networked laptop, Kinect cameras running the Open PTrack tracking system, and a projection screen visible to all students.
constraints: Target content is limited to four particle-behavior characteristics — speed, distance, attraction, and trajectory — within the states-of-matter curriculum.
target_learners: elementary school students (first and second grade)
target_learning_goals: understanding particle behaviors in the three states of matter and connections between microscopic and macroscopic characteristics
examples: Day 1 activity: students add or take away energy from a projected snowman, changing its state among snowman, puddle, or steam.
key_sources: Xintian Tu, Joshua Danish, Megan Humburg, Mengxi Zhou, Nitasha Mathayas, Noel Enyedy, Tessaly Jen. (2023). Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 18:231–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09395-z

article_title: Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies
citation: Mørch, A. I., Andersen, R., Eie, S., & Mifsud, L. (2024). Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09432-5
title: Gradient of states of intersubjectivity ordered by density of sociotechnical relations
description: The article reports a preliminary typology of six states of intersubjectivity, ordered by increasing density of sociotechnical interdependencies: vague, technical, fragmented, connected, entangled, and enmeshed intersubjectivity. The authors "adapted a qualitative gradient of intersubjectivity in terms of the density of sociotechnical relations", combining deductive STC-derived coordination needs with inductive themes. Entangled intersubjectivity covers unplanned switching between gaming and academic behavior, and enmeshed intersubjectivity occurs in role-play conversation, both including instances of emergent group understanding.
requirements: Interaction analysis with state descriptives derived by iterative coding among four researchers
constraints: States were derived from data of one profiled group (group 7), with snapshots of a 3-week process
target_learners: student teachers
seventh-grade pupils
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning with Minecraft
shared understanding of social studies topics
examples: Extracts mapped state changes from vague (task interpretation) to enmeshed (video-recorded role-play in Minecraft)
key_sources: Mørch, A. I., Andersen, R., Eie, S., & Mifsud, L. (2024). Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09432-5

article_title: Toward a Taxonomy: Insights from the 2025 CSCL paradigm building workshop
citation: Simon, S., Şener, B., Greisel, M., Pifarré Turmo, M., Borchers, C., Chernikova, O., Shahrokhian, B., Tajik, E., Sitjà Martín, M., Čarapina, M., Hu, X., & Ataş, A. H. (2026). Toward a Taxonomy: Insights from the 2025 CSCL paradigm building workshop. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09477-8
title: Use standardized taxonomy descriptors so studies can be identified by phenomenon rather than theoretical lens
description: Because CSCL lacks shared descriptors for phenomena and analytic approaches, the article recommends standardized descriptors within a community taxonomy. These mitigate the jingle-jangle fallacy, using the same terms for different concepts or different terms for the same concept, letting researchers find relevant studies across paradigms based on the phenomenon itself. The taxonomy would also serve authors as a scaffold for articulating study aspects and as a transparent checklist supporting review processes.
requirements: Variables must describe distinct aspects of the collaboration processes and carry explanatory power for understanding the phenomenon
constraints: Details on either binary or continuous variable values were not discussed by the group
target_learners: CSCL researchers
journal and conference reviewers
target_learning_goals: Improving comparability and cross-paradigm literature navigation
Supporting preregistration of CSCL studies
examples: Group members identified descriptors such as agent and temporal scope, technological mediation (online, in-presence, hybrid), and task type (knowledge building, problem-solving, co-design) that ideal CSCL contributions should communicate
key_sources: Simon, S., Şener, B., Greisel, M., Pifarré Turmo, M., Borchers, C., Chernikova, O., Shahrokhian, B., Tajik, E., Sitjà Martín, M., Čarapina, M., Hu, X., & Ataş, A. H. (2026). Toward a Taxonomy: Insights from the 2025 CSCL paradigm building workshop. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09477-8

article_title: Fostering engineering and science students’ and teachers’ systems thinking and conceptual modeling skills
citation: Peretz, R., Tal, M., Akiri, E., Dori, D., & Dori, Y. J. (2023). Fostering engineering and science students' and teachers' systems thinking and conceptual modeling skills. Instructional Science, 51, 509–543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09625-9
title: Modified Systems Thinking Assessment Rubric (STAR*) for scoring top-level OPM diagrams
description: STAR* is the study's instrument for scoring learners' OPM models, presented in Appendix 2 as the "Modified Systems Thinking Assessment Rubric (STAR*) for top-level OPM diagrams". It defines seven attributes (A1–A7) across System and Model aspects: intended purpose, main function, structural relations, level of detail, procedural relations, model readability, and OPL main-process procedural sentences, each with printed scoring scales from zero points up to two or three points. For example, A2 requires "Exactly one main process, which transforms at least one object".
requirements: Raters must score OPM diagrams attribute-by-attribute against the printed 0–2 or 0–1 (and up to three point) scales, e.g., structural relations require correct use of at least two of four kinds of links for full credit.
constraints: The rubric is specified for top-level OPM diagrams only, per its own title.
target_learners: engineering students
engineering and science teachers
target_learning_goals: assessment of systems thinking
assessment of conceptual modeling skills
examples: A1 scoring: both beneficiary and benefit correctly used, linked, and phrased earns the top score; both absent earns zero points.
key_sources: Peretz, R., Tal, M., Akiri, E., Dori, D., & Dori, Y. J. (2023). Fostering engineering and science students' and teachers' systems thinking and conceptual modeling skills. Instructional Science, 51, 509–543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09625-9

article_title: The roles that students’ ethnicity and achievement levels play in teachers’ choice of learning materials in online teaching: evidence from two experimental studies
citation: Sabine Schlag, Sabine Glock. (2024). The roles that students' ethnicity and achievement levels play in teachers' choice of learning materials in online teaching: evidence from two experimental studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09681-9
title: Stereotype-driven shortcut model of teachers' material-choice decisions
description: The article frames material choice as a decision-making process in which teachers use schemas as shortcuts that can activate stereotypes. It cites Shavelson and Stern's model in which decisions are influenced by "material and activities, teachers' beliefs about the nature of teaching, and teachers' judgments about students' abilities and behavior", and the continuum model of impression formation, under which expectation-confirming information (e.g., minority students' low achievement) triggers stereotype-based rather than individuating judgment. The two studies instantiate this by showing ethnicity and achievement cues shifting material choices.
requirements: The account presupposes student cues (names, achievement descriptions) that teachers interpret against stereotypical expectations.
constraints: The authors note they simplified the decision-making process, and preservice teachers may differ from inservice teachers, who consider more complex information.
target_learners: Ethnic minority and majority students in primary and secondary school
target_learning_goals: Understanding and improving equity in teachers' selection of learning materials
key_sources: Sabine Schlag, Sabine Glock. (2024). The roles that students' ethnicity and achievement levels play in teachers' choice of learning materials in online teaching: evidence from two experimental studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09681-9

article_title: Rigorously selected and well trained senior student tutors in problem based learning: student perceptions and study achievements
citation: Catherine De Rijdt, Janine van der Rijt, Filip Dochy, Cees van der Vleuten. (2012). Rigorously selected and well trained senior student tutors in problem based learning: student perceptions and study achievements. Instructional Science, 40, 397-411. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9173-6
title: Rigorous selection and 36-hour training programme for senior student tutors in PBL
description: The article describes a student tutor programme at Maastricht University's Faculty of Law in which students with an average final mark of seven or higher were invited to apply and "All the applicants took part in a rigorous selection procedure, based on the assessment centre method", judged on motivation, knowledge, study achievements and inherent tutor skills. The 23 selected tutors received 36 hours of intensive training in tutoring skills built around themes such as stimulating cognitive processes, scaffolding and fostering meta-cognitive strategies, using observation with reflection, peer coaching, simulations and collaborative learning, followed by further training, personal coaching and observation of experienced staff tutors.
requirements: Student tutors must be selected from high achieving students via a rigorous selection procedure and receive extensive training before and during tutoring, including observation of experienced staff tutors and weekly tutor meetings with staff tutors.
constraints: The study was conducted in one university setting with first-year PBL law courses, and the results do not warrant conclusions about the concrete impact and importance of tutor selection and training themselves.
target_learners: First-year undergraduate law students in a problem-based curriculum
Senior students serving as cross-level tutors
target_learning_goals: Effective tutorial group facilitation
Stimulating cognitive processes and active involvement
Scaffolding and meta-cognitive strategies
examples: Selected student tutors received 36 hours of intensive training during their second year and observed each of 14 tutorial sessions with an experienced staff tutor before starting; the training was similar to the obligatory 38-hour teacher training course for new staff.
key_sources: Catherine De Rijdt, Janine van der Rijt, Filip Dochy, Cees van der Vleuten. (2012). Rigorously selected and well trained senior student tutors in problem based learning: student perceptions and study achievements. Instructional Science, 40, 397-411. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9173-6

article_title: Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images
citation: Benjamin D. Jee, Bryan J. Matlen, Monica Greenlaw, Nina Simms, Dedre Gentner. (2022). Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09599-0
title: Structure-mapping theory: comparison as structural alignment of common relational systems
description: Structure-mapping theory holds that "comparison involves aligning two examples in terms of their common relational structure," placing elements into correspondence "according to their role in a common system of relations." The article applies this account to science images: a student viewing a forelimb diagram must align bones across animals by structural role, which highlights common structure (homology), supports inferences such as common ancestry, and also highlights differences connected to the shared relational system. Accurate alignment requires rejecting superficial perceptual matches.
requirements: Comparison is effective only if students create accurate structural alignments based on shared relationships rather than local perceptual matches
constraints: Novices may lack the domain knowledge to make accurate alignments without cognitive supports such as language, gestures, or spatial placement
target_learners: middle school science students
novice science learners
target_learning_goals: comprehending relational structure in science images
learning relational concepts such as homology, catalyst, and adaptation
key_sources: Benjamin D. Jee, Bryan J. Matlen, Monica Greenlaw, Nina Simms, Dedre Gentner. (2022). Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09599-0

article_title: Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis
citation: de Grave, W. S., Boshuizen, H. & Schmidt, H. (1996). Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 24(5), 321–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00118111
title: Stimulated recall procedure for tapping thinking processes during PBL problem analysis
description: The study used a stimulated recall procedure in which students' thinking processes during the tutorial group discussion were tapped, producing recall protocols analysed alongside verbatim transcripts of the group's verbal interaction. The article reports that "Thinking processes were tapped by means of a stimulated recall procedure." The method proved "sensitive for detecting conceptual change during problem analysis."
requirements: Requires verbatim transcripts of both the verbal interaction in the group and the recall protocols for analysis.
target_learners: students in problem-based learning tutorial groups
target_learning_goals: conceptual change
hypothesis evaluation
meta-reasoning
examples: The study analysed verbal communication among tutorial group members together with their stimulated recall protocols of thinking during problem analysis.
key_sources: de Grave, W. S., Boshuizen, H. & Schmidt, H. (1996). Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 24(5), 321–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00118111

article_title: Designing a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG
citation: Dillenbourg, P. (1989). The design of a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG. Instructional Science, 18(3), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00053359
title: Self-improving mechanism: learning strategy-selection criteria from student model states by concept learning from examples
description: The article's central mechanism account is that a tutor can improve itself by inducing selection criteria from its own experience. Criteria "are expressed as characteristics of the student model" and are "elaborated by comparing student model states recorded when a strategy was effective and those recorded when the same strategy was not effective". The comparison is performed by machine learning methods, "more precisely, by learning concepts from examples", so each tutoring episode contributes a labelled example of strategy success or failure.
requirements: Recorded student model states from episodes where a strategy was effective and where it was not effective
Machine learning methods able to learn concepts from examples
constraints: Criteria are limited to characteristics expressible in the student model
target_learners: geometry learners
target_learning_goals: adaptive selection of didactic strategies during tutoring
examples: The system compared student model states from effective versus ineffective uses of the same strategy to induce selection conditions
key_sources: Dillenbourg, P. (1989). The design of a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG. Instructional Science, 18(3), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00053359

article_title: Team learning: building shared mental models
citation: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3
title: Steer the Economy business simulation game as complex interdependent team task
description: "Steer the Economy", developed by Woltjer (2005), is a business simulation game in which teams act as company management making decisions in a simulated macro-economy of four markets and five actor types, with companies interlinked through a computer network. The mission is to maximize company value (equity plus goodwill). The article chose it "because of its authenticity", requiring integration of different perspectives under information overload, making members interdependent.
requirements: Face-to-face team interaction
Computer network linking all companies' decisions
constraints: Teams in the study played the game for only two weeks
target_learners: first-year International Business Economics students
target_learning_goals: managing a company in a complex simulated economy through team decision making
examples: Teams managed their company for a simulated period of circa 8 years, with equity and goodwill in the last year taken as actual performance measures
key_sources: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3

article_title: Effects of problem–example and example–problem pairs on gifted and nongifted primary school students’ learning
citation: Coppens, L. C., Hoogerheide, V., Snippe, E. M., Flunger, B., & van Gog, T. (2019). Effects of problem–example and example–problem pairs on gifted and nongifted primary school students' learning. Instructional Science, 47, 279–297. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09484-3
title: Start online learning phases with a worked example rather than a practice problem
description: The authors draw a design recommendation for online and blended learning environments from their efficiency and competence findings: "It seems solid advice to start the learning phase with an example and not a practice problem." Example–problem pairs were more efficient and beneficial for perceived competence for both gifted and nongifted primary students, even though test performance differences were not always significant.
requirements: Learning materials must include worked video modeling examples that demonstrate the solution procedure before or alongside practice problems.
constraints: Sequence effects on test performance were not always significant; the advantage lies mainly in efficiency and perceived competence, and was studied with primary school students on a puzzle-like math task.
target_learners: primary school students
gifted students
novice learners
target_learning_goals: procedural problem-solving skill acquisition
examples: Students studied two 4-minute video modeling examples and solved two isomorphic water jug practice problems in either EPEP or PEPE order before an isomorphic and near-transfer posttest.
key_sources: Coppens, L. C., Hoogerheide, V., Snippe, E. M., Flunger, B., & van Gog, T. (2019). Effects of problem–example and example–problem pairs on gifted and nongifted primary school students' learning. Instructional Science, 47, 279–297. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09484-3

article_title: The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Lyn Lim, Yizhou Fan, Jonathan Kilgour, Johanna Moore, Dragan Gašević, Maria Bannert, Inge Molenaar. (2022). The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09308-9
title: Two-dimensional framework of learning outcomes: structure (independent vs. connected concepts) and level (surface vs. deep knowledge)
description: The article operationalises learning outcomes along two dimensions of mental representation of knowledge drawn from de Jong and Ferguson-Hessler: structure, ranging from unconnected independent concepts to interconnected networks, and level, ranging from surface to deep knowledge. Four measures instantiate the combinations: a domain test, concept maps, a transfer test, and an essay. The article states that "learning outcomes can be characterised along two dimensions—the structure and the level of knowledge" and treats them as continuums rather than a dichotomy.
requirements: Outcomes must be measurable at identifiable points on both dimensions, as in the article's Table 1 operationalisation
constraints: The article notes the table might suggest a dichotomy, but the dimensions are continuums; outcomes are located on two continuums
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge
conceptual knowledge structure
transfer of knowledge
examples: The study placed a domain test (surface, independent), concept maps (surface, connected), transfer test (deep, independent), and essay (deep, connected) in a 2x2 operationalisation (Table 1)
key_sources: Joep van der Graaf, Lyn Lim, Yizhou Fan, Jonathan Kilgour, Johanna Moore, Dragan Gašević, Maria Bannert, Inge Molenaar. (2022). The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09308-9

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition
citation: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x
title: Structure-mapping theory of analogical transfer applied to metacognitive skill transfer in self-regulated learning
description: The article applies Gentner's structure-mapping theory of analogical transfer to self-regulated learning, distinguishing the source problem from the target problem and four steps of analogical transfer including retrieval and mapping. It states that "Retrieval is primarily influenced by surface similarity" while "Deep structure similarity is determined during the mapping process," and uses this distinction to define near versus far transfer of metacognitive skills between learning tasks.
requirements: A source task and a target task whose surface and deep structure similarity can be distinguished, so that transfer distance can be classified
constraints: The article notes the term transfer is inconsistently defined and that it specifically adopts the analogical transfer perspective rather than actor-oriented or situated perspectives
target_learners: fifth-grade students in secondary school
target_learning_goals: transfer of metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluating, regulating) across learning tasks and domains
examples: The article illustrates near transfer with a chemistry text and a history text both processed by text highlighting, and far transfer with a chemistry reading task versus a chemistry experiment
key_sources: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x

article_title: Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice
citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Structural belonging: institutions embed belonging or its absence in policies and routine practices
description: Structural belonging is the author's term for how institutions embed belonging—or its absence—into policies, rules, and routine practices. The article states: 'Structural belonging is the term I use to capture how institutions embed belonging—or its absence—into their policies, rules, and routine practices. It draws attention to the fact that campuses script inclusion and exclusion through their design, making clear that belonging isn't just emotional or interpersonal but tied to institutional structure.' It operates at the exosystem level through institutional rules and at the macrosystem level through cultural logics determining whose identities are recognized as legitimate.
requirements: Analysis of supposedly neutral policies (credit hour requirements, dependency definitions, promotion standards) for differential advantage
constraints: Concept introduced in this essay as an extension of Johnson (2022); empirical operationalization is not provided in the text
target_learners: higher education students, particularly those marginalized by institutional policy design
target_learning_goals: recognizing how institutional structure, not only interpersonal climate, produces inclusion and exclusion
examples: Grading practices, financial aid rules, and codes of conduct encode macrosystem ideologies such as meritocracy and neutrality
key_sources: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5

article_title: The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children’s Cognition
citation: Herold, F., Ludyga, S., Mavilidi, M. F., Benzing, V., Vazou, S., Tomporowski, P. D., & Pesce, C. (2025). The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children's Cognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10031-5
title: Structured day hypothesis
description: The structured day hypothesis proposes that in children, days that are preplanned, segmented, and supervised by an adult are associated with healthier movement behaviors, whereas unstructured days are not. As the article states, it "proposes that, in children, a less structured day that is not preplanned, segmented, and supervised by an adult is often associated with unhealthy behaviors such as less physical activity, and more sedentary behavior including screen time". The authors use it to explain why the loosely structured summer break produces reduced physical activity, and propose it as a framework for studying cognitive and academic outcomes during that period.
requirements: Predictions apply to children's days that vary in adult-imposed structure, segmentation, and supervision
constraints: The article notes the hypothesis's predictions have not been tested using cognitive and academic outcomes
target_learners: school-aged children
target_learning_goals: understanding how day structure relates to physical activity, sedentary behavior, and academic performance
examples: The article applies the hypothesis to the summer break, where days are loosely structured and children show less physical activity and more sedentary behavior
key_sources: Herold, F., Ludyga, S., Mavilidi, M. F., Benzing, V., Vazou, S., Tomporowski, P. D., & Pesce, C. (2025). The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children's Cognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10031-5

article_title: How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement
citation: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09724-6
title: Three structural causal models of the self-concept–achievement reciprocal relationship, differing in lag-2 paths and confounders
description: The article derives a taxonomy of three structural causal models for the reciprocal effects model: "(a) a model with prior scores predicting post scores; (b) a model with additional lag-2 effects ... also referred to as a full-forward model; and (c) a model with lag-2 effects and additional confounders". Model (a) assumes no hidden confounders or carry-over effects and is judged unrealistic; model (c), including time-invariant and time-varying confounders such as gender or school track, "seems to be most realistic". The taxonomy determines which statistical model can identify causal effects.
requirements: If model (c) holds, confounders must be controlled for; otherwise CLPM and FF-CLPM coefficients are biased due to unconsidered confounders.
constraints: The article states model (a) is very (and probably overly) restrictive and seems unrealistic in the context of the REM.
target_learners: lower secondary school students
target_learning_goals: causal modeling of self-concept and achievement
key_sources: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09724-6

article_title: Beyond the “Wow” Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making
citation: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x
title: Framework for student-focused GenAI educational applications that prompt generative learning activities and use GLA products as formative assessment
description: The article proposes a framework for developing student-focused GenAI educational applications grounded in generative learning theory and the select-integrate-organize framework, in which "interaction is initiated by a) the learner, b) the AIEd system, and c) the instructor." Because many learners do not spontaneously engage in sense-making, the system can systematically prompt generative learning activities and "use the quality of these products as formative assessments to inform further adjustments of learning materials and GLA support." The framework adopts an augmentation perspective in which AI complements human intelligence, and it distinguishes GenAI tools designed for students from tools merely used by students, following the Holmes and Tuomi taxonomy.
requirements: The GenAI system must be able to prompt learners who do not automatically initiate sense-making and to assess the quality of their GLA products to adapt subsequent support
constraints: The article states it is not proposing that GenAI is necessary or, in its current technological iteration, optimal for progressing from explicit instruction through scaffolded practice to independent practice
target_learners: university students in an authentic cognitive psychology course
high school psychology students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of course content
generative sense-making during lessons
examples: ChatTutor operationalizes the framework by prompting students to engage in the GLA of teaching with scaffolded feedback and by referencing course slides when generating replies
key_sources: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Three core concepts organizing introductory statistics: statistical model, distribution, and randomness
description: In their introductory statistics textbook the authors selected three core concepts to organize the domain: statistical model (captured as DATA = MODEL + ERROR), distribution (following Wild, "the pattern of variation in a variable", including the sample data, data generating process, and sampling distributions of the distribution triad), and randomness as a data generating process. They state: "we chose to focus our textbook around three core concepts: statistical model, distribution, and randomness." Concepts were chosen for being connectable throughout the course, accessible to novices, not needing later unlearning, and jointly supporting coherent understanding.
requirements: Core concepts must be accessible to novices within their zone of proximal development
Concepts must not need to be unlearned later and must form a coherent whole without introducing misconceptions
constraints: Concepts introduced to novices are almost always simplified in complex domains, and the authors warn against simplification that yields a collection of concepts failing to form a coherent whole
target_learners: Novice students in introductory statistics at the college level
target_learning_goals: Coherent conceptual understanding of statistics that transfers to advanced courses and data analysis practice
examples: The mean is introduced as the simplest statistical model; standard deviation quantifies error around model predictions; ANOVA and regression are both taught as examples of linear models.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Five key representations for introductory statistics: verbal descriptions, visualizations, word equations, GLM notation, and R code
description: The textbook asks students to repeatedly translate and connect among five representations: "verbal descriptions, visualizations, word equations, GLM (general linear model) notation, and R code." Students describe models in words, write word equations (e.g., Thumb Length = Height + other stuff), map them to DATA = MODEL + ERROR, write R code, and learn GLM notation, which the authors value for its generalizability, alignability with other representations, and ecological validity. Algebra was deliberately excluded because students do not find it accessible or useful.
requirements: Selected representations must be accessible to novices, important for the field, and productive for making connections
Learning a representational system requires an investment of time and effort, so the set must be limited
constraints: GLM notation is described as a difficult representational system for students to learn
target_learners: Novice college students in introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: Using and connecting multiple representations of statistical models
Participating in computational, reproducible data analysis practices
examples: Students fit a regression model in R, save predictions into the data frame, plot predictions against the explanatory variable, and explain why predictions coincide with a regression line while data points do not.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: “Valued” Thinking in Education: Liberating the Narrative
citation: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0
title: Standpoint epistemology: knowledge stems from socially situated positions and meaning making is value-laden and subjective
description: Standpoint epistemology is one of two theoretical perspectives the article overviews as liberating prevailing epistemic notions of valued thinking. Its unifying premise, as the article states, is that "knowledge stems from socially situated positions and that the process of meaning making is value-laden and subjective." The perspective centers the social and political realms in meaning making and liberates non-traditional epistemic notions within the narrative of valued thinking.
requirements: Within this perspective, scientists collaborate with local knowers who have firsthand, often minoritized, experiences
constraints: The article presents it as a theoretical perspective overviewed humbly, not as an empirically tested model
target_learners: educational psychology researchers and theorists
target_learning_goals: broadening conceptions of knowing and reasoning beyond narrow epistemological justification
key_sources: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0

article_title: Stressors and Turning Points in High School and Dropout
citation: Dupéré, V., Leventhal, T., Dion, E., Crosnoe, R., Archambault, I., & Janosz, M. (2014). Stressors and Turning Points in High School and Dropout: A Stress Process, Life Course Framework. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Stressors+and+Turning+Points+in+High+School+and+Dropout
title: Stress process, life course model of dropout
description: The article proposes an integrative theoretical formulation bridging major dropout theories with the stress process and life course perspectives. The stress process component details how "individuals respond to new stressors emerging in their lives differently, depending on the nature of the stressors as well as on their personal and social resources"; the life course component treats dropout trajectories as structured by turning points, timing, and wider historical, geographical, and socioeconomic contexts. The model assigns a clear role to proximal precipitating stressors while acknowledging enduring risk factors, including stress proliferation, resource moderation, and vulnerability-stress dynamics.
requirements: Research designs capable of capturing events occurring in the months or weeks before dropout, not only distal risks measured years earlier
constraints: The article notes integrative stress process, life course models had mainly been applied to health outcomes among older adults and remained to be extended to other domains and developmental periods
target_learners: high school students at risk of dropping out
adolescents from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: school perseverance and completion of secondary education
examples: The model explains, for example, how parental divorce may curb perseverance when combined with income loss, residential mobility, and social isolation in a new school
key_sources: Dupéré, V., Leventhal, T., Dion, E., Crosnoe, R., Archambault, I., & Janosz, M. (2014). Stressors and Turning Points in High School and Dropout: A Stress Process, Life Course Framework. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Stressors+and+Turning+Points+in+High+School+and+Dropout

article_title: A Meta-analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning
citation: Murray, E., Horner, A. J., & Göbel, S. M. (2023). A Meta-analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning. https://osf.io/
title: Study-phase retrieval hypothesis as an explanation for the smaller spacing effect in course-embedded settings
description: The article invokes the study-phase retrieval hypothesis, under which a key mechanism of the spacing effect is the retrieval of the initial study phase. It proposes that in course settings, where students work in classrooms or on homework, learners may have prior material or notes accessible during practice, so they "may not have to retrieve the original memory, instead relying on external guides", reducing the spacing benefit. The authors use this to explain why the course-embedded effect was numerically smaller, while noting it is difficult to know the extent to which participants actually used such materials.
requirements: For the mechanism to operate as described, learners must actually be prompted to recall the required information rather than access external guides during practice.
constraints: The article states it is difficult to understand to what extent participants made use of accessible materials, so whether retrieval occurred could not be coded accurately.
target_learners: Students learning mathematics in classroom courses or via homework, from primary school to university
target_learning_goals: Retention of mathematics material (procedures, facts, concepts) on delayed post-tests
examples: The article quotes Nazari & Ebersbach (2019) and Emeny et al. (2021) describing practice conditions in which students had access to summary sheets or their own prior written work during practice sessions.
key_sources: Murray, E., Horner, A. J., & Göbel, S. M. (2023). A Meta-analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning. https://osf.io/

article_title: Four Decades After the Big-Fish–Little-Pond Effect: Critical Boundary Tests and Integrative Models of Mean-Context, Ordinal-Standing, and Distributional-Scaling in 46 Countries
citation: Herbert W. Marsh. (2026). Four Decades After the Big-Fish–Little-Pond Effect: Critical Boundary Tests and Integrative Models of Mean-Context, Ordinal-Standing, and Distributional-Scaling in 46 Countries. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10200-0
title: The Statistical–Mechanism Gap Fallacy: statistical contextual indicators are not psychologically transparent mechanisms
description: The article names and defines the Statistical–Mechanism Gap Fallacy as "the tendency to collapse the gap between statistical indicators and the psychological, social, or cognitive mechanisms they are presumed to represent". Contextual means, ordinal ranks, and dispersion statistics are treated as "partially overlapping statistical representations of socially experienced comparison environments rather than as isolated psychological mechanisms". The framing motivates modeling mean, rank, and dispersion jointly rather than assuming any single statistic uniquely represents the comparison process.
requirements: Analyses must model contextual means, ordinal standing, and dispersion jointly so their distinct and overlapping contributions can be evaluated without assuming any single statistic uniquely represents the comparison process.
constraints: The issue is not whether students consciously compute classroom means, percentile ranks, or formal distributional statistics; the indicators are representations of evaluative environments, not the mechanisms themselves.
target_learners: Grade 8 mathematics students in cross-national assessments
target_learning_goals: Academic self-concept formation through social comparison in classrooms
examples: The study models contextual means, ordinal standing, and classroom dispersion jointly in TIMSS 2019 data rather than treating any one indicator as the mechanism.
key_sources: Herbert W. Marsh. (2026). Four Decades After the Big-Fish–Little-Pond Effect: Critical Boundary Tests and Integrative Models of Mean-Context, Ordinal-Standing, and Distributional-Scaling in 46 Countries. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10200-0

article_title: From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research
citation: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1
title: First field-specific structural variable map of STEM education interventions
description: As the toolkit's first stage, the authors "catalogued every co-occurrence of intervention, moderator, and outcome variables in the corpus, generating, to our knowledge, the first field-specific structural variable map of STEM education interventions." Coding across four layers (STEM domain, outcome, intervention, moderator theme) used iterative constant-comparative procedures until theoretical saturation, visualized as an alluvial (Sankey) diagram. The map shows moderator attention is heavily asymmetric: intervention specifications accounted for 41.61% of all moderators and sample/context variables for 23.36%, while study design/quality (10.70%), disciplinary focus (13.55%), and publication metadata (10.81%) received less attention; mathematics dominated the corpus at 49.91% of effect sizes.
requirements: Qualitative coding of interventions, moderators, and outcomes across the literature before quantitative modeling
constraints: The map reflects the 2000–2023 corpus of STEM intervention meta-analyses screened from four databases
target_learners: STEM education meta-researchers
review authors planning moderator assessments
target_learning_goals: Auditable moderator selection grounded in the evidence base
Preregisterable, theory-driven moderator sets
examples: The ten most common intervention–moderator–outcome triads accounted for 1,056 of 1,786 effect sizes (59.12%), led by instructional models with intervention-specification moderators and academic outcomes
key_sources: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1

article_title: The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects
citation: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1
title: Use the state-trait distinction to treat momentary and enduring curiosity and interest in conceptually parallel ways
description: The article recommends applying the state-trait distinction to both curiosity and interest instead of the situational/individual terminology used for interest. State and trait terms denote temporal specificity, align with the general psychological literature, and make it possible to discuss curiosity and interest in conceptually parallel ways. Trait denotes habitual patterns and does not imply genetic predisposition or immutability.
requirements: Trait is used as a descriptive category denoting habitual patterns of thought, affect, and action, not implying genetic predisposition
constraints: The article notes an asymmetry: trait curiosity is broad-situational while trait interest is re-engagement with specific contents; it remains open whether this asymmetry should be reduced
target_learners: students across educational settings
target_learning_goals: measurement and conceptual clarity about curiosity and interest
examples: The article proposes domain-specific trait curiosity and domain-general trait interest as constructs aligned with the common-core definitions
key_sources: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1

article_title: One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education
citation: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7
title: Structure-mapping theory's four domain-general processes as a framework for analyzing learning from multiple external representations
description: The article proposes theories of analogical and relational reasoning, especially structure-mapping theory, as a framework for examining how combinations of external representations trigger learning processes. It states that "Structure-mapping theory postulates four basic, domain-general processes: abstraction, re-representation, inference projection, and difference detection." Abstraction extracts a schema capturing commonalities across representations; re-representation changes an internal representation when a novel example does not fit; inference projection generates inferences from a well-understood to a less well-understood concept; difference detection distinguishes superficially similar but conceptually distinct representations. The authors use these processes to predict how MER combinations influence knowledge development.
requirements: A unified framework is needed to systematically examine cognitive aspects of learning from MERs
constraints: The authors note other processes may be involved; the four-process collection is offered as a parsimonious model
target_learners: students in mathematics and natural science education
target_learning_goals: understanding how combinations of external representations trigger learning processes
key_sources: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7

article_title: Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2
title: Provision of structure as a three-theme instructional construct (guidance, expectations, encouragement)
description: The review synthesizes how studies conceptualize provision of structure as strategies teachers use to foster students' understanding of course materials and sense of competency. Three key themes emerged: "Offer guidance, provide and clarify expectations, and encourage students." The most common components were "offering guidance, clarifying expectations, giving informational feedback, and offering encouragement", with additional components including consistent behavior, adjusting instruction to ability level, learning strategies, and explaining consequences of rule-breaking. Definitions of components such as informational feedback vary across studies.
requirements: Instructional strategies must be identifiable as guidance, expectation clarification, or encouragement to map onto the taxonomy
constraints: Components are inconsistently defined across studies; encouragement overlaps with positive feedback, and ambiguity may cause unclear teacher application
target_learners: K-12 and post-secondary students
target_learning_goals: sense of competence
academic engagement
understanding of course materials
examples: Offer guidance was referenced by 95 studies; provide and clarify expectations by 61; encourage by 32 (Table 3)
key_sources: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2

article_title: How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning
citation: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4
title: Use stop light colors rather than value-suppressing geometric contrast to visualize uncertainty in multimedia learning materials
description: The article recommends stop light colors as the uncertainty visualization style for learning materials because they support dual coding of uncertainty information. The authors state that stop light colors "should be easier to comprehend, discriminate, and transfer, thus being better for dual coding and therefore for the learning of uncertainty information compared to geometric contrast." The experiment's results on memory of uncertainty values and uncertain-element appearance are consistent with this recommendation, and the article closes by giving recommendations for designing learning material including uncertainty visualizations.
requirements: Learners must be introduced to the meaning of the color code, as done via an explanatory text and manipulation check in the study
constraints: Geometric contrast was superior for memory of the appearance of certain elements, so the recommendation is limited to learning uncertainty information
target_learners: Adult learners and students without background in the subject domain
target_learning_goals: Remembering uncertainty values and the appearance of uncertain content elements
examples: In the experiment, uncertain elements were colored red, medium yellow, and certain green in the stop light condition, versus coarse-to-fine geometric detail in the geometric contrast condition
key_sources: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4

article_title: Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships
citation: Jantine L. Spilt, Helma M. Y. Koomen, & Jochem T. Thijs. (2011). Teacher Wellbeing: The Importance of Teacher–Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9170-y
title: Student–Teacher Relationship Scale (STRS) measuring conflict, closeness, and dependency
description: The review describes the Student–Teacher Relationship Scale as a widely used and well-validated teacher-report questionnaire measuring perceptions of conflict, closeness, and sometimes dependency in relationships with specific children from preschool to upper elementary school. Conflict items include "Dealing with this child drains my energy"; closeness items include "My interactions with this child make me feel effective and confident." The review notes teachers' reports of relationship quality are unique predictors of children's school functioning above direct reports of student behavior, supporting their validity, though some researchers have questioned the validity of the dependency subscale.
requirements: Relies on teacher self-report perceptions of the dyadic relationship rather than observed behavior
constraints: Some researchers have questioned the validity of the dependency subscale, arguing it may be a marker of child adjustment problems rather than a relational dimension
target_learners: teachers of children from preschool to upper elementary school
target_learning_goals: measuring teacher-perceived relationship quality with individual students

article_title: Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students’ Cognitive Performance: a Review
citation: Lucia Mason, Angelica Ronconi, Sara Scrimin, Francesca Pazzaglia. (2022). Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students' Cognitive Performance: a Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09631-8
title: Stress Reduction Theory: nature sustains physiological stress recovery
description: Stress reduction theory (SRT; Ulrich, 1981; Ulrich et al., 1991) explains the salutary effects of nature on emotional functioning. According to SRT, exposure to nature sustains stress recovery as physiological parameters indicate, for example, reduction in blood pressure and stress hormone. Natural environments have restorative power because of the role they played during human evolution, activating the parasympathetic nervous system and reducing physiological arousal. The review pairs SRT with ART, noting the two theories are not incompatible: mental fatigue drives restoration for ART, physiological stress for SRT.
requirements: Contact with a natural environment after a stress-inducing or arousal-raising situation
constraints: SRT addresses emotional and physiological restoration, whereas ART addresses cognitive restoration of directed attention
target_learners: students at all educational levels
target_learning_goals: stress recovery and wellbeing supporting cognitive functioning
key_sources: Lucia Mason, Angelica Ronconi, Sara Scrimin, Francesca Pazzaglia. (2022). Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students' Cognitive Performance: a Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09631-8

article_title: Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods
citation: Jason C. Chow · Ruben G. Martinez. (2026). Community and Participatory Evidence and Research Synthesis: Enhancing Alignment and Usability of Research Synthesis Methods. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10152-5
title: Select and engage community members through structured, documented partner-selection processes
description: CAPERS recommends "a structured approach to partner selection and engagement that includes (a) mapping relevant community groups, (b) establishing clear engagement structures and expectations, (c) iteratively evaluating the composition of the group, and (d) documenting recruitment and decision-making processes." Teams should designate whether members are research participants or co-production partners, with implications for IRB oversight, and include individuals representing multiple roles: deliverers, receivers, indirectly impacted people, policy/legal experts, and methodological experts.
requirements: Early communication of engagement length, intensity, roles, and compensation; a decision-tracking system recording who was invited, participated, or declined
constraints: Composition should be revisited iteratively so important perspectives are not underrepresented as the project progresses
target_learners: Synthesis research teams
target_learning_goals: Ensure equitable representation and transparent, credible community engagement in synthesis
examples: Recruitment pathways include existing partnerships, professional organizations, open online recruitment, and community engagement studios for focused consultation

article_title: Study Demands–Resources Theory: Understanding Student Well-Being in Higher Education
citation: Arnold B. Bakker, Karina Mostert. (2024). Study Demands–Resources Theory: Understanding Student Well-Being in Higher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09940-8
title: Study Demands–Resources (SD–R) theory explains student burnout and engagement through demands, resources, behaviors, and feedback loops
description: SD–R theory is an explanatory framework for student well-being in higher education, built on the Job Demands–Resources model. It holds that "higher education students’ experiences can be categorized as being demanding or resourceful", that study demands and resources instigate a health impairment process and a motivational process, and that study environments trigger either reactive maladaptive behaviors or proactive adaptive behaviors. The theory includes feedback loops and is graphically depicted in the article's Fig. 1.
requirements: Study environment features must be classifiable as either a study demand or a study resource
constraints: Developed for the higher education context, although the article notes it may also be relevant for other educational contexts such as primary school and high school
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: student well-being (burnout and engagement)
academic engagement and performance
examples: The article aligns empirical evidence from existing SD–R models (e.g., Lesener et al., 2020; Salmela-Aro et al., 2022) with recent JD–R theory developments

article_title: Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading
citation: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z
title: Script Theory of Guidance (SToG): interplay of internal and external collaboration scripts with hierarchical components
description: SToG explains how external and internal scripts interplay during collaborative learning. Internal scripts are prior procedural knowledge structured from repeated experiences; external scripts are supports embedded in the environment that "activate existing internal scripts or help create new internal scripts". Knowledge of a CABLe practice "consists of a set of somewhat hierarchical components including plays, scenes, scriptlets, and roles", which this article applies to argumentation rather than collaboration as such.
requirements: External scripts are effective only when they trigger an accompanying specific constellation of internal script components, or do not conflict with or duplicate them
constraints: The article applies SToG to argumentation in CABLe settings rather than collaboration generally
Internal argumentative scripts vary among individuals and are not fixed across situations
target_learners: learners engaged in collaborative argumentation-based learning, from primary school to university
target_learning_goals: argumentation competence
collaborative knowledge co-construction
examples: The article uses SToG components to specify when feedback authoring tools should send reminder versus direct instructions during CABLe
