article_title: Student Burnout and Educational Dropout: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Dropout Behavior and Intentions
citation: Daniel J. Madigan, Hanna L. Glandorf. (2026). Student Burnout and Educational Dropout: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Dropout Behavior and Intentions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10191-y
title: Study Demands-Resources theory as an account of how student burnout develops and leads to dropout
description: The review adopts Study Demands-Resources Theory (Bakker & Mostert, 2024) as its organizing explanatory framework. It posits that "student burnout is primarily the consequence of an imbalance between study demands and resources": high demands (workload, time pressures, cognitive complexity) deplete energy and produce exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced efficacy, while resources (social support, feedback, autonomy) buffer demands. Burnout also drives self-undermining behaviors such as procrastination, creating a loss spiral, and acts as a mediator between study demands and negative academic outcomes including dropout.
requirements: Requires measurement of both study demands and study resources to model burnout development as the theory specifies
constraints: The article notes few theoretical models of student burnout exist and further work is necessary to integrate and test theory, including examining possible mechanisms underpinning these relationships
target_learners: students in post-compulsory education (secondary, undergraduate, postgraduate)
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing educational dropout risk via burnout
examples: The review draws on stress theory and self-efficacy/expectancy-value theory to explain how exhaustion and cynicism reinforce avoidant coping and withdrawal, while reduced efficacy undermines motivation
key_sources: Daniel J. Madigan, Hanna L. Glandorf. (2026). Student Burnout and Educational Dropout: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Dropout Behavior and Intentions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10191-y

article_title: Individual and Structural Factors Associated with Interactive Skills of Child-Care Professionals in Early Childhood Education and Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: Støve, L. L., Dalgaard, N. T., Mohr, J. W., Hansen, J. E., Wendelboe, K. I., Hestbaek, E., Vieira, C. C., Væver, M. S., & Smith-Nielsen, J. (2026). Individual and Structural Factors Associated with Interactive Skills of Child-Care Professionals in Early Childhood Education and Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10162-3
title: Structure-Process-Outcome and Person-Process-Context-Time models as the review's organizing framework for caregiver interactive skills
description: The review organizes factors associated with caregiver interactive skills within two frameworks. The Structure-Process-Outcome model "proposes that structural characteristics of care settings (e.g., group sizes, child-caregiver ratios) create the conditions in which caregivers operate," with process quality (caregiver-child interactions) as the proximal mechanism linking structure to child outcomes. The Person-Process-Context-Time model extends this by "emphasizing the dynamic interplay between individual and contextual characteristics over time in shaping interaction quality." The review uses this integrative lens to situate structural and individual correlates in one conceptual framework.
requirements: Studies must assess interactive skills at the individual caregiver level for the framework's individual-level correlates to be disentangled
constraints: The framework is applied to formal ECEC settings for children up to 6.0 years
target_learners: Child-care professionals working with children aged 0–6 years in formal ECEC settings
target_learning_goals: Improving quality of caregiver-child interactions (responsiveness, sensitivity, developmental stimulation)
examples: The review interprets stronger negative ratio and group-size effects in higher-quality studies through a PPCT lens, suggesting contextual systems jointly shape proximal interactions

article_title: Yes Children Need to Learn Their GPCs but There Really Is Little or No Evidence that Systematic or Explicit Phonics Is Effective: a response to Fletcher, Savage, and Sharon (2020)
citation: Jeffrey S. Bowers. (2021). Yes Children Need to Learn Their GPCs but There Really Is Little or No Evidence that Systematic or Explicit Phonics Is Effective: a response to Fletcher, Savage, and Sharon (2020). Educational Psychology Review (2021) 33:1965–1979. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09602-z
title: Structured Word Inquiry (SWI): teaching GPCs within morphology from the start, rejecting the 'phonology first' assumption
description: Structured Word Inquiry is an approach to reading instruction that explicitly teaches grapheme-phoneme correspondences together with morphology, etymology, spelling, and vocabulary from the start, rather than teaching letter-sound correspondences first in isolation. As the article states, "Structured Word Inquiry (SWI) teaches GPCs in the context of morphology in an attempt to teach GPCs more effectively." It uses tools such as word sums and morphological matrices to highlight consistent spelling-meaning connections in morphological families — for example, showing that the spelling of <do> is preserved in <does>, <doing>, and <done>, making sense of spellings phonics treats as exceptions. SWI can be used at any stage of reading instruction, unlike phonics, which is ideally finished after grade 2 or 3.
requirements: Instruction must teach phonological and semantic regularities of English spellings together from the start, because they interact in ways that make sense of GPCs
constraints: The article states the SWI approach needs more empirical support, and more work is needed on implementing SWI at larger scale given many concepts are unfamiliar to teachers
target_learners: children in the early stages of learning to read (grade 1–2 in the cited preliminary studies)
target_learning_goals: reading
spelling
vocabulary
knowledge of grapheme-phoneme correspondences and morphological structure of English spellings
examples: A SWI lesson on <does> begins with the meanings of <does> and <do> in spoken sentences, then uses word sums and morphological matrices to show the spelling of <do> is preserved in <does>, <doing>, and <done>

article_title: Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades
citation: Chen, X., Zhou, Z., & Padilla, A. M. (2026). Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10092-6
title: Stereotype threat and social cognitive theory as explanatory accounts of the male disadvantage in L2 learning
description: The article explains the female advantage in L2 achievement through two named theoretical frameworks. Stereotype threat theory (Steele & Aronson, 1995) holds that when negative stereotypes about a group become obvious in a performance context, members of the stereotyped group are threatened, which lowers task performance. Social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1991, 2011) emphasizes the interaction between personal, environmental, and behavioral factors: when males believe L2 learning is feminized, their self-efficacy weakens, they restrict effort, and achievement falls. The article applies both accounts to the L2 domain, where language learning is often stereotyped as a "female-domain" subject.
requirements: The account presupposes that learners and teachers hold gendered beliefs about language learning as a feminized subject, and that these beliefs are salient in the performance context.
constraints: The article presents these as plausible explanatory mechanisms for the observed gender gap, not as tested predictions within the meta-analysis itself; it also notes that research reporting a female biological verbal advantage was based on very small differences or none.
target_learners: Male and female L2 learners, particularly adolescents in secondary school
target_learning_goals: L2 learning achievement, motivation, self-efficacy, and persistence
examples: The article cites the Chinese context, where L2 learning is believed to be a feminized area of study and males interested in L2 learning may experience criticism or disapproval, as one setting where stereotype threat may operate.
key_sources: Chen, X., Zhou, Z., & Padilla, A. M. (2026). Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10092-6

article_title: Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches
citation: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2
title: Match dialogue structure to the intended LTA goal: low structure for sensemaking, high structure for articulation, dialectic framing for deliberation
description: The review's four study patterns show that instructional framing of argumentative dialogue aligns with the epistemic goal pursued: low-structure framing suits sensemaking, high-structure framing suits articulation and deliberation, and dialectic framing with disagreement as a starting point suits deliberation aimed at integrated arguments. The authors identify "low-structured sensemaking, high-structured articulation, high-structured deliberation, and dialectic deliberation" as the four relationships driving their findings. Designers should choose framing deliberately according to which argumentative gains they target.
requirements: The intended dialogue goal (sensemaking, articulation, or deliberation) must be identified before choosing the framing structure
constraints: The patterns derive from cross-tabulated frequencies in a review of 143 studies, not from a controlled comparison of framings; the authors note outcomes are not defined similarly across studies and methods do not always involve controlled comparison
target_learners: K-16 students in whole-class, small-group, or one-to-one dialogue settings
target_learning_goals: Learning to argue through argumentative dialogue
examples: Pattern 4 studies established disagreement as a necessary starting point and leveraged it to drive gains in counter-argumentation, rebuttals, and argument-counterargument integration
key_sources: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2

article_title: Measuring Children’s Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review
citation: Ritoša, A., Åström, F., Björck, E., Borglund, L., Karlsson, E., McHugh, E., & Nylander, E. (2023). Measuring Children's Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09815-4
title: State–trait temporality as an organizing axis of child engagement conceptualization and measurement in ECEC
description: The review organizes variation in engagement measurement around assumptions about temporality: engagement can be treated as a momentary, transient state of immersion in an activity, assessed by observations and experience sampling, or as a relatively stable tendency to behave in certain ways, assessed by questionnaires about typical behavior. It concludes that "the variations in the observational schedules, such as duration and number of observations in measuring child engagement, reflect a variety in the conceptualizations of child engagement on a state-trait continuum." This axis explains why observation schedules differ so widely across studies.
requirements: Researchers must make their temporal assumptions about engagement explicit when choosing observation duration, frequency, or questionnaire format.
constraints: The review notes conceptualizations do not always match the measurement approach, e.g., few definitions of academic engagement described it as a stable trait despite survey measurement.
target_learners: young children (approximately ages 1–6) attending ECEC settings
target_learning_goals: measuring and understanding children's engagement in learning activities
examples: The review reports 10- or 15-second time sampling in 10-minute observations as the most common time frame, with short observations repeated and averaged to obtain individual engagement scores.

article_title: Preregistration and registered reports
citation: Preregistration and Registered Reports. (2021). https://osf.io/ya594
title: Start preregistrations short and concise, then develop more detail over a research trajectory and for the study's most important parts
description: The article recommends three principles for preregistration in educational psychology: begin with short, concise documents because lower burden increases willingness to write and read them; develop more robust preregistrations as researchers gain familiarity with settings, designs, and analysis plans; and preregister more detail on correspondingly important parts of the study, such as subgroup analyses central to the theory. This follows Duflo et al.'s argument that in field settings, documenting all contingencies rapidly becomes prohibitive.
requirements: Preregistration content should match the maturity of the research line and the importance of specific analyses, with more detail where subgroup effects are predicted and theoretically central
constraints: Thorough pre-analysis plans down to analytic code may be inappropriate for less mature research lines or field settings where flexibility is needed to negotiate access
target_learners: educational psychology researchers
graduate students conducting studies
target_learning_goals: distinguishing confirmatory predictions from exploratory post hoc analyses
preserving the interpretability of null-hypothesis tests
examples: The author's own preregistrations ranged from a short narrative for a planning-prompt study to a complete package including exact analytic code for a MOOC intervention study
key_sources: Preregistration and Registered Reports. (2021). https://osf.io/ya594

article_title: Creative problem solving in primary school students
citation: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823
title: Structured creative problem solving task with vignette-based problem situations and four pre-structured steps
description: The article constructed structured tasks in which students read a short vignette describing an everyday problem (science, social, or entrepreneurial domain) and are "guided through four pre-structured steps of the task": exploring relevant knowledge in a mind map, framing the problem as a question, generating as many different and original ideas as possible in ten minutes, and selecting their three most creative ideas. Six design criteria governed the vignettes, e.g. "The problem situations are open and non-directive, enabling the participant to form his/her own interpretation of the described situation". Three problems were selected by nine-year-old students ranking six candidate situations on complexity, importance, realism, efficacy, and experience.
requirements: Problem descriptions written in short sentences with word choices suitable for children between 9 and 12 years old; problems presented on paper and read aloud
constraints: The three selected problems ranked lowest on complexity but highest on realism, efficacy, and experience per student rankings
target_learners: primary school students in grades 4-6
target_learning_goals: eliciting creative problem solving processes and products across science, social, and entrepreneurial domains
examples: The science problem described Lisa and Tom whose ice cream melted on the way home; the social problem involved Simon being distracted by his friend Julian; the entrepreneurial problem described Aron who wants a new bicycle but owns only a two-euro coin

article_title: Education, not age, linked to narrative comprehension
citation: Markus Huff, Natalia Gagarina, Ekaterina Varkentin, Irina R. Brich. (2025). Education, Not Age, Linked to Narrative Comprehension. https://aspredicted.org/WT9_TK6
title: Structure building framework as an account of codality-general narrative comprehension
description: The article adopts the structure building framework (Gernsbacher) to explain narrative comprehension across codalities. It "postulates three processes for building mental models of a narrative: laying a foundation containing the information within a scene, continually mapping new information onto the preexisting model, and, if new information is largely inconsistent with the current model, shifting to a new foundation." The mapping process draws on bridging inference generation, and the framework underpins the article's hypothesis of a general comprehension skill applying to both written and pictorial narratives.
requirements: Comprehension requires generating bridging inferences to connect explicitly depicted narrative scenes and maintain a coherent mental model held in working memory.
constraints: The article notes the framework's processes may require less effort for pictorial narratives, and that the observed pictorial advantage might instead stem from material difficulty rather than different cognitive processes.
target_learners: adults across the adult age span (18–87 years)
learners across low, middle, and high education levels
target_learning_goals: narrative comprehension via bridging inference generation

citation: Wai, J., Lubinski, D., Benbow, C. P., & Steiger, J. H. (2004). Accomplishment in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) and Its Relation to STEM Educational Dose: A 25-Year Longitudinal Study (Web Supplement). https://scholar.google.com
title: STEM educational dose measure for the graduate student cohort
description: The graduate-student cohort's STEM educational dose was scored from five components: "college courses while in high school, AP or other courses for college credit, science fair/math competitions, special classes, and research" (Table S3 note). Dose levels ranged 0-5, with the median at level 2 for males plus females (181 participants), males (82), and females (99); 150 participants had dose 0.
requirements: Dose scoring requires records of pre-college STEM enrichment such as AP courses, competitions, special classes, and research experiences
constraints: Dose levels for the graduate cohort span only 0-5, unlike the 0-10 range for talent-search cohorts
target_learners: high-ability graduate students identified in adolescence via talent search
target_learning_goals: STEM educational enrichment and acceleration leading to STEM career outcomes
examples: Table S3 reports dose distributions separately for males (median 2, n 82) and females (median 2, n 99) as well as combined

article_title: The measurement of efficiency in spelling and the overlapping of grades in combined measurements of reading, writing and spelling.
citation: Starch, D. (1910). The Measurement of Efficiency in Spelling, and the Overlapping of Grades in Combined Measurements of Reading, Writing and Spelling. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Measurement+of+Efficiency+in+Spelling
title: Starch's 600-word dictionary-sampled spelling test in six comparable 100-word lists
description: A spelling test constructed by taking the first defined word on every even-numbered page of Webster's New International Dictionary (1910 edition), yielding 1186 words, then discarding technical, scientific and obsolete words to leave 600 words arranged by length and divided into six 100-word lists by systematic rotation. The author states the method "would give a random sampling of the entire non-technical English vocabulary" and that the lists can be duplicated by anyone else. Scoring is by counting words correct, each list of 100 making the score also a percentage.
requirements: Administered as a dictated test with words pronounced clearly but not phonetically, each grade tested twice on two successive days with two different lists
Grade-specific list lengths: first 40 words in grade 1, 65 in grade 2, 80 in grade 3, and the full list in higher grades
constraints: The author notes the standard scores are probably not quite as reliable as those for reading and writing because they are based on a smaller number of tests
target_learners: Elementary school pupils in grades 1 through 8
target_learning_goals: Measuring spelling ability and attainment
examples: The full six lists of 100 words each are printed in the article, from 'add' and 'but' up to 'ineffectually' and 'irresponsibility'
key_sources: Starch, D. (1910). The Measurement of Efficiency in Spelling, and the Overlapping of Grades in Combined Measurements of Reading, Writing and Spelling. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Measurement+of+Efficiency+in+Spelling

article_title: Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning.
citation: van den Broek, G., Gerritsen, S. L., Oomen, I. T. J., Velthoven, E., van Boxtel, F. H. J., Kester, L., & van Gog, T. (2023). Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000810
title: Stepwise MCQ: a multiple-choice item that presents the question word for 4 s before the answer options appear
description: A stepwise MCQ is a modified multiple-choice item for vocabulary retrieval practice in which the question is presented before the answer options, creating an opportunity for cued recall. As the article describes the manipulation, "in stepwise MCQs, it was shown for 4 s before the translations appeared", whereas in standard MCQs a word was presented with three possible translations simultaneously. The element was tested against standard MCQs in one classroom and three online experiments.
requirements: The question must be displayed before the answer options (a 4 s delay in the reported experiments) so learners can attempt cued recall.
constraints: The retention benefit did not appear in one of the four experiments and was most robust for noncompetitive answer options.
target_learners: school students in the classroom experiment
adult online participants
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning (word-translation retention)
examples: In the reported experiments, a vocabulary word was shown for 4 s before its three possible translations appeared, and learners practiced with either standard or stepwise MCQs.
key_sources: van den Broek, G., Gerritsen, S. L., Oomen, I. T. J., Velthoven, E., van Boxtel, F. H. J., Kester, L., & van Gog, T. (2023). Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000810

article_title: Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning.
citation: van den Broek, G., Gerritsen, S. L., Oomen, I. T. J., Velthoven, E., van Boxtel, F. H. J., Kester, L., & van Gog, T. (2023). Optimizing multiple-choice questions for retrieval practice: Delayed display of answer alternatives enhances vocabulary learning. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000810
title: Use a stepwise display in MCQ-based retrieval practice: present the question before the answer options to create a cued-recall opportunity.
description: Because retrieval during MCQ practice may not always occur, for example with easy-to-guess answers, the article recommends presenting the question before the options: "a stepwise display, which presents the question before the answer options. This creates an opportunity for cued recall." The authors conclude that "a stepwise display is a promising and easy-to-implement manipulation to optimize MCQs for retrieval practice."
requirements: MCQ practice in which learners might otherwise guess without retrieving; the delay must give learners a chance to attempt retrieval from memory.
constraints: The benefit was most robust for noncompetitive answer options and for learners who reported actually retrieving during the delay; it did not appear in one of the four experiments.
target_learners: vocabulary learners in classrooms and online settings
target_learning_goals: delayed retention of vocabulary
examples: The experiments implemented the stepwise display by showing the word for 4 s before the translations appeared, in a classroom study and three online studies.

article_title: Disparity between Intelligence and Scholarship.
citation: Stone, Charles Leonard. (1924). Disparity Between Intelligence and Scholarship. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: A four-part test battery measuring tension, perseverance, environmental assimilation, and aggression
description: The article describes a battery administered to 87 summoned students to probe factors behind intelligence–scholarship discrepancy. It included "a modification of the Downey will-profile test" in which a phrase was written at normal, rapid, and slow rates to yield tension and perseverance quotients; an abbreviated Rosanoff, Martin, and Rosanoff High Standard Frequency Test scored by agreement with responses of 100 eminent men of science; and three story-based deletion tests for fear, sex, and aggression, with the aggression time divided by total time of the three tests.
requirements: Requires subjects able to write at normal, rapid, and slow rates for the Downey-derived quotients
Requires the normative response distribution of a group of 100 eminent men of science for scoring the frequency test
constraints: The aggression timing measure's intended arousal effects were reportedly not achieved according to subjects' introspections
target_learners: male college students (Dartmouth class of 1924)
target_learning_goals: measuring non-intellective factors related to the disparity between intelligence test performance and scholarship grades
examples: 87 of 98 summoned men took the tests; the discrepancy group comprised students with discrepancies of 50 per cent or over and the control group 45 men with not over 2 per cent discrepancy.
key_sources: Stone, Charles Leonard. (1924). Disparity Between Intelligence and Scholarship. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org

article_title: A New Book for Teachers of History.
citation: Rugg, E. (1921). New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Standardized history tests should be explained with concrete illustrations of diagnosing individual and class difficulties
description: The reviewer argues that a book's treatment of the movement to standardize tests and examinations in history is more helpful when it tells the teacher in detail how to use the tests. He states that "Illustration of their value in diagnosing individual and class difficulties might well have been included." The recommendation is that test coverage should go beyond description to concrete instructional use in diagnosis.
requirements: Teachers need detailed guidance on how to use standardized history tests, not merely notice of the standardization movement.
target_learners: junior and senior high school students
target_learning_goals: diagnosing individual and class difficulties in history learning
examples: The reviewer criticizes the reviewed book for giving only some space to test standardization without detailing how the teacher was to use the tests.
key_sources: Rugg, E. (1921). New Publications in Educational Psychology and Related Fields of Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: Morphology in reading comprehension among school-aged readers of English: A synthesis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling study.
citation: Zhang, D., Ke, S. (E.), & Mo, Y. (2023). Morphology in Reading Comprehension Among School-Aged Readers of English: A Synthesis and Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(5), 683–699. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000797
title: Morphological instruction should include a strong meaning focus, especially for bilingual and older school-aged readers
description: The authors recommend that morphological instruction emphasize meaning-oriented aspects of morphology (morphological problem-solving, meaning inference) rather than only code/form-based decoding. This is because the vocabulary-mediated route (Path 2) was the larger indirect effect in the whole sample and grew stronger with age, and because bilingual readers rely more on vocabulary than on word reading. As stated in the implications: "morphological instruction may need to be differentiated and responsive to children's language status and stage of schooling."
requirements: Instruction should target the specific routes (chunking for decoding, morphological problem-solving for meaning) that are developmentally most relevant to the learner group
constraints: The recommendation is based on correlational MASEM findings, not experimental intervention data
Existing morphological interventions have sometimes shown very small or non-significant effects on reading comprehension, possibly reflecting a lack of direct-effect focus
target_learners: Bilingual/L2 readers of English
Older school-aged readers (upper elementary and middle/high school)
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Vocabulary knowledge
examples: The study found that the indirect effect via vocabulary knowledge (β = .190) exceeded that via word reading (β = .140), and that bilinguals showed a more salient reliance on vocabulary than on word reading for comprehension
key_sources: Zhang, D., Ke, S. (E.), & Mo, Y. (2023). Morphology in Reading Comprehension Among School-Aged Readers of English: A Synthesis and Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(5), 683–699. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000797

article_title: Individual differences in addition strategy choice: A psychometric evaluation.
citation: Rhodes, K. T., Lukowski, S., Branum-Martin, L., Opfer, J., Geary, D. C., & Petrill, S. A. (2018). Individual Differences in Addition Strategy Choice: A Psychometric Evaluation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11360214/
title: Strategy Choice Model: adaptive strategy choice balancing goals, problem demands, and cognitive constraints
description: The SCM holds that "people's adaptive strategy choices require balancing conflicting problem-solving goals (e.g., speed and accuracy) and managing problem-specific demands (e.g., varying levels of problem difficulty) and cognitive constraints (e.g., the ability to retrieve a solution from memory)". Counting builds problem-answer associative strength, eventually yielding retrieval and decomposition strategies. The article evaluates the SCM's central tenet — that solving is a joint function of item difficulty and individual knowledge — and confirms it empirically.
requirements: Evaluation should model strategy variety across problems, mixed item/person effects, and trade-offs such as speed versus accuracy simultaneously
constraints: Most prior SCM evaluations relied on averaging methods that collapse across items or persons and can obscure individual differences
target_learners: children and adolescents learning arithmetic
target_learning_goals: addition strategy choice
development of retrieval-based problem solving
examples: Addition is described as perhaps the best understood domain of strategy development, with counting, min-counting, decomposition, and retrieval as characteristic strategies
key_sources: Rhodes, K. T., Lukowski, S., Branum-Martin, L., Opfer, J., Geary, D. C., & Petrill, S. A. (2018). Individual Differences in Addition Strategy Choice: A Psychometric Evaluation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11360214/

article_title: Problems in the scientific study of the teaching of arithmetic.
citation: Stone, C. W. (1913). Problems in the Scientific Study of the Teaching of Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(1). https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Stone's two-phase framework for determining the subject-matter of arithmetic: a practical-sociological phase and a cultural-psychological phase
description: The article organizes the question of what arithmetic ought to be taught into two phases. As printed: "There are, then, two phases of the question, viz.: the practical one, What Arithmetic is needed in order best to make a living? and the cultural one, What Arithmetic is needed in order to make the best living?" The practical phase is answered from economic and social life, including games and recreation, and asks what minimum of arithmetic all people need and what additional arithmetic each trade or profession requires. The cultural phase concerns mental-discipline values, the stages of child development, and the transferability of discipline within and beyond arithmetic.
requirements: Answers to the practical phase must rest on full knowledge of the values of arithmetic in the economic and other social needs of life
Answers to the cultural phase must rest on full knowledge of the values of arithmetic in the mental aspects of life
constraints: The article states that certain phases of the disciplinary-values problem seem at present impossible of exact solution because psychological and statistical research have not yet developed sufficiently
target_learners: all boys and girls of normal ability in public elementary schools
pupils entering respective trades and professions
target_learning_goals: determining which arithmetic topics merit inclusion in the course of study
examples: The article enumerates seven practical-phase questions, such as what minimum of arithmetic is needed by all people in the economic activities of life, and seven cultural-phase questions, including at what ages developmental stages are reached and to what extent disciplinary values are transferable
key_sources: Stone, C. W. (1913). Problems in the Scientific Study of the Teaching of Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(1). https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Standardized illustrative sentences for the Springfield Spelling List.
citation: David Spence Hill. (1917). Standardized Illustrative Sentences for the Springfield Spelling List. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Standardize the administration procedure of spelling scales, including uniform illustrative sentences, before comparing achievement results
description: The article recommends that testing procedures for standard spelling scales be made uniform, because extemporized illustrative sentences may obscure or delay children's spelling responses and vary across scores of examiners. The author wrote all sentences in advance and urges that "there is considerable room for improvement in the direction of standardizing a procedure for the actual administration of standard spelling scales."
requirements: Examiners must use the same pre-written illustrative sentences for every word on the day of the test
constraints: The article notes it is possible that failure to uniformize sentences is not a very serious defect in contemporary studies
target_learners: Elementary school children in grades 3-8
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of spelling achievement on standardized word lists
examples: The author administered the Springfield list in New Orleans with examiner-pronounced words followed by pre-written illustrative sentences, children writing the word only
key_sources: David Spence Hill. (1917). Standardized Illustrative Sentences for the Springfield Spelling List. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

article_title: Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting
citation: Thiago Cabral, Natália B. Mota, Lucia Fraga, Mauro Copelli, Mark A. McDaniel and Sidarta Ribeiro. (2018). Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0031-z
title: Stage 2 sleep account of post-learning nap benefits for declarative school content
description: The authors interpret their results through sleep-stage composition: morning naps show low slow-wave sleep and consist mostly of Stage 2 and REM sleep. Because the tested material was declarative and involved "rote learning and the association of multiple contents, but not abstract or creative thinking", they conclude "the morning nap beneﬁts were likely related to Stage 2 sleep, not REM sleep", which they link to prior work relating Stage 2 sleep to declarative memory.
requirements: Declarative, rote-style curricular material as tested here; the mechanism is hypothesized, not measured, since no sleep recording was performed
constraints: No actigraphy or EEG was collected, so sleep-stage composition during the study naps was inferred from prior literature rather than observed
target_learners: school-age learners of declarative curricular content
target_learning_goals: declarative memory consolidation after learning
examples: The article states morning naps "are comprised mostly of Stage 2 sleep and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep" and attributes the observed declarative retention gains to the Stage 2 component.
key_sources: Thiago Cabral, Natália B. Mota, Lucia Fraga, Mauro Copelli, Mark A. McDaniel and Sidarta Ribeiro. (2018). Post-class naps boost declarative learning in a naturalistic school setting. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0031-z

article_title: Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication
citation: Koch, S. B. J., Tyborowska, A., Niermann, H. C. M., Cillessen, A. H. N., Roelofs, K., Bašnáková, J., Toni, I., & Stolk, A. (2024). Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication. npj Science of Learning 9, 52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00262-6
title: Dual-contributions framework: stereotypes and interaction-based evidence provide complementary, neuroanatomically and developmentally dissociable contributions to communication
description: The article proposes a summary model (Fig. 3) in which stereotype beliefs and evidence from ongoing social interactions jointly shape communicative adjustment. Stereotypes "provide initial boundaries on mutual understanding," while interaction dynamics moderate how strongly those priors are applied. The two contributions are experimentally visible on a single metric and are independently predicted by right ACCg structural integrity and early-life social exposure, yielding "complementary, yet neuroanatomically and developmentally dissociable, contributions to interpersonal communication."
requirements: A setting where stereotype-driven and interaction-driven behavioral adjustments can be separately quantified on the same behavioral metric
constraints: Demonstrated in a nonverbal communication game minimizing linguistic conventions, with stereotype beliefs manipulated only via presumed partner age
target_learners: adolescents in dyadic communicative interactions
target_learning_goals: adjusting communicative behavior to an interaction partner by integrating prior beliefs with interaction-based evidence
examples: The game dissociated stereotype-driven adjustments (more time in the object square toward the presumed child) from interaction-driven convergence, with the two kinds of variance not accounting for each other.
key_sources: Koch, S. B. J., Tyborowska, A., Niermann, H. C. M., Cillessen, A. H. N., Roelofs, K., Bašnáková, J., Toni, I., & Stolk, A. (2024). Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication. npj Science of Learning 9, 52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00262-6

article_title: A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance
citation: Chen, P., Teo, Q.K., Foo, D.X.Y., Jiang, Y., Sun, L., Ong, X.L., Neo, D., Pereira, D.J.H., Tan, B., Chua, K.Q., Gan, J.X.F. & Ong, D.C. (2025). A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance. npj Science of Learning, 10:74. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00367-6
title: Strategic mindset: a self-prompting orientation toward strategy-eliciting questions
description: A strategic mindset is a psychological orientation in which learners frequently ask themselves questions that prompt access and use of task-appropriate methods, especially when facing difficulty or unproductivity. The article defines it as "an orientation toward asking oneself questions that elicit the access and use of task-appropriate methods." It is conceptually and empirically distinct from both growth mindset of intelligence and general metacognitive strategy use, functioning as a trigger mechanism that converts moments of difficulty into opportunities for strategy generation rather than helpless responses.
requirements: The learner must encounter moments of difficulty or unproductivity that serve as cues to trigger strategy-eliciting self-questioning
constraints: Distinct from a growth mindset of intelligence and from general metacognitive strategy use per prior factor analyses cited in the article
target_learners: Adolescent and adult students in academic settings
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning and effective strategy use during academic tasks
key_sources: Chen, P., Teo, Q.K., Foo, D.X.Y., Jiang, Y., Sun, L., Ong, X.L., Neo, D., Pereira, D.J.H., Tan, B., Chua, K.Q., Gan, J.X.F. & Ong, D.C. (2025). A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance. npj Science of Learning, 10:74. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00367-6

article_title: A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance
citation: Chen, P., Teo, Q.K., Foo, D.X.Y., Jiang, Y., Sun, L., Ong, X.L., Neo, D., Pereira, D.J.H., Tan, B., Chua, K.Q., Gan, J.X.F. & Ong, D.C. (2025). A strategic mindset predicts and promotes effective learning and academic performance. npj Science of Learning, 10:74. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00367-6
title: Online self-administered strategic mindset intervention for secondary school students
description: A scalable, cost-effective online exercise (~40 minutes) that adolescents can self-administer in classrooms. It involves "learning about the common challenges that Secondary school students often face; hearing other students'testimonials about how they had used the strategic mindset psychology to overcome these challenges, to make progress, and to learn better"; reading scientific evidence; identifying personal strategy-eliciting questions; and committing to more effective learning approaches. Crucially, it does not train specific strategies but teaches the value of self-prompting.
requirements: Delivery in a classroom environment with sufficient peer engagement and minimal disruption for fidelity
Students need some existing repertoire of learning strategies to benefit maximally
constraints: Did not include training in specific learning strategies; conveyed via slides rather than videos due to technical limitations in some schools
target_learners: Secondary school students (ages 13–17) in public school classrooms
target_learning_goals: Increasing use of effective learning strategies when studying for exams and improving exam performance
examples: Randomly assigned 1070 Secondary 2–4 students in 77 classes across 6 schools to the strategic mindset exercise or a similarly structured control about co-curricular activities, measuring later strategy use and final exam scores.

article_title: Can cognitive processes help explain the success of instructional techniques recommended by behavior analysts?
citation: Rebecca A. Markovits and Yana Weinstein. (2018). Can cognitive processes help explain the success of instructional techniques recommended by behavior analysts? npj Science of Learning 3:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0018-1
title: Behavior-analytic stimulus control account of response-card learning
description: According to behavior analysis, learning occurs when a stimulus or context requiring a particular response is repeatedly paired with reinforcement of correct responding and non-reinforcement of incorrect responding, so that correctness and fluency increase. The article describes this as the development of "stimulus control": once fluency and mastery are gained, the term itself triggers the correct response, such as giving the correct definition on a test. The article argues this process is promoted by the use of response cards, which structure antecedent–consequence contact during class.
requirements: Repeated presentations of the stimulus with feedback so correct responding is reinforced and incorrect responding is not
Opportunities for active student responding during instruction
constraints: This is the article's account of the mechanism from behavior analysis; the article presents it as an explanation rather than a directly tested result in this manuscript
target_learners: K-12 students
higher education students
target_learning_goals: fluency and accuracy of academic responses such as defining terms
examples: A student given a term to define receives feedback on early errorful attempts; with practice, correctness and fluency increase until the term controls the correct-definition response
key_sources: Rebecca A. Markovits and Yana Weinstein. (2018). Can cognitive processes help explain the success of instructional techniques recommended by behavior analysts? npj Science of Learning 3:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0018-1

article_title: Overemphasizing individual differences and overlooking systemic factors reinforces educational inequality
citation: Zengilowski, A., Maqbool, I., Deka, S. P., Niebaum, J. C., Placido, D., Katz, B., Shah, P. & Munakata, Y. (2023). Overemphasizing individual differences and overlooking systemic factors reinforces educational inequality. npj Science of Learning 8:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00164-z
title: Prioritize structural, community-participatory approaches and research-practice partnerships over individual-only interventions when addressing educational inequality
description: This principle holds that interventions addressing educational inequality should address structural and systemic barriers while ensuring community participation, rather than exporting individual-level trainings as universal solutions. The authors argue "a structural focus or combined approach may be most impactful" and that "communities are reservoirs of knowledge that can be used for supporting human ﬂourishing." They recommend research–practice partnerships that prioritize local knowledge, operationalizing constructs like executive function and well-being in ways reflecting communities' lived realities.
requirements: Programs must address structural issues while ensuring community participation, and operationalize constructs like well-being and executive function in ways that reflect the lived realities of local communities.
constraints: The authors acknowledge debates surrounding the effectiveness or continuity of some exemplary programs and explicitly do not argue for generalizability or universality of these models.
target_learners: Students facing structural and systemic barriers, including minoritized students in the U.S. and marginalized children in South Asia
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
student well-being and social-emotional functioning
reduction of educational inequality
examples: The Child-Parent Center Program combined culturally relevant instruction, parental involvement, smaller classes and health/nutrition changes; Restorative Justice for Oakland Youth shifted a district from punitive policies to restorative practices; Delhi engaged local lay counselors for student mental health; India's Mid-Day Meal Scheme and a Pakistani school lunch program combined nutrition with community engagement.
key_sources: Zengilowski, A., Maqbool, I., Deka, S. P., Niebaum, J. C., Placido, D., Katz, B., Shah, P. & Munakata, Y. (2023). Overemphasizing individual differences and overlooking systemic factors reinforces educational inequality. npj Science of Learning 8:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00164-z

article_title: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity
citation: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity. (2024). npj Science of Learning 9, 27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00240-y
title: Employ research staff who identify similarly to the participant population, or involve community members in reviewing materials and protocols
description: The review argues that hair-related conversations are not replacements for lived experience: “It is essential that labs employ research staff, both for participant-facing data collection, as well as for data analysis and study design, w ho identify similarly to the demo- graphic of the participant population.” This increases the cultural appropriateness of protocols, participant experiences, and interpretation and communication of findings. When such staffing is not possible, community members and leaders should review study materials and protocols.
requirements: When staff matching is not possible, community members and leaders should review study materials and protocols.
constraints: The authors caution that their observations and recommendations may not be appropriate for all participants, since cultural groups are not monolithic.
target_learners: Black and/or Latinx children and families participating in developmental neuroscience research
target_learning_goals: Reducing biases in participation and data acquisition in neuroscience research through culturally appropriate protocols
examples: The authors chose the terms ‘Latin’ and ‘Latinx’ in consultation with authorship team members who identify as Latina, and honor participant preferences for other terms where possible.

article_title: Structured human-LLM interaction design reveals exploration and exploitation dynamics in higher education content generation
citation: Pablo Flores Romero, Kin Nok Nicholas Fung, Guang Rong & Benjamin Ultan Cowley. (2025). Structured human-LLM interaction design reveals exploration and exploitation dynamics in higher education content generation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00332-3
title: Structured prompt-template and keyword-card interaction design for human-LLM co-creation
description: A novel interaction protocol for studying human-LLM foraging: six editable prompt templates divided into Exploration and Exploitation types, plus a shared pool of keyword cards contributed by course participants and categorized into concepts such as 'Actors', 'AI tools', 'Environments', and 'Subjects'. The templates "facilitated the exploration-exploitationbehavioral modes of IFT, standardized the interaction between participants, guided those without prior experience, and enabled systematic analysis of their foraging behavior". Participants crafted prompts by combining templates with guide or GPT-sourced keywords in 45-minute facilitated ChatGPT sessions.
requirements: Prompt templates and keyword cards derived from participants' reported interests gathered before the course
A researcher-mediated 45-minute session protocol with setup, introduction, execution, and conclusion phases
constraints: The structured design intentionally limits free-form prompting, so results do not reflect typical ChatGPT use
The specific task complicates comparisons with previous web search studies that formally assess IFT principles
target_learners: Doctoral-level educational scientists in an AI in Education course
target_learning_goals: Pedagogical content creation and study-design scenario development with generative AI
examples: In the study, exploration prompts opened new ChatGPT conversations to remove context carryover, while exploitation prompts elaborated an already generated scenario with one or two keywords
key_sources: Pablo Flores Romero, Kin Nok Nicholas Fung, Guang Rong & Benjamin Ultan Cowley. (2025). Structured human-LLM interaction design reveals exploration and exploitation dynamics in higher education content generation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00332-3

article_title: Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers
citation: Sierksma, J. (2023). Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00192-9
title: Structure cooperative and collaborative learning so that low-competence peers are not denied practice opportunities
description: Because children differentiate help by perceived competence, the article argues that educators should structure peer-to-peer helping and collaborative learning so that all children receive opportunities to practice and improve. The article states such insight "could, for example, inform how to best structure educational practices that involve cooperative and collaborative learning" so that "all children pro ﬁt from the education they receive regardless of their background". Without such structuring, peer helping may reinforce competence-based disparities rather than reduce them.
requirements: Awareness that peer helpers may give less empowering help to peers perceived as incompetent
constraints: The studies were lab-based with forced-choice measures and a within-subjects design; the article notes effects might be smaller when contrasts are less salient and classroom evidence is still needed
target_learners: children aged 6–9 in classrooms
students in cooperative and collaborative learning arrangements
target_learning_goals: equal opportunities to practice and improve skills
reducing competence-based educational inequality
examples: The article's quizmaster experiments showed children gave fewer hints to peers they overheard were not good at puzzles or math, despite endorsing that those peers could improve
key_sources: Sierksma, J. (2023). Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00192-9

article_title: Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony
citation: Qi Li, Die Wang, Weilong Xiao, Yingying Tang, Qi Sun, Binghai Sun & Zhishan Hu. (2024). Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony. npj Science of Learning 9:73. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00286-y
title: Design teacher-student interaction in flipped classrooms as a structured, planned sequence rather than leaving it spontaneous
description: The article concludes that a well-planned interaction schedule, in which students summarize content, receive feedback, ask and answer questions, and hear a teacher summary, is the active ingredient of flipped classroom learning gains. It states that "a well-planned, structured interaction is crucial for achieving positive teaching outcomes" and that "carefully planned interaction schedules can signiﬁcantly beneﬁte d u c a t i o n a l content delivery." Spontaneous interaction offered lower educational benefits in the experiment.
requirements: The teacher arranges the interaction process step by step before class, building on prior knowledge acquired from pre-class lecture videos
constraints: Demonstrated in one-on-one, laboratory-simulated flipped classes with declarative management-psychology content; the authors note it is unknown whether structured interaction after a face-to-face lecture works as well
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: declarative conceptual knowledge (management psychology theories)
examples: In the FT condition, students summarized the teaching contents, the teacher gave feedback, encouraged questions, asked questions, and summarized the knowledge concisely

article_title: Context-based learning for Inhibition of alternative conceptions: the next step forward in science education
citation: Alexandra Renouard and Yves Mazabraud. (2018). Context-based learning for Inhibition of alternative conceptions: the next step forward in science education. npj Science of Learning 3:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0026-9
title: Student profile atlas for context-based science teaching
description: An atlas of student profiles built from quantified learner-context interactions. Parameters defining each interaction are "its nature (human-human, human-object, technological, verbal, peer-to-peer, or hierarchical relationship), as well as its intensity", its stability and its resistance, quantified by criteria chosen per study. The number of profile types, their percentage and repartition "define an atlas that may be taken into account to either change the curriculum or to design temporary pedagogical projects".
requirements: Data collected via interviews or Multiple Choice Questions for small samples, or online questionnaires with automated processing for large populations
constraints: Quantification criteria need to be chosen for each study; the atlas requires an entry per individual or a statistically representative group
target_learners: students across schooling stages
target_learning_goals: targeted design of science instruction
curriculum adaptation
examples: The article describes example student profiles with weak to strong interaction links and matched targeted actions in its Figure 2

article_title: From Interactive Open Learner Modelling to Intelligent Mentoring: STyLE-OLM and Beyond
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Paul Brna. (2016). From Interactive Open Learner Modelling to Intelligent Mentoring: STyLE-OLM and Beyond. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:332–349. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0087-3
title: STyLE-OLM framework for interactive open learner modelling
description: STyLE-OLM is a computational framework in which learners and the system jointly construct, inspect, discuss and alter the learner model through structured diagnostic dialogue. The article states: "The main contribution of this work is the holistic framework for interactive open learner modelling which addresses the three main issues – providing a suitable communication means, managing a diagnostic dialogue, and maintaining a jointly constructed learner model." It combines Conceptual Graphs-based representation, a dialogue-game planner with strategies and tactics, and a belief modal operator mechanism for agreements and conflicts, and was instantiated in programming and finance domains.
requirements: A communication medium allowing both inspection of the learner model and dialogue about it
A dialogue framework giving learner and system symmetric power to negotiate the learner model
A mechanism for accommodating different beliefs about the learner's domain knowledge
constraints: Evaluation evidence came from carefully designed user studies within university conditions focusing on selected aspects, limiting broader applicability across domains and contexts
target_learners: adult learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: domain terminology and concept knowledge
metacognitive self-awareness and reflection
examples: Instantiated in STyLE-OLM for finance concepts in the LARFLAST project and for programming concepts
Adopted in OWL-OLM, PORML, SAIC and the Perico agent
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova & Paul Brna. (2016). From Interactive Open Learner Modelling to Intelligent Mentoring: STyLE-OLM and Beyond. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:332–349. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0087-3

article_title: From Interactive Open Learner Modelling to Intelligent Mentoring: STyLE-OLM and Beyond
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Paul Brna. (2016). From Interactive Open Learner Modelling to Intelligent Mentoring: STyLE-OLM and Beyond. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:332–349. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0087-3
title: STyLE-OLM communication medium: diagrammatic Conceptual Graphs with sentence openers
description: The communication medium combines a graphical construction area for propositions representing learner model beliefs with sentence openers expressing illocutionary acts. The article says it "exploited the diagrammatic external representation of Conceptual Graphs for designing a communication medium which provided a structured interface combining a graphical construction area for propositions representing beliefs from the LM." Sentence openers scaffolded the discourse structure, and the controlled expression of domain statements enabled conversion of propositions into logical axioms. The same medium was reused in OWL-OLM with OWL-based learner models.
requirements: A controlled way of expressing domain statements so propositions can be converted into logical axioms
constraints: The article notes the drawback of "the rather limited way of constructing domain propositions with the graphical apparatus provided"
target_learners: adult learners learning domain terminology
target_learning_goals: articulating and inspecting domain knowledge statements
engaging in diagnostic dialogue about the learner model
examples: OWL-OLM implemented the same communication medium using UML-like diagrammatic expressions and sentence templates

article_title: Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design
citation: Hongxin Yan, Fuhua Lin & Kinshuk. (2021). Including Learning Analytics in the Loop of Self-Paced Online Course Learning Design. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2021) 31:878–895. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00225-z
title: List of learner and learning data sources for LA applications in STEM SPOL courses
description: For STEM disciplines in SPOL, the article enumerates the data sources relevant to its LA applications, to be considered during course design: academic background (SIS), prior knowledge (diagnostic test), learning interest and approach (survey or log), knowledge state (assessment), attempts of and time spent on formative assessment (log), assessment grade (log), access to recommended learning materials (log), study schedule plan (LMS database), study pace (log), social interactions (log), social style (survey), and help-seeking frequency (log). The article states that 'students' knowledge state (or knowledge and skill proficiency) is the most critical input variable for the LA applications.'
requirements: The survey should be considered in the course learning design stage to determine the questions that can generate the genuine learner data required by the LA applications
constraints: The data sources are those the study recognizes as relevant for STEM disciplines in SPOL in higher formal education
target_learners: students in STEM self-paced online higher education courses
target_learning_goals: estimating knowledge state and supporting learning awareness, struggling-student identification, and academic intervention
examples: The COMP272 revision plans a diagnostic test for prior knowledge, a beginning-of-course survey for academic profiles, and log data from unit self-quizzes.

article_title: Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON
citation: Phaedra Mohammed & Permanand Mohan. (2015). Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:249–270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0033-9
title: Give students control over the extent of cultural contextualisation in ILEs via student-initiated controls such as a cultural density slider
description: Because system-initiated determination of cultural formality and references was not unanimously accepted and preferences fluctuate by content type, the article argues that student-initiated control should be featured in ILEs. In CRITS, "movement of the cultural density slider triggers the contextualisation changes" so that language formality, cultural references and images adjust in real time, with 0% restoring original content. The study's finding that students tolerated different densities for different content types further supports this principle.
requirements: Requires a dynamic contextualisation approach that can modify content in real time, such as the ICON architecture with a Contextual Student Model and Cultural Linguistics Adapter.
Requires an interface mechanism, such as a density slider mapped to a formality scale, through which students express their preferred level of contextualisation.
constraints: The article's supporting evidence comes from one small study (37 participants) in a Computer Science domain with content modelled only for Trinidadian culture, so the authors call the threshold findings preliminary.
Informal dialect at high densities risked perceptions of lacking professionalism and pedagogical expertise.
target_learners: students from diverse cultural subcultures, exemplified by Trinidadian university programming students
target_learning_goals: adapting problem descriptions, images, hints and instructional feedback to students' preferred level of cultural contextualisation
examples: In the CRITS study, participants moved the slider in fixed increments of 20% from 0% to 100% and rated content at each level; one student left the slider at 20% because hints at 40% were too comical and distracted her.
key_sources: Phaedra Mohammed & Permanand Mohan. (2015). Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:249–270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0033-9

article_title: Recent Meta-reviews and Meta–analyses of AIED Systems
citation: Benedict du Boulay. (2015). Recent Meta-reviews and Meta-analyses of AIED Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0060-1
title: Step-based tutoring: evaluating and reacting to each learner step in problem-solving, as the organizing distinction in ITS effectiveness research
description: The letter uses a granularity-of-feedback account to organise ITS effectiveness findings: step-based tutors "evaluates and reacts to each step that the learner makes in a problem-solving session as opposed to evaluating only the final answer given by the learner". This distinction frames which systems the surveyed meta-analyses cover. It serves as the letter's working characterisation of the ITS class whose effectiveness the reviews compare against human tutoring and conventional instruction.
requirements: Applies to problem-solving tutors whose granularity of evaluation is per-step rather than final-answer only, as the letter's definition states.
constraints: The letter uses the definition to characterise surveyed systems; it does not test whether step granularity itself causes effectiveness differences.
target_learners: Learners using intelligent tutoring systems in the surveyed studies (school pupils and university students)
target_learning_goals: Problem-solving skill in tutored domains
examples: The letter applies the definition to the ITSs surveyed by VanLehn (2011) and the step-based ITSs in the Ma et al. (2014) meta-analysis.
key_sources: Benedict du Boulay. (2015). Recent Meta-reviews and Meta-analyses of AIED Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0060-1

article_title: How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences
citation: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0
title: Student-level recency-weighted proportional correctness feature (RKC,SPFA)
description: This feature extends Galyardt and Goldin's KC-level proportional decay measure by tracking the recency-weighted proportion of correct responses at the level of the student across KCs. The authors hypothesized this additional feature "could stand in for student learning differences as well as learning transfer across KCs". It requires two ghost attempts (one incorrect, one correct) to center the measure at .5 so it can adapt upward or downward, and the authors have implemented a version in a running system.
requirements: Requires appending two ghost attempts (one failure, one success) to practice sequences so proportions are defined from the first attempt
constraints: The version computes the recency-weighted average across KCs, so it partially reflects transfer rather than pure student learning rate
target_learners: students using adaptive instructional systems
target_learning_goals: tracking individual student performance differences for mastery estimation
examples: Fit as RKC,SPFA and RKC,SEPFA variants across six datasets; a version is implemented in a running system
key_sources: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0

article_title: Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies
citation: Beemer, J., Spoon, K., He, L., Fan, J., & Levine, R.A. (2018). Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 28, 315–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0148-x
title: STAT 119 supplemental instruction section (STAT 119A) at San Diego State University
description: A one-credit supplemental instruction course attached to the large-enrollment STAT 119 introductory statistics course, enrolling 20–30 students per section meeting twice weekly for one hour. Sections are led by statistics graduate teaching assistants trained to develop "an active problem solving environment in the classroom", with students working through problems rather than watching solutions and TAs facilitating group discussion of conceptual difficulties. It deviates from the traditional UMKC SI model by using graduate students rather than near-peers and requiring enrollment in STAT 119A.
requirements: Students voluntarily enroll for one additional credit unit; students scoring below 70% on the first-week algebra assessment are strongly encouraged to enroll
Instructors are trained prior to the semester and regularly evaluated by a course coordinator
constraints: Differs from the UMKC SI model: instructors are graduate students rather than near-peers, and attendance is effectively required via enrollment and encouragement rather than voluntary drop-in
target_learners: undergraduates in a large enrollment introductory statistics bottleneck course
students scoring below 70% on an initial algebra assessment
target_learning_goals: improving final exam scores, course grades, and non-repeatable grades (C or better) in introductory statistics
examples: The Fall 2013 offering enrolled 17% of STAT 119 students; enrollees averaged 83% pass rate versus 72% for non-enrollees
key_sources: Beemer, J., Spoon, K., He, L., Fan, J., & Levine, R.A. (2018). Ensemble Learning for Estimating Individualized Treatment Effects in Student Success Studies. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 28, 315–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0148-x

article_title: An Analysis of Student Model Portability
citation: Valdés Aguirre, B., Ramírez Uresti, J. A., & du Boulay, B. (2016). An Analysis of Student Model Portability. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0113-0
title: A four-dimension classification for grading student model portability
description: The article introduces a classification that grades student models in terms of portability. Portability is measured across four dimensions — accessibility, complexity, architecture, and popularity — each composed of factors such as open source status, availability, inputs, types of data, input formats, computational techniques, data mining use, model origin, implementation, modularity, server/client architecture, and re-implementation. Each factor is graded 1 to 4 (low, mid, high restrictions, or no information), dimension grades are normalized sums mapped to 1–4, and the overall grade is the sum of the dimensions, where a grade of 4 represents "the models with least types restrictions we found (Very Low)". The authors intend it "to be used by researchers both as a methodology to measure the portability of a student model and as a guide to find existing reusable models".
requirements: Grades are calculated from questions answerable from published literature without access to source code, so published documentation of the model's inputs, implementation, and availability is required.
constraints: The authors normalize each dimension equally, which they acknowledge "is a strong assumption to make and may bias our analysis".
The classes are coarse, so "there might be considerable differences between some models that fall in the same class".
A domain independence factor was excluded because it could not be measured in a practical way.
target_learners: Researchers and developers building or reusing student models in ITSs and ILEs
target_learning_goals: Selection and reuse of existing student models when building adaptive learning systems
examples: The classification was applied to 70 student models identified from full papers at AIED 2013, EDM 2014 and ITS 2014, graded and grouped into tables from low to very high portability restrictions.
key_sources: Valdés Aguirre, B., Ramírez Uresti, J. A., & du Boulay, B. (2016). An Analysis of Student Model Portability. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0113-0

article_title: Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling
citation: Pelánek, R. (2025). Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00400-6
title: Adaptive learning environments require three interlocking models: a student model, a domain model, and a pedagogical model
description: The article describes a basic architecture for personalization consisting of three models. A student model is "an abstraction of a student that serves as a basis for adaptive decisions"; a domain model abstracts the domain into learning units and their relations; a pedagogical model specifies the personalization strategy translating model information into system actions. The author notes the terminology varies widely and that any adaptive learning environment needs these three components in some form, illustrating them with a mathematics realization using knowledge components, prerequisite relations, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, and mastery learning.
requirements: Any adaptive learning environment must realize all three model components in some form for personalization to occur.
constraints: Terminology varies widely across educational technology; the pedagogical model is often described with other terms such as instructional strategy or recommendation algorithm.
target_learners: students in mathematics, programming, and language learning domains
target_learning_goals: adaptive guidance and feedback appropriate to current student knowledge
examples: A mathematics realization maps tasks to knowledge components, defines prerequisite relations, uses Bayesian Knowledge Tracing for the student model, and drives mastery learning and recommendations from those estimates.
key_sources: Pelánek, R. (2025). Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00400-6

article_title: Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability
citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Three-source taxonomy of system complexity: structural, dynamic, and perspectival
description: Adapting Campbell (1988), the article generalizes a scheme of complexity sources into three categories shown in Fig. 2. Structural complexity concerns parts, part types, properties, and relationships (one-to-one mappings simplest, many-to-many most complex); dynamic complexity concerns systems whose properties and relationships change over time; and perspectival complexity is defined as "complexity due to multiplicity and uncertainty, including conflicting goals or subtasks", diverse stakeholder perspectives, stochastic indeterminacy, and vagueness.
requirements: Measuring these factors would require enumerating or estimating components, relationships, and dynamic behaviors of the system
constraints: The article notes perspectival factors would be measured more heuristically than the other two types, and that complexity has a quasi-subjective component involving human context and purpose
target_learners: software and authoring tool designers
learning system researchers
target_learning_goals: characterizing and comparing the complexity of tools, tasks, and user mental models

article_title: Predicting Tags for Learner Questions on Stack Overflow
citation: Olatinwo, S. O., & Demmans Epp, C. (2025). Predicting Tags for Learner Questions on Stack Overflow. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00441-x
title: Stack Overflow question and tag dataset from Kaggle and BigQuery

Each question has six features (question ID, title, body, tags, creation date, closed date), of which four were used. The dataset was split 80:20 into training and test sets.

constraints: Contains only a subset of questions and tags from the SO website
Data coverage ends December 2022

article_title: STyLE-OLM: Interactive Open Learner Modelling
citation: Vania Dimitrova. (2003). STyLE-OLM: Interactive Open Learner Modelling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197312
title: STyLE-OLM: an interactive open learner modelling demonstrator for a terminological domain
description: STyLE-OLM is "a system called STyLE-OLM", an "IOLM demonstrator" built to illustrate the interactive open learner modelling method. It operates in a terminological domain and was used in an evaluative study examining the benefits of the IOLM approach for learner modelling and learner reflection.
