article_title: A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education
citation: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1
title: The standard model of AI: a fully autonomous agent that single-mindedly maximises a pre-set objective irrespective of user needs
description: The article describes, drawing on Russell (2019), a standard model of AI in which "AI is a fully autonomous agent whose job is to single-mindedly find ways that maximise the achievement of a pre-set objective, irrespective of the users' real-time or long-term needs or contexts," with full and difficult-to-track or challenge control of the interaction. Russell's critique locates its problems in rigid insistence on local optima of limited contexts and in human fallibility in specifying objectives guaranteed to be ethical and beneficial to all stakeholders. He proposes replacing it with a flexible model "open to manipulation and personalisation by their users" that gives data back to users and whose objectives can be negotiated. The article uses this framing to position AIED's Open Learner Models as pre-eminent existing examples relevant to new forms of human-centred AI design.
requirements: A shift toward models sensitive to human needs and contextualised preferences, open to user manipulation and personalisation, whose objectives can be negotiated
constraints: Presented as the author's summary of Russell (2019)'s argument and her application of it to AIED, not as an empirical finding of this article
target_learners: all users of AI systems, including learners
target_learning_goals: human agency in human-AI interaction
AI for human good
examples: The article contrasts this standard model with AIED approaches that give users degrees of agency, control and ownership over system-generated data and over their learning processes
key_sources: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1

article_title: Implementation and use of Simulated Students for Test and Validation of new Adaptive Educational Systems: a Practical Insight
citation: Fabiano Dorça. (2015). Implementation and use of Simulated Students for Test and Validation of new Adaptive Educational Systems: a Practical Insight. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0037-0
title: Stochastic simulated student module for testing learning-styles modelling approaches
description: A software module implemented as an expert system that encapsulates knowledge about how learning styles affect student performance. It receives the student's real learning styles and a selected learning style combination, and stochastically infers session performance via P = M − (D × K × α), where difficulty D depends on the amount of unmet learning styles plus random terms for strong and moderate unmet preferences. It is uncoupled from any educational system, so it "can be easily adapted and reused for testing other student modelling approaches based on LS."
requirements: Requires setting the student's real learning styles and the strength of each preference (strong, moderate, weak or balanced) before running
constraints: Performance inference is stochastic and considers that inadequately adapted content may contribute to failure but cannot determine it
target_learners: simulated learners in adaptive educational system research
target_learning_goals: automatic learning styles modelling and teaching style selection
examples: Used to compare three reinforcement strategies over simulated courses of 30 concepts × 6 levels (at least 180 learning sessions)
key_sources: Fabiano Dorça. (2015). Implementation and use of Simulated Students for Test and Validation of new Adaptive Educational Systems: a Practical Insight. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0037-0

article_title: Keeping Up with the Trends: Analyzing the Dynamics of Online Learning and Hiring Platforms in the Software Programming Domain
citation: Ramtin Yazdanian, Robert West, Pierre Dillenbourg. (2021). Keeping Up with the Trends: Analyzing the Dynamics of Online Learning and Hiring Platforms in the Software Programming Domain. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00231-1
title: Stack Overflow tags as crowd-sourced proxies for emerging skills and topics
description: The article uses Stack Overflow tags — user-created words or phrases describing question topics — as the representation of new topics/skills in the software domain. Tens of new tags are created weekly, and moderators curate them via synonym-marking and deletion polls, making them "a set of precise and specific community-curated topics." The authors chose tags over topic modelling (e.g. LDA) for three reasons: crowdsourced manual curation, fine-grained specificity, and exact-match semantics.
requirements: Community curation signals (popularity, votes) to filter unimportant or duplicate tags
constraints: Approach "mostly excludes higher order skills" such as agile development practices or architecture redesign
target_learners: software developers
target_learning_goals: tracking emergence of new technical skills
examples: Tag vuejs2 tracked across Stack Overflow, Stack Overflow Jobs, and Udemy with first-appearance dates on each

article_title: Desktop virtual reality with scaffolded interaction and reflective explanation: effects on cognitive, motivational, and learning outcomes in engineering education
citation: Adurangba Victor Oje, Nathaniel J. Hunsu. (2026). Desktop virtual reality with scaffolded interaction and reflective explanation: effects on cognitive, motivational, and learning outcomes in engineering education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10722-y
title: Structure VR learning activities with scaffolded interaction and reflective explanation to support learning efficiency and learner confidence
description: The article recommends structuring VR learning activities as a sequenced instructional design that integrates exploration of a virtual system, scaffolded interaction tasks, and a reflective self-explanation activity. The authors conclude that "structuring VR learning activities with scaffolded interaction and reflective explanation may support learning efficiency and learner confidence in engineering contexts." This sequencing pairs generative learning strategies with interactive simulation rather than treating VR as a standalone medium.
requirements: A desktop VR simulation of the target mechanical system, with embedded on-screen scaffolding prompts available during the interaction phase
constraints: The study does not isolate the independent effects of individual instructional components, so the recommendation rests on the combined design
The small sample and use of a single VR application limit the generalizability of the findings
target_learners: Undergraduate engineering students
target_learning_goals: Engineering statics concepts, including free-body diagram construction and static force analysis
examples: Participants in the VR condition explored a desktop simulation of an excavator, completed scaffolded measurement and analysis tasks with on-screen text guidance, and responded to a structured self-explanation prompt before solving a novel statics problem.
key_sources: Adurangba Victor Oje, Nathaniel J. Hunsu. (2026). Desktop virtual reality with scaffolded interaction and reflective explanation: effects on cognitive, motivational, and learning outcomes in engineering education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10722-y

article_title: Shifting to digital: a policy perspective on ‘Student perceptions of privacy principles for learning analytics’ (Ifenthaler & Schumacher 2016)
citation: Corrin, L. (2021). Shifting to digital: a policy perspective on 'Student perceptions of privacy principles for learning analytics' (Ifenthaler & Schumacher 2016). Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09922-x
title: Include student voice in developing learning analytics policy
description: The commentary argues that policy governing the ethical use of student data in learning analytics must be developed with student input, not imposed on students. It states it is "equally important that the student voice be included in the development of such policy". This positions students as stakeholders whose understanding of data sharing purposes and benefits must be built through consultative processes around systems implementation.
requirements: Consultative processes around systems implementation that ensure transparency and accountability
constraints: Building a shared understanding and vocabulary with students about the possibilities and ethical implications of learning analytics is difficult
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness
ethical understanding of data sharing
examples: The commentary draws on Ifenthaler and Schumacher's (2016) survey of student perceptions of privacy principles for learning analytics
key_sources: Corrin, L. (2021). Shifting to digital: a policy perspective on 'Student perceptions of privacy principles for learning analytics' (Ifenthaler & Schumacher 2016). Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09922-x

article_title: Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics
citation: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8
title: 19-topic structural topic model of metacognition research in education
description: The article applies a structural topic model (STM) to the abstracts and titles of 2,568 metacognition articles, running 26 candidate models with topic numbers from 5 to 30 and selecting the 19-topic model based on semantic coherence, exclusivity (FREX), and expert verification. The 19 labeled topics include "self-regulated learning", "judgments of learning and memory accuracy", "assessment and feedback", "creative and critical thinking", and "nursing, medical, clinical, and healthcare education". The article states this "marks the inaugural application of topic modeling technology to the field of metacognition". Topics were labeled by two domain experts through a three-step procedure of interpreting discriminating terms, examining representative articles, and unifying labels.
requirements: Optimal model selection based on exclusivity and semantic coherence measures alongside human verification by two experts
constraints: Topics derived from titles and abstracts of WoS education-category articles only
target_learners: education researchers
target_learning_goals: identifying prevailing research themes in metacognition
examples: For the topic "creative and critical thinking", experts inspected discriminating terms such as "creative", "creativity", "thinking", "critical", and "divergent" and analyzed representative articles before naming the topic
key_sources: Xieling Chen, Xinyue Li, Di Zou, Haoran Xie, & Fu Lee Wang. (2025). Metacognition research in education: topic modeling and bibliometrics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10451-8

article_title: Measuring learning in serious games: a case study with structural assessment
citation: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0
title: Structural assessment measures learning by comparing a learner's knowledge organization with a referent structure
description: Structural assessment is defined as measuring the learners' knowledge organization and comparing this with a referent structure. It rests on the assumption that knowledge is organized in structures containing important concepts and the relations among them. The article proposes it as an alternative to verbal assessment for serious games, arguing that effective knowledge structures enable faster problem solving and integration of new information.
requirements: A domain analysis must identify the important concepts of the domain or task
Experts in the domain must agree about the essential concepts and relations
constraints: Agreement on essential concepts is more likely in 'hard' domains with a central body of theory than in 'soft' domains
target_learners: Novices and advanced learners in domains requiring complex skills
target_learning_goals: Knowledge organization and understanding of domain concepts
key_sources: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0

article_title: Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment
citation: Cirkony, C., Tytler, R., & Hubber, P. (2022). Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10094-z
title: STILE online learning platform with interactive canvas and written response applications
description: STILE (Student Teacher Interactive Learning Environment) is a customisable, cloud-based interactive online platform for K-12 science units, freely available to Victorian government secondary schools. In this study its modules embedded multimedia resources, assessments with automated feedback, and open-ended tools: "the interactive canvas allowed students to draw and annotate diagrams and integrate multiple media; and the written response application provided an infinitely expanded ruled pad allowing students to construct text-based responses." The platform also served as a repository for student work that teachers could access to guide discussion and refinement.
requirements: Teacher facilitation to realise guided discussion and evaluation around student-generated representations
Students need individual device access; in this study laptops with removable keyboard, Active-Pen technology, and built-in camera
constraints: Issues with internet connectivity in one lesson meant students responded in their project books instead of the platform
target_learners: K-12 science students, exemplified by Grade 9 students
target_learning_goals: Constructing and refining multimodal representations of science concepts
Inquiry-based knowledge building in blended science lessons
examples: A customised 12-module energy-transfer unit with pre- and post-test and a summative inquiry task was designed on STILE and implemented with face-to-face and online interactions
key_sources: Cirkony, C., Tytler, R., & Hubber, P. (2022). Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10094-z

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students
citation: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8
title: Student life cycle as a three-phase organizing structure for designing student support functionalities
description: The article uses the student life cycle (Sprenger et al., 2010) as an organizational structure for developing support and functionalities. The article states that "The study process comprised three phases (see Table 1), which included structured sub-dimensions that can be used to structure the development and implementation of IDSAs": before university study (recruitment to enrollment), during university study (examinations, organization, re-registration), and after university study (graduation, alumni activities). Transition phases such as arriving at a university require intensive support.
requirements: Phase-specific focus translating requirements into practical information, e.g., addressing beginning-student needs such as student financing or finding locations on campus
constraints: The structure and focus of a student life cycle may differ in terms of teaching, quality management, and campus management system cost
target_learners: Higher education students across study phases, with emphasis on early-phase students
target_learning_goals: Study organization and phase-appropriate individual support
key_sources: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8

article_title: The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains
citation: Manuel Ninaus, Rodolpho Cortez, Izabel Hazin, Kristian Kiili, Silke M. Wortha, Elise Klein, Elisabeth M. Weiss, Korbinian Moeller. (2023). The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10263-8
title: When investigating game elements, study the actual learning process, not only pretest–posttest outcomes
description: The article argues that effects of game elements can appear during the learning process even when pre-post learning outcomes do not differ, so research should measure performance during training. It states this "underscores the importance of studying the actual learning process when investigating the effects of game elements rather than analyzing learning outcomes alone (i.e., pretest–posttest differences)". In the study, only the training-phase measures revealed the accuracy and speed differences between conditions.
requirements: Behavioral performance measures (accuracy and response duration) collected during the training sessions themselves
constraints: In this study the interpretation that higher accuracy reflects increased cognitive engagement needed to be treated with caution because only behavioral indicators were available
target_learners: adult university students in game-based learning studies
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude understanding
examples: The study compared game-based and non-game-based training conditions on PAE and response duration across five sessions, revealing condition differences invisible in the pre-post measure
key_sources: Manuel Ninaus, Rodolpho Cortez, Izabel Hazin, Kristian Kiili, Silke M. Wortha, Elise Klein, Elisabeth M. Weiss, Korbinian Moeller. (2023). The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10263-8

article_title: Factors shaping faculty online teaching competencies during the Covid-19 pandemic
citation: Trevisan, O., De Rossi, M., Christensen, R., Knezek, G., & Smits, A. (2023). Factors shaping faculty online teaching competencies during the Covid-19 pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10197-1
title: Professional development for online teaching should be strength-based, embedded in daily practice, and responsive to faculty's self-identified needs
description: The article argues that developing faculty competencies for online teaching incorporates behavioral, intellectual, and attitudinal components, and that professional development "could benefit from an appreciative approach that is strength-based rather than deficiency-based, incorporated into the daily teachers' practices, and responsive to their self-identified needs and interests". Because faculty characteristics vary by profile, needs for professional support vary as well, so training pathways should be tailored to faculty's approaches and needs and support them at their own level of readiness.
requirements: Institutional support and needs-based faculty development must be available for the approach to work as described
constraints: The article notes surveyed faculty generally did not frequently attend training for OT, and the authors infer the training offered may have been inadequate or perceived as an additional overload
target_learners: higher education faculty in education departments
target_learning_goals: online teaching competence and technology integration
examples: The study's four profiles at each snapshot are used to argue that as characteristics vary by group, so do the needs for professional support and professional development
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback
citation: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel H. Chang, Philip H. Winne. (2025). A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10408-3
title: A methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns via coded pathway logs
description: The article proposes a methodology in which student-chatbot exchanges are logged, coded into a 2×2 matrix of guidance acceptance (reject/accept) by revision correctness (correct/incorrect), and mapped onto possible interaction paths whose counts reveal where chatbot instruction succeeds or fails. It extends Winne and Nesbit's critique of snapshot between-group designs by tracing each participant's conversational trajectory. The authors state they "propose a new methodology to identify where improvements can be made in conversation patterns in educational chatbots", enabling progressive redesign of chatbot scripts.
requirements: Chat histories must be automatically stored (e.g., in Rasa's backend server) and coders must resolve discrepancies to produce a final matrix per participant
constraints: The article states the small sample size constrains understanding of specific interaction pathways, and the method was piloted on one task (thesis statements, arguments and counterarguments)
target_learners: post-secondary undergraduates in writing-intensive courses
target_learning_goals: giving effective peer feedback on draft essays
examples: Participants' self-judgements were coded 0/1 and combined with CCQ correctness and revision outcomes into paths A–L (Tables 2–5), then visualized across both chatbot sessions (Fig. 7)
key_sources: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel H. Chang, Philip H. Winne. (2025). A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10408-3

article_title: Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1
title: studybuddy: an adaptive learning technology platform supporting learners' self-regulated learning
description: studybuddy is a digital platform available as both a website and an app, designed to promote SRL by providing learners with tailored and timely regulation strategies. It gathers SRL-related data over time via a brief daily survey on motivation, emotion, cognition, metacognition, and resource management, and offers feedback through prompts, strategy recommendations, a dashboard, and a planning tool. "Figure 2 depicts studybuddy's four components: an automated prompting system, a digital dashboard, personalized strategies, and a planning tool." The article focuses on the prompting system and personalized strategy delivery.
requirements: Learners respond to daily questionnaire items on a standardized 7-point Likert scale so thresholds can trigger regulation strategies
constraints: During the initial two co-design phases the authors found that although already highly adaptive, it required further development to increase its adaptiveness
target_learners: 11th-grade high school students (16-17 years old)
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, including motivation, emotion, cognition, metacognition, and resource management
examples: In the context of self-efficacy, learners are asked whether they feel optimistic about making progress, and selecting one of the four lowest values on the 7-point scale automatically suggests a regulation strategy
key_sources: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1

article_title: Exploratory studies in the use of pictures and sound for teaching foreign language vocabulary
citation: Kale, S. V., and Grosslight, J. H. (1955). Exploratory Studies in the Use of Pictures and Sound for Teaching Foreign Language Vocabulary. Technical Report SDC 269-7-53, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University.
title: Use still pictures instead of motion pictures for film-based vocabulary instruction to avoid production expense
description: The report recommends that, because still pictures appear to be as effective as motion pictures for teaching foreign vocabulary under a written criterion, "the expense of producing motion pictures be avoided by using still pictures". It is a cost-saving design recommendation grounded in the null value the studies found for motion in pictures.
requirements: Learning goal is foreign vocabulary with a criterion of writing the foreign words
constraints: Applies where still and motion pictures were found equally effective; motion showed no value in these studies
target_learners: college students learning foreign language vocabulary
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary learning measured by written word production
examples: Study 1 prepared five versions of motion pictures, including still pictures with English and Russian words, and taught Russian words to 409 college students
key_sources: Kale, S. V., and Grosslight, J. H. (1955). Exploratory Studies in the Use of Pictures and Sound for Teaching Foreign Language Vocabulary. Technical Report SDC 269-7-53, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02718464

article_title: Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment design
citation: Mäkelä, T., Fenyvesi, K., Kankaanranta, M., Pnevmatikos, D., & Christodoulou, P. (2022). Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10114-y
title: A five-category pedagogical framework of design principles for hybrid STEM learning environments
description: The co-designed framework organises design principles into five categories: General principles, Cross-curricular skills, Ways of teaching and learning, Socio-emotional aspects, and Educational compatibility. As the article states, "The co-designed framework, which is strengthened by the research literature, entails the following design principle categories". Each category holds between four and twelve principles, each with supporting literature and concrete application examples, developed to guide hybrid STEM learning environment design but presented as adaptable to other learning environments.
requirements: Principles are grounded in both stakeholder input and empirical and theoretical literature
constraints: Developed mainly to support the design of a hybrid STEM learning environment, though argued to be generic enough for other environments
target_learners: 10-18-year-old primary, lower and upper secondary school students
target_learning_goals: STEM interest and motivation
cross-curricular (twenty-first century) skills
subject-related STEM competencies
examples: Principle 1.1 Personalisation is exemplified by choosing contents and difficulty level based on personal preferences and level of understanding
key_sources: Mäkelä, T., Fenyvesi, K., Kankaanranta, M., Pnevmatikos, D., & Christodoulou, P. (2022). Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10114-y

article_title: Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment design
citation: Mäkelä, T., Fenyvesi, K., Kankaanranta, M., Pnevmatikos, D., & Christodoulou, P. (2022). Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10114-y
title: STIMEY hybrid STEM learning environment combining virtual and physical components
description: The STIMEY environment is a hybrid learning environment for 10-18-year-olds developed in a European Horizon 2020 project across Belarus, Finland, Germany, Greece and Spain. The article states it "consists of components such as a social web platform, e-portfolio, serious games, entrepreneurial tools, a digital radio (virtual learning environment) as well as physical socially assistive robots". It connects stakeholders to increase students' interest and motivation in STEM education, innovations and careers, and the co-designed principles were employed in its development.
requirements: Design guided by the co-designed pedagogical framework and its design principles
constraints: Not targeted at university students, though university students were consulted in focus groups
target_learners: young people aged 10-18
target_learning_goals: STEM interest and motivation
entrepreneurial and professional skills
cross-curricular competencies
examples: Physical socially assistive robots are combined with virtual components such as the digital radio and serious games
key_sources: Mäkelä, T., Fenyvesi, K., Kankaanranta, M., Pnevmatikos, D., & Christodoulou, P. (2022). Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10114-y

article_title: Structured or unstructured educational robotics curriculum? A study of debugging in block-based programming
citation: Chrysanthos Socratous, Andri Ioannou. (2021). Structured or unstructured educational robotics curriculum? A study of debugging in block-based programming.
title: Structured versus unstructured educational robotics curriculum comparison design for block-based programming
description: The study implements a quasi-experimental comparison of two educational robotics curricula for young learners working in block-based programming: "a structured ER curriculum group and an unstructured one". Within the quasi-experiment, "both qualitative and quantitative data are collected", covering error frequency and type, debugging ability, and engagement in the learning process.
requirements: Two comparison groups, one following a structured ER curriculum and one an unstructured ER curriculum
constraints: Quasi-experimental design with two comparison groups (n = 35), not a randomized experiment
target_learners: young learners in block-based programming contexts
target_learning_goals: debugging programs
reducing programming errors
engagement in the learning process
examples: The study compared a structured ER curriculum group with an unstructured one (n = 35), collecting qualitative and quantitative data on errors, debugging, and engagement.
key_sources: Chrysanthos Socratous, Andri Ioannou. (2021). Structured or unstructured educational robotics curriculum? A study of debugging in block-based programming. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10056-x

article_title: Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students' performance in the physics lab
citation: Gómez-Tejedor, J. A., Vidaurre, A., Tort-Ausina, I., Molina-Mateo, J., Serrano, M.-A., Meseguer-Dueñas, J. M., Martínez Sala, R. M., Quiles, S., & Riera, J. (2020). Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students’ performance in the physics lab. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103708
title: Introduce flip teaching progressively, starting with laboratory practices.
description: The article recommends that institutions adopting flip teaching begin with laboratory sessions rather than lectures, because the lab offers the clearest gain: pre-class videos free session time from long teacher explanations for discussion and experimental work. The authors state that as a general conclusion FT “works very well for lab sessions in technical degree courses” and that “For a progressive application of FT, we recommend starting the experience with the laboratory practices.”
requirements: Pre-class documents and videos must be available on an online platform, and lab-work design should be directly related in content and timing to the rest of the subject's learning activities.
constraints: Evidence comes from Physics and Electricity courses in one engineering degree; the authors advise caution in extrapolating the results to non-STEM disciplines.
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students
target_learning_goals: laboratory performance
autonomous learning
academic results in practical sessions
examples: At the Universitat Politècnica de València, FT was introduced into lab sessions from the first day of class, with teachers' explanations reduced to answering doubts about out-of-class learning.
key_sources: Gómez-Tejedor, J. A., Vidaurre, A., Tort-Ausina, I., Molina-Mateo, J., Serrano, M.-A., Meseguer-Dueñas, J. M., Martínez Sala, R. M., Quiles, S., & Riera, J. (2020). Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students’ performance in the physics lab. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103708

article_title: Immersive virtual reality serious games for evacuation training and research: A systematic literature review
citation: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://www.scopus.com
title: Static and dynamic simulated hazards in IVR evacuation serious games
description: The review categorizes simulated hazards in IVR SGs into two levels. Static hazards do not interact with participants and are used to "increase fear perception, trigger events, constrain moving area , and improve environment al realism", such as a burning vehicle blocking an evacuation way or an engine failure triggering evacuation. Dynamic hazards interact with participants and provide negative experience, such as losing visibility in smoke, blood-spattered eyes after a head hit, or falling and fragile objects hurting virtual bodies during an earthquake simulation. Participants face these realistic hazards in a completely safe environment.
requirements: IVR SGs need to integrate corresponding functions to carry out analysis for pre-defined behavior outcomes
constraints: Dynamic hazards should be chosen depending on the research purposes and participants' backgrounds
target_learners: building occupants training for indoor emergencies
target_learning_goals: hazard perception and risk awareness
self-protection strategies such as crawling under smoke
examples: Smith and Ericson (2009) suggested participants crawl on the floor to get under the smoke as the correct behavior; Li et al. (2017) used falling and fragile objects so participants needed a self-protection strategy
key_sources: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.002

article_title: Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies
citation: Jo Tondeur, Ottavia Trevisan, Sarah K. Howard, Johan van Braak. (2025). Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies. Computers & Education 232. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105262
title: Structure teacher training programs to afford opportunities for preservice teachers to experience and experiment with digital technologies and different approaches to learning
description: The review's institutional-level finding holds that teacher training programs should be deliberately designed so preservice teachers encounter and try out digital technologies and varied pedagogical approaches, including stand-alone ICT courses and modelled delivery modes such as online, hybrid and blended learning. As the article states, "Teacher training programs need to be structurally designed to afford opportunities for preservice teachers to experience and experiment with digital technologies and different approaches to learning." This underpins the SQD2 institutional vision synthesis.
requirements: Institutional guidance on expectations for different modes of delivery, and teaching courses that model desired approaches and learning designs
constraints: Grounded in qualitative evidence aggregated across 15 countries; the review notes the optimal combination of strategies depends on each teacher's unique profile
target_learners: preservice teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: digital competence and technology-integrated pedagogical design
examples: Eutsler (2022) designed learning tasks modelling the gradual release of responsibility — Teacher as Control, Teacher as Facilitator and Problem-based learning — and the review reports the value of stand-alone ICT courses (Dewa & Ndlovu, 2022; Şen & Hava, 2020)
key_sources: Jo Tondeur, Ottavia Trevisan, Sarah K. Howard, Johan van Braak. (2025). Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies. Computers & Education 232. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105262

article_title: Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study
citation: Romero-Zaldivar, V.-A., Pardo, A., Burgos, D., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2012). Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1058–1067. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.003
title: Give students control over the monitoring mechanism to comply with data protection rules
description: The article's deployment treated compliance with data protection legislation as a design requirement: students were shown an explanatory page before downloading the appliance, could disable monitoring, and a machine without monitoring was offered as an alternative. Recorded events were also kept in plain text in the student's own folder so students "may exercise the right to review, amend or delete any of the collected events". The authors state that this compliance "translates basically into giving students total control over the monitoring mechanism".
requirements: Students must be informed explicitly, precisely and unequivocally of the data file's existence, purpose, recipients, the voluntary nature of monitoring, and their rights of access, rectification, erasure and objection
constraints: The policy may have a significant impact on the amount of data collected, since students can disable monitoring at any point
target_learners: university students whose course activities are monitored
target_learning_goals: ethical, legally compliant collection of learning interaction data for analytics
examples: Before downloading the virtual machine, students saw a web page explaining the monitoring mechanism and had to agree; a non-monitored machine was also available
key_sources: Romero-Zaldivar, V.-A., Pardo, A., Burgos, D., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2012). Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1058–1067. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.003

article_title: An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS
citation: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/
title: Student knowledge components: overlay SEMs, misconception SEMs and bugs library
description: Student knowledge is constructed during interaction as overlay knowledge of the domain and diagnosed misconceptions, complemented by a bugs library. Student overlay SEMs record the instance name, strength of acquired knowledge rated between 0 and 1, the successful tutoring strategy used, and media segments used. Student misconception SEMs record incorrect answers with seriousness rated between -1 and 0, and the bugs library contains mal SEMs with common misconceptions.
requirements: student interaction with the system to construct overlay knowledge
target_learners: students interacting with the tutoring system
target_learning_goals: tracking acquired knowledge and misconceptions
key_sources: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/

article_title: Women and computers. Effects of stereotype threat on attribution of failure
citation: Koch, S. C., Müller, S. M., & Sieverding, M. (2008). Women and computers. Effects of stereotype threat on attribution of failure. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.05.007
title: Stereotype threat theory applied to the computer domain links threat to maladaptive attribution patterns
description: The article applies stereotype threat theory (Steele, 1997) to the computer domain, proposing that when a negative task-relevant stereotype about one's ingroup becomes salient, performance impairments and maladaptive attributions follow. The authors state that "maladaptive attribution patterns can be caused by stereotype threat in the minority group (in our study, women), and can be a point of reference for their future performance." The study bridges attribution theory and stereotype threat theory in the computer domain.
requirements: Conditions for stereotype threat include domain identification, task difficulty, and stereotype relevance to the situation
constraints: The effect was demonstrated only in the negative threat condition; no significant gender differences emerged in the positive or control conditions
target_learners: college-age students (16–21 years)
target_learning_goals: computer self-efficacy
attribution patterns after failure
key_sources: Koch, S. C., Müller, S. M., & Sieverding, M. (2008). Women and computers. Effects of stereotype threat on attribution of failure. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.05.007

article_title: Digital support for academic writing: A review of technologies and pedagogies
citation: Strobl, Carola; Ailhaud, Emilie; Benetos, Kalliopi; Devitt, Ann; Kruse, Otto. (2019). Digital support for academic writing : a review of technologies and pedagogies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.12.005
title: Review framework mapping writing-support technologies across writing processes, pedagogical approaches, feedback modalities and technological specifications
description: The review organises the field of digital writing-support technologies using a framework of 26 quantitative and qualitative features spanning four axes: writing processes, pedagogical approaches, feedback modalities and technological specifications. It applies this framework to a systematic analysis of 44 tools supporting first and second language writers in secondary and higher education, focusing on "instructional affordances based on their technological specifications". The framework also distinguishes micro-level revision support from macro-level strategy support, enabling the review to locate gaps in the state of the art.
requirements: Applies to technologies designed to support writing instruction in secondary and higher education, for first and second language writers
constraints: Previous studies centred on Automated Writing Evaluation, Automated Essay Scoring and rarer Intelligent Tutoring Systems, addressing mainly essay writing needs in US secondary school instruction
target_learners: secondary and higher education students, first and second language writers
target_learning_goals: academic writing
revision
writing strategies
key_sources: Strobl, Carola; Ailhaud, Emilie; Benetos, Kalliopi; Devitt, Ann; Kruse, Otto. (2019). Digital support for academic writing : a review of technologies and pedagogies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.12.005

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Storyboard design elements to maintain: abstracted interfaces, participant icons, imported data, peer feedback, test plans
description: The article enumerates elements to maintain when repeating the exercise: "Abstracted interfaces" with functionality in a black box, "Participant icons and call outs" capturing assumptions about collaborative learning, "Imported classroom data" from pupils' written strategies, "Peer feedback", and "Storyboards as test plans" for the first prototype.
requirements: Peer feedback channels must be opened through sharable storyboard documentation
target_learners: primary school pupils
target_learning_goals: collaborative mathematics learning
examples: A black box marked TOOLS reminded the designer to keep interface functionality shut; C and R icons with call outs captured hypothesised interactions
key_sources: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.01.002

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Storyboarding pitfalls to avoid: hidden assumptions, proceduralism, inefficiency
description: The article also lists elements to avoid: "Hidden assumptions", since an interface assumption grounded in the Equivalence Calculator haunted the early storyboards despite abstraction attempts; "Proceduralism", because overcoming an implementation impasse involves exposing hidden assumptions rather than following a smooth process; and "Inefficiency", as many slides were created over six months.
requirements: Awareness that interface assumptions may persist implicitly even when not represented
constraints: Storyboarding continued for six months with many slides created before guidelines were identified
target_learners: task designers and researchers
target_learning_goals: robust learning task design
key_sources: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.01.002

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Storyboards as virtual data from thought experiments
description: The article frames the storyboards produced as "virtual data" captured from thought experiments about imagined learning tasks. Thought experiments draw on the educational literature, the curriculum domain and the designer's professional intuitions, and the storyboards make their outcomes analysable and sharable: "analysable, sharable thought experiments about notational activity, pupil discourse and the role of R in imagined trials". This responds to Papert's call for a more developed culture of disciplined thought experiment.
requirements: Sharable documentation so that peers can review the thought experiments
constraints: Thought experiments have been acknowledged to lack the rigour and systematicity of actual experiments
target_learners: primary school pupils
target_learning_goals: relational understanding of the equals sign
key_sources: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2008.01.002

article_title: Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process
citation: Hujala, M., Knutas, A., Hynninen, T., & Arminen, H. (2020). Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103965
title: Streamlined four-step process for systematic analysis of written student feedback
description: The article proposes a repeatable mixed-methods pipeline that "combines text mining to pre-sort the open-ended feedback" with thematic analysis and multilevel modelling. It consists of four main steps: data collection, LDA topic model generation, evaluation of topic-model outcomes (qualitative via thematic analysis and quantitative via multilevel modelling), and reporting. The process is intended for programme- or institution-wide analysis of open-ended feedback rather than for an individual lecturer, and it connects qualitative findings to existing SET literature and quantitative feedback data.
requirements: Requires student feedback surveys that include both Likert-scale and open-ended questions, so that topic-model outcomes can be evaluated against numerical SET dimensions.
Requires large masses of open-ended text responses to distinguish meaningful themes within the feedback.
constraints: The authors state the process is novel and requires further evaluation to establish its full validity.
The process is aimed at programme- or institution-level analysis, not at an individual lecturer extracting topics from their own course feedback.
target_learners: university students
higher education institutions
target_learning_goals: evaluation of teaching quality
quality assurance of degree programmes
key_sources: Hujala, M., Knutas, A., Hynninen, T., & Arminen, H. (2020). Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103965

article_title: The Effect of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics-STEM Educational Practices on Students' Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Saraç, H. (2018). The Effect of Science, Technology, Engin eering and Mathematics-Stem Educational Practices on Students’ Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(2). https://www.tojet.net
title: STEM education as an integrated, engineering-design-based approach bridging science, technology, engineering and mathematics
description: The article frames STEM education as an approach that integrates the four disciplines rather than teaching them separately: "The aim of STEM education is to achieve an approach that focuses on the integration of learning by establishing a relationship between the disciplines, rather than being separate from each other". It describes technology and engineering design-based STEM as integrating knowledge and skills across the areas in teaching mathematics and science, and as a method by which students approach problems from a multidisciplinary point of view while gaining twenty-first century skills such as critical thinking, problem solving, co-operation, and communication.
requirements: Teaching that establishes relationships between the STEM disciplines, e.g. by connecting a unit or lesson to real-life problems
constraints: The article notes STEM integration had not yet become widespread in Turkey at the time of writing, with work in the area still in its infancy
target_learners: primary and secondary school students
higher education students
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary knowledge integration
twenty-first century skills such as problem solving, creativity and scientific thinking
examples: The reviewed STEM practices were applied across science (23 effect sizes), mathematics (17), technology (3), and other areas, at primary/secondary, high school, and university levels
key_sources: Saraç, H. (2018). The Effect of Science, Technology, Engin eering and Mathematics-Stem Educational Practices on Students’ Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis Study. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176176

article_title: The Impact of Stratified Teaching on the Academic Performance of Chinese Middle School Students: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012
title: Taxonomy of stratified teaching types: hierarchical grouped fix-class, hierarchical shift-class, and in-class hierarchical systems
description: The article defines stratified teaching as a strategy, model, and ideology in which teachers "divide students scientifically into groups of similar levels based on their current knowledge, abilities, and potential, and then teaches them accordingly". It organizes implementation into a taxonomy of three systems: the "hierarchical grouped fix-class teaching system", the "hierarchical shift-class teaching system", and the "in-class hierarchical teaching system". In-class stratification is further split into "dominant stratification", where students know their own and others' placement, and "recessive stratification", where only the teacher (or teacher and individual student/parent) knows. The meta-analysis uses this taxonomy to code and compare intervention modes.
requirements: Teachers assess students' current knowledge, abilities, and potential to assign levels, and at least two teachers teach the experimental and control groups separately per the article's inclusion criteria.
constraints: In the Chinese context, large-scale actual stratified teaching is not allowed, only small-scale experiments, according to the article.
target_learners: middle school students
high school students
target_learning_goals: academic performance in basic education subjects
examples: The 22 included studies were coded by intervention method into in-class dominant (PO), in-class recessive (NE), in-class general (GE), shift-class (TR), and combined (MI) modes.
key_sources: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012

article_title: The Impact of Stratified Teaching on the Academic Performance of Chinese Middle School Students: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012
title: Base stratification on abilities, motivation, interests, and cognitive structure — not performance alone — or stratification becomes diversion
description: The article warns that stratified teaching works as differentiated instruction only when grouping reflects more than achievement scores. It states that "in most studies, stratified teaching stratification is based on student performance and does not take into account factors such as student abilities, motivation, interests, and cognitive structure", and that without considering these factors "the stratification will evolve into a diversion", no different from fast and slow class teaching. The principle directs implementers to group on a broader profile of learner characteristics.
requirements: Teachers must gather information on student abilities, motivation, interests, and cognitive structure before assigning strata.
constraints: The article notes stratified teaching follows the principle of teaching students according to their aptitude and advancing step by step, but in practice grouping often reduces to performance-based placement.
target_learners: middle school students
high school students
target_learning_goals: academic performance
personalized learning
examples: The article's problems section describes the risk that performance-based stratification becomes diversion comparable to fast and slow class teaching in some middle schools.
key_sources: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012

article_title: A competency-based curriculum for geriatric dentistry in undergraduate and postgraduate education : a scoping review.
citation: Kim Junhewk, Kim So Yeon, Jung Hoi-In, Kang Jeong-Hyun. (2026). A competency-based curriculum for geriatric dentistry in undergraduate and postgraduate education : a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09625-6
title: A staged competency-based framework for geriatric dental education with 6 core competencies, 34 sub-competencies, and 72 enabling competencies
description: The review derives a three-level hierarchical competency framework mapping eight curricular themes onto six core competency domains. The article reports that "In total, 6 core competencies, 34 sub-competencies, and 72 enabling competencies, were identified." Core competencies guide program-level planning, sub-competencies inform course or module design, and enabling competencies support specific measurable learning outcomes and assessment criteria across undergraduate and postgraduate levels.
requirements: Themes mapped to competency domains through thematic synthesis of the included literature; the framework is intended for curriculum design at different levels of specificity
constraints: Specific learning outcomes "may require further contextual refinement according to educational level, institutional setting, and assessment purpose"
target_learners: Undergraduate dental students
Postgraduate dental trainees
target_learning_goals: Geriatric dental practice competencies including aging-related changes, oral health management, interdisciplinary communication, and ethical and legal considerations
examples: The review mapped eight thematic categories to six competency domains, e.g., merging public health and aging-related changes into core competency 1
key_sources: Kim Junhewk, Kim So Yeon, Jung Hoi-In, Kang Jeong-Hyun. (2026). A competency-based curriculum for geriatric dentistry in undergraduate and postgraduate education : a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09625-6

article_title: A competency-based curriculum for geriatric dentistry in undergraduate and postgraduate education : a scoping review.
citation: Kim Junhewk, Kim So Yeon, Jung Hoi-In, Kang Jeong-Hyun. (2026). A competency-based curriculum for geriatric dentistry in undergraduate and postgraduate education : a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09625-6
title: Stage competency expectations across educational levels: undergraduate education targets foundational knowing and applying, postgraduate training targets demonstrated performance and independent practice with frail older adults
description: The review proposes differentiating competency expectations by educational stage within a single framework. Bold enabling competencies in its Table 6 denote postgraduate and continuing education expectations, while non-bold ones represent undergraduate expectations. The article states "Undergraduate education is intended to establish foundational competencies... Postgraduate and continuing education are intended to develop advanced competencies for supervised practice with frail, dependent, or medically complex older adults in outreach settings," aligning with Miller's pyramid progression.
requirements: A hierarchical competency structure distinguishing undergraduate from postgraduate enabling competencies
constraints: The review notes one prior US competency set "did not establish clear continuity with undergraduate curricula," which this staged structure addresses
target_learners: Undergraduate dental students
Postgraduate dental trainees
target_learning_goals: Progression from explaining concepts such as oral frailty to assessing it with evaluation tools in practice
examples: At the undergraduate level students are expected to explain the concept of oral frailty, whereas postgraduate graduates are expected to assess oral frailty using appropriate evaluation tools

article_title: Instruments for Assessing Basic Life Support Knowledge in Secondary School Students: A Scoping Review and Expert Panel.
citation: Mecías‐Calvo M., Sobrido‐Prieto M., Navarro‐Patón R. (2026). Instruments for Assessing Basic Life Support Knowledge in Secondary School Students: A Scoping Review and Expert Panel. The Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.70223
title: Use standardized, psychometrically validated, and culturally/linguistically appropriate assessment tools to ensure uniform and equitable BLS training evaluation across schools
description: The review's central recommendation for school health policy and practice: BLS programs should employ standardized assessment tools incorporating all chain-of-survival elements, replacing brief ad hoc questionnaires. The authors state that "Education should focus on culturally and linguistically appropriate tools, with age‐appropriate response formats," which would improve reliability and fairness and "reduce inequalities between schools and countries." Standardized measurement is framed as the path to comparable assessments and equitable, inclusive BLS training.
requirements: Assessment instruments should include clearly defined domains such as BLS, CPR techniques, identification of cardiac arrest, calling emergency services, functional AED use, and scene safety.
constraints: Policies should promote implementation and evaluation in resource-limited settings to prevent increased disparities in emergency response capacity.
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: basic life support knowledge including CPR and AED use
examples: The review identifies gaps in content regarding scene safety, initial recognition, and AED use that should be strengthened in future questionnaires.

article_title: The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review.
citation: Amechghal A, Naciri A, Takhdat K, Loubbairi S, Mellouki A, Lahlou L, Nassik H. (2026). The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.24
title: Design observer roles as intentional pedagogy with defined learning objectives, validated observation tools, and active debriefing involvement
description: The review reframes the observer role "from a logistical compromise to an intentional teaching strategy," recommending that "observer roles should therefore be designed with defined learning objectives, validated observation tools, and active involvement in debriefing." It supports this with evidence that directed observation supported by checklists or role-specific forms may enhance active watching and listening, and that studies using structured observer tools reported outcomes as good as, or better than, those of active participants.
requirements: Faculty development and audiovisual infrastructure to support high-quality observer engagement
Defined learning objectives, validated observation tools, and active observer involvement in debriefing
constraints: Formal equivalence between roles has not been established; evidence concentrated in nursing programs in high-income countries
target_learners: Health professions students and trainees in simulation-based education
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, skills, and attitudinal outcomes comparable to active participation
examples: All 15 included studies involved observers in shared debriefing, and 7 studies used directed observation with checklists or role-specific forms
key_sources: Amechghal A, Naciri A, Takhdat K, Loubbairi S, Mellouki A, Lahlou L, Nassik H. (2026). The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.24

article_title: Mapping the evidence on public health competency assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review.
citation: Hernández Rincón Erwin Hernando, González Garcés Mariana, Montoya Jerónimo Cárdenas, Fernández Valeria Concha, Torres Mario Andrés Torres, Vargas Villafañe Nicolle Valeria, Chaves Natalia Castaño. (2026). Mapping the evidence on public health competency assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09976-0
title: Structural typology of public health competency assessment strategies organised into nine evaluative domains
description: The review proposes a structural typology (Table 3) that classifies assessment strategies into evaluative domains rather than by individual instruments. As the review states, "The analysis allowed identification of a structural typology of assessment strategies that transcends classification by individual instruments, organising itself into evaluative domains that reflect different levels of integration between competency, context and method (Table 3)." The domains span experiential evaluation in real-world contexts, evaluation in clinical settings, structured curricular evaluation, assessment of equity and social determinants competencies, structured simulation, technology-mediated assessment, longitudinal assessment, institutional/systems evaluation, and conceptual/normative development. Each domain pairs a central evaluative logic with representative strategies, competency level, context, instruments and educational contribution.
requirements: Applies to assessment of public health competencies in undergraduate medical education as mapped in the included studies
constraints: The typology is an inductive conceptual classification grounded in the 30 included studies, not a validated assessment framework
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: Public health competencies including epidemiology, health promotion, social determinants of health, community engagement and health advocacy
examples: The review maps community projects, service learning, fieldwork and patient-based learning into the experiential real-world domain, citing studies [10–13, 19, 26, 27, 33]

article_title: Characterization of the learning environment for teaching pharmaceutical care: a scoping review.
citation: Ribeiro MAL, Hohenfeld DWA, Tavares TMA, Araújo-Neto FC, Mesquita AR, Brito GC, Lyra Jr DP. (2026). Characterization of the learning environment for teaching pharmaceutical care: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08876-7
title: Student-centered active-methods pattern in pharmaceutical care teaching environments
description: The included studies' teaching environments reflect a transition from traditional teacher-centered models to student-centered pedagogical approaches using technological resources and active methods. The review reports that "Different methods were observed, and the most used were PBL (n = 2) and experience-based learning (n = 2)", alongside team-based learning, students as partners, competence-based learning, e-learning, and simulated activities. The pattern demands students be more active participants in the teaching and learning process.
requirements: Environments should explore the use of active methods
constraints: The review reports challenges in meeting the expectations of advanced students and the need for continuous innovation (e-learning study)
target_learners: Pharmacy students across course years
target_learning_goals: Pharmaceutical care competencies, clinical communication, dispensing skills, critical thinking
examples: Table 5 lists each study's strategy and main results, e.g., a PBL study where the "Prompts group overcame control group in all phases of problem solving"

article_title: Refining competency benchmarks: a scoping review of Angoff standard-setting in dental education.
citation: Lin Galvin Sim Siang, Hisham Abdul Rauf Badrul, Majid Muhammad Nazmi Abdul, Foong Chan Choong, Ho Ting Khee, Friedlander Lara T. (2026). Refining competency benchmarks: a scoping review of Angoff standard-setting in dental education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08195-9
title: Taxonomy of standard-setting methods: norm-referenced, criterion-referenced, and compromise approaches
description: The review organises standard-setting methods into three categories. Norm-referenced (relative) methods determine cut-off scores from assessment results by comparing candidates to peers, and are "not widely used for high-stakes examinations". Criterion-referenced (absolute) methods, such as the Angoff and Ebel methods, set the cut-off independently of assessment results relative to test content. Compromise methods, including Hofstee and Hofstee-Angoff, combine both approaches. The review uses this taxonomy to situate the Angoff method as a widely utilised criterion-referenced technique relying on expert judgment of the minimally competent candidate.
requirements: A panel of subject-matter experts to judge item difficulty and establish the cut-off score
constraints: Norm-referenced methods focus on relative comparison of performance and are not widely used for high-stakes examinations, per the review
target_learners: undergraduate dental students
foreign-trained dentists taking licensure proficiency tests
target_learning_goals: establishing valid cut-off scores for summative competency assessment in dental education
examples: The review's ten included studies applied Angoff, Modified Angoff, Hofstee, Cohen, Modified Cohen, relative (Mean, SD), and Borderline Regression methods across MCQ, SAQ and OSCE assessments
key_sources: Lin Galvin Sim Siang, Hisham Abdul Rauf Badrul, Majid Muhammad Nazmi Abdul, Foong Chan Choong, Ho Ting Khee, Friedlander Lara T. (2026). Refining competency benchmarks: a scoping review of Angoff standard-setting in dental education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08195-9

article_title: From operating room to leadership room: a systematic review of simulation-based interventions for leadership development in general surgery.
citation: Gulnaz Nadia, Soomro Faiza Hashim, Nazir Izza, Ansar Mehwish, Arshad Rabia. (2026). From operating room to leadership room: a systematic review of simulation-based interventions for leadership development in general surgery. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09486-z
title: Use structured debriefing as the central mechanism linking simulated leadership experience to real-life practice
description: Across all included studies, debriefing was the instructional component through which learners connected simulated crisis experience to clinical practice. The review states that "Debriefing was identified as a fundamental component that supported the concept of leadership development in all the studies." Structured formats such as the Diamond debrief (Description → Analysis → Application), the BID model, and focused video review were prevalent, and the authors recommend focusing on faculty training in debriefing to optimize educational impact.

Structured debrief formats (e.g., Diamond debrief, BID model), often including video review
constraints: Debriefing formats in the reviewed studies ranged from a few minutes of focused feedback to 30 minutes or more of structured formats
target_learners: Surgical trainees and multidisciplinary operating room teams
target_learning_goals: Leadership behaviors
Reflective practice
Crisis management skills
examples: Baste et al. (2021) used the Diamond 3-phase debrief with video feedback after high-fidelity crisis scenarios
Parsons et al. (2017) used a structured 30-minute debrief after each SimMan 3G scenario

article_title: Understanding simulation-based learning for health professions students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds: a scoping review.
citation: Zhang Luocheng, Patterson Freyr, Penman Adriana, Forbes Roma. (2025). Understanding simulation-based learning for health professions students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds: a scoping review. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10384-6
title: Provide well-structured pre-simulation preparation for CALD students without overwhelming them
description: The review recommends that SBL programs include "well-structured preparatory sessions that consider the additional needs of students from CALD backgrounds without overwhelming them", since processing information in another language can be overwhelming. Preparation such as orientation, pre-reading and goal-setting helped students understand context, set objectives, and feel more confident.

constraints: students reported challenges due to lack of preparation time before SBL experiences
target_learners: health professions students from CALD backgrounds

confidence for clinical placements
