article_title: The effects of problem-based learning (PBL) on undergraduate medical students' critical thinking and communication skills development: A scoping review across resource-rich and resource-limited settings (2015-2024).
citation: Abugri Bruce Ayabilla, Assibi Maxwell Ateni, Amalba Anthony, Gaa Patience Kanyiri, Kpebu Sophia E.A., Karikari Patience Afua Adwaapa, Mogre Victor. (2026). The effects of problem-based learning (PBL) on undergraduate medical students' critical thinking and communication skills development: A scoping review across resource-rich and resource-limited settings (2015-2024). PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342599
title: Support first-year medical students transitioning to PBL with structured orientation, guided early cases, and explicit collaboration teaching
description: The review recommends that because first-year students often struggle with self-direction and teamwork, "PBL should begin with structured orientation sessions that introduce its goals and methods". Early cases should be guided and gradually increase in complexity as students gain confidence, and educators should teach collaboration explicitly rather than assuming teamwork will develop naturally. This responds to the review's finding that first-year students face challenges transitioning from lecture-based instruction to self-directed, collaborative learning.
requirements: Structured orientation sessions introducing PBL goals and methods before full PBL participation
constraints: Recommended specifically for first-year students transitioning from traditional lecture-based instruction
target_learners: first-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
communication skills
self-directed learning
examples: The review recommends guided early cases that gradually increase in complexity as students gain confidence
key_sources: Abugri Bruce Ayabilla, Assibi Maxwell Ateni, Amalba Anthony, Gaa Patience Kanyiri, Kpebu Sophia E.A., Karikari Patience Afua Adwaapa, Mogre Victor. (2026). The effects of problem-based learning (PBL) on undergraduate medical students' critical thinking and communication skills development: A scoping review across resource-rich and resource-limited settings (2015-2024). PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342599

article_title: Early clinical exposure in undergraduate dental education: a systematic review of effectiveness, experiences, and outcomes.
citation: Gadbail AR, Gondivkar SM, Yuwanati M, Sonone A, Dhamande M, Panchbhai A, Sarode SC. (2026). Early clinical exposure in undergraduate dental education: a systematic review of effectiveness, experiences, and outcomes. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08692-z
title: Use standardized, validated, objective outcome measures in ECE research to enable comparability
description: The review finds that reliability and validity reporting varied across included studies, with about half providing clear validation evidence and others little or none. It concludes there is "necessity of employing standardized and validated outcome measures in ECE in dental education research for the sake of study comparability and enhancing confidence in results." Future studies should prioritize robust objective performance measures with multicentre designs and longitudinal follow-up.
requirements: Validated assessment instruments appropriate to study design
Objective performance measures rather than sole reliance on self-report
constraints: The review notes many existing studies relied on self-reported outcomes prone to social desirability bias that tend to overestimate positive outcomes
target_learners: Undergraduate dental students
target_learning_goals: Clinical knowledge
Psychomotor skills
Clinical reasoning
key_sources: Gadbail AR, Gondivkar SM, Yuwanati M, Sonone A, Dhamande M, Panchbhai A, Sarode SC. (2026). Early clinical exposure in undergraduate dental education: a systematic review of effectiveness, experiences, and outcomes. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08692-z

article_title: Simulate to stimulate? A systematic review of stress, learning, and performance in healthcare simulation.
citation: Vage A, Spence AD, McKeown G, Gormley GJ, Hamilton PK. (2024). Simulate to stimulate? A systematic review of stress, learning, and performance in healthcare simulation. The Ulster Medical Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11591218/
title: Design simulation courses with structured briefing and debriefing and avoid relying on extensively stressful content as a learning tool
description: The review recommends that because simulation scenarios as sole learning tools are often ineffective and potentially detrimental, course designers should add adjunctive measures. It states that "adjunctive measures such as effective briefing and debriefing should be strongly considered in course design", and that extensively stressful content may not be as beneficial as previously thought.
requirements: Structured pre-scenario briefing and post-scenario debriefing processes, which the review associates with improved instructional and learning outcomes
constraints: The review notes substantial heterogeneity between studies and a paucity of evidence, so this recommendation rests on a sparse evidence base
target_learners: healthcare students
junior medical residents
healthcare professionals in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: clinical and procedural performance under stress
resuscitation and emergency skills
examples: The review found only two of eleven impaired-performance studies mentioned structured briefing and debriefing, while three performed neither brief nor debrief
key_sources: Vage A, Spence AD, McKeown G, Gormley GJ, Hamilton PK. (2024). Simulate to stimulate? A systematic review of stress, learning, and performance in healthcare simulation. The Ulster Medical Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11591218/

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Develop standardised assessment tools with proven reliability and validity for end-point procedural skills certification
description: The review's central recommendation is that medical education needs standardised tools with proven reliability and validity for assessing procedural skills competence at the end of medical training. It argues that "There is a need to develop standardised tools with proven reliability and validity for assessment of procedural skills competence at the end of medical training", so that graduates have comparable skill levels irrespective of country of training. Currently institution-specific checklists lead to inequity of assessment before qualification.
requirements: Tools must have established reliability and validity ensuring unambiguous identification of competence or incompetence in procedural skills
constraints: Procedural skills competence is a complex entity that is not easily objectively defined and is specific not generic
target_learners: medical students at the end of their primary medical degree
target_learning_goals: procedural skills competence prior to certification
examples: The review found no currently used tool in the pre-certification setting has established construct validity, motivating the call for new validated instruments
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review.
citation: Taveira-Gomes T, Ferreira P, Taveira-Gomes I, Severo M, Ferreira MA. (2016). What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.5461
title: CBL research should continue shifting toward student-centered models, measuring online activity, and reporting instructional design
description: The review's forward-looking principle: "The shift to student-centered models needs to continue," supported by empowering students to study at their own pace, richer interactions with materials, and facilitated communication. It further recommends real-time collection of student activity with objective performance assessment for predictive value, and reporting instructional design considerations so intervention effects can be attributed.
requirements: Studies should report instructional design considerations and comparable comparison arms so intervention effects can be assessed
constraints: Only a few current reports put students at the center of the education process, focusing usually on teaching-related aspects
target_learners: medical students
medical residents
target_learning_goals: student self-directedness
engagement
predicting learning outcomes
examples: The review highlights social media, reward-based systems, collaborative user-generated content, and 3D virtual worlds as approaches to promote student-centered CBL
key_sources: Taveira-Gomes T, Ferreira P, Taveira-Gomes I, Severo M, Ferreira MA. (2016). What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.5461

article_title: Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education
citation: Chun-Yi Shen & Hsiu-Chuan Liu. (2011). Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Structured, procedural, and visualized design characteristics of the effective self-plan section
description: The authors identify three characteristics that distinguished the self-plan section, where gains were strongest: "Structured—the structure of the knowledge to be delivered was analyzed in advance"; "Procedural—Concept maps and hierarchical maps were utilized to display how to use metacognitive strategies step by step"; and "Visualized—complicated concepts could be clearly expressed through use of visualizing tools." This pattern links advance analysis of knowledge structure, step-by-step strategy display, and visualization to metacognitive skill gains.
requirements: The structure of the knowledge to be delivered must be analyzed in advance and displayed with multimedia to enhance comprehension and memory
constraints: The authors state this explanation is their inference about why the self-plan section succeeded, not a separately tested result
target_learners: college students in web-based instruction
target_learning_goals: self-planning and organized use of metacognitive strategies
examples: The self-plan section used a concept map and hierarchical graphics to display metacognitive strategy use step by step
key_sources: Chun-Yi Shen & Hsiu-Chuan Liu. (2011). Metacognitive Skills Development: A Web-Based Approach in Higher Education. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ932234

article_title: The Effect of Reflective Science Journal Writing on Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies
citation: Nawar M. Al-Rawahi & Sulaiman M. Al-Balushi. (2015). The Effect of Reflective Science Journal Writing on Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 10(3), 367-379.
title: Structured reflective science journal writing model with six components
description: A journal-writing model (Figure 1) in which students write after each science lesson using six components drawn from Table 1: lesson goals, dialogues with the self, teacher and classmates, scientific observations, main conclusions, assessment of their level of understanding, and personal feelings. The article states the model "encourages students to produce internal feedback on their learning process" and that students were given a model journal to complete after lessons, starting in class and finishing at home.
requirements: Journals are structured around self-reflections on learning goals, learning strategies, observations, understanding, feeling, and dialogues with oneself and others
Students need time during each lesson to start writing and complete journals at home
The teacher collects, comments on, and returns the journals each lesson
constraints: The journal writing used is structured writing in which students fill in spaces in response to pre-determined questions, which the authors name as a limitation of the study
target_learners: tenth-grade science students (15 years old)
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategies in school science (motivation and learning strategies)
examples: Students reflected on an endothermic reaction experiment, on station activities, and on difficulties such as distinguishing single from double displacement reactions
key_sources: Nawar M. Al-Rawahi & Sulaiman M. Al-Balushi. (2015). The Effect of Reflective Science Journal Writing on Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 10(3), 367-379. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1069260

article_title: Scaffolding in a Medicine Education Intervention for Student Teachers Based on the PROFILES Three Stage Model
citation: Sirpa Kärkkäinen, Jari Kukkonen and Tuula Keinonen. (2014). Scaffolding in a Medicine Education Intervention for Student Teachers Based on the PROFILES Three Stage Model. ceps Journal, Vol. 4, No. 1. https://journals.cepsj.si
title: Structure collaborative inquiry tasks with templates so scaffolding supports intensive work and sense making
description: The article's structuring principle holds that scaffolding collaborative inquiry through prepared templates and a shared online environment helps learners work intensively and make sense of the task. The authors conclude that "by structuring the activity with Google Sites and presentation templates, scaffolding helps student teachers to work intensively and to prepare their presentations", and that "presentation modelling seems to be beneficial to the students’ sense making process during the investigation". In the study this was implemented as a presentation template covering all three PROFILES stages.
requirements: A structured environment (Google Sites with case and presentation templates) covering the phases of the inquiry task
constraints: Evidence comes from a small qualitative study of six student teachers in two groups; the article calls for further research on scaffolding and ICT in medicine education
target_learners: primary school teacher students
target_learning_goals: sense making during inquiry
collaborative case-based reasoning
preparing and justifying presentations
examples: The scaffolded group annotated and uploaded a presentation template spanning the Scenario, Inquiry and Decision-making Stages, while the unscaffolded group built their presentations themselves in Word documents
key_sources: Sirpa Kärkkäinen, Jari Kukkonen and Tuula Keinonen. (2014). Scaffolding in a Medicine Education Intervention for Student Teachers Based on the PROFILES Three Stage Model. ceps Journal, Vol. 4, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1129505

article_title: The Effect of Instructional Methods (Lecture-Discussion versus Group Discussion) and Teaching Talent on Teacher Trainees Student Learning Outcomes
citation: Mutrofin, Degeng, I.N.S., Ardhana, I.W., & Setyosari, P. (2017). The Effect of Instructional Methods (Lecture-Discussion versus Group Discussion) and Teaching Talent on Teacher Trainees Student Learning Outcomes. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143985
title: Standardized achievement test of learning and instruction based on Merrill's Component Display Theory
description: Student learning outcomes were measured by a standardized achievement test of the subject of learning and instruction, with indicators based on Merrill (1983)'s taxonomy of Component Display Theory (CDT), i.e. "remembering and retrieving the facts, concepts, principles, and procedures of learning theory and instruction". The outcome was defined specifically as a retention rate, the amount of information students can still remember or retrieve after a certain period of time. The test was administered at the end of the experiments, which took over eight face-to-face meetings of 100 minutes each.
requirements: Administered as a standardized achievement test at the end of the experiments
constraints: Outcome measured is retention of facts, concepts, principles, and procedures of learning theory and instruction, not broader teaching performance
target_learners: teacher trainees in higher education
target_learning_goals: retention of facts, concepts, principles, and procedures of learning theory and instruction
examples: Used as the dependent variable (ScoreTest) in the two-way ANOVA of the 168-trainee quasi-experiment
key_sources: Mutrofin, Degeng, I.N.S., Ardhana, I.W., & Setyosari, P. (2017). The Effect of Instructional Methods (Lecture-Discussion versus Group Discussion) and Teaching Talent on Teacher Trainees Student Learning Outcomes. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1138824

article_title: TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Maxwell, B., Connolly, P., Demack, S., O'Hare, L., Stevens, A., & Clague, L. (2014). TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Prefer highly structured tutoring programmes: well-trained tutors, lessons focused on specific reading skills, and systematically timetabled sessions
description: Drawing on a systematic review of randomised trials of adult volunteer tutoring (Ritter, Barnett, Denny, & Albin, 2009), the report concludes that "existing evidence also suggests that highly structured tutoring programmes provide the  best effects on outcomes", where highly structured means tutors are well trained, lessons focus on specific reading skills, and sessions are timetabled systematically. Of the implementation factors reviewed (tutor type, tutee age, structure), only level of programme structure significantly influenced effectiveness. The report flags that this recommendation may be counter to TextNow's choice-enjoyment-comprehension model.
requirements: Tutors are well trained; lessons focus on specific reading skills; sessions are timetabled systematically
constraints: The report notes this recommendation may be counter to the Text Now underpinning model of 'choice - enjoyment - comprehension'
target_learners: Struggling readers receiving one-to-one or volunteer tutoring
target_learning_goals: Reading outcomes including standardised reading achievement, letters and words, oral fluency, and writing
examples: The cited review reported small but significant effects of volunteer tutoring programmes on reading outcomes (hedges g = 0.23 overall; g = 0.26 for standardised reading achievement), but no significant effects on reading comprehension or mathematics
key_sources: Maxwell, B., Connolly, P., Demack, S., O'Hare, L., Stevens, A., & Clague, L. (2014). TextNow Transition Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581131

article_title: Benefits of Structured After-School Literacy Tutoring by University Students for Struggling Elementary Readers
citation: Lindo, E. J., Weiser, B., Cheatham, J. P., & Allor, J. H. (2018). Benefits of structured after-school literacy tutoring by university students for struggling elementary readers. Reading & Writing Quarterly, 34(2), 117–131. https://doi.org/10.1080/10573569.2017.1357156
title: Highly structured scripted tutoring lesson pattern: sequenced phonics routines, leveled book reading with prediction routines, immediate corrective feedback, and motivational games and points
description: Each 25–45-minute session followed a fixed sequence: 15–20 minutes of scripted phonics chart routines, 10–20 minutes of book reading at the student's instructional level, and 5–15 minutes of supplemental games, with a 100-point chart for effort. The article states "The lessons were very structured, which means that they followed a systematic phonics scope and sequence, implemented routine book reading procedures (e.g., making predictions, summarizing), and included explicit instruction with corrective feedback." All materials were provided so tutors made no curricular decisions.
requirements: Tutors follow scripted directions and a predetermined lesson sequence rather than selecting activities or materials themselves
Texts are matched to each student's instructional level (approximately 90% accuracy) and placement is set by placement tests administered by professionals
constraints: The study did not compare different amounts of tutoring or levels of supervision, so the contribution of structure alone is not isolated
target_learners: Struggling elementary readers in Grades K–6 at risk for reading failure from low-income families
target_learning_goals: Word identification and decoding (phonics and word attack)
Oral reading fluency
Passage comprehension
examples: Tutors used the sound-and-say decoding strategy in every lesson, with letter combinations underlined to scaffold sounding out, and repeated the corrective-feedback routine for any mistake, even during book reading or games
key_sources: Lindo, E. J., Weiser, B., Cheatham, J. P., & Allor, J. H. (2018). Benefits of structured after-school literacy tutoring by university students for struggling elementary readers. Reading & Writing Quarterly, 34(2), 117–131. https://doi.org/10.1080/10573569.2017.1357156

article_title: Influence of Web Based Cooperative Learning Strategy and Achiever Motivation on Student Study Outcome
citation: Bambang Hariadi, Tutut Wurijanto. (2016). Influence of Web Based Cooperative Learning Strategy and Achiever Motivation on Student Study Outcome. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), Vol.5, No.3, pp. 189~199. http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
title: STAD cooperative learning with heterogeneous small groups and a facilitator lecturer
description: This pattern organizes class activities around small student teams under a lecturer acting as facilitator. In STAD-type cooperative learning, "lecturers become facilitator for the purpose of making learning process to involve more group activities, which these groups consists of between three and five students." Groups are formed to be heterogeneous in gender, performance level, ethnicity, and other characteristics, so members can help each other toward learning objectives. Assignments require students not only to complete ordered tasks as a team but to learn something as a team.
requirements: Groups of three to five students formed with heterogeneous genders, performance levels, tribes/races, and other student characteristics
Lecturer acts as facilitator rather than transmitter
target_learners: undergraduate students
school students in prior STAD studies cited by the article
target_learning_goals: comprehension of new information
cooperative attitudes and soft skills such as mutual respect and responsibility
examples: The experimental and control classes both used STAD-type cooperative learning, differing only in whether materials were delivered web-based or text-based
key_sources: Bambang Hariadi, Tutut Wurijanto. (2016). Influence of Web Based Cooperative Learning Strategy and Achiever Motivation on Student Study Outcome. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), Vol.5, No.3, pp. 189~199. http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE

article_title: Effects of Student Teams-Achievement Divisions Cooperative Learning with Models on Students' Understanding of Electrochemical Cells
citation: Ataman Karaçöp. (2016). Effects of Student Teams-Achievement Divisions Cooperative Learning with Models on Students' Understanding of Electrochemical Cells. International Education Studies, 9(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n11p104
title: STAD cooperative learning cycle with heterogeneous teams, worksheets, quizzes and improvement scores
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern in which students work in small heterogeneous cooperative teams toward a common goal of all members learning the content. As the article describes it, "This method is conducted as the students get prepared for end of subject or weekly exams by teaching the course contents, worksheets, test applications presented by the teacher to each other through the activities they perform together." Individual quiz scores feed a team progress score so higher-achieving students support teammates. In this study the pattern was applied to electrochemical cells over two weeks with first-year university students.
requirements: Heterogeneous groups so that students who achieve the collective goal can support others and act as teachers
A group reward based on the learning progress of each group member, as in STAD
target_learners: first-year undergraduate science teacher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding electrochemical cells at macroscopic, microscopic and symbolic levels
examples: Students in CLG and CLMG studied topics including electrolysis vs. galvanic cell, anode and cathode, and half-reactions in cooperative groups over two weeks, then took quizzes scored individually and converted to team progress scores.
key_sources: Ataman Karaçöp. (2016). Effects of Student Teams-Achievement Divisions Cooperative Learning with Models on Students' Understanding of Electrochemical Cells. International Education Studies, 9(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n11p104

article_title: The Use of Personalized Texts for Teaching Turkish as a Second Language
citation: Kardaş, D. (2016). The use of personalized texts for teaching Turkish as a second language. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2538
title: Student-completed personal information form for generating personalized Turkish texts
description: A 19-item form collecting personal information used to build personalized grammar examples and test questions for foreign learners of Turkish. It was developed after a literature review, consultation with specialists, and asking 45 foreign students which three pieces of personal information they would like to see in a text. Items covered "name and surname, country, date and place of birth, names of parents" and other details such as profession, height, and place of residence.
requirements: Personal information must be collected from students before instruction so examples can reference their lives
target_learners: adult foreign learners of Turkish at A1-A2 level
target_learning_goals: Turkish grammar (possessive, plural, case and tense suffixes) at A1-A2 levels
examples: Experimental-group students were taught for six weeks with examples generated from the form, and their pretest and post-test questions were also built from the same personal information
key_sources: Kardaş, D. (2016). The use of personalized texts for teaching Turkish as a second language. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2538

article_title: Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues
citation: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579
title: Student and teacher guides for the Humanity and the Environment unit
description: Two guides were developed to support holistic learning of the unit. The students' guide enriched objective-based text with pictures, charts, and tables, placing activities, worksheets, and assessment activities within the text so it served "as a scientific source and as an implementation guide for the students". The teachers' guide contained objectives, allocated time, and flowcharts showing how activities would be carried out. Guides were reviewed by a biology faculty member and a science teacher before finalization.
requirements: Review by subject-matter and pedagogical experts before finalization
A table matching each objective with a relevant activity and time allocation
constraints: Teachers reported a problem of time because several activities were carried out on some subjects
target_learners: 7th-grade science students and their teachers
target_learning_goals: Holistic learning of ecosystem, biodiversity, and environmental issues
examples: After the pilot study, concept maps and pictures were revised, activities modified or added, and end-of-unit assessment questions added
key_sources: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579

article_title: Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons
citation: Teke, H., Dogan, B., & Duran, A. (2015). Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(2), 111-118. https://www.ijres.net
title: Science and Technology Achievement Test (STAT), a 30-item multiple-choice instrument
description: The STAT is a multiple-choice achievement test covering the 'Systems of the Human Body' unit (digestive system, urinary system, nervous system and sense organs). It was developed from an initial pool of 50 questions administered to 95 eighth-grade students for item analysis, after which "the validity and reliability of the items were ensured (Cronbach's = 0.831)" and the final 30-question test was created. It served as both pretest and post-test in the study.
requirements: Expert opinion was consulted before preparing the test, and items were analyzed for difficulty and distinctiveness before the final form was fixed
constraints: The test covers only the seventh-grade 'Systems of the Human Body' unit topics
target_learners: Seventh-grade primary education students
target_learning_goals: Achievement in science-and-technology topics on human body systems
examples: Administered as pretest (T1) and post-test (T2) to 35 experimental and 35 control students; scores analyzed with SPSS 15.0
key_sources: Teke, H., Dogan, B., & Duran, A. (2015). Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(2), 111-118. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105195

article_title: Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners’ Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217732335
title: Pair training in high-impact instructional strategies with an explicit collaboration framework and ongoing school-based support
description: The article recommends that PD for teachers of English learners combine specific strategy training with a structured collaboration framework (working alliance plus time, structure, and accountability) and ongoing supports such as coaching and follow-up modules. The authors write that "providing specific training in high-impact instructional strategies along with a framework for professional collaboration supports teachers in their implementation of new practices."
requirements: School policies must allow weekly collaboration time between ESL and classroom teachers
Coaching must be available during the school year
constraints: Recommendation drawn from a pilot RCT with a small number of schools; the authors call for a larger efficacy trial
target_learners: elementary school ESL and classroom teachers of English learners
target_learning_goals: teacher implementation of high-impact instructional strategies for English learners
sustained use of new instructional practices
examples: In the trial, intervention teams collaborated 30 minutes weekly, received coaching about every six weeks, and attended four follow-up modules during the school year
key_sources: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners’ Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217732335

article_title: Developing a Fidelity Measure of Early Intervention Programs for Children with Neuromotor Disorders
citation: Mihee An, Jayden Nord, Natalie A Koziol, Stacey C Dusing, Audrey E Kane, Michele A Lobo, Sarah W McCoy, Regina T Harbourne. (2020). Developing a fidelity measure of early intervention programs for children with neuromotor disorders. Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology. https://doi.org/10.1111/dmcn.14702
title: START-Play intervention-specific fidelity measure
description: A coding instrument developed to quantify fidelity of the START-Play intervention, which the authors call "the first intervention-specific measure used in pediatric rehabilitation". It codes six START-Play behaviors and five non-START-Play behaviors each minute (coded 1 if observed, 0 if not), plus four 1–4 Likert gestalt quality scales scored per 10-minute segment. Variables cover adherence rates, dosage in minutes, quality and responsiveness averages, and program differentiation. It can be used for replicating efficacy studies and by therapists to examine their own delivery of key components.
requirements: Training and practice for coding took more time than other fidelity measures, roughly estimated at 16 hours, due to a complex measurement system using rates of occurrence rather than a checklist
constraints: The 'flexible and not rigid' item did not reach acceptable reliability within usual early intervention services and needs refinement; the instrument was developed for START-Play, and the authors note the process rather than the instrument is more likely useful for comparing other specific approaches
target_learners: infants with neuromotor disorders receiving early intervention
target_learning_goals: measuring implementation fidelity of intervention key components
differentiating an experimental intervention from usual care
examples: Two coders blind to group assignment independently coded 103 trial videos randomly assigned between them
key_sources: Mihee An, Jayden Nord, Natalie A Koziol, Stacey C Dusing, Audrey E Kane, Michele A Lobo, Sarah W McCoy, Regina T Harbourne. (2020). Developing a fidelity measure of early intervention programs for children with neuromotor disorders. Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology. https://doi.org/10.1111/dmcn.14702

article_title: The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL
citation: Salem Saleh Khalaf Ibnian. (2010). The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 4. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Story-mapping technique as a graphic organizer for EFL short story writing
description: The story-mapping technique is a visual, graphic-organizer-based instructional method in which students map the elements of a short story. The article defines it as "A graphic organizer used to help tenth grade students identify elements of the short story in EFL composition classes", and describes story maps as depicting settings and the sequence of major events so students can relate story events and perceive structure. In the study it was applied to the experimental group's composition classes over one term.
requirements: Used during composition classes with teacher support; the researcher visited schools to help teachers overcome obstacles while using the technique
constraints: Studied only with tenth-grade male students in Amman public education schools over one three-month term
target_learners: tenth grade EFL students
target_learning_goals: short story writing skills in EFL
examples: The experimental group (42 students in two classes at Tareq bin Ziad and Tawfiq Abul Huda Secondary Schools) received instruction through the story-mapping technique while control classes used the traditional method.
key_sources: Salem Saleh Khalaf Ibnian. (2010). The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 4. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: Should Peer E-Comments Replace Traditional Peer Comments?
citation: Ho, P. V. P., Phung, L. T. K., Oanh, T. T. T., & Giao, N. Q. (2020). Should Peer E-Comments Replace Traditional Peer Comments? International Journal of Instruction, 13(1), 295-314. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13120a
title: Structured peer-commenting training cycle with fixed small groups, guidelines, and teacher credit
description: The article's peer commentary design combines fixed small groups, explicit comment guidelines, staged writing cycles, and teacher accountability. Students worked in "groups of four members" kept constant across the semester; the teacher "provided the students with the guidelines, explained the details in the guidelines and demonst rated to them how to use the guidelines to give peer comments"; in-class conferences checked compliance; and students were told in advance their comments would be read and marked. Each two-week cycle moved from topic introduction through drafting, peer commenting, and teacher comments to final drafts.
requirements: instruction in peer response and comment guidelines
groups small enough to run efficiently
teacher reads peer comments and gives students credit
constraints: Group size depends on task nature, time limits, proficiency, and maturity, per Liu and Hansen
target_learners: university EFL writing students
target_learning_goals: giving qualified peer comments
improving writing quality through revision
examples: Both groups followed the same cycle three times for three writing assignments, differing only in whether comments were exchanged on paper face-to-face or on the Facebook group
key_sources: Ho, P. V. P., Phung, L. T. K., Oanh, T. T. T., & Giao, N. Q. (2020). Should Peer E-Comments Replace Traditional Peer Comments? International Journal of Instruction, 13(1), 295-314. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13120a

article_title: Embedded Instruction Improves Vocabulary Learning during Automated Storybook Reading among High-Risk Preschoolers
citation: Howard Goldstein, Elizabeth Kelley, Charles Greenwood, Luke McCune, Judith Carta, Jane Atwater, Gabriela Guerrero, Tanya McCarthy, Naomi Schneider, and Trina Spencer. (2016). Embedded Instruction Improves Vocabulary Learning During Automated Storybook Reading Among High-Risk Preschoolers. Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research. https://doi.org/10.1044/2015_JSLHR-L-15-0227
title: Story Friends: automated Tier 2 pre-K curriculum with embedded vocabulary and comprehension lessons
description: Story Friends is a supplemental preschool program delivering vocabulary and comprehension instruction via prerecorded storybooks played at small-group listening centers. Each instructional book includes "two embedded lessons for each of two challenging vocabulary words" and one lesson for each of three inferential story questions. The automated format is designed so that key elements of explicit instruction are delivered consistently, requiring only minimal training of educational staff. Vocabulary targets follow Beck and McKeown's recommendations for challenging, high-utility words.
requirements: Requires classroom staff to facilitate the listening center (e.g., helping children keep headphones on or turn pages) and set up materials
Requires children to listen through headphones in small groups and follow along in accompanying storybooks
constraints: Procedural fidelity is the responsibility of educational staff, whereas fidelity of instructional components is accomplished via the automated instruction
target_learners: preschool children with limited vocabulary knowledge at risk for language and reading disabilities
target_learning_goals: vocabulary knowledge of challenging, high-utility words
answering inferential questions about stories
examples: In the trial, children heard each instructional book three times per week across six units, receiving about 10 hr total of instruction delivered by educational staff

article_title: The Effects of Metacognitive Strategy in Reading Expository Text
citation: Yahya Othman, Zamri Mahamud & Noradinah Jaidi. (2014). The Effects of Metacognitive Strategy in Reading Expository Text. International Education Studies, 7(13). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n13p102
title: START-based framework of metacognitive strategy application across before-, during- and after-reading processes
description: The study's theoretical framework, modified from the Students and Teachers Actively Reading Text (START) Reading Strategies Diagram in Scharlach (2008) and grounded in constructivism, organises metacognitive strategy use across "all three reading processes, namely before reading, during reading and after reading". Before reading, students guess and construct questions; during reading, they examine difficult words, connect text to existing knowledge and answer formulated questions; after reading, they summarise and assess key ideas. The framework holds that this constructive application helps readers build understanding during information acquisition.
requirements: Application across all three reading processes (before, during, after) as depicted in the framework
constraints: Framed for reading and comprehension lessons with expository texts in primary school contexts
target_learners: primary school students (Standard 4, ages 10-11)
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of expository text
examples: The experimental teaching preparation emphasised application of metacognitive strategy in reading and understanding the text across the three reading processes
key_sources: Yahya Othman, Zamri Mahamud & Noradinah Jaidi. (2014). The Effects of Metacognitive Strategy in Reading Expository Text. International Education Studies, 7(13). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n13p102

article_title: The Effect of Prediction, Observation, Explanation Supported Project-Based Environmental Education on the Levels of Attitude and Behavior toward the Environment
citation: Calis, D. & Yildirim, H.I. (2020). The Effect of Prediction, Observation, Explanation Supported Project-Based Environmental Education on the Levels of Attitude and Behavior Toward the Environment. Educational Policy Analysis and Strategic Research, 15(1), 22-43. https://doi.org/10.29329/epasr.2020.236.2
title: Prefer student-centered, learning-by-doing-living approaches over teacher-centered methods in environmental education
description: The article concludes that improving environmental attitudes and turning them into environmentally friendly behaviors is not possible through traditional education disconnected from real life. It recommends that "instead of teacher-centered methods in environmental education, student-centered learning-teaching approaches, which are based on learning by questioning-doing-living, enable an active attendance in the learning environment, and can establish a relationship with life, should be preferred." The recommendation rests on the study's comparison results.
requirements: Methods must enable active attendance in the learning environment and establish a relationship with life
constraints: The study could not examine the effects of POE technique and PBL method individually because only two classes were available; the authors suggest studies comparing teacher-centered teaching, POESPBEE, POE and PBL separately
target_learners: eighth-grade secondary school students
target_learning_goals: positive environmental attitudes
environmentally friendly behaviors
examples: The experimental group's POESPBEE applications had students design projects, make predictions, observations and explanations, and share their ideas in class

The Effect of Prediction, Observation, Explanation Supported Project-Based Environmental Education on the Levels of Attitude and Behavior Toward the Environment. article_title: The Experimental Effects of the Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) on a Scenarios-Based Reading Comprehension Assessment
citation: James Kim, Lowry Hemphill, Margaret Troyer, Stephanie Jones, Maria LaRusso, Ha-Yeon Kim, Suzanne Donovan, Catherine Snow. (2016). The Experimental Effects of the Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) on a Scenarios-Based Reading Comprehension Assessment. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract.
title: STARI: a year-long multicomponent Tier-2 reading intervention for struggling middle school readers
description: STARI is a comprehension-focused supplemental reading program developed by the first author and SERP for middle school students scoring below proficient on state literacy assessments. It incorporates "strands on decoding, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension" and provides roughly 60 additional minutes of targeted instruction per session in one teaching block 3-5 days per week. Teachers receive student workbooks, unit novels and non-fiction books, slides, and detailed daily lesson plans.
requirements: Delivered by teachers who received an intensive graduate course and on-site coaching as part of the intervention package
Students scoring below proficient on the state ELA assessment, approximately two levels below grade norms
constraints: Excluded students in substantially separate special education classes, level 1 or 2 English language learners, and students with rules-based phonics intervention plans
target_learners: Struggling middle school readers in grades 6-8, mostly low-income (68% eligible for free or reduced lunch)
target_learning_goals: Decoding multisyllabic words
Reading fluency
Vocabulary and comprehension strategies
Developing personal stances on text content
examples: In the 2013-14 trial, 9 middle schools across four Massachusetts districts participated and 562 students were randomized to STARI or control via rank-ordered lottery
key_sources: James Kim, Lowry Hemphill, Margaret Troyer, Stephanie Jones, Maria LaRusso, Ha-Yeon Kim, Suzanne Donovan, Catherine Snow. (2016). The Experimental Effects of the Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) on a Scenarios-Based Reading Comprehension Assessment. article_title: The Experimental Effects of the Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) on a Scenarios-Based Reading Comprehension Assessment
citation: James Kim, Lowry Hemphill, Margaret Troyer, Stephanie Jones, Maria LaRusso, Ha-Yeon Kim, Suzanne Donovan, Catherine Snow. (2016). The Experimental Effects of the Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) on a Scenarios-Based Reading Comprehension Assessment. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract.
title: STARI's instructional design: partner fluency cycles, small-group and partner strategy reading, and unit debates
description: The intervention's daily block combines recurring activity structures: 15 minutes of leveled fluency work in partners (timed, repeated, and phrase-cued reading with partner discussion of a controversy or personal response), 30-40 minutes of novel and nonfiction reading in teacher-guided small groups and pairs with workbook prompts for "questioning, summarizing, and predicting," and debates on controversial issues for which teams gather textual evidence. Key features named by the authors are extensive themed reading, multiple talk opportunities, and personal stances.
requirements: Project-authored workbooks, unit texts, slides, and daily lesson plans
One teaching block 3-5 days per week
target_learners: Middle school students reading approximately two levels below grade norms
target_learning_goals: Fluency
Comprehension strategy use
Evidence-based argumentation
examples: Each two-day fluency cycle included a partner discussion about a controversy or personal response plus literal comprehension checks; each thematic unit included one or more debates
key_sources: James Kim, Lowry Hemphill, Margaret Troyer, Stephanie Jones, Maria LaRusso, Ha-Yeon Kim, Suzanne Donovan, Catherine Snow. (2016). The Experimental Effects of the Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) on a Scenarios-Based Reading Comprehension Assessment. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567033

article_title: Developing a Theory of Treatment Effect Heterogeneity through Better Design: Where Do Behavioral Science Interventions Work Best?
citation: Tipton, E., Yeager, D., & Iachan, R. (2016). Developing a theory of treatment effect heterogeneity through better design: Where do behavioral science interventions work best? SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Stratify study samples on covariates explaining variation in treatment impacts, not on outcome correlates
description: The paper's stratified selection procedure deviates from standard survey-sampling practice: strata should be based on covariates that explain variation in treatment impacts rather than variables correlated with outcomes. The article states that stratifying schools on free-and-reduced-lunch status, 'a variable often highly correlated with outcomes,' 'makes little sense, unless the intervention effects also vary in relation to this variable.'
requirements: Moderators must be identified in advance from prior research, the theory of change, and policy questions
Dimension reduction (e.g., k-means clustering or latent-variable approaches) may be needed when the moderator list is large
constraints: Stratifying on p covariates leads to at least 2p strata, which can be far too many given a small number of clusters
target_learners: students in U.S. public high schools
target_learning_goals: designing generalizable behavioral science intervention experiments
examples: In the NGMI study, strata were created from school achievement (a latent variable based on GreatSchools.org and College Board data) and school minority composition, yielding five strata
key_sources: Tipton, E., Yeager, D., & Iachan, R. (2016). Developing a theory of treatment effect heterogeneity through better design: Where do behavioral science interventions work best? SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567217

article_title: The Role of Independent Activities in Development of Strategic Learning Competences and Increase of School Performance Level, within the Study of High School Pedagogy
citation: Monica-Iuliana Anca & Muşata Bocoş. (2017). The Role of Independent Activities in Development of Strategic Learning Competences and Increase of School Performance Level, within the Study of High School Pedagogy. Educatia 21 Journal, (15). https://doi.org/10.24193/ed21.2017.15.07
title: Strategic learning competence as choosing and valorising efficient learning strategies individually and collectively
description: The article defines strategic learning competence within the family of learning-to-learn key competences: it involves "choosing and valorisation of the most efficient strategies in order to successfully perform the learning tasks", both individually and collectively. It builds on learning-to-learn competences of coordinating learning processes, time and information management, self-knowledge of learning needs, and self-motivation to overcome cognitive obstacles. The experimental programme was designed to shape this competence through independent activities.
requirements: Learners must analyse tasks, choose strategies for approaching tasks, evaluate the tasks' solving manner, and monitor performances, as the article states independent activities require
target_learners: 11th-grade high school students of pedagogical profile, specialisation primary school-kindergarten teacher
target_learning_goals: strategic learning competence
learning-to-learn key competences
examples: The support Curriculum taught students to identify key words and phrases in the subject Students' Class Management and to complete reflection/self-evaluation exercises for strategic learning
key_sources: Monica-Iuliana Anca & Muşata Bocoş. (2017). The Role of Independent Activities in Development of Strategic Learning Competences and Increase of School Performance Level, within the Study of High School Pedagogy. Educatia 21 Journal, (15). https://doi.org/10.24193/ed21.2017.15.07

article_title: The Effects of Processing Instruction and Traditional Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Ability
citation: Hossein Hashemnezhad & Sanaz Khalili Zangalani. (2012). The Effects of Processing Instruction and Traditional Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Ability. English Language Teaching, 5(11). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p125
title: Structured input activity sequence: referential activities followed by affective activities
description: This instructional pattern sequences structured input activities so that learners first process form to obtain meaning and then respond personally. VanPatten distinguishes two types: "Referential activities are those for which there is a right or wrong answer and for which the learner must rely on the targeted grammatical form to get meaning", while affective activities have learners express opinions or beliefs. Normally, as Wong and VanPatten indicate, a sequence begins with two or three referential activities followed by affective ones. In this study each tense received two referential and one affective activity.
requirements: Input must be manipulated so learners become dependent on the targeted form to get meaning, and activities must not require production of the target structure
constraints: The article notes learners can do many ordinary activities without understanding the content, which is not acceptable within the PI model; activities must force processing for meaning
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners
target_learning_goals: processing target grammatical forms for meaning
form-meaning connections for English tenses
examples: In the study's PI package, referential activities required participants to find the correct answer among alternatives, and affective activities were based on participants' opinions about a subject specific to the activity.
key_sources: Hossein Hashemnezhad & Sanaz Khalili Zangalani. (2012). The Effects of Processing Instruction and Traditional Instruction on Iranian EFL Learners' Writing Ability. English Language Teaching, 5(11). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p125

article_title: The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students' Performance in Fractions
citation: Charalambos Lemonidis & Ioanna Kaiafa. (2019). The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students’ Performance in Fractions. Journal of Education and Learning, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v8n2p165
title: Story-anchored concept introduction sequence: interactive story reading, discussion, then story-related activities
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern in which each new mathematical concept is introduced by the teacher reading a teaching story with displayed pictures, followed by a brief classroom discussion of the story content and then math activities related to the story and the learning objectives. The reading is done "in an interactive way that fostered communication to accomplish the goal of meaningful student engagement", so that students are active participants rather than passive listeners. Only the concept introduction differs from the comparison condition; both groups then process the same textbook activities.
requirements: the same curriculum and textbook activities follow the story-based introduction
interactive reading that fosters communication and meaningful engagement
constraints: in this study the pattern was used only when introducing a new mathematical concept, not throughout the lesson
target_learners: third grade primary students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of fractions
examples: Experimental group: story reading with pictures, discussion, story-related activities; control group: manipulative materials (objects, area models, fraction walls, fraction strips, number lines) for the same concepts
key_sources: Charalambos Lemonidis & Ioanna Kaiafa. (2019). The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students’ Performance in Fractions. Journal of Education and Learning, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v8n2p165

article_title: Implementation of Structured Inquiry Based Model Learning toward Students' Understanding of Geometry
citation: Salim, K. & Tiawa, D.H. (2015). Implementation of Structured Inquiry Based Model Learning Toward Students' Understanding of Geometry. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(1), 75-83. http://www.ijres.net
title: Structured inquiry learning model
description: The structured inquiry model is a constructivist-based instructional model that "promotes the involvement of learners actively and creatively in the search for, examine, formulate concepts and principles of geometry". Learning is student-centered: students formulate hypotheses, perform experiments related to the geometry material, and draw conclusions to answer the hypotheses under teacher guidance. The article applies it to abstract three-dimensional geometry content for high-school students whose concrete-operational stage makes abstract concepts hard to grasp.
requirements: Teachers guide students to rediscover concepts (guided reinvention) rather than transfer knowledge intact
Student attitudes such as curiosity, flexibility, critical reflection and honesty support the process
constraints: Success is judged by how actively students search and find, not only by mastery of the material, per Sanjaya (2009) as cited
target_learners: high school grade 10 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: understanding of geometry concepts
intellectual thinking skills and problem solving
examples: Two classes of 29 students at SMAN 3 Tanjungpinang studied geometry of space either via structured inquiry or conventional instruction, compared with a 20-item multiple-choice understanding test
key_sources: Salim, K. & Tiawa, D.H. (2015). Implementation of Structured Inquiry Based Model Learning Toward Students' Understanding of Geometry. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(1), 75-83. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105196

article_title: A Randomized Controlled Study Evaluating a Brief, Bystander Bullying Intervention with Junior High School Students
citation: Midgett, A., Doumas, D., Trull, R., & Johnston, A. (2016). A Randomized Controlled Study Evaluating a Brief, Bystander Bullying Intervention with Junior High School Students. Boise State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Randomized+Controlled+Study+Evaluating+a+Brief+Bystander+Bullying+Intervention
title: STAC bystander bullying intervention program
description: STAC (stealing the show, turning it over, accompanying others, and coaching compassion) is a brief bystander bullying intervention that "encourages students to act as defenders on behalf of victims." Implementation includes a 90-minute training with didactic and role-play components delivered by counseling graduate students, followed by the school counselor facilitating two 20-minute small-group follow-ups. A unique feature is that school counselors, not classroom teachers, lead implementation.
requirements: A school counselor to facilitate two 20-minute follow-up group meetings per grade level over the 30 days after training
Trainers prepared via a STAC training video, with fidelity checks on teaching the definition and types of bullying, the STAC strategies, and role-plays
constraints: Adapted from the CARES bystander component of the Bully-Proofing program, modified to focus on bystanders, reduce implementation time, and shift delivery from teachers to school counselors
target_learners: junior high school students selected for leadership qualities
target_learning_goals: knowledge of bullying and defender strategies
confidence and skills to intervene as defenders on behalf of bullying victims
examples: In this study, 31 students were randomized to the intervention and completed a 90-minute training during classroom time plus two 20-minute counselor-led follow-up meetings

article_title: Assessing the Effect of Cooperative Learning on Financial Accounting Achievement among Secondary School Students
citation: Inuwa, U., Abdullah, Z. & Hassan, H. (2017). Assessing the Effect of Cooperative Learning on Financial Accounting Achievement among Secondary School Students. International Journal of Instruction, 10(3), 31-46. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.1033a
title: Slavin's Student Teams-Achievement Divisions (STAD) three-day cycle for cooperative learning
description: The study implemented cooperative learning using Slavin's (1994) STAD technique: students were randomly divided into five heterogeneous sub-groups of four members per class, and instruction ran in a repeating three-day cycle of teacher presentation, team worksheet work, and individual testing with team improvement scores. As the article describes it, "the students were randomly divided into five heterogeneous sub-groups of four members each", and high-scoring teams were recognized as super, excellent and good teams. The cycle continued for four weeks.
requirements: A trained teacher presents the lesson conventionally on day one before team work begins
Teams work so that all team members master the lesson before individual testing
Team scores are calculated based on team member's improvement scores
constraints: The treatment covered a period of four weeks in this study
Implemented with senior secondary level two financial accounting students in Gombe state, Nigeria
target_learners: senior secondary school level two (SSII) financial accounting students
target_learning_goals: financial accounting achievement
mastery of lesson content within teams
examples: In each class the teacher presented the lesson conventionally for 40 minutes on day one, teams worked on a worksheet for 40 minutes on day two, and students took an individual 20-minute test on day three without helping one another.
key_sources: Inuwa, U., Abdullah, Z. & Hassan, H. (2017). Assessing the Effect of Cooperative Learning on Financial Accounting Achievement among Secondary School Students. International Journal of Instruction, 10(3), 31-46. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.1033a

article_title: Exploration of the Factors That Support Learning: Web-Based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra
citation: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Two-dimensional framework of learning environments: adaptability and basis in an explicit model of learning
description: The article proposes that learning environments vary along two dimensions: "the extent to which they adaptively respond to student behavior and (2) the extent to which they are based on a careful cognitive model." Crossing these yields static environments (non-adaptive, no cognitive model, e.g., online problem sets giving "Correct" or "Incorrect" feedback), dynamic environments that track student behavior and use programmed decision trees to select problem sets and feedback (e.g., ALEKS, Khan Academy mastery challenges), and cognitively-based "intelligent" tutoring systems (e.g., Cognitive Tutor) whose scaffolds are informed by a theoretical model of the cognitive processing needed for skill acquisition and can themselves be adaptive and faded.
requirements: Dynamic environments require tracking of student behavior such as errors, error rates, or time-on-problem to drive the programmed decision tree
constraints: The framework is presented as a conceptual framing for the study, not a tested result
target_learners: community college elementary algebra students
target_learning_goals: algebraic knowledge and skills
examples: Table 1 classifies textbook problem sets, ALEKS/Khan Academy-style adaptive systems, and Cognitive Tutor-style intelligent tutoring systems by adaptability and cognitive-model basis
key_sources: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567766

article_title: Exploration of the Factors That Support Learning: Web-Based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra
citation: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Stratified cluster-analysis sampling for multi-site trial recruitment
description: To support generalization, the researchers conducted a cluster analysis on all 112 eligible community college sites based on college-level characteristics possibly related to student learning (e.g., average student age, proportion of adjunct faculty), yielding five clusters. Recruitment then aimed to include a proportionate number of colleges within each cluster. The authors state "the primary value of this approach is that it allows more appropriate generalization of study findings to the target population (Tipton, 2014)", and the recruited sample of 38 colleges matched the target distribution across clusters.
requirements: College-level characteristic data for all eligible sites to perform the cluster analysis
constraints: Applies to multi-site trials seeking generalization to a defined target population of colleges
target_learners: community college students in elementary algebra
target_learning_goals: algebraic knowledge
examples: Cluster analysis of 112 eligible colleges produced five clusters; recruitment of the first cohort yielded 38 colleges with a distribution similar to the target
key_sources: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567766

article_title: Effects of Automated Tier 2 Storybook Intervention on Vocabulary and Comprehension Learning in Preschool Children with Limited Oral Language Skills
citation: Kelley, E. S., Goldstein, H., Spencer, T. D., & Sherman, A. (2015). Effects of automated Tier 2 storybook intervention on vocabulary and comprehension of preschool children with limited oral language skills. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 31, 47-61. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2014.12.004
title: Story Friends automated Tier-2 storybook intervention
description: Story Friends is "a small-group intervention in which vocabulary and question-answering lessons are embedded in a series of storybooks", delivered via prerecorded audio on mp3 players with headphones at classroom listening centers. The series includes 13 books (one introductory, nine instructional, three review) teaching 18 challenging Tier-2 words, 15 basic concept words, and 27 inferential story questions. An adult facilitator manages materials but provides no instruction.
requirements: Prerecorded audio narration with embedded lessons, storybooks, mp3 players, and headphones
Small-group listening centers of three children with an adult facilitator for logistics only
constraints: Because lessons were prerecorded, feedback was the same regardless of participant behavior; children heard the correct answer and encouragement whether or not they responded
target_learners: prekindergarten children with limited oral language skills from families with low income
target_learning_goals: Tier-2 vocabulary knowledge
answering inferential questions about stories
examples: Children listened to each plain storybook once and each instructional book three times, with review books after every three instructional books

Effects of automated Tier 2 storybook intervention on vocabulary and comprehension of preschool children with limited oral language skills.
