article_title: Impact of Early Numeracy Training on Kindergarteners from Middle-Income Families
citation: Carla Meloni, Rachele Fanari, Andrea Bertucci and Sara Berretti. (2017). IMPACT OF EARLY NUMERACY TRAINING ON KINDERGARTENERS FROM MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES. 14th International Conference on Cognition and Exploratory Learning in Digital Age (CELDA 2017). https://isbnsearch.org/isbn/978-989-8533-68-5
title: Structured early numeracy training materials targeting four areas of early numerical competence
description: The training materials were structured learning materials such as short stories, games, and practical activities about numbers, developed for early math training for children from three to six years of age (Lucangeli et al., 2003) and for consolidation interventions (Judica et al., 2010). Activities focused on "the lexical area", "the semantic area", "the counting area", and operations in the pre-syntactic area (comparing and ordering quantities of up to five elements). Each math activity comprised a manipulation or movement game followed by a paper-and-pencil consolidation task, and the same materials were used for both the cooperative and individual training groups.
requirements: Delivered in 12 weekly meetings alongside the standard kindergarten math curriculum, with sessions of about 30-40 minutes for individual training and about an hour for cooperative learning
target_learners: typically developing 4-5 year old kindergarten children
target_learning_goals: early numerical competence: counting, number words and symbols, comparing and ordering quantities
examples: Both experimental groups in the study were exposed to the same learning materials; the only difference between the two groups was the way the lesson was implemented: cooperative versus individual.
key_sources: Carla Meloni, Rachele Fanari, Andrea Bertucci and Sara Berretti. (2017). IMPACT OF EARLY NUMERACY TRAINING ON KINDERGARTENERS FROM MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES. 14th International Conference on Cognition and Exploratory Learning in Digital Age (CELDA 2017). https://isbnsearch.org/isbn/978-989-8533-68-5

article_title: Effectiveness of Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary
citation: Malik Behlol & Hukam Dad. (2010). Effectiveness of Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary. English Language Teaching, 3(3). https://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Structural method of teaching vocabulary (SMTV)
description: The structural method of teaching vocabulary is an approach based on "the morphological analyses of the word", breaking words into prefixes, root and suffixes to illustrate meanings. Students analyze the word rather than the sentence, generate new words from the root form (for example forming adjectives and adverbs from nouns or verbs), and act as partners who manage their own learning, with the teacher as facilitator. In this study it was operationalized in 20 validated lesson plans and contrasted with the definitional method of looking up meanings in a dictionary or glossary or drill.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to analyze words morphologically and to design generation exercises from root words
constraints: Studied only with ninth-grade Federal Government Urdu-medium school students in Islamabad, on the first three chapters of the 9th-class textbook
target_learners: secondary-level (9th grade) English learners of mixed achievement levels
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary knowledge, retention and use across listening, semantics, syntax and word formation
examples: The experimental group was taught with SMTV for 20 days (20 hours) while the control group received DMTV, with the same test used as pretest, posttest and retention test
key_sources: Malik Behlol & Hukam Dad. (2010). Effectiveness of Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary. English Language Teaching, 3(3). https://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: Pedagogical Interaction in High School, the Structural and Functional Model of Pedagogical Interaction
citation: Semenova, L. A., Kazantseva, A. I., Sergeyeva, V. V., Raklova, Y. M., & Baiseitova, Z. B. (2016). Pedagogical Interaction in Hugh School, the Structural and Functional Model of Pedagogical Interaction. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(9), 2553-2566.
title: Structural and functional model of pedagogical interaction
description: The article offers "a structural and functional model of pedagogical interaction was developed (Figure 2), which includes the main elements of subject-subject interaction". The model organises interaction around three measured components — cognitive, emotional and behavioural — and defines interaction as "a process of mutual influence, the result whereof is a positive change in the characteristics of the pedagogical process subjects". It is used to derive a monitoring system and four conditions for improving interaction.
requirements: Monitoring and diagnostic techniques to verify the model's effectiveness
Focus on the three components: cognitive, emotional and behavioural
constraints: The authors state the research "does not provide a final solution to the studied problem"
target_learners: high school and university students
target_learning_goals: teacher-student communication skills
student motivation
academic performance
examples: The model was implemented in an educational process with 122 humanities students in experimental and control groups, with levels measured before and after.
key_sources: Semenova, L. A., Kazantseva, A. I., Sergeyeva, V. V., Raklova, Y. M., & Baiseitova, Z. B. (2016). Pedagogical Interaction in Hugh School, the Structural and Functional Model of Pedagogical Interaction. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(9), 2553-2566. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114604

article_title: The Relative Impact of Aligning Tier 2 Intervention Materials with Classroom Core Reading Materials in Grades K-2
citation: Foorman, B. R., Herrera, S., & Dombek, J. (2018). The relative impact of aligning Tier 2 intervention materials with classroom core reading materials in grades K–2. The Elementary School Journal, 118(3). https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/journals/esj
title: Stand-alone Tier 2 intervention: Sound Partners plus Bridge of Vocabulary and Language in Motion
description: A supplementary Tier 2 intervention combining three externally developed programs: Sound Partners, a scripted program providing "explicit and systematic instruction in phonemic awareness, phonics, spelling, and reading"; Bridge of Vocabulary, a semiscripted vocabulary program using manipulatives and discussion; and Language in Motion, a scripted program building syntax and listening comprehension through science-based manipulatives, interactive stories, and games. It was delivered as a 25–30-minute daily reading component plus a 15-minute daily language component.
requirements: Interventionists administer skill assessments after every 10 Sound Partners lessons and repeat lessons when skills are not mastered
Two-day training in late September plus manuals and instructional materials
constraints: No WWC-rated language intervention programs existed for at-risk K–2 students, so vocabulary and language components were selected on clinical and efficacy evidence rather than WWC ratings
target_learners: K–2 students below the 30th percentile in vocabulary and reading-related skills
target_learning_goals: Phonemic awareness, phonics, spelling, word reading, vocabulary, syntax, and listening comprehension
examples: Delivered daily in 45-minute small groups of four to five students for 27 weeks across 55 Florida schools
key_sources: Foorman, B. R., Herrera, S., & Dombek, J. (2018). The relative impact of aligning Tier 2 intervention materials with classroom core reading materials in grades K–2. The Elementary School Journal, 118(3). https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/journals/esj

article_title: Application of Interactive Multimedia Tools in Teaching Mathematics--Examples of Lessons from Geometry
citation: Marina Milovanoviü, Jasmina Obradoviü, Aleksandar Milajiü. (2013). APPLICATION OF INTERACTIVE MULTIMEDIA TOOLS IN TEACHING MATHEMATICS – EXAMPLES OF LESSONS FROM GEOMETRY. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Multimedia lesson pattern: guided discovery through chapters with step-by-step animation before solutions are shown
description: Each transformation lesson is organized into chapters (Basics, Examples, Some characteristics, Exercises, Problems and Examples from everyday life), and each problem is animated incrementally rather than revealed at once. The authors state that "Animations do not show the whole solution at once, but steb by step" and that in most tasks "lecturer leads a student to think and to find a conclusion before it is shown on the screen", with special attention to enabling students to find solutions individually.
requirements: Tasks ordered by difficulty, from basic to more demanding, each containing an explicit solution or instructions
constraints: Designed for topics where visualizing movement in three-dimensional space matters, which the authors call the weak links of traditional lectures
target_learners: First-year university students
Primary and secondary students encountering these geometry topics
target_learning_goals: Developing abstract thinking and intuitive understanding of geometric transformations and solids
examples: Example 1 asks students to recognize the common characteristic of figures and find which two do not belong before the line-reflection definition is given; the animation then shows folding along the symmetry line.
key_sources: Marina Milovanoviü, Jasmina Obradoviü, Aleksandar Milajiü. (2013). APPLICATION OF INTERACTIVE MULTIMEDIA TOOLS IN TEACHING MATHEMATICS – EXAMPLES OF LESSONS FROM GEOMETRY. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1008863

article_title: Enhancing Educators' Skills for Promoting Critical Thinking in Their Classroom Discourses: A Randomized Control Trial
citation: Gul, R. B., Khan, S., Ahmed, A., Cassum, S., Saeed, T., Parpio, Y., Profetto-McGrath, J., & Schopflocher, D. (2014). Enhancing Educators' Skills for Promoting Critical Thinking in Their Classroom Discourses: A Randomized Control Trial. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 26(1), 37-54. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/
title: Educators need structured formal training to foster critical thinking in their teaching practices
description: The article argues that teachers cannot be assumed to know how to promote critical thinking unless they learned it in their own training, and that formal training and coaching can improve questioning and facilitation skills. Its RCT evidence shows a structured 40-hour workshop intervention produced significant gains in higher-order questioning and selected facilitation behaviors. The authors conclude that "some formal training is necessary to enhance educators' CT skills if they are expected to enhance CT in their teaching practices."
requirements: Training should address CT ontology and epistemology, questioning skills, active strategies, and opportunities to externalize attitudes and dispel myths about barriers
constraints: In contexts with centralized content-heavy assessments and heavy faculty workload, gains in active teaching strategy use may not reach significance
target_learners: higher education faculty, particularly nursing educators
target_learning_goals: promoting students' critical thinking through questioning, active strategies, and facilitation
examples: The RCT randomly assigned 91 consenting educators from 14 Pakistani schools of nursing to intervention or control and measured classroom practice via observation and audiotaping
key_sources: Gul, R. B., Khan, S., Ahmed, A., Cassum, S., Saeed, T., Parpio, Y., Profetto-McGrath, J., & Schopflocher, D. (2014). Enhancing Educators' Skills for Promoting Critical Thinking in Their Classroom Discourses: A Randomized Control Trial. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 26(1), 37-54. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/

article_title: Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course
citation: B. Lyazzat Rakhimzhanova, N. Darazha Issabayeva, Tiyshtik Khakimova & J. Madina Bolyskhanova. (2015). Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course. International Education Studies, 8(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n8p166
title: Step-by-step formation of mental actions as the basis of the modeling teaching technique
description: The article's formation technique rests on Galperin and Talyzina's (1968) theory of step-by-step formation of mental actions, applied "by a method of 'undelivered' tasks". The conclusion lists as a result a "formalized approach for development and research of models in the form of scheme defining an indicative basis of activities". Modeling is framed as developing pupils' mental actions and intellectual abilities, meeting modern didactic requirements including undelivered and nonstationary tasks.
requirements: A system of basic concepts of modeling with a logical sequence of study
An indicative basis of activities in formalized scheme form
target_learners: secondary school pupils; future teachers in pedagogical higher education
target_learning_goals: formation of conceptions of mathematical modeling and computing experiment methodology
examples: The training experiment tested the effectiveness of the developed system of tasks and technique of their solution built on this theory
key_sources: B. Lyazzat Rakhimzhanova, N. Darazha Issabayeva, Tiyshtik Khakimova & J. Madina Bolyskhanova. (2015). Methodical Approaches to Teaching of Computer Modeling in Computer Science Course. International Education Studies, 8(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n8p166

article_title: Comparative Effect of Memory and Cognitive Strategies Training on EFL Intermediate Learners' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Maryam Banisaeid. (2013). Comparative Effect of Memory and Cognitive Strategies Training on EFL Intermediate Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 6(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p108
title: Strategy pamphlets for overt memory and cognitive strategy training
description: Two ten-page pamphlets of activities and exercises, one for cognitive strategies and one for memory strategies, were distributed to give learners "more time, context, opportunity and control over his/her vocabulary learning approach". Each pamphlet introduced and practiced one strategy group and its subsets, supporting the overt (explicit) training model in which learners know the strategy being taught. The treatment also used English Book 1, whose chapters contextualize new vocabulary and end with word lists.
requirements: Overt instruction: learners are made aware of the definition and understanding of the strategies for future use
constraints: Designed for school learners whose speaking and listening are not taught, which shaped the choice of the Nelson 250B proficiency test
target_learners: fourth-grade pre-university EFL students in Tehran
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning via memory strategies (keyword, semantic map) or cognitive strategies (repetition, flashcards)
examples: Each two-hour session taught six new words through the assigned strategies, with further strategy practice assigned as homework
key_sources: Maryam Banisaeid. (2013). Comparative Effect of Memory and Cognitive Strategies Training on EFL Intermediate Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 6(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p108

article_title: Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach
citation: Elena A. Shakuto, Evgenij M. Dorozhkin and Anastasia A. Kozlova. (2016). Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(16), 8834-8845. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Structural-functional model of managing teacher scientific-methodical work with five components
description: The article presents a structural-functional model of management of teacher scientific-methodical work grounded in project-target, systemic, activity-based and axiological approaches. As printed, "They are target -based, methodological, content, organizational and procedural, evaluation -resultative (Figure 1)". The target component aims at systematic improvement of teachers' scientific-methodical competence; the content component covers planning, motivation building, organization and control; the evaluation-resultative component has motivation-axiological, cognitive-activity and professionally-reflexive blocks.
requirements: Implementation requires the organizational-pedagogical conditions the model specifies: a management system, purposeful teacher motivation, and a teacher training system
constraints: Developed and tested in secondary vocational educational institutions in Ekaterinburg, Russia
target_learners: teachers of secondary vocational educational institutions
Deputy heads controlling methodical work
target_learning_goals: scientific-methodical competence of teachers
designing educational programs and methodical materials
examples: Figure 1 of the article diagrams the five components and their blocks, principles, methods, forms and tools
key_sources: Elena A. Shakuto, Evgenij M. Dorozhkin and Anastasia A. Kozlova. (2016). Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(16), 8834-8845. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

article_title: Efficacy of an Electronic Editing Strategy with College Students with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities
citation: Suzanne Woods-Groves, Youjia Hua, Jeremy W. Ford, Katelyn M. Neil. (2017). Efficacy of an Electronic Editing Strategy with College Students with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities. Education and Training in Autism and Developmental Disabilities, 52(4), 422-436. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=EDIT+Strategy+editing+college+students+intellectual+developmental+disabilities
title: Strategy instruction lesson pattern: assessment, systematic explicit instruction, mastery-based learning, and self-regulation
description: The article describes a recurring lesson-level design for strategy instruction in writing. "Elements of strategy instruction include the following (a) pre- and post-instructional assessment, (b) explicit instruction to teach skills in a systematic and sequential fashion, (c) mastery-based learning (i.e., students do not move to the next skill until they master the current skill meeting a predetermined criterion-80%), and (d) self-regulation skills such as goal setting and self-evaluation." The EDIT intervention instantiated this pattern with advance organizers, think-aloud modeling, guided practice with immediate corrective feedback, and student graphing of scored independent work.
requirements: Pre- and post-instructional assessment
Systematic, sequential explicit instruction
Mastery criterion (80%) before advancing
Self-regulation components such as goal setting and self-evaluation
target_learners: learners with disabilities who struggle with written expression
postsecondary students with IDD
target_learning_goals: written expression and editing skills
acquisition and retention of strategy steps
examples: EDIT lessons used an advance organizer, think-aloud modeling, guided practice with immediate corrective feedback, and independent mastery exercises graphed by students
key_sources: Suzanne Woods-Groves, Youjia Hua, Jeremy W. Ford, Katelyn M. Neil. (2017). Efficacy of an Electronic Editing Strategy with College Students with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities. Education and Training in Autism and Developmental Disabilities, 52(4), 422-436. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1160277

article_title: The Effectiveness of Content-Based Instruction in English Language Teaching
citation: Evangelin Arulselvi. (2016). The Effectiveness of Content-Based Instruction in English Language Teaching. Excellence in Education Journal, 5(2). https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Effectiveness+of+Content-Based+Instruction+in+English+Language+Teaching%22
title: Eight practices for natural content integration in CBI classrooms
description: The article presents Stoller's (2002) list of eight practices that "allow for natural content integration": extended input with meaningful output and feedback; information gathering, processing, and reporting; integrated skills; task-based activities and project work enhanced by cooperative learning; strategy training; visual support such as images and graphic organizers; contextualized grammar instruction; and culminating synthesis activities in which knowledge is displayed in writing and orally. The study's CBI treatment instantiated several of these practices.
requirements: Content that is taught through the language rather than as separate language instruction
target_learners: non-native English language learners in ESL and EFL settings
target_learning_goals: integrated language skills
content grasp
metacognitive strategy awareness
examples: The experimental lessons used small-group research tasks, visual support, and culminating group reports
key_sources: Evangelin Arulselvi. (2016). The Effectiveness of Content-Based Instruction in English Language Teaching. Excellence in Education Journal, 5(2). https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Effectiveness+of+Content-Based+Instruction+in+English+Language+Teaching%22

article_title: Effective Game Based Citizenship Education in the Age of New Media
citation: Chee, Y.S., Mehrotra, S. and Liu, Q. (2013). Effective Game Based Citizenship Education in the Age of new Media. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning, Vol 11 Issue 1, pp16-28. https://www.ejel.org
title: Statecraft X multiplayer mobile game on governance
description: Statecraft X is a multiplayer client-server mobile game, typically played on Apple iPhones, in which students take the role of town governors in the medieval fantasy kingdom of Velar. The article states: "Students are assigned the role of town governor in the game. When the game begins, each student is the governor of one town." Students expand their influence across towns, compete ideologically within factions, and manage embedded tensions between economic wealth and citizen happiness. A typical game session supports 20 concurrent players across four factions and lasts about three weeks, running continuously as a 24/7 game.
requirements: Access controlled by the server
A functionally equivalent Web version allows play on tablet devices such as the Apple iPad
constraints: Game play was not permitted on Sundays, a condition imposed by the school administration
target_learners: 15-year-old secondary school students in the Social Studies curriculum
target_learning_goals: governance and its relation to citizenship
value-laden trade-offs in governing
examples: In-game events such as epidemics, bandit attacks, and invasion by a neighboring kingdom are triggered at times predetermined by the game administrator.
key_sources: Chee, Y.S., Mehrotra, S. and Liu, Q. (2013). Effective Game Based Citizenship Education in the Age of new Media. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning, Vol 11 Issue 1, pp16-28. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1012864

article_title: The Impact of Peer Observation and Feedback on Technical Seminar Presentations: A Constructive Model
citation: V. Vijaya Vani. (2015). The Impact of Peer Observation and Feedback on Technical Seminar Presentations: A Constructive Model. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 5, No. 3, July-September. https://www.teachingenglish.org.uk/article/peer-observation
title: Structured seven-parameter peer feedback format with a four-point rating scale
description: A printed feedback rubric the author generated to guide peer observers after the unstructured first spell. It rates seven presentation parameters — displayed title and key words, relevant vocabulary, fluency, tone of speech, clarity of oral and written instructions, slides/materials, and body language — on a scale where "Scope for Improvement = 1, Average = 2, Effective = 3, Very effective =4". Completed forms for named student pairs (e.g., feedback to Karthik kumar by Sai Teja) appear in Table 1 and the appendix.
requirements: Peer observers need the format before observing so they know what components to focus on while watching a seminar
constraints: Developed and used with third-year B.Tech students giving technical seminar presentations at one engineering college
target_learners: tertiary-level engineering students giving technical seminar presentations
target_learning_goals: technical seminar presentation skills, including language use, organization, materials and body language
examples: In the second spell, each of 10 presenters was observed by one of 10 peer observers using this format; completed forms are shown in Table 1 and the appendix
key_sources: V. Vijaya Vani. (2015). The Impact of Peer Observation and Feedback on Technical Seminar Presentations: A Constructive Model. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 5, No. 3, July-September. https://www.teachingenglish.org.uk/article/peer-observation

article_title: Development of Polytechnic Knowledge and Abilities in the Course of Studying Physics
citation: Imashev, G., Abykanova, B. T., Rakhmetova, M. T., Tumysheva, A. A., Moldasheva, R. N., Ilyasova, S. S. & Shahimova, A. A. (2016). Development of Polytechnic Knowledge and Abilities in the Course of Studying Physics. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(10), 3595-3606. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Staged formation of polytechnic skills across four phases from familiarization to testing
description: The article organizes the formation of polytechnic knowledge and skills into sequential stages tied to methods, learning tools and forms of organizing training sessions. As printed: "Depending on the stage of formation of polytechnic knowledge and skills, they can be: 1. Familiarization of students with physical and technical principles of operation of individual technical objects and technological processes." The stages proceed through compilation and systematization of polytechnic materials, mastery of individual skill elements, and testing of the system of polytechnic skills. The article states complex techniques are required because single methods serve only one training task.
requirements: Use of complex techniques and learning tools, since selected methods are usually aimed at solving one goal of polytechnic training
target_learners: 10th-grade secondary school physics students
target_learning_goals: polytechnic knowledge and skills formation in physics
examples: The authors developed physics lesson systems and methods for 10th grade across the 2010-2012 and 2012-2014 experimental stages
key_sources: Imashev, G., Abykanova, B. T., Rakhmetova, M. T., Tumysheva, A. A., Moldasheva, R. N., Ilyasova, S. S. & Shahimova, A. A. (2016). Development of Polytechnic Knowledge and Abilities in the Course of Studying Physics. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(10), 3595-3606. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

article_title: Effects of Instruction-Supported Learning with Worked Examples in Quantitative Method Training
citation: Kai Wagner, Martin Klein, Eric Klopp, Thomas Puhl & Robin Stark. (2013). Effects of Instruction-Supported Learning with Worked Examples in Quantitative Method Training. Higher Education Studies, 3(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v3n3p1
title: Structure-emphasizing example sets with ascending complexity and multiple perspectives
description: The learning environment arranged worked examples in a structure-emphasizing example set (Quilici & Mayer, 1996), "a sequence of worked examples characterized by ha ving an analogue underlying structure" with complexity increasing across the sequence. Consecutive examples shared the same statistical test, and multiple perspectives were constructed by placing tests in different contexts and analytical perspectives. The first four examples covered descriptive statistics and internal validity, later ones mean differences, moderator effects and effect size.
requirements: Worked examples must share an analogue underlying structure and be sequenced by ascending complexity
target_learners: advanced university students in educational science
target_learning_goals: acquisition of problem-solving schemata for statistical methods
examples: Consecutive worked examples based on the same statistical test, with the test placed in different contexts such as mediation- versus moderation-hypotheses
key_sources: Kai Wagner, Martin Klein, Eric Klopp, Thomas Puhl & Robin Stark. (2013). Effects of Instruction-Supported Learning with Worked Examples in Quantitative Method Training. Higher Education Studies, 3(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v3n3p1

article_title: Assessing the Effectiveness of STAD Model and Problem Based Learning in Mathematics Learning Achievement and Problem Solving Ability
citation: Tawachai Rattanatumma and Dr.Vichian Puncreobutr. (2016). Assessing the Effectiveness of STAD Model and Problem Based Learning in Mathematics Learning Achievement and Problem Solving Ability. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.12. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105110
title: STAD (Student Teams Achievement Divisions) model of cooperative learning
description: STAD is one of five models of cooperative-based learning developed and evaluated at Johns Hopkins University by the Center for Social Organization of Schools. Learning management using STAD focuses on students, beginning from teachers providing knowledge to learners using appropriate context while allowing students to have more roles in activities. The model uses group process so learners work together and mutually obtain benefits and achievement for groups.
requirements: Students must be qualified enough to work in group
constraints: The article notes four of the five cooperative learning models are adjustable to all subjects and levels, while the CIRC model could be used for reading and writing only
target_learners: First-year undergraduate students studying mathematics
target_learning_goals: Mathematics learning achievement
Problem solving ability
examples: In this study, STAD was implemented through 16 learning plans over 16 hours with 25 first-year mathematics students.
key_sources: Tawachai Rattanatumma and Dr.Vichian Puncreobutr. (2016). Assessing the Effectiveness of STAD Model and Problem Based Learning in Mathematics Learning Achievement and Problem Solving Ability. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.12. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099565

article_title: Electronic School Atlas as an Innovative Means of Development of Geographic Education in Kazakhstan Schools
citation: Damekova, S. K., Zharkinbekova, T. N., Turtkarayeva, G. B., Han, S. I., & Damekova, O. Z. (2016). Electronic School Atlas as an Innovative Means of Development of Geographic Education in Kazakhstan Schools. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(18), 12668-12679.
title: Staged development of GIS competence across secondary grades
description: The article proposes a two-stage model for forming GIS competence. The first stage, in grades 6-7, covers initial acquaintance with the atlas and basic techniques of working with electronic information. The second stage, in grades 8-9 studying 'Geography of Kazakhstan', adds digital overlay of map layers, preparation of territory descriptions, statistical data analysis, and construction of students' own thematic maps.
requirements: Progressive availability of atlas-based tasks aligned with the geography curriculum across grade levels
constraints: Stages are tied to the Kazakhstan geography course structure (initial course grades 6-7; 'Geography of Kazakhstan' grades 8-9)
target_learners: Students in grades 6-9
target_learning_goals: Progressive GIS competence
Thematic map construction
Spatial data analysis
examples: The second stage includes tasks such as overlaying hydrography and freezing-rivers layers, and physical and soil maps of Kazakhstan
key_sources: Damekova, S. K., Zharkinbekova, T. N., Turtkarayeva, G. B., Han, S. I., & Damekova, O. Z. (2016). Electronic School Atlas as an Innovative Means of Development of Geographic Education in Kazakhstan Schools. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(18), 12668-12679. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1124623

article_title: The Effect of Buzz Group Technique and Clustering Technique in Teaching Writing at the First Class of SMA HKBP I Tarutung
citation: Tagor Pangaribuan & Sondang Manik. (2018). The Effect of Buzz Group Technique and Clustering Technique in Teaching Writing at the First Class of SMA HKBP I Tarutung. English Language Teaching, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n1p164
title: Use structured small-group pre-writing discussion with assigned roles to maximize participation
description: The article prescribes a specific procedure for implementing buzz groups effectively: divide the class into small groups of about six, explain the discussion question clearly, assign a leader and recorder, orient students to their responsibilities beforehand, monitor progress by circulating among groups, and summarize briefly at the end. The article states "The leader should encourage less aggressive individuals to join in the discussion, so that a few highly verbal students do not control the discussion and prevent goo d group interaction." This procedure is designed to ensure equitable participation and accurate recording of ideas.
requirements: The topic "must also be simple enough that students do not become discourage in trying to discuss it in so short time."
constraints: The article states buzz groups are "not intended to be a full meeting but used as a supplement to other methods."
target_learners: first-year senior high school students (Class X)
target_learning_goals: participating equitably in pre-writing discussion and generating ideas for descriptive writing
examples: The article's Figure 1 illustrates the buzz group procedure steps from dividing the class through teacher summarization.
key_sources: Tagor Pangaribuan & Sondang Manik. (2018). The Effect of Buzz Group Technique and Clustering Technique in Teaching Writing at the First Class of SMA HKBP I Tarutung. English Language Teaching, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n1p164

article_title: Effects of a Graphic Organizer Intervention Package on the Mathematics Word Problem Solving Abilities of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorders
citation: Delisio, L. A., Bukaty, C. A., & Taylor, M. (2018). Effects of a Graphic Organizer Intervention Package on the Mathematics Word Problem Solving Abilities of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorders. The Journal of Special Education Apprenticeship, 7(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1180604
title: Strategy instruction may not be the best solution for every student with disability or every type of word problem
description: The authors argue that while an extensive research base suggests strategy instruction such as SBI and CSI benefits students who struggle with word problems, this study's results suggest "strategy instruction may not be the only -- or the best -- solution for all students who struggle with mathematics". They question whether providing every SWD with strategies that may not work for them supports individualized education.
requirements: Educators should assess what individual students do and do not know before applying interventions
constraints: The finding is based on a study with small disaggregated group sizes and should be interpreted with caution
target_learners: students with disabilities in elementary inclusive classrooms
target_learning_goals: mathematical word problem solving
examples: The authors ask why the field is providing every SWD with strategies that may not work for them, given that individualized education is the cornerstone of special education
key_sources: Delisio, L. A., Bukaty, C. A., & Taylor, M. (2018). Effects of a Graphic Organizer Intervention Package on the Mathematics Word Problem Solving Abilities of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorders. The Journal of Special Education Apprenticeship, 7(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1185372

article_title: Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level
citation: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28
title: Feuerstein's structural cognitive modifiability and mediated learning experience
description: The article leans especially on Feuerstein's idea of structural cognitive modifiability: the cognitive process is "a dynamic quality that occurs in the interaction process between two people: a learner and a teacher", so a learner's skills can and must be evolved and remediated. A mediated learning experience is central to remediating cognitive basic skills, and its essential components are "purposefulness, reciprocity and its meaning content". The teacher acts as a model and filter between learner and stimuli, moulding the order, intensity and content of stimuli without blocking direct learner–environment contact.
requirements: A learning situation must be purposeful and reciprocal, with teacher and learner committed to the task
The teacher must inform learners of distant learning goals (transcendence) and give here-and-now feedback
constraints: The teacher's influence should be neither too strong nor too weak, so direct connections between learner and surroundings are not prevented
target_learners: primary-level pupils needing guidance to learn cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: repair of defective cognitive processes
learning and working skills
examples: The intervention created structured, artificial learning situations in which pupils detected and learned relations between things
key_sources: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28

article_title: Learning How to Learn: A Student Success Course for at Risk Students
citation: Bowering, E. R., Mills, J., & Merritt, A. (2017). Learning How to Learn: A Student Success Course for At Risk Students. The Canadian Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 8(3). http://ir.lib.uwo.ca/cjsotl_rcacea/vol8/iss3/12
title: Student Success Course (SSC): a mandatory 14-week noncredit intervention for students on academic probation
description: The SSC is a mandatory, noncredit intervention developed at Mount St. Vincent University for undergraduates placed on academic probation (term GPA between 1.0 and 1.7). Its stated objectives are to identify academic strengths and weaknesses, enhance motivation, and develop effective study skills and personal developmental skills. The article describes it as follows: "The course consists of  36 contact hours across a 14-week academic term, costs the student $350, and is taught by q ualified instructors who hold graduate degrees in Education and/or Psychology". Instruction uses diagnostic assessment (the LASSI, re-administered at the last class), lecture, group discussion, written assignments, presentations, and in-class application exercises, with classes capped at no more than 20 students.
requirements: Mandatory registration for all AP students, with payment of the cost-recovery tuition fee
Diagnostic assessment with individual feedback, and instructors who hold graduate degrees in Education and/or Psychology
constraints: The SSC grade does not appear on the university transcript or affect GPA; students who do not pass must remain on AP and re-take the course
Whether academic gains were maintained over time and whether students persisted to degree completion were not assessed
target_learners: Undergraduate students on academic probation (cumulative GPA below 1.7)
target_learning_goals: Learning strategies and study skills
Motivation and self-regulation
Reduced test anxiety and procrastination
Improved GPA and removal of academic probation status
examples: Students complete the LASSI at the first and last class, with results interpreted individually to reinforce positive change
Writing assignments such as journals and one minute papers, plus a group presentation near the end of the course, provide practice and constructive feedback
key_sources: Bowering, E. R., Mills, J., & Merritt, A. (2017). Learning How to Learn: A Student Success Course for At Risk Students. The Canadian Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 8(3). http://ir.lib.uwo.ca/cjsotl_rcacea/vol8/iss3/12

article_title: Extended Discourse in First and Second Language Acquisition: A Challenge and an Opportunity
citation: Catherine E. Snow. (2014). Extended discourse in first and second language acquisition: A challenge and an opportunity! Journal of Japanese Linguistics 30. https://www.wordgen.serpmedia.org
title: Use discussion-based approaches to teaching in all language-learning situations because students learn more from talking than from listening
description: The article's key takeaway from the Word Generation studies and the broader literature on classroom discussion is that incorporating classroom discussion of challenging but engaging topics is a highly promising approach for promoting foreign language proficiency and second language skills. Discussion creates authentic contexts for using newly taught vocabulary and strong motivation to use it, replicating the rich conversations in which well-educated parents involve young first language learners.
requirements: Teachers and students need preparation for discussion-based learning, which the article notes was lacking in participating classrooms
Sufficient time must be protected, since curricular coverage pressures often limited discussion time
constraints: Not all observed discussions were exemplary: students got off topic, a few students dominated the floor, and quiet students' contributions were sometimes ignored
Discussions of delicate or personally relevant topics sometimes descended into unproductive and possibly hurtful exchanges
Students still in early stages of English learning require careful adaptation, such as extending 20-minute activities to 45 minutes or a one-week unit over 10 days
target_learners: second and foreign language learners
urban middle school students
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
oral language skills as preparation for literacy achievement
examples: The article reports that students greatly enjoyed the debate activity and many teachers said they had never fully appreciated the depth and subtlety of their students' thinking before launching the classroom debates.
key_sources: Catherine E. Snow. (2014). Extended discourse in first and second language acquisition: A challenge and an opportunity! Journal of Japanese Linguistics 30. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED571513

article_title: Classmate Peer-Coaching: "A Study Buddy Support Scheme"
citation: Thalluri, Jyothi; O'Flaherty, Jackie A.; and Shepherd, Paul L. (2014). Classmate peer-coaching: "A Study Buddy Support scheme". Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 92-104. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/8
title: Study Buddy Support (SBS) scheme
description: The SBS scheme is a same-year-level classmate peer-coaching initiative for first-year Nursing science courses. At-risk students (Buddies) and academically gifted students (Buddy Leaders) are identified early from performance in assessments "conducted in the first two weeks of their study period". Buddy Leaders receive a training handbook and face-to-face training; sessions run for eight weeks, two hours each, with each Leader allocated 7-10 Buddies, focusing on forthcoming assessments, with staff accessible for assistance.
requirements: Early identification of at-risk students and high achievers via early-semester assessments
Buddy Leaders attend a training session and receive an SBS training handbook
Teaching staff organise time, venue, weekly topics, and remain accessible during sessions
constraints: Buddy Leaders were not paid for their time; recognition was via certificates and book gift vouchers
target_learners: first-year Bachelor of Nursing and Midwifery students at risk of failing a Bioscience course
target_learning_goals: understanding of human anatomy and physiology course content
improved pass rates and retention of at-risk students
examples: In 2012-2013, 272 of 1280 enrolled HB1 students (21%) were classified as at risk; 141 participated in SBS and 131 did not.
key_sources: Thalluri, Jyothi; O'Flaherty, Jackie A.; and Shepherd, Paul L. (2014). Classmate peer-coaching: "A Study Buddy Support scheme". Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 92-104. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/8

article_title: A Student-Centered Guest Lecturing: A Constructivism Approach to Promote Student Engagement
citation: Lei Li; Rong Guo. (2015). A student-centered guest lecturing: A constructivism approach to promote student engagement. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies, 15. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html
title: Student-centered guest lecturing process: team question-generation, question-and-answer interview, recorded video, reflection, and term paper
description: The article defines a repeatable lesson-level sequence for guest lecturing in online courses. Students study course content and work in groups to determine questions for the guest speaker; the speaker is interviewed in a pure question-and-answer format by an on-site representative or instructor, remotely if needed; the interview is recorded and shared; students revisit the video and reflect in discussion forums; the cycle may repeat with more speakers; finally students review the video series and write a term paper summarizing lessons learned. Teams are formed and coordinated through discussion forums in the course management tool.
requirements: Guest speakers carefully aligned with course content
Discussion forums in the course management tool for team formation and group activities
Recorded interviews made available to all students
Required discussions and a term paper to encourage participation
constraints: Ideally multiple speakers repeat the process, which the article treats as an ideal rather than a guaranteed condition
target_learners: online graduate students
target_learning_goals: student engagement
active construction of course knowledge
reflection on guest-expert content
examples: In the pilot, students formed teams via a discussion forum, generated questions for the speaker, watched the recorded interview, discussed reflections in forums, and wrote a term paper
key_sources: Lei Li; Rong Guo. (2015). A student-centered guest lecturing: A constructivism approach to promote student engagement. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies, 15. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html

article_title: Determination Instructions Efficiency of Teaching Methods in Teaching Physics in the Case of Teaching Unit "Viscosity. Newtonian and Stokes Law"
citation: Branka Radulović, Maja Stojanović. (2015). Determination Instructions Efficiency of Teaching Methods in Teaching Physics in the Case of Teaching Unit „Viscosity. Newtonian and Stokes law“. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 8, Number 2. https://adn.teaching.ro
title: Stokes-method falling-ball experiment for teaching viscosity
description: The experimental treatment used the Stokes method: "Students measured the distance traveled and the time for which the balls fall through the liquid uniformly certain density." Based on the measured quantities, pupils calculated the coefficient of viscosity of the fluid. The unit connected everyday occurrences of viscosity (tap water flow, wind in narrow streets) with fluid mechanics and mechanical engineering.
requirements: Students must understand viscosity as a basic concept of fluid mechanics for the experiment to be meaningful
constraints: The experiment was applied to one specific teaching unit (viscosity, Newtonian and Stokes law) in second-grade high-school physics
target_learners: second-grade high-school students (natural sciences and mathematics profile)
target_learning_goals: understanding viscosity and calculating a fluid's viscosity coefficient
examples: Students measured falling-ball distance and time, then calculated the viscosity coefficient of the liquid
key_sources: Branka Radulović, Maja Stojanović. (2015). Determination Instructions Efficiency of Teaching Methods in Teaching Physics in the Case of Teaching Unit „Viscosity. Newtonian and Stokes law“. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 8, Number 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1073276

article_title: Problem Solving Instruction for Overcoming Students' Difficulties in Stoichiometric Problems
citation: Mandina Shadreck, Ochonogor Chukunoye Enunuwe. (2017). Problem Solving Instruction for Overcoming Students' Difficulties in Stoichiometric Problems. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 10, Number 4. https://adi.uab.ro
title: Validated stoichiometry achievement test (Cronbach alpha 0.84)
description: The study's data-collection instrument was an achievement test in stoichiometry consisting of both multiple choice and open ended items. It was validated by experts in chemistry education, and its internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach alpha, "found to be 0.84, which is an acceptable level of reliability". It was administered as a 1.5-hour pre-test and again as a post-test after the intervention.
requirements: Validated by experts in chemistry education
target_learners: Advanced level high school chemistry students
target_learning_goals: Stoichiometry problem-solving competence
examples: Administered as pre-test in week 2 and post-test in week 5 of the five-week study
key_sources: Mandina Shadreck, Ochonogor Chukunoye Enunuwe. (2017). Problem Solving Instruction for Overcoming Students' Difficulties in Stoichiometric Problems. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 10, Number 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1164987

article_title: The Effects of a Female Role Model on Academic Performance and Persistence of Women in STEM Courses
citation: Sarah D. Herrmann, Robert Mark Adelman, Jessica E. Bodford, Oliver Graudejus, Morris A. Okun, and Virginia S. Y. Kwan (2016). The Effects of a Female Role Model on Academic Performance and Persistence of Women in STEM Courses. Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 38(5), 258-268. https://doi.org/10.1080/01973533.2016.1209757
title: Story-editing approach: brief interventions that reframe personal narratives yield sustainable academic benefits
description: The article frames its intervention within the story-editing approach, which posits that people can redirect their narratives about themselves to lead to lasting behavioral changes. Small psychological changes can yield large effects that persist over time; validated intervention families include teaching incremental theories of intelligence, values affirmation to buffer stereotype threat, and enhancing belonging by changing attribution styles. The present studies integrate role model, belonging, and investment themes into one narrative delivered online.
requirements: Changes in narratives from brief interventions result in sustainable, positive benefits when individuals reframe narratives about themselves and their story in the world
constraints: The article notes properly demonstrating mediation is challenging, citing identified issues such as overreliance on null hypothesis significance testing and use of mediation in cross-sectional research without clear time precedence
target_learners: college students, particularly women in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: academic performance
persistence in STEM majors
examples: The intervention letter drew on attribution themes (a lower-than-expected first test grade), belonging themes (questioning whether the investment in tuition and time was worthwhile), and the value of a college degree
key_sources: Sarah D. Herrmann, Robert Mark Adelman, Jessica E. Bodford, Oliver Graudejus, Morris A. Okun, and Virginia S. Y. Kwan (2016). The Effects of a Female Role Model on Academic Performance and Persistence of Women in STEM Courses. Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 38(5), 258-268. https://doi.org/10.1080/01973533.2016.1209757

article_title: The Effects of Problem-Based Learning on Pre-Service Teachers' Critical Thinking Dispositions and Perceptions of Problem-Solving Ability
citation: Senar Temel. (2014). The effects of problem-based learning on pre-service teachers’ critical thinking dispositions and perceptions of problem-solving ability. South African Journal of Education, 34(1), Art. #769. https://www.sajournalofeducation.co.za
title: Employ student-centred learning approaches in teacher education classes to develop critical thinking dispositions and problem-solving perceptions
description: The article recommends that teacher education deliberately develops pre-service teachers' critical thinking dispositions and perceptions of problem-solving ability by first describing the levels at which those skills are possessed, identifying hindering situations, providing models and opportunities, and employing student-centred approaches. It states: "student- centred learning approaches should be employed in classes to enable them to develop skills such as critical thinking dispositions and perceptions of problem-solving ability".
requirements: Levels of pre-service teachers' skills should first be described
Situations likely to hinder development should be determined
A model and opportunities should be provided to pre-service teachers
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from a single study in one chemistry topic with first-year students; the article notes critical thinking requires more time to develop than problem-solving
target_learners: pre-service teachers
university science students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking disposition
perception of problem-solving ability
examples: The study itself implemented PBL across five sessions on the acid-base topic as a student-centred approach, compared against traditional direct-explanation teaching
key_sources: Senar Temel. (2014). The effects of problem-based learning on pre-service teachers’ critical thinking dispositions and perceptions of problem-solving ability. South African Journal of Education, 34(1), Art. #769. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1136398

article_title: Is Storytelling Effective in Improving the English Vocabulary Learning among Iranian Children in Kindergartens?
citation: Maasumeh Abasi, Afshin Soori. (2014). Is Storytelling Effective in Improving the English Vocabulary Learning among Iranian Children in Kindergartens? International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 2(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.3p.7
title: Dolakova's content-based taxonomy of children's story types for language teaching
description: The article presents, citing Dolakova (2008), a classification of stories by content: "classical tales, animal tales or fables, repetitive and cumulative tales, adventures and romantic stories, poem, rhymes, songs and chants". Classical tales are described as most common across cultures, letting children guess unknown words from familiar plots; repetitive and cumulative tales are called very suitable for language learning because short plots and repetitive rhythms help children remember and reproduce words and structures quickly.
requirements: For classroom use, the article notes classical tales pose problems of story length and large numbers of words that can keep teachers from using them
constraints: The taxonomy is reported second-hand from Dolakova (2008) as cited in the article, not tested in the study itself
target_learners: young children in kindergartens and primary classes learning a foreign language
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary and listening comprehension through stories
examples: The article reports children especially like animal tales because the animal characters talk and think like human beings, and adventure/romance stories such as Cinderella for their happy endings
key_sources: Maasumeh Abasi, Afshin Soori. (2014). Is Storytelling Effective in Improving the English Vocabulary Learning among Iranian Children in Kindergartens? International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 2(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.3p.7

article_title: Is Storytelling Effective in Improving the English Vocabulary Learning among Iranian Children in Kindergartens?
citation: Maasumeh Abasi, Afshin Soori. (2014). Is Storytelling Effective in Improving the English Vocabulary Learning among Iranian Children in Kindergartens? International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 2(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.3p.7
title: Use storytelling so children learn vocabulary in context rather than by rote
description: The article argues that common Iranian kindergarten vocabulary practice — rote repetition, word-picture matching, songs whose words children repeat without understanding — is not meaningful, whereas storytelling lets children meet words inside a meaningful story context. Its conclusion states that "storytelling enables children to learn the vocabulary in context", and that the results let teachers and course designers see the potential of storytelling for vocabulary learning.
requirements: A suitable storybook and a teacher able to deliver staged storytelling sessions
constraints: The article notes that because adequate studies of story effectiveness are lacking, storybooks are not widely used in Iranian kindergartens, preschools and nursery schools
target_learners: children in kindergartens and preschools learning a second or foreign language
target_learning_goals: meaningful second/foreign language vocabulary learning
examples: In the study, new vocabulary was drawn from the storybook Three Bears and taught through flashcards, pictures, story reading, and post-storytelling questions linking words to children's real lives
key_sources: Maasumeh Abasi, Afshin Soori. (2014). Is Storytelling Effective in Improving the English Vocabulary Learning among Iranian Children in Kindergartens? International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 2(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.3p.7

article_title: The Impact of Task Type and Cognitive Style on Vocabulary Learning
citation: Gholam Reza Haji Pour Nezhad & Nasrin Shokrpour. (2012). The Impact of Task Type and Cognitive Style on Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 5(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n9p17
title: Static versus dynamic task-type dichotomy in task-based language teaching
description: The article adopts Ellis's (2003) classic dichotomy of task types in task-based language teaching. The static type "pays more attention to form and transfers information in a linear sequence through the prescribed language" with material learned consciously, giving more control to the learner and more linguistic context. The dynamic type describes situations or actions and narrates, involving two-way conversations without prescribed language content, learned unconsciously, emphasizing free uncontrolled production and extra-linguistic context. The study operationalizes these as its control and experimental treatments.
requirements: Both task types must fit within a balanced language course of meaning-focused input, deliberate language-focused learning, meaning-focused output, and fluency development strands
constraints: Studies cited by the article suggest static tasks are in general easier than dynamic ones
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners at university BS level
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary learning
reading comprehension
examples: The control group received vocabulary instruction through static task-type technique while the experimental group underwent dynamic task-type technique across 32 Academic Encounters reading passages over four months
key_sources: Gholam Reza Haji Pour Nezhad & Nasrin Shokrpour. (2012). The Impact of Task Type and Cognitive Style on Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 5(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n9p17

article_title: Effect of Edmark Program on Reading Fluency in Third-Grade Students with Disabilities
citation: Meeks, B. T., Martinez, J., & Pienta, R. S. (2014). Effect of Edmark Program on Reading Fluency in Third-Grade Students with Disabilities. International Journal of Instruction, 7(2). https://www.e-iji.net
title: STAR Reading assessment and Estimated ORF measure
description: STAR is a computer-adaptive reading assessment by Renaissance Learning used here to measure estimated oral reading fluency (ORF) in correct words per minute. Items adapt in difficulty to student responses, and the diagnostic report provides grade equivalency, reading range, and estimated ORF. The article cites U.S. Department of Education reviews (one with n = 63,291) finding "convincing evidence" of STAR's reliability and validity. In this study students took the 25-question test before and after the intervention.
requirements: Administered at individual computers before and after the intervention to derive pre/post Estimated ORF scores
target_learners: elementary students reading below grade level
target_learning_goals: measuring oral reading fluency growth
examples: All six participants were reading below the 25th percentile; the four lowest readers' Estimated ORF rates ranged from 13-26 words per minute against a third-grade target of 120 words correct per minute
key_sources: Meeks, B. T., Martinez, J., & Pienta, R. S. (2014). Effect of Edmark Program on Reading Fluency in Third-Grade Students with Disabilities. International Journal of Instruction, 7(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085264

article_title: Inculcating Positive Thinking in the Self-Concept of Children with Learning Difficulties
citation: Mohaned Ghazi Abed. (2016). Inculcating Positive Thinking in the Self-Concept of Children with Learning Difficulties. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 10, No. 3. https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: Focus children with learning difficulties on their identified strengths rather than their weaknesses to support self-concept
description: The article's guiding principle is that children with learning difficulties tend to attend to their weaknesses, so interventions should identify each child's character strengths and redirect attention toward abilities. It states that "Assisting children in establishing their main strengths can help to redirect focus away from their problems and issues and instead towards their abilities." The study operationalized this through the VIA Survey plus positive psychology lectures, though its overall SDQ hypothesis was not validated.
requirements: An instrument such as the VIA Survey to establish each child's individual strengths
class lectures on positive psychology delivered alongside strengths identification
constraints: The overall hypothesis of improved SDQ scores was not statistically validated in this study
the sample was small (40 boys) and drawn by purposive convenience sampling in Jeddah
target_learners: children with learning difficulties in intermediate school
target_learning_goals: self-concept improvement
resiliency
examples: Forty boys were randomly assigned to intervention or control groups; the intervention group completed the VIA Survey and three positive psychology lectures over five weeks
key_sources: Mohaned Ghazi Abed. (2016). Inculcating Positive Thinking in the Self-Concept of Children with Learning Difficulties. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 10, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1138669

article_title: An Effort to Close Achievement Gaps at Scale through Self-Affirmation
citation: Borman, G. D., & Grigg, J. (2013). An Effort to Close Achievement Gaps at Scale through Self-Affirmation. SREE Spring 2013 Conference.
title: Stereotype threat as an explanation of group achievement gaps
description: The article situates its intervention in stereotype threat theory: the apprehension individuals experience when confronted with a personally relevant stereotype, which elicits anxiety and counterproductive responses interfering with performance on evaluative activities. Over time it may pressure students to protectively disidentify with achievement. Self-affirmation, or "compensatory self-inflation," is the strategy of managing threatening situations by shoring up one's self-concept.
requirements: A personally relevant stereotype threatening social identity or self-esteem in an evaluative context
constraints: The article's own large-scale replication found no evidence the self-affirmation intervention closed the Black-White achievement gap on high-stakes test scores
target_learners: middle school students from groups subject to negative stereotypes (Black, Latino students; girls in mathematics)
target_learning_goals: closing racial and gender achievement gaps in standardized test performance
key_sources: Borman, G. D., & Grigg, J. (2013). An Effort to Close Achievement Gaps at Scale through Self-Affirmation. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563077

article_title: The Effect of Geogebra on Students' Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge: The Case of Applications of Derivative
citation: Mehmet Fatih Ocal. (2017). The Effect of Geogebra on Students’ Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge: The Case of Applications of Derivative. Higher Education Studies, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v7n2p67
title: Conceptual and procedural knowledge framework (Star, 2005) as applied to calculus learning
description: The article adopts Star's (2005) definitions in which conceptual knowledge encompasses "not only what is known (knowledge of concepts) but also one way that concepts can be known (e.g., deeply and with rich connections)", while procedural knowledge involves "the rules, the algorithms and operational procedures to be followed in fulfilling mathematical tasks". The framework holds that the two knowledge types develop simultaneously and interact, so gains in one lead to gains in the other. The article uses this framework to categorize test questions and interpret group differences.
requirements: Both knowledge types should be developed in balance for meaningful comprehension of a topic
constraints: There is no precise distinction between conceptual and procedural knowledge; one type may include parts of the other or be dominant
target_learners: calculus students at secondary and university level
target_learning_goals: understanding concepts and relations among concepts in mathematics; executing algorithms and procedures in mathematical tasks
examples: The study categorized ADT questions as conceptual or procedural using this framework, acknowledging students may have greater knowledge of one type for a specific topic
key_sources: Mehmet Fatih Ocal. (2017). The Effect of Geogebra on Students’ Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge: The Case of Applications of Derivative. Higher Education Studies, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v7n2p67

article_title: Students' Psychosocial Empowerment with the 'Steps for Life' Personal and Social Skills Greek Elementary Programme
citation: Kourmousi, N., Markogiannakis, G., Tzavara, C., Kounenou, K., Mandrikas, A., Christopoulou, E., & Koutras, V. (2018). Students’ Psychosocial Empowerment With The ‘Steps For Life’ Personal and Social Skills Greek Elementary Programme. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 10(5), 535-549. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2018541303
title: 'Steps for Life' Elementary curriculum: a question-based, multi-theoretical social-emotional programme for grades 1–2
description: A Greek universal, annual, teacher-taught mental health promotion programme for first and second graders aiming to enhance self-esteem, empathy, and personal and social skills. It "refrains from didacticism" and by "the almost sole use of questions during teaching, it guides the students in learning how to think for themselves". It draws on Bandura's Social Learning Theory (role-modelling, role-playing), the cognitive problem-solving approach of Shure and Spivack, the Eco-Behavioral Systems Model, Psychoanalytic Theory elements, and Rogers' person-centered approach. It comprises 27 two-hour weekly lessons in four modules, delivered within the Greek 'Flexible Zone'.
requirements: Teacher training including initial presentation, three whole-day experiential workshops, and monthly support meetings
A Teacher's Manual, Lesson Guide, hand-puppets, 76 pictures, and Letters to the Family
constraints: Designed for implementation within the Greek 'Flexible Zone' weekly two-hour period
Designed for first and second grade elementary students
target_learners: first and second grade elementary students
target_learning_goals: self-esteem
empathy
emotion management
problem-solving
personal and social skills
examples: The nine-step question-based procedure for safe emotions' teaching, from naming the emotion to choosing the best ideas
key_sources: Kourmousi, N., Markogiannakis, G., Tzavara, C., Kounenou, K., Mandrikas, A., Christopoulou, E., & Koutras, V. (2018). citation: Kourmousi, N., Markogiannakis, G., Tzavara, C., Kounenou, K., Mandrikas, A., Christopoulou, E., & Koutras, V. (2018). title: Letters to the Family: parental involvement component of 'Steps for Life'
description: One of five curriculum components, the Letters to the Family "inform parents of the taught skills and provide them with simple guidelines and indicative ways of dialoguing, thus supporting the continuation of the child's learning at home". Families received the letters during lessons that required them, containing "guidelines concerning the continuation of learning of the taught skills". This parental involvement is one of the programme's three distinguishing design features alongside question-based teaching and diffusion in formal and hidden curriculum.
requirements: Delivery during the lessons that required so, as part of the weekly lesson structure
target_learners: first and second grade elementary students and their families
target_learning_goals: consolidation of taught personal and social skills at home

article_title: The Effect of Explicit Instruction of Meta Cognitive Learning Strategies on Promoting Jordanian Language Learners' Reading Competence
citation: ABEER AL-GHAZO. (2016). The Effect of Explicit Instruction of Meta Cognitive Learning Strategies on Promoting Jordanian Language Learners' reading competence. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.10. https://www.iiste.org
title: Strategy training should teach language learning strategies together with feelings, beliefs, responsibility and trust, and encourage collaborative work
description: In the conclusion the article states, citing Tashtosh (2008), that teachers need to learn how to facilitate the process of reading and that conscious learning can be achieved through strategy training. It asserts that "The best strategy training not only teaches language learning strategies but also deals with feelings and beliefs about taking on responsibility and trust", and that giving instructions on how to implement and employ different strategies makes learning and teaching more meaningful and purposeful and encourages learners to work collaboratively. The article offers this as an author interpretation rather than a tested result of the study.
requirements: Instruction on how to implement and employ different strategies in the classroom
constraints: Stated in the article's conclusion as an interpretation; the study itself measured reading comprehension outcomes only
target_learners: EFL learners
University language learners
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Learner responsibility and collaboration in language learning
examples: The author reports that the experimental group's strategy instruction was associated with improved reading comprehension and vocabulary development in the post-test

article_title: Investigating the Effectiveness of a Dynamic Integrated Approach to Teacher Professional Development
citation: Antoniou, P., Kyriakides, L., & Creemers, B. (2011). Investigating the Effectiveness of a Dynamic Integrated Approach to Teacher Professional Development. ceps Journal, 1(1). https://cepsj.si
title: Focus professional development on stage-specific groupings of teaching skills rather than unfocused reflection
description: The article argues that professional development should focus on "specific groupings of teacher factors associated with student learning rather than with an isolated teaching factor or with the whole range of teacher factors". Reflection should be directed at the improvement priorities implied by each teacher's developmental stage, complementing rather than replacing critical reflection. In the study, this stage-focused design produced teaching-skill gains and student achievement gains that unfocused reflection did not.
requirements: Validated measurement of each teacher's developmental stage before assigning content
Professional development content drawn from factors empirically associated with student achievement
constraints: Findings come from one school year with volunteer teachers in Cyprus; generalisability and long-term effects are flagged as needing further study
target_learners: elementary school teachers across developmental stages
target_learning_goals: developing teaching skills linked to student achievement gains
examples: Teachers at stage 1 in the HA group attempted differentiation without prerequisite classroom management and structuring skills, and their attempts were not successful

article_title: Using Online Computer Games in the ELT Classroom: A Case Study
citation: Ioanna Vasileiadou & Zafiri Makrina. (2017). Using Online Computer Games in the ELT Classroom: A Case Study. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p134
title: Start each course by eliciting students' preferences about how the lesson should take place and incorporate those preferences into regular lessons
description: The article's educational implication is that teachers should begin the year by finding out how students want to learn and build those preferences into lessons. It reports that this freedom of choice, grounded in differentiated instruction, had a radical impact on performance, particularly of weaker students, and increased motivation. In the study this was done through semi-structured interviews that identified computer games as the students' preferred vocabulary method.
requirements: Teachers must investigate students' preferences regarding vocabulary-teaching methods before deciding the instructional approach, as the researchers did with semi-structured interviews.
constraints: The article states its results cannot be generalized to students of the same level across Greece because the research was small-scale, rural, and involved very few students.
target_learners: young primary-school EFL learners (4th grade)
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary learning and retention
examples: The researchers interviewed students about seven candidate methods, found 61% preferred computer games, and let the experimental class practise vocabulary with free online games chosen according to their likes, interests and abilities.

article_title: An Examination of the Impact of Early Intervention on Learning Outcomes of At-Risk Students
citation: Yi Zhang, Qiang Fei, Munir Quddus, Carolyn Davis. (2014). An examination of the impact of early intervention on learning outcomes of at-risk students. Research in Higher Education Journal, Volume 26. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html
title: Structured student information form for early intervention advising sessions
description: The early intervention program at the College of Business at PVAMU used a structured student information form (Appendix A) as the advising instrument. As the article states, "A structured student information form (see appendix A) is used as a guide to determine students' problem areas so that students and advisors can discuss ways to improve their course performance for the rest of the semester." The form collects student data (GPA, credit hours, major, grades, absences), student responses on study hours, working hours, tutoring use, and access to course materials, plus instructor suggestions and follow-up progress discussions. It supported developmental rather than prescriptive advising.
requirements: Students must be identified as at-risk by failing midterm grades (below C) before the form is used in an advising session
constraints: The advising was voluntary, so only students who responded and came in were covered by the form
target_learners: academically at-risk undergraduate business students at a minority-serving university
target_learning_goals: improving course performance and passing rates for at-risk students
examples: Students were asked how many hours per week they study and work, whether they had the required course material, and why they thought they were performing poorly
