article_title: Effect of Inquiry-Based Learning Approach on Student Resistance in a Science and Technology Course
citation: Demet SEVER, Meral GÜVEN. (2014). Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Approach on Student Resistance in a Science and Technology Course. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.4.1919
title: Student resistance as an affective problem distinct from unwanted student behaviors
description: The article defines student resistance behavior as "an affective problem perceived as oppositional behavior toward instructional activities", distinguishing it from unwanted student behaviors because it "affects each component of the teaching–learning process negatively". The literature it cites identifies sources including direct teacher instruction, insufficient learning experience, lack of self-confidence, low academic achievement, and unfair behaviors toward students. Resistance can sometimes improve teaching because resistant students complain about improper instruction.
requirements: Identification of resistance behaviors through observations and interviews with teachers
constraints: Resistance behaviors are sometimes constructive, as complaints about improper instruction can improve the teaching–learning process
target_learners: elementary and secondary students
target_learning_goals: affective engagement in instruction
reduction of oppositional behavior toward instructional activities
examples: The study identified 25 7th-grade students with resistance behaviors via observations and interviews with 14 teachers
key_sources: Demet SEVER, Meral GÜVEN. (2014). Effect of Inquiry-based Learning Approach on Student Resistance in a Science and Technology Course. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.4.1919

article_title: The Effects of Structured Transfer Pathways in Community Colleges
citation: Baker, R. (2016). The Effects of Structured Transfer Pathways in Community Colleges. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373716651491
title: Structured transfer pathways with guaranteed admission and standardized curricula reduce informational barriers and increase degree attainment
description: The article finds that transfer degree programs combining set curricula, guaranteed admission to a 4-year system, junior standing, and priority consideration can significantly increase associate degree attainment. The author concludes that "strategies that address structural impediments present in community colleges (a profusion of potential pathways, uncoordinated scheduling, a lack of coordination between sectors, and insufficient information and support) are promising because they are affordable, scalable, and relatively easy to sell politically."
requirements: Requires coordination between 2-year and 4-year institutions to establish common curricula and admission guarantees across campuses.
constraints: The article notes that not all ADTs are accepted at all CSU campuses and that the modest GPA bump given with the ADT might not be enough for students to get accepted to a local campus.
target_learners: community college students intending to transfer
target_learning_goals: associate degree completion
transfer to 4-year institutions
credit efficiency
examples: California's SB 1440 established ADTs jointly created by community colleges and CSUs, with guaranteed admission, junior standing, and priority consideration for capacity-constrained programs.
key_sources: Baker, R. (2016). The Effects of Structured Transfer Pathways in Community Colleges. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373716651491

article_title: Beyond Behavioral Modification: Benefits of Socio-Emotional/Self-Regulation Training for Preschoolers with Behavior Problems
citation: Graziano, P. A., & Hart, K. (2016). Beyond behavior modification: Benefits of social–emotional/self-regulation training for preschoolers with behavior problems. Journal of School Psychology, 58, 91–111. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2016.07.004
title: STP-PreK Enhanced: intensive kindergarten summer readiness class with social–emotional and self-regulation training
description: The STP-PreK Enhanced is an 8-week, full-day (8 a.m.–5 p.m.) kindergarten summer readiness class for pre-kindergarteners with behavior problems. It combines a behavioral modification point and response-cost system, an academic curriculum (Literacy Express), and added social–emotional training (30 min daily) and self-regulation training including EF games and "a daily 15 min computerized working memory training (Cogmed JM)." Families in this condition also received the weekly School Readiness Parenting Program.
requirements: Staffing at a 2:5 staff-to-student ratio with certified lead teachers, graduate-student lead counselors, and paraprofessional aides; a manual available from the authors details each component
constraints: Evaluated as part of a small randomized trial with 45 children; the enhanced curriculum was delivered daily for 8 weeks during the summer before kindergarten
target_learners: preschool children with externalizing behavior problems entering kindergarten
target_learning_goals: school readiness
executive functioning
emotion regulation
social skills
pre-academic skills
examples: Children learned to cope with negative emotions via the Turtle Shell Technique and engaged in EF games such as red light/green light adapted from Tominey and McClelland (2011)
key_sources: Graziano, P. A., & Hart, K. (2016). Beyond behavior modification: Benefits of social–emotional/self-regulation training for preschoolers with behavior problems. Journal of School Psychology, 58, 91–111. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2016.07.004

article_title: Success Training for Academic Resiliency: An Advising Intervention Program for Undergraduate Students on Probation
citation: Liu, C., Bruner, J., & Ammigan, R. (2022). Success Training for Academic Resiliency: An Advising Intervention Program for Undergraduate Students on Probation. Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies in Education, 11(2). https://ojed.org/jise
title: Student Success Model as conceptual framework for STAR Lite
description: The Student Success Model (Royal et al., 2015) addresses three variables: academic proficiency, institutional navigation, and socio-emotional engagement. The article adopts it as the conceptual framework for the STAR Lite program, using each variable as a guiding principle for serving students on probation. The model "focuses on three key success indicators to increase undergraduate student's (a) academic proficiency; (b) institutional navigation; and (c) socio-emotional engagement." It was integrated with the NACADA academic advising core competencies model (conceptual, informational, relational) to center the student in advising work.
requirements: Requires integration with NACADA academic advising core competencies to center students in advising work
constraints: The article applies the model specifically to undergraduate students on academic probation at one institution
target_learners: Undergraduate students on academic probation
target_learning_goals: Return to good academic standing
Academic proficiency
Institutional navigation
Socio-emotional engagement

article_title: Success Training for Academic Resiliency: An Advising Intervention Program for Undergraduate Students on Probation
citation: Liu, C., Bruner, J., & Ammigan, R. (2022). Success Training for Academic Resiliency: An Advising Intervention Program for Undergraduate Students on Probation. Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies in Education, 11(2). https://ojed.org/jise
title: STAR Lite advising intervention program
description: STAR Lite is a one-semester advising intervention for undergraduate students on academic probation, grounded in a strength-based mindset and tailored to individual student needs. Participation requires "meeting with an assigned STAR Lite advisor at least three times during the academic semester." The program uses a cohort model allowing students to work together and share experiences, building peer-to-peer community support guided by the Neighborhood Student Success Model. Students with GPA under 2.0 who are Exploratory Preference (undeclared) majors are invited to participate.
requirements: Students meet with an assigned advisor at least three times during the semester
Participation limited to one semester immediately after probation placement
constraints: Served only Exploratory Preference (undeclared) majors at one Midwestern research university
Pre-COVID data with all services provided in person
target_learners: Undergraduate students on academic probation with undeclared majors
target_learning_goals: Return to good academic standing
Persistence and graduation

title: Obtain stability of observed teaching practices before drawing inference from classroom observation measures
description: The paper concludes that "the present study highlights the importance of obtaining stability of observed teaching practices" and recommends further investigation of methods to improve stability of instructional variables, such as controlling for the type of academic content observed and observing consecutive days of instruction. Low stability attenuates relationships between observed practices and student outcomes.

constraints: Many instructional variables fell below a reliability threshold of .70 with three observations

Kindergarten students

Beginning mathematics

article_title: Gamifying Outdoor Social Inquiry Learning with Context-Aware Technology
citation: Morris Siu-Yung Jong, Tom Chan, Vincent Tam and Ming-Tak Hue. (2017). Gamifying Outdoor Social Inquiry Learning with Context-Aware Technology. International Conference Educational Technologies 2017.
title: Star-and-leaderboard gamification layer with real-time progress display
description: After completing tasks at a spot, students are awarded a star. The "leader board in the App will dynamically indicate how many stars each student has obtained and how much time he/she has spent on obtaining the stars in a real-time manner", providing a competitive game mechanic intended to sustain engagement during outdoor inquiry activities.

title: Stripling's social inquiry model as the pedagogic framework for the app's scaffolds
description: The article adopts Stripling's (2003, 2008) social inquiry model as one of two guiding frameworks for the app design. article_title: Using Story Structure for Lesson Design in Teaching about Sexual Assault
citation: Erbe, R. G., & Kearns, K. D. (2016). Using story structure for lesson design in teaching about sexual assault. The Health Educator, 48(2), 23-27. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1130703
title: Story-structured lesson design using the four C's (characters, complications, conflict, causality)
description: A lesson design pattern in which content is organized as a story divided into segments built on Willingham's (2009) 4 C's of stories: characters, complications, conflict, and causality. In this study, students read different segments of a story about sexual assault, predicted what occurred before or after their segment, reflected personally, discussed in groups, and concluded with whole-class discussion. The segments were 'created based on Willingham's (2009) 4 C elements' with each segment 'causally connected to each other and revolving around the Conflict'.
requirements: A story relevant and relatable to students, divided into segments each embodying the 4 C elements
constraints: Authors note sensitivity of topic may make some students uncomfortable participating in group discussion
target_learners: college undergraduates
target_learning_goals: increase concern about sexual assault
understand consent
identify effective prevention strategies
examples: A 60-minute sexual assault prevention lesson in a 300-level Men's Health class: video, statistics, group reading of story segments, personal reflection, group discussion, whole-class discussion

article_title: Fostering Team Creativity in Higher Education Settings
citation: de Villiers Scheepers, M. J. & Maree, L. (2015). Fostering Team Creativity in Higher Education Settings. e-Journal of Business Education & Scholarship of Teaching, 9(1). http://www.ejbest.org
title: Stickiness stages framework applied to team creative skills development
description: The article applies Szulanski's stickiness framework to creativity education, defining stickiness as "the difficulty learners have to internalise knowledge and skills, enabling them to perform a task successfully". Four stages — initiation, implementation, ramp-up and integration — mark where skill losses may occur during creative skills development. The framework structures when skills should be measured: before training, immediately after, and after three months. It provides a lens for designing interventions that minimise barriers to knowledge transfer.
requirements: Skills should be assessed at multiple time intervals aligned to the four stickiness stages to determine whether effects endure
constraints: Creative skills are particularly vulnerable in an unsupportive team climate, and new skills could be discarded if problems are encountered
target_learners: final-year undergraduate business and food science students
target_learning_goals: team creativity
creative problem-solving skills
examples: The study aligned measurement times O1, O2 and O3 to initiation, implementation & ramp-up, and integration stages

citation: Wekesa, Noah Wafula and Ongunya, Raphael Odhiambo. (2016). Project Based Learning on Students’ Performance in the Concept of Classification of Organisms Among Secondary Schools in Kenya. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.16. https://www.iiste.org
title: Students' Attitude Questionnaire
description: The Students' Attitude Questionnaire (Attitude Test Questionnaire) was used to collect information about students' attitude towards classification of organisms when taught using project based learning compared with conventional methods. Post-test results were analysed by ANOVA, yielding F = 3.94, significant at the 0.05 level.

article_title: Development of Subject Position as a Condition for Forming Communicative Competence of a Future Teacher
citation: Yarullina, A. Sh., & Araslanova, A. T. (2016). Development of Subject Position as a Condition for Forming Communicative Competence of a Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(9), 2311-2322.
title: Structural-functional model of forming communicative competence of the future teacher
description: The article works out a functional-structural model of forming communicative competence of a future teacher under transforming pedagogical education. It includes purposeful, methodological, content, organizational-processual and regulative components, built on competent, businesslike and module approaches. The model reflects "four levels of structural contents of educating the future teacher, possessing communicative competence: informational, methodological, methodical and practical". Its basic condition is development of the student's subjective position.
requirements: Educational process built on competent, businesslike and module approaches with leading principles including putting a student into a position of his own activity
constraints: The model was developed and tested in the context of pedagogical university education in Russia
target_learners: university students in pedagogical education programs
target_learning_goals: communicative competence of a future teacher

article_title: Fostering the Computation Competence of Low Achievers through Cooperative Learning in Inclusive Classrooms: A Longitudinal Study
citation: Moser Opitz, E., Grob, U., Wittich, C., Häsel-Weide, U., & Nührenbörger, M. (2018). Fostering the Computation Competence of Low Achievers Through Cooperative Learning in Inclusive Classrooms: A Longitudinal Study. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 16(1), 19-35.
title: Structured learning settings are crucial for successfully implementing cooperative learning with low achievers in mathematics
description: Based on inconsistent prior CL research, the article hypothesizes that "structured learning settings are crucial for successfully teaching low achievers in mathematics and for the implementation of CL." The intervention operationalized structure through detailed lesson plans with a fixed lesson sequence of introduction, seatwork, reflection, and discussion, and cooperative pairs selected by the teacher working on tasks at different difficulty levels.
requirements: Detailed lesson plans and teacher training to guarantee fidelity of implementation
constraints: Prior research findings on CL effectiveness are inconsistent; Kroesbergen and Van Luit found CL less effective than direct instruction for children with learning problems
target_learners: Low achievers in mathematics in inclusive grade-2 classrooms
target_learning_goals: Computation competence and flexible strategy use
examples: Teachers received a manual with standardized lesson plans introduced in two three-hour training meetings, and one program unit per classroom was videotaped to check fidelity

article_title: The Use of Geospatial Technologies Instruction within a Student/Teacher/Scientist Partnership: Increasing Students' Geospatial Skills and Atmospheric Concept Knowledge
citation: Hedley, M. L., Templin, M. A., Czajkowski, K., & Czerniak, C. (2013). Journal of Geoscience Education. https://doi.org/10.5408/11-237.1
title: STS partnership model combining scientist-led teacher training, field data collection, and inquiry-based student projects
description: The STS partnership model involves scientists teaching teachers geospatial technologies in a summer institute, followed by a master teacher providing standards-based pedagogy instruction. During the school year, teachers instruct students in geospatial skills, students collect field data shared with scientists, and complete inquiry-based projects presented at a mini-science conference. The article states "An STS partnership, therefore, must meet a number of requirements in order for it to succeed: (1) Teachers and students must be able to understand the science involved; (2) the cost of instrumentation must be low; (3) the research in which the teacher and students will participate should require more manpower or observers than scientists alone can provide, and (4) the research must be conducted in multiple locations that are geographically diverse."
requirements: Teachers and students must be able to understand the science involved
the cost of instrumentation must be low
the research should require more manpower or observers than scientists alone can provide
the research must be conducted in multiple locations that are geographically diverse
target_learners: grades 7-12 students in high-needs schools
target_learning_goals: geospatial skills
atmospheric science concept knowledge
inquiry-based science skills
examples: Scientists taught teachers remote sensing, GIS, and GPS in a 5-day summer institute; students collected surface temperature data at two field sites and presented inquiry projects at a mini-science conference at the Great Lakes Science Museum.

citation: Nian Zhixuan, Li Mingchun, Liang Junwen, Li Yijia, Wei Ziting, Pan Liqiang, Fang Sen, Yang Xudong, Du Wenjia, Yun Xiangdong. (2026). description: The article concludes that interdisciplinary collaboration skills "cannot be developed solely through situational exposure but still require more explicit, structured guidance from instructors—such as a unified discussion framework, clear objectives for each discipline's contributions, and enhanced feedback sessions." Enhanced feedback sessions
constraints: Derived from a single-center study with a relatively small sample size; generalizability requires further validation in larger, multicenter studies

medical students in multidisciplinary clinical education

clinical judgment
integration of diverse expert perspectives

article_title: Learning curve of Versius-assisted radical prostatectomy: role of prior experience and proctoring.
citation: Fernández-Conejo G, González Álvarez C, Del Olmo Durán P, Tagalos Muñoz A, Sanz Mayayo E, Diez Nicolás V, García Barreras S, Subiela Henríquez JD, Rodríguez-Patrón R, Pérez-Fernández E, Gómez Dos Santos V, Burgos Revilla FJ. description: The article recommends integrating structured, proficiency-based VR simulation curricula into early surgical training because its prospective comparative study found that novices completing such a curriculum outperformed controls given unstructured deliberate practice. The authors state these findings "support the integration of structured, proficiency-based VR simulation curricula into early surgical training to enhance technical skill acquisition and procedural competence." Procedural proficiency in laparoscopic cholecystectomy

VR simulators (LaparoS VR trainers) and experienced laparoscopic surgeon instructors

citation: Yang Yuehang, Sheng Li, Huang Liang, Guo Qiannan, Hu Yuting, Shi Jiawei. (2026). Application of an AI-enabled personalized medical education model for improving clinical thinking among cardiovascular surgery trainees. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09993-z
title: Staged case-based teaching that presents clinical information progressively to reduce cognitive load
description: The intervention organized complex cardiovascular scenarios into sequential learning steps: an introductory module using problem-based learning principles with common scenarios (e.g., acute chest pain, postoperative low cardiac output), and an advanced module with complex scenarios containing multiple clinical variables and distracting information. "By dividing complex cardiovascular surgery scenarios into sequential learning steps, this approach may reduce cognitive load and provide more opportunities for active reasoning." Interactive questions guided next-step examination choices, diagnosis identification, and management decisions.
requirements: Case materials integrating history, examination, laboratory, and imaging data
Embedded interactive questions and guideline-based explanatory notes
Progression from common introductory scenarios to complex advanced scenarios
constraints: The authors state this may reduce cognitive load; the cognitive-load mechanism was not directly measured in the study
target_learners: Cardiovascular surgery trainees in specialized training
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning and diagnostic decision-making
Synthesizing complex clinical information
examples: The introductory module covered scenarios such as acute chest pain and postoperative bleeding; the advanced module covered perioperative multiple organ dysfunction, ARDS, and acute kidney injury

article_title: Nursing Students' Perceptions of a Clinical Simulation Experience in Community Care: Strengths and Limitations.
citation: Gómez‐Torres, P., S. Galarreta‐Aperte, I. Blázquez‐Ornat, I. Antón‐Solanas, and E. Ramón‐Arbués. (2026). Nursing Students' Perceptions of a Clinical Simulation Experience in Community Care: Strengths and Limitations. Nursing Open 13, no. 9: e70807. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70807
title: Use structured prebriefing to define objectives, roles and expectations before each simulation scenario to promote psychological safety
description: A design principle for simulation-based education drawn from the study's implications section. The authors state that "Educators should use structured prebriefing to define learning objectives, roles and expectations before each scenario, thereby promoting psychological safety and meaningful engagement." Prebriefing establishes a fiction contract and a safe environment in which mistakes are treated as learning opportunities, which the study links to students' valued sense of practicing without fear and to mitigating performance anxiety.
requirements: Facilitators who provide consistent support throughout the activity and tailor guidance to students' needs
constraints: Performing individually while being observed and evaluated created anxiety and vulnerability for some students despite the safe-environment design
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students in simulation-based education
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning, communication and decision-making competencies in community care
examples: In the study, each 45-minute session opened with 5–10 minutes of prebriefing covering case presentation and clarification of questions before scenario enactment.

citation: Zhu Xiaocheng, Tang Anliu, Chin Munle, Chang Huan. (2026). Developing purposeful observation during early clinical exposure in anesthesiology: a cluster-randomized study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10042-y
title: Structured perioperative observation pattern: explicit objectives plus checklist-guided observation and reflective summary within existing clinical exposure time
description: A lesson-level pattern in which early clinical exposure is reorganized rather than extended: the model "did not extend clerkship duration or increase students' direct participation in clinical procedures" but reduced passive didactic time and added explicit objectives, a workflow-oriented observation checklist, instructor prompts, and summary reflection. The checklist covered preoperative assessment, surgical entry verification, anesthesia implementation and intraoperative management, PACU recovery, postoperative management, patient safety, and team collaboration.
requirements: Same total instructional and clinical exposure time as the conventional clerkship
Standardized safety orientation before entering clinical areas
Instructor and student checklist versions to standardize prompts and discussion
constraints: Designed for high-safety clinical environments where student participation must be limited and teaching cannot interfere with clinical workflow
The checklist was used as an observation guide rather than an assessment tool and was not included in outcome scoring
target_learners: Novice undergraduate medical students without systematic clinical training
target_learning_goals: Transforming passive clinical exposure into goal-directed learning
Developing observation ability during early clinical exposure
examples: Students observed in subgroups of two per operating room across approximately 20 min preoperative assessment, 10 min surgical waiting area, 60 min operating theatre, and 30 min PACU

citation: Liao Ting, Zou Jinmei, Wang Min, Song Yuqing, Cai Li, Yin Jin, Chen Yao, Wang Yating. (2026). Professional Identity, Educator Competence Perception and Willingness to Engage in Geriatric Nursing Among Nursing Students: A Cross‐Sectional Study. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70804
title: Nursing education should strengthen both students' professional identity and geriatric nursing educators' professional competence
description: Based on the finding that PI and educator competence perception are both positively associated with willingness to engage in geriatric nursing, and that educator competence perception partially mediates the PI–willingness association, the authors recommend that nursing education practice should not focus solely on developing students' PI but should also emphasise teachers' professional competence. They suggest providing positive learning experiences in geriatric nursing may help students develop clearer career perceptions.
requirements: Educational interventions targeting both PI development and gerontological nurse educator professional competence
constraints: The cross-sectional design means the mediating pathway is associative, not established causally; the authors call for longitudinal or interventional studies
target_learners: vocational college nursing students
target_learning_goals: willingness to pursue geriatric nursing careers
examples: The study measured educator competence perception with the Chinese-version Gerontological Nurse Teacher Scale across five dimensions including theoretical knowledge, practical training, and social ethics.

title: Safe adoption of complex surgical procedures requires structured, team-based, proctored training beyond simulation alone
description: The article argues that implementing complex minimally invasive procedures should proceed through a structured curriculum combining simulation, video-based learning, observation, and proctoring, rather than the traditional apprenticeship model. It concludes that "safe adoption of complex procedures requires structured, team-based, proctored training beyond simulation alone," and that structured training "should no longer be viewed as optional but rather as a prerequisite for the ethical introduction of complex surgical innovations." The LEARNBOT program operationalized this by decoupling the learning curve from patient outcomes via preclinical biotissue training with a graduation gate.
requirements: High-volume center setting with sufficient annual procedure volume to sustain the trained team
A consistent operative team of at least two trained surgeons per center (console and tableside roles)
constraints: The article states a residual learning-curve effect (POPF) remained detectable per center despite simulation establishing standardized technical competency
The exact added value of the program remains unknown because no control group without training was included
target_learners: Surgeon teams adopting a new complex minimally invasive procedure
target_learning_goals: Transfer of the learning curve from the intraoperative setting to a preoperative training environment to protect patient safety
examples: The article cites a post hoc analysis of the LAELAPS-3 program in which centers adhering to a structured curriculum achieved significantly shorter learning curves compared with pioneering institutions

description: A renal biopsy simulator ("JIN Senshi-kun", Taisei Medical, Japan) mimicking a human kidney with approximately 10 cm diameter and 20 mm cortical thickness, made of "three types of styrene-based soft resins" reproducing cortical, medullary, and encapsulating layers. Ultrasonography showed distinct cortical-medullary contrast and real-time needle visualization. It maintained structural integrity after more than 100 punctures, enabling repeated use across a large student cohort.
requirements: Requires ultrasound equipment for real-time needle visualization during puncture practice
constraints: Developed based on the previously reported boiled egg model; durability claim derives from preliminary testing and the authors' previous work
target_learners: fifth-year medical students
target_learning_goals: ultrasound-guided renal biopsy technique
handling an 18-gauge biopsy needle
selecting the puncture site
examples: Students practiced puncture site selection and 18-gauge needle handling under real-time ultrasound guidance for approximately five minutes each

description: The article recommends integrating scheduled post-proficiency refreshers into robotic curricula, stating that "structured refreshers near the 3-month mark and extended practice should be integrated into robotic curricula to sustain readiness." target_learning_goals: Retention of robotic surgical technical skill and procedural efficiency
examples: ROC analysis identified 84 days as the cutoff for performance decay and 188 days for efficiency loss

title: Professionals should advise parents on creating structured, low-chaos homework routines to strengthen self-efficacy and reduce conflict
description: The article recommends that professionals incorporate practical advice on organizing homework routines, minimizing distractions, and establishing predictable practice moments. This is particularly relevant given evidence that frequent and consistent practice is critical for poor readers. Encouraging regular practice in a calm and organized setting may enhance learning opportunities, reduce parental stress, and strengthen parents' sense of efficacy, which is known to support more positive interactions.
requirements: Parents are expected to assist their child with homework assigned as part of dyslexia treatment on a near-daily basis
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and does not establish causality
target_learners: Mothers of children with dyslexia receiving clinic-based treatment
target_learning_goals: Supporting children's reading and spelling practice at home
Reducing mother–child conflict during homework
examples: The study measured household chaos using items from the Chaos, Hubbub, and Order Scale

asthma crisis management knowledge

title: Structured autonomy model balancing surgical education with patient safety
description: The article proposes a model in which resident autonomy is implemented through a structured, competency-based progression framework rather than time-based seniority alone. description: The authors propose viewing standardized testing as one component within a comprehensive, evidence-informed admissions process rather than as a standalone admission criterion. They state: "our findings support viewing standardized testing as one component of a comprehensive, evidence-informed admissions process, rather than as a standalone admission criterion." This framework positions test scores alongside GPA, structured interviews, and noncognitive assessments, with the incremental value of any single component diminishing when multiple robust measures are already incorporated.

constraints: The incremental contribution of standardized tests may become smaller when admissions systems already incorporate multiple academic and nonacademic measures; institutional differences may produce different outcomes elsewhere
target_learners: Medical school applicants
target_learning_goals: Designing holistic admissions processes that balance cognitive metrics with interpersonal, ethical, and professional attributes

title: Grant students autonomy to choose their examination pacing structure, since preference alone need not align with psychological benefit.
description: The article concludes that empowering students with choice in how they engage in assessments may be a key strategy to buffer test anxiety, especially in high-stakes, time-constrained settings. Because students were assigned rather than allowed to choose their pacing condition, the authors suggest the disconnect between pacing preference and test anxiety outcomes may reflect a psychological reactance effect, and that simply granting students the autonomy to choose their pacing structure may itself mitigate test anxiety.
requirements: Assessment designs that offer students a genuine choice of pacing structure rather than random assignment.
constraints: The article states this possibility is raised, not tested: the autonomy-to-choose idea is supported by open-text feedback from a subsequent unpublished study, and the present study's randomized crossover design denied students choice.
target_learners: upper-year undergraduate anatomy students
target_learning_goals: buffering test anxiety during high-stakes, time-constrained assessments
examples: Students in the randomized crossover study were assigned to bell-paced and self-paced conditions for the midterm and final laboratory examinations, and 23 of 35 preferred bell-pacing despite its higher reactive test anxiety.
key_sources: Bentley DC, Sotto A, Lombardi P. Comparison of examination performance and test anxiety during bell‐paced and self‐paced gross anatomy laboratory examinations. Anat Sci Educ. 2026;19:732–742. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70215

article_title: Efficacy of laparoscopic simulator training in standardized obstetrics and gynecology residents: a prospective study demonstrating skill convergence.
citation: Li Congqing, Song Fei, Xu Youjiang, Zhang Liwei, Wang Wenyan. (2026). Efficacy of laparoscopic simulator training in standardized obstetrics and gynecology residents: a prospective study demonstrating skill convergence. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-46957-1
title: Structured simulator-based curricula should serve as a standard adjunct to traditional clinical training for foundational laparoscopic skills, rather than relying on apprenticeship alone.
description: The article argues that traditional apprenticeship models are inconsistent, time-intensive, and raise patient safety concerns during the highest-risk phase of the learning curve. A structured, risk-free simulator curriculum enables systematic skill acquisition and promotes comparable outcomes across trainees, making it "a valuable adjunct to traditional clinical education".
requirements: A standardized curriculum with defined weekly sessions and core skill modules (e.g., 90-minute weekly sessions over four weeks covering camera navigation, hand-eye coordination, bimanual coordination, and suturing).
Regular objective assessment (e.g., weekly task completion time) to track skill acquisition and convergence.
constraints: Simulation serves as a preparatory adjunct; supervised clinical experience remains essential for developing full operative competence.
Low-cost box trainers may be preferable in resource-limited settings where high-fidelity equipment is inaccessible.
target_learners: obstetrics and gynecology residents (PGY-1 to PGY-3)
target_learning_goals: foundational laparoscopic surgical skills
examples: Thirty residents undertook a standardized 90-minute weekly session for four consecutive weeks on an Ethicon box trainer, covering four core skill modules assessed by task completion time.
key_sources: Li Congqing, Song Fei, Xu Youjiang, Zhang Liwei, Wang Wenyan. (2026). Efficacy of laparoscopic simulator training in standardized obstetrics and gynecology residents: a prospective study demonstrating skill convergence. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-46957-1

article_title: USMLE Step 2 Clinical Knowledge performance by disability, race, and ethnicity in U.S. medical students: A multi-site study.
citation: Nguyen Mytien, Kim Michael, Pereira-Lima Karina, Hodgens Tiffany, Juliao Jordan, Holman Elizabeth, Sangsland J. T., Boatright Dowin, Meeks Lisa M. (2026). USMLE Step 2 Clinical Knowledge performance by disability, race, and ethnicity in U.S. medical students: A multi-site study. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0349774
title: Structural barriers in assessment and accommodation access as explanation for Step 2 CK disparities
description: The article proposes that observed Step 2 CK disparities reflect "the cumulative influence of structural and contextual factors operating across training and assessment environments" rather than differences in clinical knowledge or preparedness. These factors include differential access to or utilization of accommodations, variability in institutional support, negative perceptions of learning environments shaped by ableism and fear of bias, and barriers such as requirements for updated neuropsychological documentation. The theory holds that "observed score differences may reflect variation in access to the exam rather than differences in clinical knowledge or preparedness."
requirements: Examination of accommodation access and institutional support processes to distinguish access barriers from knowledge differences
constraints: Step 2 CK–specific accommodation data were not available in this study, so the pathway could not be examined directly; residual confounding from unmeasured academic indicators cannot be excluded
target_learners: medical students with disabilities
medical students with intersecting marginalized identities
target_learning_goals: equitable access to high-stakes assessment of clinical knowledge
examples: The article cites 2025 AAMC graduation questionnaire data suggesting 7.1% of medical students with disabilities do not request accommodations because they lack documentation to support their request
key_sources: Nguyen Mytien, Kim Michael, Pereira-Lima Karina, Hodgens Tiffany, Juliao Jordan, Holman Elizabeth, Sangsland J. T., Boatright Dowin, Meeks Lisa M. (2026). USMLE Step 2 Clinical Knowledge performance by disability, race, and ethnicity in U.S. medical students: A multi-site study. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0349774

article_title: Comparing Early and Long-Term Outcomes of "Truly Autonomous" Senior Resident-Led with Consultant-Led Cardiac Surgery: A 10-Year Propensity-Matched Study.
citation: Kumar Ujjawal Aditya, Rao Eteesha, Al-Zubaidi Fadi Ibrahim, Page Aravinda, Smith Harry, Sitaranjan Daniel, De Silva Ravi, Farid Shakil. (2026). Comparing Early and Long-Term Outcomes of “Truly Autonomous” Senior Resident-Led with Consultant-Led Cardiac Surgery: A 10-Year Propensity-Matched Study. Interdisciplinary Cardiovascular and Thoracic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1093/icvts/ivag099
title: Structured progressive autonomy model for surgical residency training
description: A training-structure account in which residents progress through supervised involvement toward fully autonomous operating, supported by competency assessment and case selection tailored to experience. The article describes that "Only in the final months of residency are residents typically allowed to perform independent cases, once consultants are familiar with their capabilities as being safe to operate without direct supervision." It links this model to JCST supervision levels progressing from direct to indirect supervision, and attributes the safe outcomes to "robust institutional training standards rather than exceptional individual performance."
requirements: Systematic competency assessment through workplace-based assessments across multiple clinical settings
Consultant familiarity with resident capabilities before authorising autonomous cases
A local curriculum of wet lab, dry lab and didactic teaching plus high-fidelity simulation
constraints: Studied at a single high-volume quaternary centre with a long training tradition; the article notes the study period included the UK switch to exclusively integrated training, affecting resident experience levels
target_learners: cardiac surgical residents in integrated training programmes
target_learning_goals: progressive operative independence
day 1 consultant readiness
emergency operative proficiency
examples: Royal Papworth Hospital's residency programme, in which 803 truly autonomous resident-led cases across multiple surgeons were completed over 10 years with outcomes comparable to consultant-led cases
key_sources: Kumar Ujjawal Aditya, Rao Eteesha, Al-Zubaidi Fadi Ibrahim, Page Aravinda, Smith Harry, Sitaranjan Daniel, De Silva Ravi, Farid Shakil. (2026). article_title: Factors influencing the competence of student midwives in symphysis-fundal height measurement: A quantitative study.
citation: Cele, W.D., Mbeje, P.N. & Mhlongo, E.M., 2026, 'Factors influencing the competence of student midwives in symphysis-fundal height measurement: A quantitative study', Curationis 49(1), a2855. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v49i1.2855
title: Structure and standardise clinical teaching, mentorship and the clinical learning environment for SFH skills
description: The article concludes that variability across clinical units in communication, preceptor support and displayed learning objectives undermines consistent skill development, and that a supportive clinical environment complements classroom teaching and simulation. It states that "variability across units highlighted the need for a more structured and standardised approach to clinical teaching and mentorship" and that "strengthening the clinical learning environment is essential to complement existing teaching strategies".
requirements: A supportive clinical environment with mentoring, supervision and constructive feedback, alongside clear display of clinical objectives in units
constraints: The study was conducted in one province, so the authors state results cannot be generalised to other provinces; findings rest on subjective questionnaire data with no objective competence assessment
target_learners: Undergraduate student midwives in the R425 programme
Community service nurses
target_learning_goals: Competence and confidence in measuring, plotting and interpreting symphysis-fundal height
examples: In the survey, 141 students reported the learning environment maintained by clinical lecturers was conducive to learning, while variability across units showed inconsistent preceptor support
key_sources: Cele, W.D., Mbeje, P.N. & Mhlongo, E.M., 2026, 'Factors influencing the competence of student midwives in symphysis-fundal height measurement: A quantitative study', Curationis 49(1), a2855. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v49i1.2855

article_title: Trainee involvement in laparoscopic pyloromyotomy does not compromise outcomes: evidence from a longitudinal institutional experience.
citation: Martinho S, Nóbrega S, Barroso C, Correia-Pinto J. (2026). Trainee involvement in laparoscopic pyloromyotomy does not compromise outcomes: evidence from a longitudinal institutional experience. Pediatric Surgery International. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00383-026-06435-1
title: Structure early, supervised trainee involvement in neonatal minimally invasive surgery around direct in-room supervision plus early MIS immersion, simulation and video-based learning
description: The department's educational philosophy embeds pediatric surgery trainees in a strongly MIS-oriented culture from the outset of residency, with trainees operating as primary surgeons under direct in-room supervision of a consultant. The article states their model "includes early exposure to neonatal laparoscopy, progressive entrustment of procedural steps, access to ex-vivo laparoscopic simulation" and systematic video-based learning. In this 14-year cohort this model produced outcomes comparable to specialists, supporting early structured involvement rather than delaying trainee operative participation.
requirements: Direct in-room supervision of a consultant pediatric surgeon for trainee-performed procedures
Early exposure to neonatal laparoscopy during residency
Progressive entrustment of procedural steps
Access to ex-vivo laparoscopic simulation and video-based learning
constraints: Findings come from a single tertiary center with a southern European training paradigm (pediatric surgery from the outset, no general surgery residency); the article calls for replication across differing training systems
Retrospective, non-randomized design with small sample size limits statistical power and generalizability
target_learners: pediatric surgery trainees/residents
target_learning_goals: acquisition of independent neonatal minimally invasive surgical competency
examples: Between February 2017 and June 2025, three supervised trainees performed 8–13 laparoscopic pyloromyotomies each as primary operators, with no surgery-related complications and no adverse institutional CUSUM drift
key_sources: Martinho S, Nóbrega S, Barroso C, Correia-Pinto J. (2026). Trainee involvement in laparoscopic pyloromyotomy does not compromise outcomes: evidence from a longitudinal institutional experience. Pediatric Surgery International. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00383-026-06435-1

article_title: Enhancing gynecological examination training for international medical students: a comparative study of peer role-play and peer assessment.
citation: Lv Pingping, Chen Jianpeng, Chen Xijing, Wang Xiao, Xu Xiangrong, Li Jingyi. (2026). Enhancing gynecological examination training for international medical students: a comparative study of peer role-play and peer assessment. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09102-0
title: Structured peer feedback forms and scenario cases with psychosocial backstories for student-simulated patients
description: An instructional component consisting of three standardized simulated-patient scenarios (abnormal uterine bleeding, lower abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea), each with a detailed backstory including psychosocial elements such as anxiety about pelvic examinations, plus structured feedback forms. Student-simulated patients "use structured feedback forms to evaluate peers on empathy, clarity of explanation and respect for privacy", supporting assessment of technical skills and patient-centered communication during role-play.
requirements: Students select one scenario for role-play; simulated patients must be instructed to respond to student questions and complete the structured feedback forms.
constraints: Scenarios were designed for gynecological examination training of international medical students in this course.
target_learners: International medical students learning gynecological examination
target_learning_goals: Patient-centered communication, empathy, privacy respect, and technical examination skills
examples: Cases incorporate "psychosocial elements (e.g., anxiety about pelvic examinations) to enhance authenticity".

article_title: Educational impact of a structured simulation-based orthopedic training program on technical and non-technical competency development: a prospective pre-post study.
citation: Dudau Ionut, Sutoi Dumitru, Chiu Bogdan, Radbea Raluca, Marin George, Ciontos Anda Nicoleta, Mulcutan-Chis Vlad, Sutoi Maria, Mederle Ovidiu Alexandru, Deleanu Bogdan Nicolae. (2026). Educational impact of a structured simulation-based orthopedic training program on technical and non-technical competency development: a prospective pre–post study. Journal of Medicine and Life. https://doi.org/10.25122/jml-2026-0021
title: Structured two-part simulation-based orthopedic workshop (fracture first aid and basic surgical techniques)
description: A hands-on orthopedic workshop integrating theoretical concepts with practical skill acquisition in a simulated environment, delivered in two parts: Part I covered "fracture assessment and first aid, indications and principles of fracture immobilization" including plaster splint demonstration and supervised individual practice; Part II covered basic surgical instruments, simulated incision and dissection, fracture fixation with plates and screws, and wound closure techniques. The workshop emphasized step-by-step procedural learning, safety principles, and non-technical skills including communication, situational awareness, and task management.
requirements: Instructor demonstration followed by supervised hands-on practice; educational materials including plaster splint materials, basic orthopedic surgical instruments, synthetic models and simulation materials, and standardized wound-dressing supplies
constraints: Outcomes were assessed immediately after the workshop, precluding evaluation of long-term retention and transfer to clinical practice; the study did not assess cost-effectiveness or resource implications
target_learners: medical students across all 6 years of undergraduate training
target_learning_goals: fracture first aid and immobilization skills
basic orthopedic surgical techniques
non-technical skills (communication, teamwork, situational awareness)
examples: Participants individually performed plaster splint application after a live instructor demonstration, then practiced simulated incision, dissection, fracture fixation, and suturing techniques

article_title: Construction and practice of a certification system for clinical nursing preceptors: a " license to teach" approach in China.
citation: Tang Yinying, Linyue Tan, Chen Xiuwen, Chen Huiqiong (2026). Construction and practice of a certification system for clinical nursing preceptors: a “license to teach” approach in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08953-x
title: Strengthen interactive-teaching training — especially teaching ward rounds — when certifying clinical preceptors, since it is their weakest skill area
description: Because the teaching ward rounds assessment showed the lowest pass rate and participants most often requested more pre-assessment training for it, the article recommends that "in the training and certification of clinical nursing chief teachers, strengthening specialized training in the concepts and methods of interactive teaching is key to improving the quality of teaching ward rounds." It treats interactive teaching — teacher-student, teaching-media, and teacher-student emotional interaction — as the crucial competency for cultivating students' comprehensive clinical competence beyond one-way knowledge transmission.
requirements: Certification and training programs that include an interactive component such as teaching ward rounds, with pre-assessment demonstrations and interpretations of comprehensive ability assessments.
constraints: Domestically, the article notes interactive teaching is mostly concentrated in university classroom settings with insufficient application in frontline clinical teaching, and heavy clinical workloads limit training effectiveness.
target_learners: Clinical nursing chief teachers and preceptor candidates
target_learning_goals: High-level interactive clinical teaching, guiding student clinical reasoning during patient encounters
examples: Candidates conducted a ward round on a common disease within their specialty, assessed on preparation, clinical guidance, communication, and overall teaching performance.
key_sources: Tang Yinying, Linyue Tan, Chen Xiuwen, Chen Huiqiong (2026). Construction and practice of a certification system for clinical nursing preceptors: a “license to teach” approach in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08953-x

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation.
citation: B. Jones, A. Desu, and C. D. F. Honig. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation. European Journal of Dental Education 30(2): 447–456. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13135
title: Two interconnected GPT-4 chatbots simulating a dental patient and a clinical supervisor, built in Streamlit
description: The system comprised "two interconnected chatbots, built using Streamlit for the front‐end user interface," initially powered by GPT-3.5 Turbo and later upgraded to GPT-4. The patient chatbot represented a 41-year-old individual named Alena responding to inquiries about symptoms and medical history, while the supervisor chatbot embodied a dental professional with over 20 years of experience, guided diagnosis, and provided access to embedded diagnostic tests such as radiographs, photographs, and test videos. Careful prompt engineering defined roles, constraints, and available information, with temperature 0.1 settings for both chatbots.
requirements: Backend Python scripts to deploy the chatbot and manage API fetch requests between the user interface and the LLM
Careful prompt engineering to define roles, constraints, and available information for each chatbot
constraints: The article notes optimising system prompts remains an ongoing challenge, and the AI patient could be 'too helpful' and volunteer excessive information
target_learners: second-year and final-year oral health students in a Bachelor of Oral Health program
target_learning_goals: systematic pain history taking
diagnostic test selection and interpretation
clinical reasoning and communication with a supervisor
examples: Implemented with 46 second-year students in a 60-min tutorial in April 2024 and 24 final-year students in a July 2024 seminar with a 20-min time limit
key_sources: B. Jones, A. Desu, and C. D. F. Honig. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation. European Journal of Dental Education 30(2): 447–456. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13135

article_title: Reducing misdiagnoses and cognitive errors using virtual patients and automated feedback in a clinical reasoning curriculum.
citation: Waechter Jason, Kusnoor Anita, Eickman Kara, Smith David, Wong Matt, Rogers Suzanne, Lee Chel Hee. (2026). Reducing misdiagnoses and cognitive errors using virtual patients and automated feedback in a clinical reasoning curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08647-4
title: Start clinical reasoning training with virtual patient deliberate practice at the beginning of first year, before significant medical knowledge is acquired
description: The article argues that beliefs that clinical reasoning cannot be trained among students with low medical knowledge are a barrier, and its data contradict this: "in contrast to a common misperception, we demonstrated that implementation of a CR curriculum is successful for CR skill development at the start of 1 st year medical school prior to students' acquisition of significant medical knowledge". Educators should therefore implement structured CR practice with feedback early in medical school and continue it longitudinally, since learning curves did not plateau at 20 cases.
requirements: Virtual patients with automated scoring and feedback to overcome faculty workload, expertise, time, and cost barriers
Common diseases with typical presentations
Formative feedback and self-reflection opportunities
constraints: Findings are from a simulated curriculum; it remains unclear how well they translate to real-life clinical environments
Observational design without comparison to other assessment methods
target_learners: First-year medical students beginning pre-clerkship training
target_learning_goals: Diagnostic accuracy, diagnostic justification, test ordering, reduction of cognitive errors and misdiagnoses
examples: First-year students who completed 20 cases outperformed second-year students who completed 10 in all CR metrics by end of pre-clerkship
key_sources: Waechter Jason, Kusnoor Anita, Eickman Kara, Smith David, Wong Matt, Rogers Suzanne, Lee Chel Hee. (2026). Reducing misdiagnoses and cognitive errors using virtual patients and automated feedback in a clinical reasoning curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08647-4

article_title: When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education.
citation: Al-Shawee N, McElvaney G, Strawbridge J, Spooner M. (2026). When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2033
title: Structured prompts combining structural formatting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought reasoning shape AI-generated MCQ quality
description: The article's institutional workshop prompt was designed around three key strategies: "structural formatting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought reasoning." As illustrated in supplementary figure 2, the degree of contextual information provided to the LLM shapes the alignment of output with assessment intent and the overall quality of AI-generated MCQs — their validity, reliability, and educational impact. Well-structured prompts also reduce post-generation editing, improving cost-efficiency.
requirements: Specification of parameters such as learner stage, clinical context, cognitive domain, and item structure
constraints: Even with well-structured prompts, GenAI may produce factually inaccurate, poorly calibrated, or misaligned content, so review remains essential
target_learners: Medical educators writing SBA items with GenAI
target_learning_goals: Generating curriculum-aligned, cognitively appropriate assessment items
examples: The structured prompt was implemented as part of a faculty development workshop on AI-assisted item-writing at the authors' institution
key_sources: Al-Shawee N, McElvaney G, Strawbridge J, Spooner M. (2026). When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2033

article_title: Exploring the effects of the health transformation plan on the quality of clinical education in teaching hospitals: a qualitative study.
citation: Ahari Saeid Sadeghieh S, Khodabandeh S, Zandian H, Kamran A. (2026). Exploring the effects of the health transformation plan on the quality of clinical education in teaching hospitals: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08848-x
title: Core category: tension between service and education as a process of structural misalignment in teaching hospitals under health reform
description: The study's grounded theory core category describes an ongoing process in which faculty navigate competing institutional expectations, with service-oriented priorities becoming increasingly prominent alongside educational goals after the HTP. Two interrelated main categories were identified: structural expansion with latent educational potential, and service-centered reorganization of academic practice, plus contextual conditions shaping educational practice. The authors state the tension was 'experienced as being shaped by changes in workload, incentive structures, and policy signals'.
requirements: Participants with teaching experience spanning before and after the reform to perceive changed conditions
constraints: Findings are faculty perceptions at a single university, not objective educational outcomes
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in teaching hospitals
target_learning_goals: Clinical competencies and professional readiness for practice
examples: Coding example: the meaning unit 'I spend more time on patient care due to performance targets' was coded as 'increased clinical workload' and integrated into the theme 'Shift in faculty role priorities under the HTP'

article_title: How digital stress affects academic procrastination and subjective well-being: mediating effect of ego depletion.
citation: Acaray Ali. (2026). How digital stress affects academic procrastination and subjective well-being: mediating effect of ego depletion. BMC Psychology, 14, 449. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04164-7
title: Stress–strain–outcome model (Koeske and Koeske) as the theoretical framework linking digital stress to procrastination and well-being
description: The article adopts the stress–strain–outcome model as its framework for how digital stress affects students. It describes the model as consisting of three parts: "stress factors, resulting tension, and outcomes" — excessive, uncontrolled digital media use creates stress (strain) that produces negative psychological consequences and raises academic procrastination, or lowers psychological well-being. Self-determination theory is additionally invoked to explain well-being effects via autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs.
requirements: The framework presumes the individual's perception of stressors matters, as the article states stress perception becomes important when stress is considered as a process.
constraints: The article applies it to undergraduate students in Türkiye interacting with social media and digital tools; it is a hypothesised explanatory framework, tested by cross-sectional self-report data.
target_learners: undergraduate university students
target_learning_goals: reducing academic procrastination
protecting psychological well-being
supporting academic achievement
examples: The article's conceptual model (Fig. 1) maps digital stress subdimensions through ego depletion to academic procrastination, psychological well-being, and academic achievement.
key_sources: Acaray Ali. (2026). How digital stress affects academic procrastination and subjective well-being: mediating effect of ego depletion. BMC Psychology, 14, 449. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04164-7

article_title: A Novel Competency-Based Simulation Model for Thoracoscopic Lung Resection.
citation: Liu Ganwei, Yang Feng, Zhou Zuli, Jiang Guanchao. (2025). A Novel Competency-Based Simulation Model for Thoracoscopic Lung Resection. The Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgeon. https://doi.org/10.1055/a-2702-2239

Both groups trained in small teams with real-time faculty feedback and peer observation.
requirements: Standardized preparatory materials to ensure consistent foundational knowledge
Small-team training with a trainee-to-instructor ratio of 5:1 and real-time faculty feedback
constraints: The FLS comparison curriculum focused on core laparoscopic skills and did not replicate full procedural steps
target_learners: surgical residents
target_learning_goals: thoracoscopic wedge resection technique
anatomical recognition
technical skill acquisition
examples: The lung model group's sessions emphasized anatomical recognition, thoracoscopic orientation, stapling technique, and safe specimen retrieval

article_title: Impact of a Structured Training Program on Medical Student Confidence and Behavior During Their First Radial Arterial Puncture: Comparative Study.
citation: Rolland-Debord C, Juret L, Simon M, El Mouhajer A, Londner C, Morélot-Panzini C, Chenivesse C, Similowski T. (2026). Impact of a Structured Training Program on Medical Student Confidence and Behavior During Their First Radial Arterial Puncture: Comparative Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/78086
title: Structured arterial puncture training program combining theoretical instruction, simulator practice, and debriefing
description: A training session of at least 1 hour delivered by a single instructor to groups of approximately 7 students, combining "theoretical instruction, simulation-based practice, and debriefing." It includes a reviewed slide deck, individual hands-on practice on an artificial arm simulator until self-reported confidence, peer-to-peer exercises, a standardized communication script practiced in pairs, and a structured debriefing following French simulation guidelines. The program was routinely implemented in the department and evaluated against usual heterogeneous bedside teaching.
requirements: A single instructor, an artificial arm simulator with palpable pulse and visible blood return, reviewed slide deck and communication script, and time of at least 1 hour per session
constraints: The training was not delivered by certified simulation instructors as recommended by the French National Authority for Health, which the authors state may have affected debriefing quality
target_learners: Third-year medical students performing their first arterial puncture
target_learning_goals: Radial arterial puncture technique, patient communication, and procedural confidence
examples: Students repeated the procedure on the simulator until self-reported confidence and practiced palpation, the Allen test, and patient communication in pairs

article_title: Enacted practices and developmental experiences of senior medical student tutors in a structured peer tutoring program.
citation: Yoo Dong Mi, Cho A Ra, Kim Sun. (2026). Enacted practices and developmental experiences of senior medical student tutors in a structured peer tutoring program. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.111
title: Structured near-peer tutoring program with orientation, individualized matching, weekly meetings, and faculty oversight
description: A structured peer tutoring program implemented in 2022 and 2023 at a Korean medical school to support academically underperforming students in a near-peer (senior–junior) configuration. The article states "The tutoring program followed a standardized sequence consisting of tutor orientation, individualized matching, weekly meetings, and ongoing faculty oversight." Tutors attended a structured orientation led by the Associate Dean for Student Affairs covering peer tutoring principles, academic coaching strategies, and communication approaches, and pairs met at least weekly with additional sessions near examinations.
requirements: Tutors selected through a competitive review process based on a written application and an interview
Structured tutor orientation before duties begin
Regular tutor activity reports for program monitoring
constraints: Implemented at a single institution with 14 tutor–tutee pairs across two one-semester cycles
target_learners: Academically underperforming premedical year 2 and medical year 1 students
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning and stable study routines
Academic performance in preclinical medical coursework
examples: Seven tutor–tutee pairs operated in each of the 2022 and 2023 cycles, with tutors submitting activity reports documenting session content and observed changes in tutees' routines

article_title: Maintaining teaching consistency across repeated sessions using structured pre-session planning in medical education.
citation: Alotiby Amna. (2025). Maintaining teaching consistency across repeated sessions using structured pre-session planning in medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08506-8
title: Use structured pre-session planning to maintain teaching consistency across repeated delivery of identical sessions
description: Structured pre-session planning involves deliberate preparation before each repeated delivery of identical content: notes aligned with predefined learning outcomes, annotated notes highlighting key points and examples, and a fixed sequence and timing for content delivery across all sessions. The article reports it was implemented uniformly across four student groups to reduce variability and prevent content omissions, and that perceptions and exam scores were consistent across groups. It is characterized as a feasible, low-cost strategy suitable for faculty development.
requirements: Notes ensuring all essential session content aligned with predefined learning outcomes
Annotated notes highlighting key points and examples
A fixed sequence and timing for content delivery across all sessions
constraints: Evidence comes from a single institution with a single tutor and a cross-sectional design without causal inference
Student ratings may be influenced by familiarity with the tutor, personal biases, or contextual factors
target_learners: second-year medical students in repeated-session teaching groups
target_learning_goals: consistent instructional delivery aligned with intended learning objectives across repeated sessions
examples: A single haematology tutor delivered an identical nine-week lecture series to four groups of 35–39 students using the structured plan, with all 147 students completing the post-module survey

article_title: Impact of problem-based learning on the development of clinical reasoning skills in esophageal cancer teaching.
citation: Zhao L, He J, Han Z, Zhang Y, Li L. (2026). Impact of problem-based learning on the development of clinical reasoning skills in esophageal cancer teaching. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000047451
title: Structured PBL module for esophageal cancer teaching (small fixed groups, authentic cases, facilitator-guided reasoning, formative assessment)
description: The intervention is a structured PBL framework for thoracic surgery interns: "Students were divided into small fixed learning groups (6–8 interns per group)" and each unit began with real clinical case scenarios covering presentation, imaging, endoscopy, and therapeutic decision points. Students identified learning objectives, retrieved guideline-based evidence, built diagnostic reasoning chains, and proposed differential diagnoses through iterative group discussion. The instructor acted as a facilitator "to guide cognitive reasoning and ensure accuracy of clinical conclusions without providing prestructured answers", and modules ended with oral reporting, peer feedback, and formative assessment focused on reasoning rather than recall.
requirements: Full-time clinical internship participation in the esophageal cancer teaching module, completion of the entire teaching cycle, and completion of all required theoretical and practical assessments.
constraints: Prior exposure to PBL-based thoracic oncology teaching was an exclusion criterion; a concurrent randomized design was not feasible because the curriculum allocates each academic year to one teaching model.
target_learners: medical interns on thoracic surgery rotations
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning in esophageal cancer
differential diagnosis formulation
guideline-concordant treatment decision-making
theoretical knowledge of esophageal cancer
examples: Interns rotating September 2024–June 2025 received the PBL module; those rotating September 2023–June 2024 received lecture-based teaching.

Implementation as described pairs authentic case scenarios with small fixed groups, instructor facilitation, and formative assessment targeting reasoning. Programs teaching other thoracic or gastrointestinal malignancies "may consider analogous PBL structures".

residents in oncologic rotations

diagnostic accuracy

article_title: Evaluation of healthcare simulation centers: development of the "STRIVE" tool using the Delphi method.
citation: Zhang Yan, Lu Yihong, Yuan Huiyun, Meng Chao, Mu Yifei, Qian Xiaolei, Konge Lars, Bian Zhengqian. (2025). Evaluation of healthcare simulation centers: development of the “STRIVE” tool using the Delphi method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08332-y
title: STRIVE evaluation tool for healthcare simulation centers
description: STRIVE is a 24-item evaluation model for healthcare simulation centers, named as an acronym of its six categories: "simulation curricula, training of faculty, result of training, internal resources, variety of activities, effect of activities". Each item can be scored, quantified and compared across centers. Each category totals 10 points, with two items weighted at 2 points and two at 3 points, and category scores are plotted on a hexagonal radar scheme for visual comparison, supporting self-assessment and identification of strengths and weaknesses.
requirements: Requires expert consensus items scored per category; a weighted scoring system assigns each category 10 total points
constraints: Developed with and for HSCs in mainland China; some assessment items can only be used for HSCs in China, per the authors' limitations section
target_learners: HSC managers and administrators in medical education
target_learning_goals: Institutional evaluation and continuous quality improvement of simulation-based medical education centers
examples: The final Table 2 lists items such as skills training courses for residents and medical students, annual simulation instructors training courses, and a pass rate for the practical part of the annual National Practitioners Exam at or above 90%

article_title: Combining Problem-Based Learning Methods With the WeChat Platform in Teaching Ophthalmology: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Fang Fang, Bu Bing, Jiang Wenmin. (2026). Combining Problem-Based Learning Methods With the WeChat Platform in Teaching Ophthalmology: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/65279
title: Minute-by-minute structured PBL session format (recap, presentation, cross-group challenge, synthesis, reflection)
description: Each WeChat-based PBL session followed a fixed internal structure intended to ensure balanced pacing and consistent coverage across groups. "The guide provided a minute-by-minute timetable covering the entire 2-hour process (10 min recap, 45 min group presentation, 30 min cross-groups challenge, 25 min instructor synthesis, and 10 min reflection)." The guide also specified 5 must-cover learning objectives, prompt questions addressing common misconceptions identified during the pilot phase, and a required 1-slide take-home summary displayed at the end of each session.

Instructors intervene only when discussion drifts more than 2 minutes off task or critical misconceptions arise, otherwise guiding by inquiry-based questioning
Instructors complete a structured checklist after the session documenting which objectives were achieved
constraints: The pattern was applied to a single ophthalmology topic (PACG) in one institution
target_learners: undergraduate medical students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: covering mandated syllabus objectives
correcting misconceptions
peer presentation and cross-group critique
examples: A representative student from each group presented their understanding of the assigned disease and summarized unresolved problems identified during preclass discussions

citation: Thompson, M. B., Gandhi, V., Richardson-Newton, A., & Campitelli, G. (2026). Detecting expertise in decision making under pressure: a virtual reality assessment environment and empirical evaluation. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 11, 6. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-025-00695-6
title: Strategic time-allocation assessment pattern with constrained exploitation
description: A reusable assessment design embedding multiple tasks within an immersive environment where learners must continuously decide how to allocate limited time across competing activities. The design "incorporates structural limitations that prevent simple exploitation strategies from dominating performance", such as games allowing only limited plays or having diminishing yields. These constraints ensure that "good performance requires strategic switching decisions rather than mere persistence in high-ability domains".
requirements: Multiple tasks with unknown and dynamically changing relative profitability
A global time budget
Structural constraints on repeating single tasks
Continuous second-by-second stay-or-switch decisions
constraints: Measures sustained resource allocation rather than acute deadline pressure
target_learners: adults in safety-critical professions
university students
target_learning_goals: strategic decision making
resource allocation under uncertainty
metacognitive monitoring
examples: Mental Rotation allows only two plays maximum; other games have diminishing ticket yields over time; switching games consumes time through physical navigation

title: Stepwise LAS training pattern: lecture, pre-learning with videos and simulators, then hands-on live-animal practice
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern for laboratory animal skills training in which each session follows a fixed sequence: a faculty lecture with handouts distributed in advance, a preparatory phase with training videos and mouse simulators used at students' discretion, and finally hands-on training with live mice. The article reports that "a stepwise program, including handout distribution, a lecture, pre-learning with alternative educational tools (videos and simulators), and hands-on training with live mice was conducted". The pattern was applied to habituation, restraint, and vaginal smear sampling with one mouse per 2–3 students.
requirements: Alternative tools must remain available during both the pre-learning period and as review resources after live training
Teaching assistant support during hands-on sessions
constraints: Hands-on training using live animals remains essential for mastering psychomotor techniques
Utility of each tool may vary depending on learner prior experience, technique type, and student numbers
target_learners: novice veterinary students with no prior live-mouse handling experience
target_learning_goals: basic mouse handling techniques: habituation, restraint, and vaginal smear sampling for estrous cycle determination
examples: 149 second-year veterinary students completed the three-session program; one mouse was allocated per group of 2–3 students, with two iPads and two of each simulator per group of 8–9 students
