article_title: A nursing-led pathway to safe task sharing in Japan: Interprofessional simulation and a common competency credential.
citation: Kubota, K., Nishimura, A., & Funaki, J. (2026). A nursing‐led pathway to safe task sharing in Japan: Interprofessional simulation and a common competency credential. Japan Journal of Nursing Science, 23(1), e70036. https://doi.org/10.1111/jjns.70036
title: Embed stop rules, defined supervision levels, and scripted escalation to manage risk when delegating clinical tasks
description: The article holds that safety is the foremost criterion for task sharing and that credentials must build risk management into the point of care: "The CCC embeds stop rules, defined supervision levels, and scripted escalation to manage risk at the point of care." Standardization reduces unwarranted variation, and simulation provides a safe environment to identify and remedy system defects before they reach patients. Institutions should align credential scopes with bylaws, credentialing committees, and risk management processes, with clear documentation of responsibility to mitigate medicolegal ambiguity.
requirements: Documentation delineating delegated tasks, supervision levels, and escalation triggers aligned with institutional policies and Japanese law
Alignment of credential scopes with bylaws, credentialing committees, and risk management processes
constraints: Cultural barriers in hierarchical settings can slow escalation and are stated to require psychological safety and structured communication tools such as SBAR
target_learners: delegating and delegated clinical team members across professions
target_learning_goals: safe escalation and error recovery during delegated clinical tasks
examples: Each scenario in the proposed CCC library would embed explicit stop rules, supervision levels, checklists, and escalation criteria reflecting real-world safety boundaries.

description: The State-Trait Anxiety Inventory consists of two 20-item subscales measuring state anxiety (STAI-X1) and trait anxiety (STAI-X2), self-rated on a 4-point Likert scale, with subscale scores ranging from 20 to 80. The article describes it as having "good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha > 0.85 for both subscales) and well-established validity across different populations." constraints: Self-assessment is recommended for formative rather than summative evaluation
Overestimating self-efficacy can be a barrier to development, so trainer collaboration is needed
target_learners: first-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: patient-physician communication skills
accurate self-perception and self-regulated learning
examples: After simulated patient interviews, students and trainers completed parallel online evaluation forms with identical questions, and results were used to identify where trainers should give more individual feedback

article_title: The effect of educational intervention using surgery preference cards on anxiety and clinical competence among operating room nursing students in general surgeries: a randomized controlled trial study.
citation: Bagheri Majid, Shiryani Morteza, Mehralizade Sara, Basirinezhad Mohammad Hasan, Bagheri Hossein, Abbasi Ali. (2025). The effect of educational intervention using surgery preference cards on anxiety and clinical competence among operating room nursing students in general surgeries: a randomized controlled trial study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07930-0
title: Structured procedural information reduces clinical anxiety by reducing ambiguity and uncertainty
description: The authors' explanatory account of why preference card training lowered anxiety: cards act as a roadmap that makes surgical stages explicit in the student's mind. As they put it, "By clearly outlining the necessary instruments, steps, and responsibilities before, during, and after surgery, SPCs help reduce ambiguity and uncertainty, which are known contributors to anxiety in clinical environments." The account holds that a clear roadmap enhances students' sense of preparedness and control, which are associated with lower performance-related stress, and that greater knowledge decreases fear of the unknown. It is an interpretation offered in the discussion, not a tested mechanism in the trial.
requirements: The informational tool must clearly outline instruments, steps and responsibilities across the pre-, intra- and post-operative phases
constraints: Offered as the authors' explanation; the trial measured anxiety outcomes but did not test the mechanism directly
target_learners: Operating room nursing students in clinical training
target_learning_goals: Managing anxiety in the clinical learning environment
Building preparedness and perceived control before surgical procedures
examples: The trial's intervention group received step-by-step teaching of surgical phases using preference cards, and showed significant anxiety reductions relative to lecture-trained controls

Comparing the Effectiveness of Multimodal Learning Using Computer-Based and Immersive Virtual Reality Simulation–Based Interprofessional Education With Co-Debriefing, Medical Movies, and Massive Online Open Courses for Mitigating Stress and Long-Term Burnout in Medical Training: Quasi-Experimental Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/70726
title: Steeling effect: resilience cultivated through manageable exposure to adversity rather than avoidance
description: To justify exposing learners to a stressful simulated crisis, the article invokes the steeling effect, described as "the idea that resilience can be cultivated through exposure to manageable risk rather than through avoidance of all adversity." Appropriate exposure may organize, calibrate, or tune the adaptive systems of an individual or team for future adversity. The article pairs this with a bidimensional resilience framework distinguishing intrinsic and external factors, and warns that exposure exceeding adaptive capacity produces a sensitizing effect in individuals and collective breakdown in teams.
requirements: The type, degree, and duration of stressor exposure must remain within a range manageable for the learner or team
constraints: Unmanageable exposure may sensitize individuals to future stressors and erode team cohesion; the study excluded students with elevated PHQ-9 scores out of safety concern
target_learners: undergraduate health care professional students
target_learning_goals: building resilience and stress tolerance for high-pressure clinical environments
examples: The SIMBIE scenario simulated a COVID-19 pneumonia crisis, exposing interprofessional teams to a high-acuity event in a safe, controlled setting

article_title: Academic performance and anxiety in the evaluation of health science undergraduate students using osce: a pre- and post-covid-19 cohort study.
citation: Polonio-López Begoña et al. (2025). Academic performance and anxiety in the evaluation of health science undergraduate students using osce: a pre- and post-covid-19 cohort study. BMC Medical Education 25:1171. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07780-w
title: State-trait anxiety distinction underlying OSCE emotional-response measurement
description: The article adopts the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory framework distinguishing two interrelated anxiety types measured by the STAI: state anxiety (STAI-SA), a transient response to a stressful evaluative situation, and trait anxiety (STAI-TA), a stable personal disposition to perceive situations as threatening. The framework guides the study's measurement design: trait anxiety was measured only at baseline to verify cohort equivalence, while state anxiety was measured before and after the OSCE. State anxiety is defined as "a transient and fluctuating emotional response characterized by a composite feeling of tension, apprehension, and autonomic activation, which occurs when being tested in performance-based situations".
requirements: A validated instrument such as the Spanish STAI (Cronbach's α 0.93 for STAI-TA and 0.92 for STAI-SA as reported)
Measurement timed to the pre- and post-test situation to capture transient state anxiety
constraints: The anxiety discussed is examination-related state anxiety, not anxiety as a mental disorder or illness
target_learners: Higher education students in performance-based practical assessments
target_learning_goals: Understanding and measuring students' emotional response to high-stakes practical assessment
examples: The study applied the STAI while students waited for the OSCE and again after completion, measuring trait anxiety only at the start of the session.

article_title: Improving Confidence in Performing Clinical Procedures Through Peer-Driven Training Sessions for Preclinical Medical Students.
citation: Bohrer Maxwell B. MD, Rodgers David L. EdD. (2025). Improving Confidence in Performing Clinical Procedures Through Peer-Driven Training Sessions for Preclinical Medical Students. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11542
title: Involve medical students in designing and facilitating clinical procedure training to provide early clinical exposure with minimal faculty resources
description: The article argues that student-designed and student-facilitated procedure training can overcome faculty-resource barriers to early clinical exposure. It states the SLPTS "provides a framework by which medical students can take ownership of their medical education through a program that can be replicated with minimal faculty resources," and that with expert review during planning, students can fulfill the roles of curriculum planner and resource developer. The authors suggest collaboration between students and faculty could further integrate such training into the official curriculum.
requirements: Expert review of content and educational processes during curriculum design (Kern's six-step approach)
Peer instructor training with faculty oversight before delivery
constraints: Confidence was the only outcome measured; no objective skills assessment was performed
Peer instructors may teach improper technique unless mitigated by advance training with faculty present
target_learners: Preclinical medical students (MS1 and MS2)
target_learning_goals: Procedural skills confidence prior to clinical rotations
examples: The SLPTS was designed by a medical student completing a medical education scholarly concentration, mentored by a faculty curriculum expert, and implemented with seven peer instructors and 37 learners

title: Standardized two-hour TBL session sequence with pre-class preparation, IRAT, GRAT, feedback, mini-lecture, and application activities
description: Ewha Womans University College of Medicine developed a standardized manual for implementing TBL when converting traditional lectures to the format. "Each TBL session was designed to last 2 hours", and after self-directed pre-class preparation the in-class session follows a fixed sequence of course introduction, IRAT, GRAT, immediate feedback, a mini-lecture, and application activities. This systematic structure is the perceived class-management quality the study found associated with active participation.
requirements: Instructors design and deliver courses in accordance with TBL protocols; the article notes some instructors question whether strictly adhering to all aspects of TBL is essential
constraints: Findings about systematic management come from student perceptions in pre-clinical medical courses at one institution

target_learning_goals: Active engagement in knowledge-acquisition sessions
examples: The 575 students' feedback came from TBL sessions following this sequence across three semesters

article_title: Training in the use of basic functions of the daVinci Xi(®) robot: a comparative study of residents' skills.
citation: Cannata G, Leone N, Salzano A, Rebecchi F, Morino M (2025). Training in the use of basic functions of the daVinci Xi® robot: a comparative study of residents’ skills. Updates in Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13304-025-02150-z
title: Standardized robotic surgery training is needed because no universal training program exists and video tutorials alone are insufficient for patient-cart skills
description: The article argues that the rapid spread of robotic surgical systems has not been matched by standardized training courses, and that the need for effective, robotic surgery-specific training programs is particularly important for residents to ensure adequate surgical skills and patient safety. In its own study, video tutorials sufficed for console learning but the authors report that participants "encountered difficulties primarily related to operating the patient cart" and that "video tutorials alone proved insufficient," highlighting the need for targeted and more intensive training. The rating scale used in the study is proposed as a tool for residents to monitor their progress in specific skills.
requirements: Practical, hands-on training courses beyond theoretical training, which the authors tie to overcoming the absence of tactile and haptic feedback and reducing time of use
constraints: Further studies are needed to validate and standardize a training model and to evaluate how training improvements translate into actual surgical performance
target_learners: Surgical residents and young surgeons in training
target_learning_goals: Independent, safe operation of robotic surgical platforms in basic functions
examples: The study used two video tutorials plus practice; console performance was similar across experience levels while patient-cart performance differentiated groups

article_title: Bridging teacher motivation and instruction: Relevance of student-oriented goals for teaching alongside personal achievement goals and self-efficacy.
citation: Daumiller, M., Gaspard, H., Dickhäuser, O., & Dresel, M. (2025). Bridging teacher motivation and instruction: Relevance of student‐oriented goals for teaching alongside personal achievement goals and self‐efficacy. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S98–S114. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12776
title: Student-oriented goals as a cognitive process element linking teacher motivation to instructional behaviour
description: This framework holds that teachers' motivation translates into instruction partly through goals teachers set for their students, distinct from personal self-directed achievement goals. Student-oriented goals can be mastery-oriented (focused on understanding and skill development) or performance-oriented (focused on achieving better results compared to peers). The article positions them as a process element: "student‐oriented goals could plausibly serve as an important process element that translates teachers' personal achievement goals and self‐efficacy into actionable instructional behaviours". The study tests this with two-level path modelling and finds student-oriented mastery goals especially relevant, though not a full mediator.
requirements: Requires joint consideration of personal achievement goals and self-efficacy beliefs as predictors alongside the student-oriented goals
constraints: The article notes this perspective necessarily simplifies a more complex interplay of psychological factors, and the mastery/performance dichotomy employed may omit further goal distinctions
target_learners: Secondary school teachers (grades 7–9 mathematics, lower-track schools)
target_learning_goals: Understanding how teacher motivation translates into specific instructional practices
examples: The study measured student-oriented mastery and performance goals at baseline and modelled their associations with ten lesson-diary teaching practices among 70 teachers

Bridging teacher motivation and instruction: Relevance of student‐oriented goals for teaching alongside personal achievement goals and self‐efficacy. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S98–S114. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12776

title: Establish a standardized endoscopic training curriculum specifically designed for metabolic and bariatric surgeons
description: The article recommends coordinated efforts by educators, institutions, and professional societies to standardize endoscopic education for bariatric surgeons, because its survey revealed "significant gaps in structured endoscopic training" alongside low procedural volumes and confidence. It notes that no standardized endoscopic training curriculum has yet been formally recommended by professional societies dedicated to metabolic and bariatric surgery, and that existing certifications such as FES do not cover EBTs or MBS.
requirements: Coordinated efforts by educators, institutions, and professional societies
Curriculum content covering diagnostic endoscopy, complication management, and EBTs, which the article says are essential components of contemporary MBS
constraints: The article notes existing FES certification's core curriculum does not include didactic content related to EBTs or MBS
Global heterogeneity and limited-resource settings make establishing training pathways challenging

Endoscopic management of MBS-related postoperative complications
Endoscopic bariatric therapies (IGB, ESG, TORe)
examples: The survey found 83.4% of respondents expressed interest in attending formal upper endoscopy training courses, and institutions offering structured training did so primarily through simulation (30.6%), dry labs (16.6%), and animal courses (13.6%)

description: A structured educational activity in which undergraduate pharmacy students, working in pairs, select and analyze recent research articles relevant to their current pharmacology or hospital pharmacy coursework and present their findings to peers and instructors. The activity was evaluated with a validated four-domain survey covering general experience, learning outcomes, perception and attitude, and feedback and future improvements.

Articles selected must be recent research relevant to the coursework of the semester

research and literature evaluation skills
presentation skills
teamwork and collaboration
examples: 207 students in Cardiovascular Pharmacology (3rd year) and Hospital Pharmacy (5th year) courses at Umm Al-Qura University completed the paired journal club during the 2024 academic year

description: The study's training and assessment materials: a standardised video training session covering gallbladder, liver, and pancreas normal findings and pathologies, in which "The video training for both groups was identical in duration, spoken text, and displayed captions, differing only in the format of the sonographic findings." The accompanying digital theory test comprised 54 multiple-choice questions (16 gallbladder, 20 liver, 18 pancreas) with four answer options each and a 30-second per-question limit. Materials were developed by an interdisciplinary expert team and pretested by five DEGUM Level II/III experts for content validity.

target_learning_goals: theoretical ultrasound competencies in abdominal sonography covering normal findings and pathologies of the gallbladder, liver, and pancreas
examples: The study group viewed dynamic video clips while the control group viewed static images of the same findings, each topic lasting six minutes

interpreting case components
formulating a differential diagnosis

article_title: Simulation-Based Echocardiography Training Enhanced Competence and Self-Confidence in Neonatal Residents.
citation: Blanchetière Amélie, Guillouët Erwan, Favrais Géraldine, Lardennois Caroline, Bellot Anne, Savey Baptiste. (2025). Simulation‐Based Echocardiography Training Enhanced Competence and Self‐Confidence in Neonatal Residents. Acta Paediatrica. https://doi.org/10.1111/apa.70003
title: Standardised small-group simulator session using the modified Peyton four-step process with a mastery-learning passing standard
description: A reusable session design for introducing a procedural skill: each session involves a maximum of four residents, one teacher and one simulator, and teaches a normal neonatal TTE "through the modified Peyton four‐step process: demonstration, deconstruction, comprehension and performance", followed by pathology cases and an evaluated performance. Mastery learning is enforced because "The minimum passing score for validation of the training session was 12 out of 14", with additional sessions until the requirement is met. The whole session typically lasted 2.5–3.0 h.
requirements: One EchoCom Neo simulator and one teacher per session of up to four residents
Pre-recorded videos covering the session presentation, the simulator and Peyton's first and second steps
A minimum passing score of 12 out of 14 with additional training sessions until met
constraints: The session served as an introduction to neonatal TTE, developing fundamental skills before bedside practice
The simulator was set to a normal heart scenario, followed by persistent ductus arteriosus and pericardial effusion cases
target_learners: Neonatology residents with all levels of training who had completed a 6-month residency or at least night shifts in neonatology
target_learning_goals: Performing the seven standard sections of a normal neonatal transthoracic echocardiography
Recognising visible anatomical structures in each section
examples: The same teacher conducted all sessions at each hospital throughout the study, and incorporating videos on Peyton's first and second steps meant the training could be delivered by a trained resident
The authors report the ratio of 2.5–3.0 h of teacher availability for every four residents required only 45 min per resident

title: Standardize prebriefing across cognitive, technical, and affective domains to prepare learners psychologically before simulation
description: The article applies Ludlow's three-stage prebriefing: preparation for the cognitive domain (prior knowledge and brief lectures), orientation for the technical domain (equipment and environment familiarization), and pre-briefing for the affective domain (psychological safety, fiction contract, expectations). examples: In the affective stage, learners were told they could request help from team members if they made mistakes, to reduce psychological anxiety.

article_title: Learning curve analysis of 100 consecutive robotic liver resections.
citation: Rahimli M, Gumbs AA, Perrakis A, Al-Madhi S, Dölling M, Stelter F, Lorenz E, Andric M, Franz M, Arend J, Croner RS. (2025). Learning curve analysis of 100 consecutive robotic liver resections. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-11551-5
title: Structure surgical training with standardized protocols, mentorship, and a graduated case-complexity progression to support safe learning-curve progression
description: The article recommends that learning curves in robotic liver surgery be supported by "standardized training protocols" and structured mentorship, with case complexity graduated so that basic skills are built on minor resections before indications are expanded to major resections. It also stresses that "Standardized procedures and consistent team composition are essential for facilitating smoother transitions through the learning phases and minimizing variability in surgical outcomes." The principle treats the learning curve as a plannable, phased progression rather than an unstructured accumulation of cases.
requirements: Institutional support and structured mentorship; starting with less complex (minor) resections before progressing to major resections; consistent team composition
constraints: The 65-case benchmark applies to surgeons already experienced in open and laparoscopic liver surgery; evidence comes from one surgeon's retrospective series
target_learners: surgeons transitioning to robotic liver surgery
surgical training program designers
target_learning_goals: safe and efficient acquisition of robotic liver resection proficiency
examples: In the studied series the surgeon performed the first 21 minor resections before expanding to major resections starting with the 22nd operation, and the authors cite evidence that structured fellowship programs can accelerate learning

article_title: Heart and lung point-of-care ultrasonography tutoring in internal medicine: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Leidi Antonio, Krauer Juliette, Soret Guillaume, Parent Thibault, Marti Christophe, Meyer Philippe, Juillerat André, Bex Stijn, Suh Noémie, Rouyer Frédéric, Siegenthaler Nils, Grosgurin Olivier. (2024). Heart and lung point-of-care ultrasonography tutoring in internal medicine: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Ultrasound. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40477-024-00968-8
title: Pair hands-on point-of-care ultrasound courses with structured longitudinal supervision including scheduled bedside time slots
description: The article recommends that after a short practical course, learners receive structured tutoring in which a certified tutor and pre-agreed bedside supervision time slots are scheduled over the following months, transitioning to asynchronous logbook validation once core competencies are acquired. The trial showed that "Structured POCUS tutoring can significantly enhance training and practice", while encouragement alone left control residents with almost no supervised practice.
requirements: A certified POCUS tutor pool and scheduled time slots agreed between trainees and supervisors
An environment with available ultrasound devices for bedside practice
constraints: Supervision slots were scheduled on top of an already demanding clinical workload; unavailability of tutors or trainees may have influenced success rates
Dedicated supervision time slots during acute medicine rounds are suggested as a further improvement to be explored in future trials
target_learners: Internal medicine residents with little or no POCUS experience
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and retention of heart and lung point-of-care ultrasonography skills
examples: Residents in the intervention arm were paired with a certified tutor and time slots were scheduled for direct bedside supervision over 6 months, with later asynchronous validation through an electronic logbook.
key_sources: Leidi Antonio, Krauer Juliette, Soret Guillaume, Parent Thibault, Marti Christophe, Meyer Philippe, Juillerat André, Bex Stijn, Suh Noémie, Rouyer Frédéric, Siegenthaler Nils, Grosgurin Olivier. (2024). Heart and lung point-of-care ultrasonography tutoring in internal medicine: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Ultrasound. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40477-024-00968-8

article_title: The impact of perinatal mental health training on knowledge and practice of primary care physicians: a systems strengthening initiative in Telangana, India.
citation: Akkineni Raveena, Ganjekar Sundarnag, Satyanarayana Veena, Kondapuram Nithin, Tiwari Khyati, Medisetti Sowjanya, Padmaja S., Karnan R. V., Chandra Prabha S. (2025). The impact of perinatal mental health training on knowledge and practice of primary care physicians: a systems strengthening initiative in Telangana, India. BMC Primary Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-025-02782-5
title: Stepped-care integration of perinatal mental health into maternal and child health services (WHO framework)
description: The program used the WHO framework for integrating perinatal mental health into maternal and child health services, organizing care in tiers. "An algorithm was developed to screen, identify, and refer women with perinatal mental health conditions using a stepped-care approach with clear referral pathways." Frontline workers (Auxiliary Nurse Midwives) provide screening and first-level interventions, medical officers perform case identification and treatment, and specialist care is reserved for severe mental illness or suicidal risk. Training PCPs is positioned as the first systems-strengthening step within this framework.
requirements: Training, handholding, and supervision of non-specialist providers at the forefront of care delivery
constraints: Specialist referral is reserved for severe mental illness or suicidal risk
target_learners: Primary care physicians, community health workers, and auxiliary nurse midwives
target_learning_goals: Screening, identification, management, and referral of perinatal mental health conditions
examples: Telangana integrated PMH into the existing maternal nutrition and high-risk obstetric protocols using this framework
key_sources: Akkineni Raveena, Ganjekar Sundarnag, Satyanarayana Veena, Kondapuram Nithin, Tiwari Khyati, Medisetti Sowjanya, Padmaja S., Karnan R. V., Chandra Prabha S. (2025). The impact of perinatal mental health training on knowledge and practice of primary care physicians: a systems strengthening initiative in Telangana, India. BMC Primary Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-025-02782-5

article_title: Stakeholder perspectives of an experiential learning program at a children's museum to promote healthy eating and physical activity.
citation: Varman Sumantla Devi, Kelly Bridget, Cliff Dylan P., English Josef, Hammersley Megan L., Jones Rachel A. (2025). Stakeholder perspectives of an experiential learning program at a children's museum to promote healthy eating and physical activity. BMC Public Health 25:1239. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22364-5
title: Co-develop health-promotion programs with host-site staff to maximise feasibility and sustainability
description: The article recommends sustained, consultative collaboration between researchers and implementing staff when designing health-promotion programs. Including researchers and museum staff in the development team was described as "important to increase the likelihood of successful implementation and sustainability", and staff focus-group data identified the intentional, consultative collaboration as critical to the program's high feasibility. The principle applies to embedding interventions in non-traditional education settings such as museums.
requirements: Sustained collaboration requires time and energy from all stakeholders
Staff input during both development and implementation stages
constraints: Benefits of sustained collaborations may outweigh potential difficulties but require justification of stakeholder time
target_learners: children aged 0-10 years in informal learning settings
target_learning_goals: healthy eating and physical activity habits
examples: The HL program was developed by a multi-disciplinary team including researchers and Discovery Space staff, and was implemented in all 56 planned sessions
key_sources: Varman Sumantla Devi, Kelly Bridget, Cliff Dylan P., English Josef, Hammersley Megan L., Jones Rachel A. (2025). Stakeholder perspectives of an experiential learning program at a children's museum to promote healthy eating and physical activity. BMC Public Health 25:1239. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22364-5

article_title: Self-Testing and Follow-Through of Learning Strategies Supports Student Success.
citation: Hazlett, Z. S., Jimenez, P. C., & Knight, J. K. (2025). Self-Testing and Follow-Through of Learning Strategies Supports Student Success. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-04-0128
title: Provide structured, feedback-rich practice opportunities in courseware, linked to learning objectives, to support adoption of effective strategies
description: The article recommends that instructors help students adopt high-utility learning strategies by building structured practice into courseware. In the authors' words, instructors can "provide structured opportunities for practicing, ideally through courseware that provides feedback and makes the process transparent and straightforward", with practice "directly linked to course LOs". The study's own course embedded optional, ungraded practice questions and practice tests in the Codon Learning platform, and measured self-testing there predicted course performance.
requirements: Practice opportunities must be structured and accessible within the courseware, with feedback on answers and alignment to course learning objectives.
constraints: The article notes awareness of learning behaviors does not always lead to change; students may still choose easier, less effective strategies.
target_learners: introductory molecular biology majors (second-course students)
target_learning_goals: adoption of effective study strategies such as self-testing
metacognitive awareness of what topics students do and do not understand
examples: The studied genetics course offered optional, ungraded practice questions and practice tests in the Codon Learning platform before each quiz, with feedback on all answer choices, and students' measured completion of these questions predicted final course score.
key_sources: Hazlett, Z. S., Jimenez, P. C., & Knight, J. K. (2025). Self-Testing and Follow-Through of Learning Strategies Supports Student Success. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-04-0128

article_title: A Standardized Clinical Case-Based Assessment for Evaluating Medical Students' Oral Spanish Communication Skills.
citation: Mai AM, Molina RL, Aguayo-Mazzucato C, Diaz AA, Canenguez K, Cheung HC, Graupera NR, Martel B, Bonilla S. (2025). A Standardized Clinical Case-Based Assessment for Evaluating Medical Students' Oral Spanish Communication Skills. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11518
title: Standardized clinical case with SP script for end-of-course oral Spanish assessment
description: The authors developed a standardized clinical case "outlined by a lead instructor and then circulated it amongst the rest of the Medical Spanish course instructors," with each instructor reviewing content and wording and a final version agreed by consensus. The case includes chief concern; medical and surgical history; medications; allergies; family and social history; and health beliefs. An SP script was created in Spanish and English, and volunteer native-level Spanish-speaking SPs practiced mock interviews with instructors before the assessment. The case and script are released as openly accessible appendices.
requirements: Native-level Spanish-speaking standardized patients who rehearse the script with instructors
Facilitators who are Spanish-speaking physicians with native-level proficiency
constraints: SPs were unpaid volunteers, mostly physicians or medical students already serving as teaching assistants, which the authors note is not representative of the broader patient demographic students will encounter
target_learners: medical and dental students in Medical Spanish courses
target_learning_goals: oral Spanish communication with patients
medical history taking in Spanish
examples: In Fall 2021 the case was administered virtually on Zoom, with students rotating through breakout rooms each containing an SP and a facilitator
key_sources: Mai AM, Molina RL, Aguayo-Mazzucato C, Diaz AA, Canenguez K, Cheung HC, Graupera NR, Martel B, Bonilla S. (2025). A Standardized Clinical Case-Based Assessment for Evaluating Medical Students' Oral Spanish Communication Skills. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11518

article_title: Comparing Virtual Reality-Based and Traditional Physical Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) Stations for Clinical Competency Assessments: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Mühling T, Schreiner V, Appel M, Leutritz T, König S. (2025). Comparing Virtual Reality–Based and Traditional Physical Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) Stations for Clinical Competency Assessments: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/55066
title: STEP-VR virtual reality simulation station for emergency-medicine OSCE assessment
description: STEP-VR (version 0.13b; ThreeDee GmbH) is the VR-based simulation of complex medical emergencies used as the VRS in the curricular OSCE, run with head-mounted displays and controllers. Students read the case, then manage septic or anaphylactic shock scenarios with dynamic vital parameters; the first-person view is transmitted to a screen for assessors, who rate performance with standardized candidate assessment forms. The article reports that "53 of 57 students (93%) were able to use the VR technology without any issues."
requirements: Hardware and software maturity sufficient to avoid interruptions from technical issues
Scenarios aligned with the learning and assessment objectives of the curriculum
A backup VR setup on hand to address technical issues
constraints: Blinding of participants and assessors was not possible because VRS and PHS were substantially different
Students with reservations such as simulation sickness could have a tutor operate the headset, and their data were excluded
target_learners: fifth-year medical students
target_learning_goals: assessment of clinical competency in managing medical emergencies (septic and anaphylactic shock)
examples: Used as the tenth station of a 10-station curricular OSCE at University of Würzburg, with two emergency scenarios (septic shock day 1, anaphylactic shock day 2) randomized across parallel circuits
key_sources: Mühling T, Schreiner V, Appel M, Leutritz T, König S. (2025). Comparing Virtual Reality–Based and Traditional Physical Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) Stations for Clinical Competency Assessments: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/55066

article_title: Effectiveness of deliberate practices versus conventional lecture in trauma training for medical students.
citation: Kanoksin Suksan, Songkhla Bhapapak Na, Tansawet Amarit, Laopeamthong Issaree, Sukhvibul Pakkapol, Techapongsatorn Suphakarn. (2025). Effectiveness of deliberate practices versus conventional lecture in trauma training for medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06732-8
title: Staggered deliberate-practice session structure: three 1-hour sessions over three days with readiness assessments before progression
description: The deliberate practice condition divided three hours of training into "three separate 1-hour sessions over three consecutive days," each targeting a specific step of the procedure with hands-on practice, immediate feedback, and readiness assessments at the end of each session. Students worked in small groups of 4–6 participants to allow effective supervision and individualized feedback, and those not meeting competency standards received tailored guidance and additional practice before advancing. This staggered structure was designed to let participants consolidate learning and progressively build skills.
requirements: Standardized models simulating real-life trauma scenarios; structured checklists assessing accuracy, safety, and procedural steps; instructor availability for immediate feedback
constraints: The article notes the distributed schedule itself may have contributed to the group's superior performance, and calls for future studies to separate the effect of time distribution from teaching method
target_learners: first- to third-year medical students
target_learning_goals: stepwise mastery of trauma procedures (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure)
examples: Each session focused on specific trauma procedures with step-by-step practice on models and readiness assessment at the end
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: Evaluating an online stroke training programme for Saudi Arabian physiotherapists for improving their knowledge and confidence in long-term stroke care: a pilot mixed-methods study.
citation: Temehy Basema, Soundy Andrew, Rosewilliam Sheeba. (2025). Evaluating an online stroke training programme for Saudi Arabian physiotherapists for improving their knowledge and confidence in long-term stroke care: a pilot mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06837-0
title: Stroke Training Programme (STP): a four-module online training programme for physiotherapists on long-term stroke care
description: The STP is an online training programme developed to build physiotherapists' knowledge and skills for long-term stroke care after discharge. It "consisted of four modules and was delivered via an online platform": Module 1 introduced stroke pathology and rehabilitation; Module 2 covered carer education, discharge planning and home needs assessments; Module 3 covered assessment procedures, outcome measures and goal setting; Module 4 covered supported patient self-management and telerehabilitation. Supplementary resources, guides and links to educational materials were provided to facilitate learning.
requirements: Participants needed access to online technology such as Zoom or Teams to participate remotely
Participants were physiotherapists currently providing therapy to stroke patients and working in SA
constraints: Evaluated as a pilot with a convenience sample of 26 completers in one Saudi city; participants were excluded if working outside the city for which ethical approval was sought
target_learners: Physiotherapists in Saudi Arabia working with stroke patients
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of stroke assessment, goal-setting, self-management and telerehabilitation
Confidence in delivering long-term stroke care
examples: 26 physiotherapists completed the STP and outcome measures; 16 were interviewed one month post-training
key_sources: Temehy Basema, Soundy Andrew, Rosewilliam Sheeba. (2025). Evaluating an online stroke training programme for Saudi Arabian physiotherapists for improving their knowledge and confidence in long-term stroke care: a pilot mixed-methods study. article_title: How effective and sustainable is proctoring in robotic surgery? A retrospective analysis based on interviews with surgeons.
citation: Günther V, Nees F, Maass N, von Otte S, Ruchay Z, Pape J, Ackermann J, Alkatout I. (2025). How effective and sustainable is proctoring in robotic surgery? A retrospective analysis based on interviews with surgeons. Surgical Endoscopy 39(3):1985–1995. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11503-5
title: Pair proctoring with a structured curriculum and regular feedback modules tailored to individual learning needs
description: The article recommends that proctoring be embedded in a structured curriculum with regular feedback rather than offered as isolated sessions. It states "Depending on learning needs, a structured curriculum is crucial and should be established for the future. Regular feedback modules should be a part of any surgical training concept." The recommendation follows from the finding that learning needs differ by experience, position, qualification and robotic-surgery frequency, and that the feedback form acted as an individual curriculum.
requirements: Learning needs of individual surgeons must be assessed, since they differ by medical function, work experience, and frequency of robotic surgery
constraints: The study notes that a large majority of clinics in Germany lack the financial resources and/or time needed for prolonged clinical leave, and calls for extending perioperative feedback in content, structure and quantity
target_learners: surgeons learning robot-assisted surgery, from novices to experienced chief and senior physicians
target_learning_goals: acquisition of robotic surgical skills
transfer of trained skills to clinical routine
lifelong professional development
examples: The proctor accompanied the operational team for one day (1.3 appointments on average, 5.6 hours on average), gave intraoperative feedback to surgeon, assistants, anesthesia and nursing staff, and afterwards sent a detailed feedback sheet by e-mail
key_sources: Günther V, Nees F, Maass N, von Otte S, Ruchay Z, Pape J, Ackermann J, Alkatout I. (2025). How effective and sustainable is proctoring in robotic surgery? A retrospective analysis based on interviews with surgeons. Surgical Endoscopy 39(3):1985–1995. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11503-5

article_title: Development and user experience of a three-dimensional object-based virtual reality-simulation tool for dental radiography training: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Im Ji-Eun, Gu Ja-Young, Bae Jung-Hee, Lee Jae-Gi. (2025). Development and user experience of a three-dimensional object-based virtual reality-simulation tool for dental radiography training: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06623-4
title: Step-gated sequential task structure with immediate correct/incorrect feedback in procedural VR training
description: The 3DOVR-DR organizes a clinical procedure into a fixed sequence of tasks, each begun and ended on an operational panel, with progression gated on successful completion. "The graphical user interface for the 'Next' option was designed to activate only after the successful completion of the current task." Correct actions triggered a green 'Next' button while incorrect actions produced a red indicator prompting repetition, giving learners repeated practice of individual steps or the whole process until performed correctly.
requirements: Interactive 3D objects with clearly delineated response areas, an operational panel guiding each task, and controller-based interaction in the VR environment
constraints: Increased complexity in VR-learning scenarios can lead to higher cognitive load and stress, which the authors say future studies should analyze
target_learners: preclinical health-science students learning a hands-on clinical procedure
target_learning_goals: mastery of a multi-step clinical procedure through repeated, feedback-guided practice
examples: The 12 tasks ranged from verifying patient information and assisting with the lead apron to operating the positioning device, irradiating, verifying film, and guiding the patient to the waiting area
key_sources: Im Ji-Eun, Gu Ja-Young, Bae Jung-Hee, Lee Jae-Gi. (2025). Development and user experience of a three-dimensional object-based virtual reality-simulation tool for dental radiography training: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06623-4
grain_size: lesson-level design pattern for simulation-based procedural training

article_title: Strategies and barriers to implementing physically active teaching in universities from the perspective of lecturers: a qualitative study.
citation: Rupp Robert, Wallmann-Sperlich Birgit, Bucksch Jens. (2025). Strategies and barriers to implementing physically active teaching in universities from the perspective of lecturers: a qualitative study. BMC Public Health 25, Article 855. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22075-x
title: Design physically active university teaching as stealth health: synchronise physical activity with learning rather than interrupting it
description: Rather than inserting breaks that cost learning time, physically activating teaching methods make physical activity itself learning time, achieving a double activation of students. The article states: "Physically activating teaching methods are thus characterised by the fact that they lead to a double activation of the students — physically as well as cognitively — while pursuing specific learning objectives." Compared with breaks and sit-stand desks, these methods "appear to be advantageous because they are cost-effective, close to the subject and save learning time."
requirements: Methods must be congruent with the subject matter and pursue primary pedagogical-didactic goals so health promotion is incidental
constraints: Physical activity breaks are invariably associated with a loss of teaching time; sit-stand desks entail cost implications that hinder scaling
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: cognitive and physical activation in service of learning while reducing sedentary time
examples: In a gallery walk, students stand up and walk around the classroom to view and discuss other groups' exhibited work results, so the physically active time is also learning time
key_sources: Rupp Robert, Wallmann-Sperlich Birgit, Bucksch Jens. (2025). Strategies and barriers to implementing physically active teaching in universities from the perspective of lecturers: a qualitative study. BMC Public Health 25, Article 855. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22075-x

article_title: ChatGPT-4 Omni Performance in USMLE Disciplines and Clinical Skills: Comparative Analysis.
citation: Brenton T Bicknell, Danner Butler, Sydney Whalen, James Ricks, Cory J Dixon, Abigail B Clark, Olivia Spaedy, Adam Skelton, Neel Edupuganti, Lance Dzubinski, Hudson Tate, Garrett Dyess, Brenessa Lindeman, Lisa Soleymani Lehmann. (2024). ChatGPT-4 Omni Performance in USMLE Disciplines and Clinical Skills: Comparative Analysis. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/63430
title: Integrate LLMs into medical education through structured curricula, formal guidelines, and continuous oversight rather than unguided use
description: The article argues that high LLM accuracy alone does not justify unstructured adoption: integration should occur "emphasizing the importance of structured curricula to guide their appropriate use". Institutions are advised to "implement clear guidelines for AI use, including regular audits of AI performance and mandatory training for students and faculty", and program directors should "establish mechanisms to continuously monitor the performance and impact of LLMs". This principle translates the study's accuracy findings into a guardrail for educational use.
requirements: Mechanisms to continuously monitor LLM performance and impact in clinical and educational settings
constraints: Correct USMLE question answering is not the same as synthesizing and reasoning about a patient's history, symptoms, exam findings, and laboratory data
target_learners: Medical students
Medical school faculty
Residency program directors
target_learning_goals: Safe and appropriate use of AI tools in study and clinical reasoning
Preservation of students' own diagnostic and problem-solving skills
examples: The study recommends creating a national registry of feedback from students and faculty to identify errors and unintended consequences associated with LLM use in medical education and clinical care, and establishing dedicated oversight committees to monitor AI integration.

article_title: Examining interviewer bias in medical school admissions: The interplay between applicant and interviewer gender and its effects on interview outcomes.
citation: Tsikas Stefanos A., Dauer Karina. (2024). Examining interviewer bias in medical school admissions: The interplay between applicant and interviewer gender and its effects on interview outcomes. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0309293
title: Selection interviews should be highly standardized, with a common interview guide, comprehensive interviewer training, and shared rating standards, to prevent bias
description: The article recommends that where selection interviews are used, procedural standardization is the primary safeguard against differential ratings. It states that observed inequalities "could have been prevented with a higher degree of standardization", including a clearly defined interview guide with questions posed to all candidates, comprehensive interview training and shared rating standards, and fewer interviewers conducting a larger number of interviews in fixed commissions. Among known procedures, the authors judge Multiple Mini-Interviews best meet these criteria.
requirements: A clearly defined interview guide with questions posed to all candidates
Comprehensive interview training and shared rating standards
Fewer interviewers conducting a larger number of interviews in fixed commissions
constraints: At the studied school, interviewer trainings and general agreements were rather cursory, and participation was de facto not mandatory; the interviews were not standardized
target_learners: medical school applicants
target_learning_goals: fair and objective assessment of social competence, motivation, and self-reflection in admissions selection
examples: At MHH, interviews were not standardized, no uniform questions were asked, and the authors link the observed committee-type differences to this lack of standardization.
key_sources: Tsikas Stefanos A., Dauer Karina. (2024). Examining interviewer bias in medical school admissions: The interplay between applicant and interviewer gender and its effects on interview outcomes. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0309293

article_title: Designing simulation-based curriculum content for emergency medicine residents in France: a Delphi method.
citation: Thiebaud Pierre-Clément, Philippon Anne-Laure, Plaisance Patrick, Chauvin Anthony, Houze-Cerfon Charles-Henri, Truchot Jennifer, and the CNUMU-SIMU Group. (2024). Designing simulation-based curriculum content for emergency medicine residents in France: a Delphi method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05901-5
title: Standardize curriculum content while leaving educators flexibility to align teaching goals with learner expertise and local resources
description: The article argues a national curriculum should tend toward uniformity and standardization of simulation training while preserving teacher autonomy. Because "the alignment of teaching objectives with the students’ level of expertise is a major challenge in simulation-based training," the authors conclude "it seems wise to leave a certain degree of freedom to educators to align teaching goals to the respective level of expertise of students." They also note the technology itself is not that relevant to learning quality, so the selected items serve as guidelines adaptable to local human and material resources.
requirements: A competency-based approach with milestones to identify level of progression for each skill or knowledge
constraints: Curriculum must be adjusted to local needs given barriers such as lack of time, teacher training, and equipment cost
target_learners: Emergency medicine residents across all French universities
target_learning_goals: Progressive, step-by-step acquisition of technical and non-technical skills matched to resident expertise level
examples: The curriculum was approved by the CNUMU and distributed to regional directors, with implementation evaluation scheduled two years after implementation
key_sources: Thiebaud Pierre-Clément, Philippon Anne-Laure, Plaisance Patrick, Chauvin Anthony, Houze-Cerfon Charles-Henri, Truchot Jennifer, and the CNUMU-SIMU Group. (2024). Designing simulation-based curriculum content for emergency medicine residents in France: a Delphi method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05901-5

article_title: Robotic hepaticojejunostomy training in novices using robotic simulation and dry-lab suturing (ROSIM): randomized controlled crossover trial.
citation: Menso Julia E., Rahimi A. Masie, Zwart Maurice J. W., Daams Freek, de Hondt Joey, Karadza Emir, Montorsi Roberto M., Nickel Felix, Bonjer H. Jaap, van Dijkum Els J. M. Nieveen, Besselink Marc G. (2024). Robotic hepaticojejunostomy training in novices using robotic simulation and dry-lab suturing (ROSIM): randomized controlled crossover trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-10914-8
title: Sequence robotic suturing curricula to start with robotic simulation followed by suture-pad dry-lab training
description: The article recommends that a robotic suturing curriculum combining SimNow robotic simulation and suture-pad dry-lab training "should ideally start with robotic simulation", because initial simulation exposure lets novices practice the system and its features before realistic dry-lab suturing. This follows directly from the trial's finding of significantly better OSATS performance after the simulation-first sequence. The authors also state the SimNow "cannot replace suture-pad training", so both modalities are included.
requirements: Access to both a SimNow robotic simulator and a da Vinci system with suture-pads and biotissue models
Novice trainees without prior robotic suturing experience
constraints: The advantage was shown in robotic novices performing a hepaticojejunostomy in biotissue, not in live procedures
The sensitivity analysis excluding experienced participants showed no significant difference between sequences
Participants themselves preferred suture-pad training over simulation
target_learners: Surgical residents without robotic experience
target_learning_goals: Robotic suturing and hepaticojejunostomy technical skill
examples: In the trial, the intervention group completed 15 minutes each of 'Running suture' and 'Knot tying' SimNow exercises followed by 30 minutes of suture-pad interrupted suturing, then crossed over

Nieveen, Besselink Marc G. (2024). Robotic hepaticojejunostomy training in novices using robotic simulation and dry-lab suturing (ROSIM): randomized controlled crossover trial. article_title: Impact of laparoscopic training course for surgical trainees based on an evidence-based pedagogical framework: randomized trial.
citation: Pan Ruijun, Zhou Xueliang, Wu Chao, Zhang Luyang, Wang Jiayu, Zheng Minhua, Shi Ting, Cai Wei, Sun Jing. (2024). Impact of laparoscopic training course for surgical trainees based on an evidence-based pedagogical framework: randomized trial. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrae109
title: Structure procedural-skill courses around a staged framework that bridges simulation to clinical practice
description: The article recommends organizing procedural-skill training as a staged progression rather than an undifferentiated lecture-plus-practice course, "guiding the trainees from 'virtual simulation' to 'live animal' and ultimately to 'clinical practice'". In the trial this meant adding demonstration video, summative simulator assessment before clinical exposure, operating theatre rotations, and protected self-directed maintenance time to an otherwise identical lecture and skills curriculum.
requirements: Simulator-based assessment should be passed before trainees perform skills on patients under direct supervision
constraints: Simulation is valuable but "does not replace the need for training in real-life clinical environments"; long-term maintenance effects were not assessed
target_learners: surgical residents learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: procedural (laparoscopic) skills
technical and non-technical surgical performance
examples: The pedagogical group's course added a 30-min instructional video, an Operational Assessment Sheet 'prove' step, 1 day per week of operating theatre rotation, and an additional hour per week of self-directed skills learning to the shared lecture and simulator content
key_sources: Pan Ruijun, Zhou Xueliang, Wu Chao, Zhang Luyang, Wang Jiayu, Zheng Minhua, Shi Ting, Cai Wei, Sun Jing. (2024). Impact of laparoscopic training course for surgical trainees based on an evidence-based pedagogical framework: randomized trial. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrae109

article_title: Improving learning experience through implementing standardized team-based learning process in undergraduate medical education.
citation: Andrews-Dickert Rebecca, Nagaraj Ranjini, Zhan Lilian, Knittig Laura, Zhao Yuan. (2024). Improving learning experience through implementing standardized team-based learning process in undergraduate medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06025-6
title: The standardized TBL process framework: a prescribed sequence of steps plus four key components
description: The article describes Team-Based Learning as "a highly structured form of learning, involving the performance of a prescribed sequence of steps and the implementation of key components." The sequence runs pre-class preparation, readiness assurance (IRAT, TRAT, immediate feedback and clarification), problem-solving activities, and a closing summary. The framework's four key components are "carefully formed and managed teams, frequent and timely feedback, problem-solving activities, and student peer evaluation." Application activities follow the 4 S's: Significant problem, Same problem, Specific choice, Simultaneous reporting. The study implemented this full framework in a 6-week systems course and assessed its effect on student perception.
requirements: Faculty trained in TBL design and facilitation; the article notes faculty received basic training and that quality of training and facilitation skills appear key to institutional effectiveness of TBL
constraints: The article notes evidence of frequent modifications of TBL design and delivery upon implementation, and that implementation of the standardized framework can be complex
target_learners: Undergraduate medical (osteopathic) students in preclinical courses
target_learning_goals: Application of pre-class preparatory knowledge to clinical problem-solving
Teamwork and professional skills such as communication and giving and receiving feedback
examples: In the ERG course, three 2-hour TBL sessions used identical IRAT and TRAT items, mini-cases with time goals, A-D placard simultaneous reporting, and anonymous peer evaluations with a completion grade
key_sources: Andrews-Dickert Rebecca, Nagaraj Ranjini, Zhan Lilian, Knittig Laura, Zhao Yuan. (2024). Improving learning experience through implementing standardized team-based learning process in undergraduate medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06025-6

article_title: Construction and implementation of a laparoscopic skill training course based on a smartphone application and virtual reality.
citation: Liang Yao, Huang Hua, Tan Yu-Bao, Li Tang, Huang Wan, Zhang Qing-Long, Liu Zhuo-Wei, Kuang Ming. (2024). Construction and implementation of a laparoscopic skill training course based on a smartphone application and virtual reality. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06066-x
title: STALS three-stage progressive course structure integrating theory, practice, assessment, and feedback
description: The STALS course organizes laparoscopic training into three stages of progressively increasing difficulty, each combining online and offline components. The article states "Each stage incorporates both online and offline components, consisting of theory, practice, assessment, and feedback (Table 1)". Trainees must pass each stage's assessment before progressing, retaking a stage on failure, and complete a feedback questionnaire at each stage's end. Stage one uses box trainers, stage two the LapSim VR simulator, and stage three animal organ perfusion simulation.
requirements: Assessment thresholds must be met before progression to the next stage; failed trainees retake the current stage
constraints: The extended learning cycle across all three stages poses a challenge due to the time-consuming nature of full implementation
target_learners: surgical residents and fellows at varying experience levels
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic skills progression from basic tasks toward operating-room practice
examples: Stage one assessed Peg Transfer, Precision Cutting, and Suture with Intracorporeal Knot on the DM-LAP-S simulator with a 30-point rating scale and TABLT scoring
key_sources: Liang Yao, Huang Hua, Tan Yu-Bao, Li Tang, Huang Wan, Zhang Qing-Long, Liu Zhuo-Wei, Kuang Ming. (2024). Construction and implementation of a laparoscopic skill training course based on a smartphone application and virtual reality. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06066-x

article_title: Work stress and competency among radiology residents: the mediating effect of resilience.
citation: Shen Lijun, Lu Yuanmei, He Yanrong, Wang Peicheng, Chen Yanhua, Li Hange, Yang Zhenghan, Zhang Jingfeng, Wang Zhenchang, Jiang Maoqing, Zheng Jianjun, Zhu Jiming. (2024). Work stress and competency among radiology residents: the mediating effect of resilience. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1415351
title: Stress-process model explaining resilience's mediating role between work stress and competency
description: The stress-process model (SPM) is the explanatory framework the article employs to account for resilience's mediating role between work stress and competency. Under SPM, "the processes of perception, appraisal and coping would mitigate work stress, and bring positive or negative responses and outcomes". Resilience enters the model as one of the coping strategies that can mitigate the impacts of work stress on competence.
requirements: Exposure to work stressors together with perception, appraisal and coping processes through which resilience operates as a coping strategy
constraints: The article employs SPM as an explanation for the observed mediating effect rather than directly testing its perceptual and appraisal processes
target_learners: radiology residents experiencing work stress during residency training
target_learning_goals: sustaining competency under work stress
coping with stress through resilience
key_sources: Shen Lijun, Lu Yuanmei, He Yanrong, Wang Peicheng, Chen Yanhua, Li Hange, Yang Zhenghan, Zhang Jingfeng, Wang Zhenchang, Jiang Maoqing, Zheng Jianjun, Zhu Jiming. (2024). Work stress and competency among radiology residents: the mediating effect of resilience. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1415351

article_title: Anesthesiological Preoperative Interview with a Palliative Care Patient: A Simulation-Based Experiment Using Standardized Patients.
citation: Lassen Christoph L., Jaschinsky Fabian, Stamouli Elena, Lindenberg Nicole, Wiese Christoph H. R. (2024). Anesthesiological Preoperative Interview with a Palliative Care Patient: A Simulation-Based Experiment Using Standardized Patients. Medicina (Kaunas). https://doi.org/10.3390/medicina60101577
title: Standardized-patient preoperative interview simulation with embedded palliative-care problems under prompted and unprompted conditions
description: A simulation-based scenario in which trained standardized patients portrayed a 64-year-old palliative-care patient with a mechanical ileus scheduled for palliative gastrostomy, embedding four problems: port catheter use, nausea and vomiting, a transdermal fentanyl patch, and an advance directive with a DNR order. The authors "simulated a preoperative anesthesiological interview using standardized patients" under two conditions: in group 1 problems were present but not actively raised, while in group 2 the standardized patient asked about unaddressed issues at the end of the interview.
requirements: standardized patients who were previously trained and deployed by the medical student training and education center of the university
all interviews recorded on an audio and video recording system and transcribed
constraints: the study was only carried out at one location in Germany
no debriefing feedback was obtained, purposefully, to prevent the handling of advance directives being passed on among participants
target_learners: anesthesiologists in training or fully trained anesthesiologists without prior palliative care training
target_learning_goals: identifying and addressing perioperative medical and psychosocial challenges of patients under palliative care
examples: Group 2 standardized patients asked four scripted questions, including "I have an advanced directive. It is important for me that I do not want to be resuscitated. Is this a problem?"
key_sources: Lassen Christoph L., Jaschinsky Fabian, Stamouli Elena, Lindenberg Nicole, Wiese Christoph H. R. (2024). Anesthesiological Preoperative Interview with a Palliative Care Patient: A Simulation-Based Experiment Using Standardized Patients. Medicina (Kaunas). https://doi.org/10.3390/medicina60101577

article_title: Virtual reality simulation training in laparoscopic surgery - does it really matter, what simulator to use? Results of a cross-sectional study.
citation: Sparn Moritz B., Teixeira Hugo, Chatziisaak Dimitrios, Schmied Bruno, Hahnloser Dieter, Bischofberger Stephan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation training in laparoscopic surgery – does it really matter, what simulator to use? Results of a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education 24, 589. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05574-0
title: Implement standardized outcome metrics so that training results are comparable across different virtual reality simulators
description: Because each manufacturer's proprietary metrics cannot be compared across simulators, the article recommends standardized, universally applicable outcome measures. The authors used total instrument path length and total time as surrogate parameters for proficiency, noting both metrics are "widely used and enable universal comparability of different simulators and exercises without having to rely on proprietary evaluation algorithms". They call for standardized and validated metrics to reliably measure trainee proficiency.
requirements: Metrics must be measurable on any simulator platform; total time and total instrument path length satisfy this and were collected for every participant in the study
constraints: Time and path length are surrogates: a task can be performed quickly but badly executed, and path length is only a surrogate for movement efficacy
target_learners: surgical trainees assessed on virtual reality simulators
target_learning_goals: reliable measurement of laparoscopic proficiency and performance across simulator platforms
examples: The study recorded total path length of all instruments and time to complete exercises at entry and exit examinations, comparing them with Welch's t-test and LOESS scatterplot smoothers
key_sources: Sparn Moritz B., Teixeira Hugo, Chatziisaak Dimitrios, Schmied Bruno, Hahnloser Dieter, Bischofberger Stephan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation training in laparoscopic surgery – does it really matter, what simulator to use? Results of a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education 24, 589. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05574-0

article_title: Construction and application of procedural pathways combined with information management in nursing staff skills training system.
citation: Cui Liping, Dong Yuting, Zhang Shan, Ma Wenxia, Li Min. (2024). Construction and application of procedural pathways combined with information management in nursing staff skills training system. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05593-x
title: Standardized operation pathway structure for skills training
description: A reusable lesson-level design in which each clinical operation is converted into a procedural pathway with fixed components. The article states that "Every operation procedure formed different but regular operation pathways, including quality requirements, pre-operation preparation, operation process, post-operation treatment, and effect evaluation." Scores are detailed for the operation assessment standards, reducing invigilator subjectivity, and scientific predictions of reasonable mistakes during procedures are emphasized and analyzed during lesson preparation.
requirements: Collective and individual lesson preparation by a trained skills operation group
Reference to textbooks, guidelines, consensus, and literature when condensing teaching content
constraints: Developed and evaluated for hospital nursing skills training; the article does not claim generalization beyond that setting
target_learners: Newly admitted nurses in hospital in-service training
target_learning_goals: Standardized, safe execution of clinical nursing operations
Error prevention in nursing procedures
examples: Operation demonstrations were guided by clinical problems, based on the 6th edition of Basic Nursing, combined with clinical cases and standardized patients
key_sources: Cui Liping, Dong Yuting, Zhang Shan, Ma Wenxia, Li Min. (2024). Construction and application of procedural pathways combined with information management in nursing staff skills training system. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05593-x

article_title: Does clinical experience influence the effects of team simulation training in stroke thrombolysis? A prospective cohort study.
citation: Ajmi Soffien, Kurz Martin, Lindner Thomas Werner, Dalen Ingvild, Ersdal Hege Langli. (2024). Does clinical experience influence the effects of team simulation training in stroke thrombolysis? A prospective cohort study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-086413
title: Weekly in situ team simulation training programme for acute stroke thrombolysis at Stavanger University Hospital
description: A team simulation training programme introduced in February 2017 as part of a quality improvement project at a Norwegian stroke centre. Sessions were weekly and "focused on improving procedural adherence and team leadership skills for neurology registrars (eg, improving team situational awareness through briefs and summaries, using closed-loop communication)". Attendance dates per registrar were registered from the first session, and attendance prior to a patient's admission defined the exposure in the cohort analysis.
requirements: Registration of registrar attendance dates and treating-registrar identity in the thrombolysis registry
constraints: Its effects cannot be reliably separated from concurrent protocol-streamlining interventions in the same QI project
target_learners: neurology registrars and the in-hospital stroke team
target_learning_goals: procedural adherence
team leadership
team situational awareness
examples: The first year after introduction, median DNT was reduced from 27 min to 13 min in the centre's prior quality improvement publication
key_sources: Ajmi Soffien, Kurz Martin, Lindner Thomas Werner, Dalen Ingvild, Ersdal Hege Langli. (2024). Does clinical experience influence the effects of team simulation training in stroke thrombolysis? A prospective cohort study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-086413

article_title: Measuring personal characteristics in applicants to German medical schools: Piloting an online Situational Judgement Test with an open-ended response format.
citation: Knorr Mirjana, Mielke Ina, Amelung Dorothee, Safari Mahla, Gröne Oana R., Breil Simon M., MacIntosh Alexander. (2024). Measuring personal characteristics in applicants to German medical schools: Piloting an online Situational Judgement Test with an open-ended response format. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2024-41/zma001685.shtml
title: Stav central research database matching admission, sociodemographic, and study-performance data
description: The Studierendenauswahlverbund (stav) is an ongoing research project with "a central database" in which "admission data, study performance data of admitted students, and data from other research studies and a sociodemographic questionnaire ... are matched and stored". It enabled this pilot to link Casper scores to Abitur grades, TMS, HAM-Nat, HAM-SJT, and OSCE results without separate data collection. The R code, full data analysis report, appendices, and information on requesting the original data are available via the project's OSF page.
requirements: Participants must have consented to data collection, storage and matching of their data
constraints: Sociodemographic information was available for only around 64% of the pilot participants
target_learners: medical school applicants
medical students
target_learning_goals: evaluation of medical school admission criteria and study success
examples: Casper data were matched to OSCE communication-station results from exams taken between 2016 and 2022
key_sources: Knorr Mirjana, Mielke Ina, Amelung Dorothee, Safari Mahla, Gröne Oana R., Breil Simon M., MacIntosh Alexander. (2024).
