article_title: UK and Ireland Joint Advisory Group (JAG) consensus statements for training and certification in diagnostic endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).
citation: El Menabawey Tareq, McCrudden Raymond, Shetty Dushyant, Hopper Andrew D, Huggett Matthew T, Bekkali Noor, Carroll Nicholas R, Henry Elaine, Johnson Gavin J, Keane Margaret G, Love Mark, McKay Colin J, Norton Sally, Oppong Kofi, Penman Ian, Ramesh Jayapal, Ryan Barbara, Siau Keith, Nayar Manu. (2024). UK and Ireland Joint Advisory Group (JAG) consensus statements for training and certification in diagnostic endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). Gut. https://doi.org/10.1136/gutjnl-2023-329800
title: Staged EUS training sequence: imaging familiarisation before scope handling, then formal hands-on training on a TTT ladder
description: The guideline prescribes training delivered at specific levels: pre-procedure preparation (indications, consent, imaging review), a period of observation before handling the echoendoscope, formal hands-on training using the EUS Train the Trainers ladder, then postprocedure care and report writing, with trainees auditing their own practice. Trainees "should spend a period familiarising themselves with image acquisition and interpretation prior to echoendoscope handling", combining observing EUS cases with time spent with ultrasonographers.
requirements: Trainers delivering EUS training should have undertaken an endoscopy-specific TTT course, preferably in EUS
Trainers should ensure trainees are empowered to give honest and critical feedback on their training
constraints: The panel notes there is currently no evidence base on which to base a recommendation for the period of attendance at ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging lists and hands-off observation
target_learners: EUS trainees from gastroenterology, radiology and surgery backgrounds
target_learning_goals: safe echoendoscope handling, ultrasound image acquisition and interpretation, structured reporting
examples: Non-radiology trainees are recommended to shadow radiologists performing transabdominal ultrasound and attend cross-sectional imaging lists to learn terminology and reporting.
key_sources: El Menabawey Tareq, McCrudden Raymond, Shetty Dushyant, Hopper Andrew D, Huggett Matthew T, Bekkali Noor, Carroll Nicholas R, Henry Elaine, Johnson Gavin J, Keane Margaret G, Love Mark, McKay Colin J, Norton Sally, Oppong Kofi, Penman Ian, Ramesh Jayapal, Ryan Barbara, Siau Keith, Nayar Manu. (2024). UK and Ireland Joint Advisory Group (JAG) consensus statements for training and certification in diagnostic endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). Gut. https://doi.org/10.1136/gutjnl-2023-329800

article_title: Study on the status and problems of teaching system of "medical advanced mathematics": data based on a research of 11 universities in China.
citation: Sun Jiangjie, Liu Tong, Li Hui. (2024). Study on the status and problems of teaching system of “medical advanced mathematics”: data based on a research of 11 universities in China. BMC Medical Education, 24, 36. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-05012-7
title: STC teaching mode: self-directed learning, traditional teaching, and cross-collaborative learning for medical advanced mathematics
description: The STC teaching mode, formally proposed by the authors' group in 2016, combines three learning components: “S refers to the self-directed learning”, “T refers to the traditional teaching”, and “C refers to cross-collaborative learning”. It is delivered through a smart classroom integrating “student side, teacher side and interconnected cloud side”, intended to free teaching from fixed class schedules and align content with professional needs. The article positions it as the proposed solution to the surveyed problems of content-profession disconnect and unrealized educational-model innovation.
requirements: Internet-based quality learning resources for the self-directed learning component
a smart classroom infrastructure integrating student, teacher and cloud sides
coordination across multiple university departments for implementation
constraints: The article reports no controlled evaluation of the mode's learning effects; support consists of the authors' own teaching awards and student outcomes
data come from China only, which the authors state may lead to biased results
target_learners: undergraduate medical university students in majors offering advanced mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematical operation and data analysis ability
applying mathematical methods and tools to solve practical problems in medicine
examples: The authors completed a provincial-level smart classroom project in 2020 and report teaching-competition awards and students publishing SCI and EI papers
key_sources: Sun Jiangjie, Liu Tong, Li Hui. (2024). Study on the status and problems of teaching system of “medical advanced mathematics”: data based on a research of 11 universities in China. BMC Medical Education, 24, 36. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-05012-7

article_title: Predicting academic achievement from the collaborative influences of executive function, physical fitness, and demographic factors among primary school students in China: ensemble learning methods.
citation: Sun Zhiyuan, Yuan Yunhao, Xiong Xuan, Meng Shuqiao, Shi Yifan, Chen Aiguo. (2024). Predicting academic achievement from the collaborative influences of executive function, physical fitness, and demographic factors among primary school students in China: ensemble learning methods. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-024-17769-7
title: Stacking ensemble learning model built from SVM, DT, LR, and LDA base classifiers with a meta-classifier
description: A Stacking ensemble learning model in which four heterogeneous individual learners—Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, and Linear Discriminant Analysis—serve as base classifiers. Their outputs form a meta-dataset passed to a next-layer meta-classifier that produces the final prediction, with base outputs treated as new features and raw labels retained. In this study it was used to predict primary school students' academic achievement and achieved 68.33% average cross-validation accuracy.
requirements: Base classifiers are heterogeneous individual learners so they observe data from various data spaces and structures
constraints: Its average accuracy (68.33%) was below XGB (70.21%) and RF (70.42%) in this study's training-set cross-validation
target_learners: primary school students in grades 4-6
target_learning_goals: predicting academic achievement (Chinese, mathematics, foreign language exam performance) for early identification of academically disadvantaged students
examples: The study trained the Stacking model on an 80% training set with repeated five-fold cross-validation and evaluated it on held-out test samples with accuracy, precision, and recall
key_sources: Sun Zhiyuan, Yuan Yunhao, Xiong Xuan, Meng Shuqiao, Shi Yifan, Chen Aiguo. (2024). Predicting academic achievement from the collaborative influences of executive function, physical fitness, and demographic factors among primary school students in China: ensemble learning methods. article_title: Relationships of gaming disorder, ADHD, and academic performance in university students: A mediation analysis.
citation: Hawi Nazir, Samaha Maya. (2024). Relationships of gaming disorder, ADHD, and academic performance in university students: A mediation analysis. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0300680
title: Structured time and alternative leisure activities should be part of therapeutic approaches to gaming disorder
description: Because GD correlated more strongly with gaming hours on non-university days (r = .487) than university days (r = .365), the authors argue free time may exacerbate gaming behaviors. The discussion states this "highlights the importance of structured time and alternative leisure activities as part of the therapeutic approach". The principle applies to managing gaming behavior in students at risk of gaming disorder.
requirements: Identification of students at risk of gaming disorder, e.g., via a validated instrument such as the IGD-20 Test
constraints: The underlying correlation is cross-sectional and observational; the article does not test whether structuring time reduces gaming disorder
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: reducing excessive gaming behavior that interferes with academic functioning
examples: The study found the disordered gaming group averaged 7.7 hours (SD = 4.8) of gaming on non-university days versus 3.6 hours (SD = 2.7) on university days
key_sources: Hawi Nazir, Samaha Maya. (2024). Relationships of gaming disorder, ADHD, and academic performance in university students: A mediation analysis. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0300680

article_title: A simulation training of family management for parents of children with epilepsy: a randomized clinical trial.
citation: Liu Hua-yan, Zeng Shan, Chen Yue-wei, Yi Min, Tan Xiao-yan, Xie Jian-hui, Wu Xia, Zhu Li-hui. (2024). A simulation training of family management for parents of children with epilepsy: a randomized clinical trial. Italian Journal of Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13052-024-01646-5
title: STOFMS: simulation training of family management style intervention
description: STOFMS is "a flexible and family-centered intervention that focuses on improving caregivers' perceptions of disease and problem-solving capability". It teaches family members to manage both the child's chronic condition and daily living, adding simulated post-discharge family management during hospitalization and Internet-based ongoing support. In the trial it was delivered across four sessions from admission to 6-month follow-up against a routine FMSF control.
requirements: Multidisciplinary team of physicians, pharmacists and nurses to assess the child and set the treatment regimen
A family ward setting in which staff act as family members during the simulation
An Internet-based application for post-discharge reminders, education materials and follow-up
constraints: Evaluated only in children with epilepsy aged over 28 days to 14 years at one tertiary hospital in China
The article notes the STOFMS group received only a short-term intervention, so long-term efficacy is yet to be examined
target_learners: Parents and family caregivers of children with epilepsy
target_learning_goals: Family management of childhood chronic illness
Medication adherence behaviors
Seizure prevention, early identification and emergency response
examples: In the trial, 231 families were assigned to STOFMS and received simulation training three days after admission, with follow-up every two weeks for 6 months after discharge
key_sources: Liu Hua-yan, Zeng Shan, Chen Yue-wei, Yi Min, Tan Xiao-yan, Xie Jian-hui, Wu Xia, Zhu Li-hui. (2024). A simulation training of family management for parents of children with epilepsy: a randomized clinical trial. Italian Journal of Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13052-024-01646-5

article_title: Development and validation of the student ratings in clinical teaching scale in Australia: a methodological study.
citation: Huang Pin-Hsiang, O'Sullivan Anthony John, Shulruf Boaz. (2023). Development and validation of the student ratings in clinical teaching scale in Australia: a methodological study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2023.20.26
title: STRICT: a 78-item student-ratings scale measuring frequency of clinical teaching practices
description: STRICT is a questionnaire for medical students to rate how often clinical teaching practices occur, developed from a meta-analysis of effective teaching-learning factors. The article states the item pool "was then reviewed by 3 experts (1 scale expert and 2 clinicians)" and piloted, reducing "the number of items from 202 to 78". It applies 6-point frequency scales from never to always so respondents recall how often behaviors occur rather than judge them.
requirements: Responses require students with direct clinical teaching experience; the scale was administered to medical students in clinical training years
constraints: The scale's four measured domains derive from one prior meta-analysis of effective clinical teaching-learning factors
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical training years (2, 3, and 6)
target_learning_goals: evaluation of clinical teaching practices across student-centered learning, visual technology, problem-solving learning, and self-directed learning
examples: Applied to 834 invited UNSW medical students, of whom 352 completed the questionnaire in 2018
key_sources: Huang Pin-Hsiang, O'Sullivan Anthony John, Shulruf Boaz. (2023). Development and validation of the student ratings in clinical teaching scale in Australia: a methodological study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2023.20.26

article_title: Impact of simulation training on the management of shoulder dystocia and incidence of permanent brachial plexus birth injury: An observational study.
citation: Kaijomaa M, Gissler M, Äyräs O, Sten A, Grahn P. (2023). Impact of simulation training on the management of shoulder dystocia and incidence of permanent brachial plexus birth injury: An observational study. BJOG. https://doi.org/10.1111/1471-0528.17278
title: Standardised stepwise shoulder dystocia management protocol taught with emphasis on posterior arm delivery technique
description: The training teaches a fixed sequence of SD actions — recognising and stating SD, calling for help, informing anaesthetist and paediatrician, lowering the headboard, stopping oxytocin, McRoberts manoeuvre, episiotomy, suprapubic pressure, internal rotation, posterior arm delivery, and escalation to all-fours position or hysterotomy. "A particular emphasis is placed on the technique for posterior arm delivery", taught individually each session. No one manoeuvre is taught as superior; participants always try McRoberts and suprapubic pressure first, and are taught to avoid fundal pressure and excessive traction, which increase anterior shoulder impaction and brachial plexus damage risk.
requirements: Simulation equipment including a high-fidelity birthing simulator and a simple pelvic model for manoeuvre practice
Certified trainers able to demonstrate and individually teach the posterior arm technique
constraints: Midwives are encouraged to perform posterior arm delivery in real SD situations before the obstetrician arrives only if indicated
target_learners: Midwives
Obstetric doctors
target_learning_goals: Technical management of shoulder dystocia
Safe selection and sequencing of obstetric manoeuvres
examples: A lateroposterior approach with the whole hand inserted into the vagina is discussed, demonstrated and individually taught in each training session
key_sources: Kaijomaa M, Gissler M, Äyräs O, Sten A, Grahn P. (2023). Impact of simulation training on the management of shoulder dystocia and incidence of permanent brachial plexus birth injury: An observational study. BJOG. https://doi.org/10.1111/1471-0528.17278

article_title: Preparing for obstetric anaesthesia-An educational randomised controlled trial comparing e-learning to written course material.
citation: Andersson ML, Duch P, Bessmann EL, Lundstrøm LH, Ekelund K. (2023). Preparing for obstetric anaesthesia—An educational randomised controlled trial comparing e‐learning to written course material. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aas.14148
title: Two e-learning modules on postpartum haemorrhage and preeclampsia built on the StringLearning platform
description: The authors created two e-learning modules covering all learning objectives of the obstetric anaesthesia course curriculum in PPH and PE, using the platform StringLearning ApS. The modules "consisted of obstetric cases, segments of conference videos and online lectures, pictures and summary tables with voice‐over explanation", with MCQs presented during learning to stimulate reflective thinking. Expert panels approved academic content and usability was tested on obstetric anaesthetists and residents before the trial.
requirements: Developed according to contemporary principles for effective learning and approved by experts in obstetric anaesthesia
Requires resources, time, and technical and pedagogical qualifications to develop
constraints: Each module covers only a single obstetric anaesthesia subject, not the entire course curriculum
target_learners: second-year resident anaesthetists
target_learning_goals: knowledge of postpartum haemorrhage and preeclampsia management for obstetric anaesthesia
examples: Participants randomised to e-learning in one subject and written material in the other, with access to StringLearning restricted to the assigned module
key_sources: Andersson ML, Duch P, Bessmann EL, Lundstrøm LH, Ekelund K. (2023). Preparing for obstetric anaesthesia—An educational randomised controlled trial comparing e‐learning to written course material. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aas.14148

article_title: An international collaborative approach to learning histology using a virtual microscope.
citation: Then, S.-M., Kokolski, M., Mbaki, Y., Merrick, D., & Anderson, S. (2023). An international collaborative approach to learning histology using a virtual microscope. Anatomia, Histologia, Embryologia, 52, 21-30. https://doi.org/10.1111/ahe.12888
title: Engage students in actively creating their own annotated revision resources (e-workbooks) from virtual microscope sessions.
description: The principle is that students should generate their own learning resources by finding, inserting and annotating virtual microscope images, rather than passively receiving material. The article states that "student participation in generating their own learning resources increased active learning, engagement, and motivation in addition to providing a valuable revision aid". In the study, all students were expected to find, insert and annotate images from the VM for all sessions across modules.
requirements: Access to a web-based virtual microscope so all students can retrieve the same digitised slides
A worksheet or workbook structure into which students insert and annotate screenshots
constraints: The e-workbook itself was not part of summative assessment in the reported implementation
target_learners: First- and second-year undergraduate BSc students in biomedical sciences and medical physiology
target_learning_goals: Histology and microanatomy knowledge
Relating tissue structure to function
examples: Students saved VM screenshots into worksheets, annotated and labelled their own examples, and supplemented them during summing-up sessions

article_title: Time for a simulation strategy?
citation: Shiner N. (2023). Time for a simulation strategy? Journal of Medical Radiation Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1002/jmrs.685
title: Adopt a strategic, curriculum-wide approach to integrating traditional simulation and VR rather than sporadic uptake
description: The editorial argues that after rapid, often necessity-driven adoption of simulation during the pandemic, educators should "take a strategic approach to implement both traditional simulation and VR into a radiography curriculum, to maximise investments and promote successful student learning outcomes". A strategy should balance learning objectives, be led by a vision, and be informed by audits, student feedback, placement provision and evidence-based practice.
requirements: A strategy should be led by a vision and informed by audits, student feedback, placement provision, evidenced-based practice and regulatory and societal bodies' guidance
constraints: Answers on what to teach with simulation and how much to invest will vary from institute to institute
target_learners: Undergraduate radiography students
target_learning_goals: Preparation for clinical practice across technical and non-technical skills
examples: The editorial cites Rowe et al.'s VR-only first-year training and Ketterer et al.'s blended simulated placements as contrasting implementation strategies.

article_title: The Impact of Systematic Laparoscopic Skills and Suture Training on Laparoscopic Hysterectomy Outcomes in a Brazilian Teaching Hospital.
citation: Lobão Gonçalves Anna Luiza, Ayroza-Ribeiro Helizabet Abdala, Lima Raquel Ferreira, Yonamine Aline Estefane Eras, Ohara Fabio, Ayroza-Ribeiro Paulo Augusto Galvão. (2019). RBGO Gynecology & Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0039-1700587
title: Standardized step-ordered total laparoscopic hysterectomy technique
description: Since 2008, all TLHs at the institution follow a standardized intrafascial technique in which "the same standard steps are performed in the same order for every TLH." The fixed sequence covers patient positioning and pneumoperitoneum, trocar placement, round ligament and broad ligament dissection, uterine vessel section, colpotomy, transvaginal uterus removal, and x-shaped plus continuous colporrhaphy sutures. The authors report that standardization made surgical outcomes comparable regardless of surgeon and eased resident training by removing exposure to multiple technique variations.
requirements: All surgeons in the group perform the identical step sequence for every procedure
constraints: Described for the intrafascial TLH technique at one institution
target_learners: Gynecologic endoscopy fellowship residents
target_learning_goals: Surgical technique consistency
comparable patient outcomes across surgeons
learnable procedure structure for trainees
examples: The Methods section enumerates the fixed steps, including Veress needle safety maneuvers, 5-mm accessory portals, and no. 0 Vicryl colporrhaphy with x-shaped angle stitches

article_title: [Virtual training of practical competences in sonography].
citation: Everad F., Seifert L., Mansour N., Hofauer B., Knopf A., Offergeld C. (2024). Sonographie als Gegenstand virtuellen Wissenstransfers zum praktischen Kompetenzerwerb. HNO. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00106-024-01476-1
title: Digital teaching of practical skills requires standardized units, recognized teaching methods, and frequent repetition
description: The article's conclusions for practice state that effective digital teaching of sonography depends on structural and methodological conditions: "Eine Standardisierung der Lehreinheiten, die Verwendung von anerkannten Lehrmethoden und die häufige Wiederholung sind unverzichtbar." In the online setting this meant a highly structured, standardized lesson sequence, standardized visual presentations, strict division into small groups, and constant repetition of content alongside Peyton-based practical execution.
requirements: Highly structured, standardized lesson flow to overcome the barrier of the virtual space
Strict small-group division to create an effective learning atmosphere
Constant repetition of teaching content
constraints: The course required high personnel resources: small groups of at most 4 students were supervised by student tutors under constant supervision of a DEGUM-III status holder
target_learners: medical students
target_learning_goals: practical (psychomotor) clinical skills such as sonography
examples: In the online course, two new regions were learned each study day "sowie die bereits erlernten wiederholt" (and the already learned ones repeated)

article_title: Making Effective Educational Videos for Clinical Teaching.
citation: Krumm Ilana Roberts MD, Miles Matthew C. MD, MEd, FCCP, Clay Alison MD, Carlos II W. Graham MD, Adamson Rosemary MBBS. (2021). Making Effective Educational Videos for Clinical Teaching. Chest. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chest.2021.09.015
title: A stepwise eight-step approach to creating educational videos for clinical teaching
description: The article summarizes "our approach to creating educational videos" (Fig 1) as a stepwise sequence: choose a durable topic, identify specific learning objectives and a target length, pick software, plan the video (storyboarding, privacy review, equipment testing), consider adding activities, produce (images, webcam use), watch the final product with a reviewer, and make it available to learners. Objectives are limited to "no more than five per video" to reduce cognitive load, and topics unlikely to become obsolete are preferred.
requirements: A group of colleagues (and potentially learners) to help in development and peer review
Checking whether a suitable high-quality video already exists before investing time
constraints: Topics likely to change rapidly, such as developing guidelines or recent research findings, may not be worth the time investment
target_learners: busy clinical educators creating videos for residents, fellows, and students
target_learning_goals: efficient production of durable, high-yield educational video content
examples: The lung slide video was chosen because lung slide appearance is unlikely to become obsolete, with three narrow objectives and a 2-min duration

article_title: Simulation-based team training improves door-to-needle time for intravenous thrombolysis.
citation: Svobodová Veronika, Maršálková Hana, Volevach Ekaterina, Mikulík Robert. (2023). Simulation-based team training improves door-to-needle time for intravenous thrombolysis. BMJ Open Quality 12(1):e002107. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjoq-2022-002107
title: Half-day simulation course pattern: briefing–simulation–debriefing–conclusion with real-case scenarios, trainee-played patient, observer checklists and four learning-objective elements
description: The programme's reusable course pattern runs scenarios "in a usual format (briefing–simulation–debriefing–conclusion)" with at least two simulation rounds per course. Scenarios reproduce the full clinical workflow from EMS prenotification through CT interpretation to thrombolysis, use real cases adapted for education, assign trainees to roles including the patient to build communication insight, and use four auditorium observers with checklists feeding a three-phase debriefing. Learning objectives cover logistics/workflow, decision-making, teamwork (crew resource management principles) and patient communication.
requirements: A standardly equipped simulation centre (hospital bed, patient monitor, artificial CT scanner, audio-visual equipment, control room)
A neurologist experienced in thrombolytic treatment leading sessions with at least a simulation technician and a methodologist/lecturer
Attendance by all healthcare professionals in the logistics pathway, with department heads encouraged to attend
constraints: Scenarios were adapted for educational purposes rather than being exact clinical reproductions
The patient role is played by a trainee rather than a trained actor
target_learners: Stroke-centre physicians, nurses, paramedics and radiologists involved in acute stroke logistics
target_learning_goals: Shortening door-to-needle time
Teamwork and closed-loop communication
Thrombolysis decision-making
Communication with patients
examples: Ten courses between 2016 and 2017 trained 10 stroke teams (62 physicians and 32 nurses) from 9 of 45 Czech stroke centres, all without previous simulation experience

article_title: Team-based learning versus interactive lecture in achieving learning outcomes and improving clinical reasoning skills: a randomized crossover study.
citation: Imran M, Halawa TF, Baig M, Almanjoumi AM, Badri MM, Alghamdi WA. (2022). Team-based learning versus interactive lecture in achieving learning outcomes and improving clinical reasoning skills: a randomized crossover study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03411-w
title: Structured TBL session format: advance preparation, iRAT, tRAT, instructor clarification, and team application
description: The TBL session implemented in this study was an 85-minute in-class sequence conducted per the literature: teams of five to six members formed by the instructor, an individual readiness assurance test of ten single-best-answer MCQs (15 minutes), the same test as a team readiness assurance test (15 minutes), instructor clarification review (15 minutes), then a 40-minute team application. In team application, "Different scenarios, with all relevant details, were provided to all teams" under rules requiring identical scenarios, practice-relevant problems, specific choices, and simultaneous answer display with defense. Students most often named team application as TBL's most interesting element.
requirements: Preparation time was assured in the study guide before the in-class session
One instructor can conduct TBL even for a class of more than a hundred students
constraints: In this study TBL's in-class duration (85 min) exceeded IL's (60 min), with IL compensated by two supervised library self-study hours
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students working in teams of five to six
target_learning_goals: Readiness on assigned topics
Applying knowledge to clinical scenarios
Teamwork and immediate error correction via iRAT followed by tRAT
examples: The authors implemented this format in endocrinology and emergency modules with scenarios relevant to clinical practice
A student remarked that "iRAT followed by tRAT helps to correct our mistakes immediately"
key_sources: Imran M, Halawa TF, Baig M, Almanjoumi AM, Badri MM, Alghamdi WA. (2022). Team-based learning versus interactive lecture in achieving learning outcomes and improving clinical reasoning skills: a randomized crossover study. article_title: Comparing computer-assisted learning activities for learning clinical neuroscience: a randomized control trial.
citation: Rajan Kiran, Pandit Anand S. (2022). Comparing computer-assisted learning activities for learning clinical neuroscience: a randomized control trial. BMC Medical Education 22:522. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03578-2
title: Interactive case-based neuroscience eModule built in Storyline 360

It used "a case-based approach with clinically relevant neuroimaging" and Storyline 360 software enabled "drag-and-drop, multiple-choice and click-and-point questions". It cost $649 per academic user per annum via an Articulate 360 subscription.
requirements: Development required multidisciplinary input including a senior neurology professor, an educational specialist and supervision by an academic neurosurgical fellow
constraints: Development, delivery and maintenance carry opportunity costs; the module was designed to take approximately 20 to 30 min to complete

Know the anatomy of the cerebral arterial system
Understand the relationship between the arterial system and clinical presentation
Understand core clinical management for stroke

article_title: Study smart - impact of a learning strategy training on students' study behavior and academic performance.
citation: Biwer Felicitas, de Bruin Anique, Persky Adam. (2022). Study smart – impact of a learning strategy training on students’ study behavior and academic performance. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9397154/
title: Study Smart program: three-session learning strategy training for all first-year students
description: The Study Smart program is a mandatory learning strategy training for all first-year pharmacy students consisting of three 90-minute online sessions — "awareness, practice, and reflection" — held during the first four weeks of a bridging course. The awareness session challenges beliefs about strategy effectiveness using evidence from Dunlosky et al. (2013) and demonstrations of the testing effect; the practice session has students apply strategies (self-explanation, retrieval practice, visualization) to real course material and write implementation intentions; the reflection session targets study motivation and obstacles via questionnaires and the critical incident method.
requirements: A facilitator-led structure with pre-session exercises, access to students' actual course materials for guided strategy practice, and a culminating exam to schedule study for
constraints: Evaluated in a single first-year pharmacy course at one university; delivered online due to COVID-19; sessions were mandatory within a competence-based curriculum
target_learners: first-year professional pharmacy (health sciences) students, average age 23
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive knowledge about effective learning strategies
self-regulated use of effective strategies for long-term retention and application
examples: Students kept a photolog of their study behavior between sessions and discussed common obstacles; after 15 minutes they switched groups and applied another strategy to other course material
key_sources: Biwer Felicitas, de Bruin Anique, Persky Adam. (2022). Study smart – impact of a learning strategy training on students’ study behavior and academic performance. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9397154/

article_title: Study smart - impact of a learning strategy training on students' study behavior and academic performance.
citation: Biwer Felicitas, de Bruin Anique, Persky Adam. (2022). Study smart – impact of a learning strategy training on students’ study behavior and academic performance. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9397154/
title: Provide all first-year students a learning strategy training with a remediation track for lower performers to support effective study and equal chances
description: The article argues that formal learning strategy instruction should be embedded for all first-year students, combined with continuous additional support for lower-performing students. It reports that such a program "can thus support students to study more effectively and enhance equal chances for all students at university", because students not prepared to study self-regulated are likely to struggle and build shallow knowledge as admission numbers rise.
requirements: Training components addressing declarative and conditional knowledge, beliefs, motivation, and guided practice, plus a remediation track for lower performers with weekly reinforcement in context of actual course work
constraints: In assessment cultures rewarding rote memorization, cramming may suffice and effortful strategies may be less appealing; generalization to other organizational and assessment structures is an open question
target_learners: first-year university (professional/health sciences) students, especially lower achievers
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and application of knowledge
self-regulated strategy use and study habits
examples: The 2020 cohort received the three-session Study Smart program as a mandatory part of the PHCY 500 course, and the bottom 20% of midterm 1 additionally completed the remediation pathway

article_title: Using virtual reality in lumbar puncture training improves students learning experience.

residents and attendings

citation: Nair Akshay Gopinathan et al. (2021). Effectiveness of simulation-based training for manual small incision cataract surgery among novice surgeons: a randomized controlled trial. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-90410-4
title: Structured simulation-based surgical curriculum combining self-study, classroom instruction, dry-lab, simulator practice and live surgery
description: The experimental curriculum is a structured, reproducible training program for scleral tunnel construction that sequences self-study using an eBook, instructor-led classroom instruction, hands-on dry-lab activities, training with the HelpMeSee Eye Surgery Simulator, and a live surgery phase. It spanned 6 days (35 h total), of which 80% of the time was dedicated to hands-on training on the simulator. During live surgery, a HelpMeSee surgeon was physically present in the operating room solely as an observer for the first 20 procedures.
requirements: Trainees allowed time off from clinical responsibilities to attend the simulation-based training phase
Instructor assessment of competence in individual tasks before progression
constraints: The article states the curriculum was evaluated in three highly specialized tertiary eye care centres, so the observed effect is not necessarily applicable to trainees across all training institutions
target_learners: novice ophthalmology residents within 3 months of matriculation
target_learning_goals: safe and efficient scleral tunnel construction in MSICS
examples: The trial deployed this curriculum with consistency at multiple academic institutions in India, which the authors describe as proof of feasibility

article_title: Immersive virtual reality enables technical skill acquisition for scrub nurses in complex revision total knee arthroplasty.
citation: Edwards Thomas C., Patel Arjun, Szyszka Bartosz, Coombs Alexander W., Liddle Alexander D., Kucheria Rakesh, Cobb Justin P., Logishetty Kartik. (2021). Immersive virtual reality enables technical skill acquisition for scrub nurses in complex revision total knee arthroplasty. Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00402-021-04050-4
title: Train for infrequently performed, equipment-heavy operations before they occur, because unstructured ad hoc learning compromises safety and efficiency
description: Because scrub nurses typically learn complex procedures ad hoc — from industry representatives or double-scrubbing — they report high anxiety, low confidence and concern that patient safety is compromised. The article argues that "targeted training for these operations could improve procedural knowledge and operative efficiency, thus protecting patient safety", since prolonged operative time is correlated with increased complication risk. Pre-procedural simulation training such as the iVR curriculum addresses this gap by building proficiency before the operation rather than during it.
requirements: Training must target operations with multiple pieces of equipment or steps that are performed infrequently
Assessment of baseline competence to measure skill acquisition
constraints: The evidence base presented is a single-arm study of one operation with no real-theatre or patient-outcome validation
target_learners: Scrub nurses and perioperative teams facing staff shortages and frequent specialty rotation
target_learning_goals: Procedural knowledge and operative efficiency for complex operations
Reduction of intraoperative errors and delays
examples: The rTKA inventory exceeds 500 separate pieces of equipment and revisions have almost double the complication rate of primary TKA, motivating the training intervention

article_title: Aptitude and attitude: predictors of performance during and after basic laparoscopic skills training.
citation: Beattie Kirsty L., Hill Andrew, Horswill Mark S., Grove Philip M., Stevenson Andrew R. L. (2022). Aptitude and attitude: predictors of performance during and after basic laparoscopic skills training. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-021-08668-8
title: Predictors of laparoscopic performance change with task demands and trainee development, so multi-variable prediction models should match the training stage and task
description: The article's central interpretive principle is that no single ability predicts laparoscopic performance across all stages and tasks. It reports that "the predictors may change with both task demands and the development of the trainee": psychological variables dominated early training, bimanual dexterity predicted training while assembly dexterity predicted later testing, and visual-spatial ability mattered only for the spatially complex novel task. Prediction and selection tools should therefore combine physical, cognitive, visual, and psychological variables suited to the criterion of interest.
requirements: Criterion-specific regression or assessment covering multiple ability and psychological domains, as the study conducted per-criterion analyses
constraints: Findings come from a single sample of 34 novices in simulation-based training; the authors note future studies may benefit from larger sample sizes
target_learners: medical students and surgical trainees (laparoscopic novices)
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic technical skill acquisition and prediction of surgical potential
examples: The study ran separate stepwise regressions for training repetitions, training score, test score, NIS score, and follow-up score, yielding different final models for each criterion

article_title: What really impacts the use of active learning in undergraduate STEM education? Results from a national survey of chemistry, mathematics, and physics instructors.
citation: Apkarian, N., Henderson, C., Stains, M., Raker, J., Johnson, E., & Dancy, M. (2021). What really impacts the use of active learning in undergraduate STEM education? Results from a national survey of chemistry, mathematics, and physics instructors. PLoS ONE 16(2): e0247544. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0247544
title: Institutions seeking more active learning should combine structural changes (class size, active learning classrooms, reduced SET emphasis) with professional development
description: Based on survey evidence that contextual factors correlate with lecture time, the article recommends that institutions "continue to make targeted structural changes such as maintaining and seeking smaller class sizes, building and supporting active learning classrooms, and emphasizing methods beyond SET scores for the evaluation of teaching effectiveness." It further affirms professional development, since instructors "are more likely to implement active learning if they do not have to figure out everything on their own." The recommendation rests on correlational survey data combined with prior research.
requirements: Requires institutional decision-makers able to enact policy and structural changes such as classroom construction and evaluation practices
Requires professional development activities focused on local needs and contexts
constraints: The article states its data are correlational and do not allow causal claims, so recommendations are based on the correlations found as well as other research
target_learners: Undergraduate students in introductory STEM (general chemistry, single-variable calculus, introductory quantitative physics) courses
target_learning_goals: Increased use of active learning instructional strategies in introductory undergraduate STEM courses
examples: Instructors selecting active learning strategies compatible with a large class or a particular classroom setup, supported by local professional development
key_sources: Apkarian, N., Henderson, C., Stains, M., Raker, J., Johnson, E., & Dancy, M. (2021). What really impacts the use of active learning in undergraduate STEM education? article_title: Massive Open Online Courses-based blended versus face-to-face classroom teaching methods for fundamental nursing course.
citation: Cao W, Hu L, Li X, Li X, Chen C, Zhang Q, Cao S. (2021). Massive Open Online Courses-based blended versus face-to-face classroom teaching methods for fundamental nursing course. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000024829
title: Blend MOOC self-study with structured in-class application rather than replacing face-to-face teaching wholesale
description: The article argues MOOCs should not fully replace classroom teaching but be combined with it: blended learning is "defined as the combination of traditional face-to-face learning techniques, and a number of pedagogic approaches supported by information and communication technology." Its trial implemented this by having students self-study recorded lectures before class and reserving class time for case application, scenario demonstration, group reports, and discussion of key and difficult points, with post-class group homework on the platform.
requirements: Highly structured blended teaching with a focus on higher quality methods and utilizing tutorials
Pre-class video study with a survey form feeding into classroom design
In-class flipped activities targeting higher levels of thinking skills such as synthesis or evaluation
constraints: Only if blended teaching was highly structured would it be beneficial over purely traditional learning, per the authors' discussion
Some students accustomed to traditional methods may resist spending more time in self-directed learning
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students
Higher education students in health professions
target_learning_goals: Theoretical knowledge and operational nursing skills
Critical thinking dispositions
Student satisfaction with teaching
examples: The trial's blended group watched recorded lectures before class, then attended in-class group discussions, case application, and demonstrations, and completed group homework and a book report after class
key_sources: Cao W, Hu L, Li X, Li X, Chen C, Zhang Q, Cao S. (2021). Massive Open Online Courses-based blended versus face-to-face classroom teaching methods for fundamental nursing course. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000024829

article_title: Study on the effect of education for insulin injection in diabetic patients with new simulation tools.
citation: Liang K, Xie Q, Nie J, Deng J. (2021). Study on the effect of education for insulin injection in diabetic patients with new simulation tools. Medicine. 2021;100:14(e25424). https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000025424
title: Standard training procedure: staged simulation-based practice with review before and after discharge
description: A three-stage in-hospital training sequence: a simple teaching stage where a specialist nurse dictates and demonstrates the technique, a detailed teaching stage where patients practice with the simulation device while asking questions and repeating until proficient, and a review stage on the training day, next day, and third day with video, booklets, and simulated skin, followed by post-discharge review of videos and text guidelines. It differs from traditional training only in the added simulation-tool practice opportunities.
requirements: Specialized nurses proficient in insulin injection; simulation tool, operating video, and manual booklets; training one-on-one or in groups of 3 guided by the supervising nurse.
constraints: Evaluated in a single-site study with patients who were first-time insulin pen users and without serious comorbidities or cognitive impairment.
target_learners: Hospitalized diabetic patients beginning insulin therapy
target_learning_goals: Standardized insulin injection technique and related knowledge
examples: Intervention group patients practiced with the wearable simulation tool through the detailed teaching and review stages, then reviewed videos and guidelines at home after discharge.

article_title: Multicultural personality and effectiveness in an intercultural training simulation: The role of stress and pro-active communication.
citation: Hofhuis, J., Schilderman, M. F., & Verdooren, A. (2020). Multicultural personality and effectiveness in an intercultural training simulation: The role of stress and pro‐active communication. International Journal of Psychology, 55(5), 812–821. https://doi.org/10.1002/ijop.12647
title: Division of MPQ traits into stress-related and social-perceptual subsets with distinct mediators
description: Drawing on Van der Zee and Van Oudenhoven (2013), the article endorses a two-subset organisation of the MPQ: "The stress-related traits, Emotional Stability and Flexibility, are said to reduce the sense of threat" in intercultural encounters, while the social-perceptual traits (Cultural Empathy, Openmindedness, Social Initiative) increase the likelihood interactions are seen as challenge rather than threat. The study's mediation results provide "additional evidence for the distinction between stress‐related and social‐perceptual traits": emotional stability works via stress reduction, social initiative via communication.
requirements: Mediator measurement (stress and pro-active communication) to distinguish the pathways
constraints: In this simulation, flexibility showed no effects, and the mediators were measured only once, after round 4
target_learners: adults in intercultural training
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms of intercultural competence
examples: Emotional stability enhanced outcomes via reduced perceived stress; social initiative enhanced outcomes via pro-active non-verbal communication

Public Health 17(11):3889. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17113889
title: Start procedural breakdowns from validated checklists to reduce resource demands and expert bias
description: The article recommends beginning a procedure breakdown from one or more validated evaluation checklists, because these instruments have "proven useful in abstracting those activities considered critical when evaluating the achievement of a competence". This avoids the hours of interviews, trained personnel, and specialty-dependent bias of classical cognitive task analysis. Checklists alone cannot express decision points or alternative paths, so they serve only as the basis for a fuller BPMN model.
requirements: Access to checklists psychometrically validated and of proven impact on clinical outcomes for the target procedure
constraints: Checklists are an abstraction that omits critical decision points and alternative paths, so they are insufficient on their own
target_learners: medical residents in procedural training
target_learning_goals: efficient generation of procedural curricula
standardized procedure teaching
examples: The CVC model was built from the Barsuk et al. dialysis catheter checklist, extended with the Nguyen et al. ultrasound checklist and reviews by McKinley et al. and Ma et al.

article_title: Outperforming yet undervalued: Undergraduate women in STEM.
citation: Bloodhart, B., Balgopal, M. M., Casper, A. M. A., Sample McMeeking, L. B., & Fischer, E. V. (2020). Outperforming yet undervalued: Undergraduate women in STEM. PLoS ONE 15(6): e0234685. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0234685
title: Stereotype-consistent information processing account of persistent gender bias despite counter-stereotypic performance
description: The article explains its central finding through social-psychological accounts of stereotype information processing: "information that is inconsistent with one's stereotype or worldview is often discounted, forgotten," or processed as a subtype that leaves the overarching stereotype intact. Women's strong academic performance can additionally be explained away in system-justifying ways, such as attributing it to hard work rather than innate ability, preserving the perception that men possess greater natural STEM talent. Counter-stereotypic examples can, given enough time and exposure, change stereotypes, which is why representation and public recognition of women's success matter.
requirements: Stereotypes already formed among peers prior to or during coursework
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of prior social science research, not a mechanism tested in this study
Intersectional effects for women of color could not be statistically examined due to insufficient sample power
target_learners: Undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: Understanding why peer gender bias persists despite women's superior academic performance
examples: Applied to explain why classmates continued to nominate men as best students even in courses where women both outnumbered and outperformed them.
key_sources: Bloodhart, B., Balgopal, M. M., Casper, A. M. A., Sample McMeeking, L. B., & Fischer, E. V. (2020). Outperforming yet undervalued: Undergraduate women in STEM. PLoS ONE 15(6): e0234685. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0234685

article_title: Formative assessment of practical skills with peer-assessors: quality features of an OSCE in general medicine at the Heidelberg Medical Faculty.
citation: Möltner Andreas, Lehmann Mirijam, Wachter Cornelia, Kurczyk Sonia, Schwill Simon, Loukanova Svetla. (2020). Formative assessment of practical skills with peer-assessors: quality features of an OSCE in general medicine at the Heidelberg Medical Faculty. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(4), Doc42. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001335.shtml
title: Use trained senior students as examiners in formative OSCEs to overcome faculty examiner shortages
description: The article recommends that medical faculties use students in higher semesters as examiners for formative practical examinations, because implementation of such structured formative assessments "often fails at the faculties due to the availability of examiners from the teaching staff". With precisely defined tutor training courses and checklists, student examiners produced assessments matching those of medical expert supervisors, allowing a large cohort to be assessed at low cost.
requirements: Precisely defined student tutor training courses and checklists
Basic didactic training for the student examiners
Supervisory second assessments for quality assurance
constraints: Evidence comes from a single formative OSCE at one faculty; the article states it is not possible to generalize to other institutions or general conditions
target_learners: Pre-clinical medical students in large cohorts
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment of practical clinical and communication skills
examples: In the 2018 OSCE, 32 student examiners assessed 300 fourth-semester students across four stations, with five supervisors performing 135 random second evaluations

citation: Rouleau G, Pelletier J, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Martel-Laferrière V, Lévesque R, SimforHealth, Fontaine G. (2020). Codeveloping a Virtual Patient Simulation to Foster Nurses’ Relational Skills Consistent With Motivational Interviewing: A Situation of Antiretroviral Therapy Nonadherence. title: Target stable, transversal clinical behaviors such as relational skills to maximize a simulation's adaptability and sustainability
description: The authors argue that focusing on relational skills, which are "used by all nurses, from novice to expert, and by all other health care professionals", ensures the simulation's "adaptability, sustainability, and efficiency". Because behavioral change counseling techniques such as open-ended questions and summarizing are timeless, the simulation does not need the regular updates a pharmacology-focused simulation would require after scientific breakthroughs.

other health care practitioners

article_title: Signatures of medical student applicants and academic success.
citation: Baron Tal, Grossman Robert I., Abramson Steven B., Pusic Martin V., Rivera Rafael, Triola Marc M., Yanai Itai. (2020). Signatures of medical student applicants and academic success. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0227108
title: The student-signature approach to admissions and personalized education
description: The article proposes replacing a 'one-size-fits-all' admissions reading of applicants with a data-driven account of "distinct clusters of students" delineated by pattern of achievement. It works by feature-engineering applicant records, K-means clustering to define signatures, and logistic regression using the signature to predict medical school success. The authors present it as an example of how "learning analytics may allow for the personalized education of health professions" and for "the implementation of personalized education for more successful student training".
requirements: Requires application records with sufficient quantitative features and engineered trajectory features
Requires longitudinal outcome data on subsequent academic performance to validate signatures
constraints: Data come from a single highly-selective institution and require replication at others
The dataset included only accepted and matriculated students, not the full applicant pool
Only quantitative application aspects were analyzed
target_learners: medical school applicants and matriculants
target_learning_goals: predicting and supporting academic success in medical school
examples: The article names the four signatures statics, solids, risers, and improvers and shows risers favored when a trajectory of improvement outweighs a small GPA difference

citation: Stocco AU, Miranda CH. (2020). Clinical Competence in ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction Management by Recently Graduated Physicians Applying for a Medical Residency Program. Arquivos Brasileiros de Cardiologia. https://doi.org/10.36660/abc.20180309
title: Undergraduate medical curricula should emphasize STEMI temporality, assistance flows and transfer persistence within the health network
description: The article concludes that "STEMI approach needs to be improved during medical undergraduate courses, highlighting practical aspects such as temporality for starting treatment and the assistance flows of these patients" within the Brazilian Unified Health System. Because most students remembered antiplatelet agents but a significant proportion did not reinforce immediate transfer, the authors argue education must integrate pharmacological treatment with the urgency network so patients reach reperfusion-capable centers even without available beds.
requirements: Teaching of the hierarchical network structure of the SUS and regional assistance flows
Discussion of the Federal Medicine Council "zero vacancy" resolution on urgencies and emergencies
constraints: The authors note telemedicine support for ECG interpretation will be useless if physicians lack knowledge of how to speed up transfer according to the established assistance flow
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: time-dependent STEMI treatment
transfer persistence and network navigation
patient communication
examples: Only 25% of applicants insisted on transfer when no beds were available, which the authors link to the need to teach the zero-vacancy concept

article_title: Knowledge and confidence in managing obstructive sleep apnea patients in Canadian otolaryngology - head and neck surgery residents: a cross sectional survey.
citation: Ansari Saad, Hu Amanda. (2020). Knowledge and confidence in managing obstructive sleep apnea patients in Canadian otolaryngology - head and neck surgery residents: a cross sectional survey. Journal of Otolaryngology - Head & Neck Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40463-020-00417-6
title: Residency programs should strengthen sleep surgery training opportunities, including access to subspecialty-trained sleep surgeons, to build resident confidence in managing OSA
description: The article argues that high knowledge paired with low management confidence indicates "limited or missed opportunities in residency programs to manage OSA patients who are surgical candidates". It cites a US program-director survey finding that only 41.3% of programs have faculty dedicating over 50% of their time to sleep surgery, and that about 70% of respondents agreed a subspecialty-trained sleep surgeon on faculty would benefit residents. The principle is that programs should ensure residents gain hands-on OSA management and sleep surgery experience to meet competency expectations.
requirements: Programs must provide opportunities for residents to manage OSA patients who are surgical candidates, ideally with subspecialty-trained sleep surgery faculty available.
constraints: The article states further research is needed to ascertain the reasons for the lack of confidence, and that its data do not audit the sleep medicine curriculum or count procedures performed.
target_learners: Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery residents (PGY1–5)
target_learning_goals: Managing patients with obstructive sleep apnea and sleep-disordered breathing, including CPAP therapy and OSA-related surgeries
examples: The survey identified perceived strengths and weaknesses in OSA training among Canadian otolaryngology residents, with lowest confidence in OSA-specific procedures such as tongue base suspension (1.5%).

article_title: Insights into student assessment outcomes in rural clinical campuses.
citation: Shulruf Boaz, Velan Gary, Forster Lesley, O'Sullivan Anthony, Harris Peter, Taylor Silas. (2019). Insights into student assessment outcomes in rural clinical campuses. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1828-z
title: Standardised Assessment Item Bank questions combined with identical grading criteria and Examiner Guidelines minimise variation between examination sites
description: The article concludes that rural and metropolitan examination outcomes can be kept comparable through standardised assessment logistics: 'the selection and use of questions from a standardised Assessment Item Bank, combined with the use of identical grading criteria and Examiner Guidelines can minimise variation between examination sites'. In the studied program, all sites sat identical questions at the same date and time, with grading performed on iPads under identical criteria.
requirements: "For the OSCE and management viva examinations, questions are selected from an Assessment Item Bank so that all questions are the same at all rural and metropolitan sites for examinations held at the same date and time"
"Examination supervisor and examiners guidelines are prepared and distributed to all examination sites in advance"
constraints: Evidence comes from one cohort in one medical program; "extracting information about the reliability or any other psychometric properties of the assessments was outside the scope of this study"
target_learners: undergraduate medical students at rural and metropolitan clinical campuses
target_learning_goals: equitable assessment outcomes across examination sites
clinical skills and knowledge assessment performance
examples: The rural OSCE and management viva examinations were always held at the same date and time as metropolitan sites, and "the grading is performed on iPads and the grading criteria are identical for all metropolitan and rural sites"

Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) in non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: evaluation of an educational programme. description: The article recommends that implementation of a new prehospital procedure such as REBOA be preceded by a structured, stepwise training programme and objective assessment of skills, because such procedures "requires special training before implemented in clinical practice". citation: Moll-Khosrawi P, Kamphausen A, Hampe W, Schulte-Uentrop L, Zimmermann S, Kubitz JC. (2019). Anaesthesiology students’ Non-Technical skills: development and evaluation of a behavioural marker system for students (AS-NTS). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1609-8

description: The article develops AS-NTS through four steps combining qualitative and quantitative methods: an expert-group literature search producing an NTS list, focus groups and half-structured interviews building a hierarchical structure, field observations testing whether skills were observable, and implementation and validation across 98 simulation scenarios. Skills not observable in enough field observations were excluded following the guideline that "items to be excluded, if they are not observable in at least 50% of field observations".

constraints: Skills highly important but not fully developed in undergraduates had to be redefined or excluded, since existing taxonomies target specialist-level postgraduate training

article_title: Stress response in the daily lives of simulation repeaters. A randomized controlled trial assessing stress evolution over one year of repetitive immersive simulations.
citation: Ghazali Daniel Aiham, Breque Cyril, Sosner Philippe, Lesbordes Mathieu, Chavagnat Jean-Jacques, Ragot Stéphanie, Oriot Denis. (2019). Stress response in the daily lives of simulation repeaters. A randomized controlled trial assessing stress evolution over one year of repetitive immersive simulations. title: Use standardized conditions, good-judgment debriefing, and consistent manikin-death policy across repeated simulations to limit psychological risk
description: The article links the absence of PTSD among 48 participants to study design choices: "The use of standardized debriefing with 'good-judgment' [26] may have contributed to the absence of PTSD, as suggested by a decrease in HR and LF/HF ratio during all the debriefings." The authors also note "non-occurrence of death of the simulated patient in our experiments may have helped to limit risk of PTSD," while acknowledging controversy over whether manikins should die. They recommend all repeated simulations be carried out under similar conditions to avoid bias.

constraints: The article notes emotional reactions to simulated death can have serious psychological impact, particularly when death results from learners' actions, and experts disagree on announcing possible death beforehand

target_learning_goals: managing life-threatening events without lasting psychological harm
examples: All 72 sessions used identical preprogrammed infant-shock scenarios, the manikin deteriorated but did not die, and each session included 15 min briefing, 25–30 min simulation, and 30–45 min good-judgment debriefing
