article_title: The Mediating Role of Self-Concept between Sports-Related Physical Activity and Mathematical Achievement in Fourth Graders.
citation: Dapp Laura C., Roebers Claudia M. (2019). The Mediating Role of Self-Concept between Sports-Related Physical Activity and Mathematical Achievement in Fourth Graders. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16152658
title: Children benefit most from physical activity that is structured, lasts at least two hours per week, and empowers self-concept
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that children gain the most academic benefit when their physical activity is organized and adult-led, sustained for a minimum weekly duration, and experienced in a way that builds confidence. As the authors state, "the results indicate that children benefit most from PA if (a) it is structured, (b) it lasts for at least two hours per week, and (c) it has empowering effects on children's self-concept." This makes structured leisure-time sports a lever for both self-concept and academic success.
requirements: Structured (sports-club) settings with adult guidance
at least two hours per week of participation
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional and correlational; causal direction was not established
PA was assessed by self-report
target_learners: primary school children
target_learning_goals: mathematical achievement
academic self-concept
examples: In the study, children spending two or more weekly hours in sports clubs scored significantly higher on the HRT math test than low-duration club members, while low-duration members did not differ from non-participants
key_sources: Dapp Laura C., Roebers Claudia M. (2019). The Mediating Role of Self-Concept between Sports-Related Physical Activity and Mathematical Achievement in Fourth Graders. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16152658

article_title: Small changes, big gains: A curriculum-wide study of teaching practices and student learning in undergraduate biology.
citation: Weir Laura K., Barker Megan K., McDonnell Lisa M., Schimpf Natalie G., Rodela Tamara M., Schulte Patricia M. (2019). Small changes, big gains: A curriculum-wide study of teaching practices and student learning in undergraduate biology. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0220900
title: Use structured in-class worksheets as a low-barrier active-learning tool to increase student-centered class time
description: The article recommends that educators use structured worksheets during class because they are simple, low-technology, and promote collaboration and problem solving. As the authors state, "we would suggest that educators consider the use of structured worksheets as a way to increase student-centered use of class-time." Worksheets encourage students to articulate, evaluate, and reflect on written answers and inform instructors about student struggles.
requirements: Worksheets can be built from previous test or problem-set questions and need not be handed in for grading or require special technology.
constraints: The study observed varied worksheet implementations and could not distinguish implementation quality; effectiveness evidence is observational, not experimental.
target_learners: undergraduate biology students in large-enrollment lecture courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of core biology content
problem solving and collaboration skills
examples: In the observed courses, many worksheets were guided activities embedded within lectures or case-study approaches requiring students to examine multiple aspects of a problem.
key_sources: Weir Laura K., Barker Megan K., McDonnell Lisa M., Schimpf Natalie G., Rodela Tamara M., Schulte Patricia M. (2019). Small changes, big gains: A curriculum-wide study of teaching practices and student learning in undergraduate biology. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0220900

article_title: The podiatric surgery theatre environment in the UK; is it conducive to learning? A quantitative study using the surgical theatre educational environment measure (STEEM).
citation: Austen Thomas, Otter Simon. (2019). The podiatric surgery theatre environment in the UK; is it conducive to learning? A quantitative study using the surgical theatre educational environment measure (STEEM). Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-018-0312-z
title: Surgical Theatre Educational Environment Measure (STEEM), 40-item questionnaire
description: The STEEM is a 40-item questionnaire developed by Cassar at the University of Aberdeen, evolved from PHEEM through a literature review and interviews with surgical trainers and trainees, and validated with Scottish basic surgical trainees. It measures the surgical operating theatre learning environment across four subscales — Teaching and training, Learning Opportunities, Atmosphere, and Supervision/workload/support — each item on a 0–4 Likert scale with reverse coding of 19 negative items, giving a maximum of 160. The article applies it online to podiatric surgery trainees for the first time.
requirements: Reverse coding of negative questions so higher scores indicate more positive perception; the 0–4 scale is used to avoid the overestimation a 1–5 score may introduce
constraints: First applied to the podiatric surgery theatre in this study; some items (emergency procedures) may not suit podiatric surgery's elective day-case caseload and would need re-validation if removed
target_learners: Surgical and podiatric surgical trainees in theatre-based training
target_learning_goals: Assessment of the educational environment of the operating theatre
examples: The article reports each statement's median and interquartile range for the 16 respondents, identifying Q17 opportunity to assist and the discrimination items as highest rated and Q20–22 emergency items as lowest
key_sources: Austen Thomas, Otter Simon. (2019). The podiatric surgery theatre environment in the UK; is it conducive to learning? A quantitative study using the surgical theatre educational environment measure (STEEM). Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-018-0312-z

article_title: Critical Appraisal Worksheets for Integration Into an Existing Small-Group Problem-Based Learning Curriculum.
citation: O'Neil Jessica, Croniger Colleen. (2018). Critical Appraisal Worksheets for Integration Into an Existing Small-Group Problem-Based Learning Curriculum. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10682
title: Use structured worksheets with detailed answer keys so faculty need little training and classroom time stays small
description: The article recommends structured critical appraisal worksheets as a low-resource integration: "CAWs require a relatively small amount of dedicated classroom time as compared to other methods for teaching EBM, such as lectures and journal club presentations," and the worksheets were designed so students could work through them with relatively little faculty instruction. Answer sheets were designed to be straightforward but sufficiently detailed so faculty would not need extensive training to facilitate discussion.
requirements: Answer keys must be detailed enough that faculty can facilitate discussion without extensive training, and worksheets must be user friendly for independent student completion.
constraints: The authors believe the worksheets are most valuable in small-group settings where thoughtful student discussion can take place; in lecture-based curricula a portion of lecture time would be needed to review answers.
target_learners: preclinical medical students
learners in team-based or small-group settings
target_learning_goals: critical appraisal skills
evidence-based medicine
examples: The article suggests CAWs could be assigned before a TBL session with answers debated within and among student groups, or reviewed during lecture with clicker questions for closed-ended items.
key_sources: O'Neil Jessica, Croniger Colleen. (2018). Critical Appraisal Worksheets for Integration Into an Existing Small-Group Problem-Based Learning Curriculum. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10682

article_title: Is the clinician an independent variable in embryo transfer outcomes under standardized direct and indirect supervision? A 5-year observational cohort study.
citation: Mittal Monica, Supramaniam Prasanna Raj, Lim Lee Nai, Hamoda Haitham, Savvas Mike, Narvekar Nitish. (2019). Is the clinician an independent variable in embryo transfer outcomes under standardized direct and indirect supervision? A 5-year observational cohort study. GMS Journal for Medical Education. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001215.shtml
title: Staged direct-to-indirect supervision competency framework for embryo transfer training
description: A unit-level competency framework governing when trainees may progress from observing to independently performing embryo transfers. It specifies "a minimum of 20 ETs to be observed prior to being able to perform them under direct supervision", then a further 20 under direct supervision before the trainee is deemed competent for indirect supervision, and competency is reassessed after a further minimum of 20 ETs before independent performance. The framework operated within a unit culture with "a strong emphasis on adequate direct and indirect supervision".
requirements: Trainees must complete the specified minimum observed and supervised procedure counts before progressing to each stage
Competency reassessment before independent practice
constraints: Findings reflect the training culture of a single fertility unit; difficult or anticipated-difficult transfers were more likely carried out by an experienced clinician
target_learners: Postgraduate trainee fellows naive to embryo transfer in a fertility unit
target_learning_goals: Acquiring clinical competence in embryo transfer under graded supervision
examples: All trainees were trained by one or more experienced consultants in the same unit before performing ETs independently; the number 50 was based on the British Fertility Society Embryo Transfer Training Module minimum
key_sources: Mittal Monica, Supramaniam Prasanna Raj, Lim Lee Nai, Hamoda Haitham, Savvas Mike, Narvekar Nitish. (2019). Is the clinician an independent variable in embryo transfer outcomes under standardized direct and indirect supervision? A 5-year observational cohort study. GMS Journal for Medical Education. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001215.shtml

article_title: Effect of wet-laboratory training on resident performed manual small-incision cataract surgery.
citation: Ramani Soumya; Pradeep Thanuja Gopal; Sundaresh Divya D. (2018). Effect of wet-laboratory training on resident performed manual small-incision cataract surgery. Indian Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijo.IJO_1041_17
title: Structured wet-laboratory curriculum for ophthalmology residents (foam suturing then goat-eye steps before supervised operating)
description: A stepwise pre-operative skills curriculum introduced in March 2013 at the study institute, which residents had to complete before entering the operating theater. It begins with hand–eye coordination training, described as "suturing on foam under microscope (3-step, Leica microscope) for two classes", followed by goat-eye practice of "the scleral tunnel, entry into anterior chamber and capsulotomy for 6 weeks (12 Goat's eye each)", then two months of wet-laboratory training before supervised surgery and regular monthly training of 6 h/month during the first two residency years.
requirements: Residents complete the wet-laboratory curriculum before being allowed to operate on patients
Continued monthly wet-laboratory training of 6 h/month during the first two years of residency
Supervised operating in the theater after wet-laboratory training
constraints: The article notes the cost involved in setting up and maintaining the wet laboratory as a pitfall
target_learners: Ophthalmology residents (first- to third-year) in a postgraduate training program
target_learning_goals: Hand–eye coordination and microsurgical skills for manual small-incision cataract surgery
Mastery of cataract surgery steps (scleral tunnel, anterior chamber entry, capsulotomy) before live surgery
examples: Introduced at Ramaiah Medical College in March 2013; resident cases before and after its introduction formed Groups A and B of the comparative study
key_sources: Ramani Soumya; Pradeep Thanuja Gopal; Sundaresh Divya D. (2018). Effect of wet-laboratory training on resident performed manual small-incision cataract surgery. Indian Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijo.IJO_1041_17

article_title: Validation of a new study skills scale to provide an explanation for depressive symptoms among medical students.
citation: AlFaris Eiad, Irfan Farhana, AlSayyari Shuaa, AlDahlawi Waad, Almuhaideb Shahad, Almehaidib Alanood, Almoqati Shaikha, Ahmed Abdullah M. A., Ponnamperuma Gominda, AlMughthim Muhannad, Shaffi Ahamed Shaik, Al Maflehi Nassr, van der Vleuten Cees. (2018). Validation of a new study skills scale to provide an explanation for depressive symptoms among medical students. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199037
title: Study Skills Inventory (SSI): a 23-item, five-subscale self-report instrument for medical students
description: The SSI is a short self-report inventory measuring study skills as 'the conscious and intentional use of processes around organizing and retaining new information'. Developed by expert consensus from four non-validated inventories, it was reduced from 97 items to 23 items across five subscales: reading, concentration and memory, time management, emotional management, and other learning practices, each scored 0-3 per item.
requirements: Administered as a self-report inventory; developed to be short and easy to complete for non-native English speakers, unlike longer inventories such as LASSI and ASSIST
constraints: Developed and validated with medical students at a single medical school (King Saud University, Riyadh)
target_learners: medical students
target_learning_goals: study skills: reading, concentration and memory, time management, emotional management, other learning practices
examples: The final inventory comprised 23 items after exclusion of all items with loading <0.4, with varimax rotation
key_sources: AlFaris Eiad, Irfan Farhana, AlSayyari Shuaa, AlDahlawi Waad, Almuhaideb Shahad, Almehaidib Alanood, Almoqati Shaikha, Ahmed Abdullah M. A., Ponnamperuma Gominda, AlMughthim Muhannad, Shaffi Ahamed Shaik, Al Maflehi Nassr, van der Vleuten Cees. (2018). Validation of a new study skills scale to provide an explanation for depressive symptoms among medical students. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199037

article_title: Medical students create multiple-choice questions for learning in pathology education: a pilot study.
citation: Grainger R, Dai W, Osborne E, Kenwright D. (2018). Medical students create multiple-choice questions for learning in pathology education: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1312-1
title: Structured student MCQ-writing task with per-module quotas, quality ratings and scaffolding
description: A reusable course-level design in which each student creates at least two MCQs per topic module and correctly answers at least twenty peer-generated MCQs per module. Each MCQ comprises "a stem, one correct answer and three or four plausible distractors" with required explanations justifying the correct option and distractors. Questions are peer-rated on a six-point scale, tagged by topic, and a 30-minute scaffolding session introduces the rationale and question-writing guidance before implementation.
requirements: A 30-min instructional scaffolding session covering pedagogical rationale and technical support
Timetabled class time for authoring/answering within one to two weeks of relevant teaching
Course credit allocation (here 20% of the final grade) to support compulsory participation
constraints: Peer feedback via rating and commenting was strongly encouraged but not required, and engagement remained shallow
The authors note the high cognitive load required for task completion may have seemed excessive to students
target_learners: fourth-year medical students
target_learning_goals: deep learning including knowledge analysis, evaluation, and creation
preparation for high-stakes MCQ examinations
examples: Students received 20% of their final grade for the PeerWise activity: half for achieving an Answer Score of 800 and half for externally rated quality of one MCQ per module.
key_sources: Grainger R, Dai W, Osborne E, Kenwright D. (2018). Medical students create multiple-choice questions for learning in pathology education: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1312-1

article_title: Evaluating a dialogue-based approach to teaching about values and policy in graduate transdisciplinary environmental science programs.
citation: Hall Troy E., Piso Zachary, Engebretson Jesse, & O'Rourke Michael. (2018). Evaluating a dialogue-based approach to teaching about values and policy in graduate transdisciplinary environmental science programs. PLoS ONE 13(9): e0202948. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0202948
title: Structure values-and-policy dialogue with scaffolding while preserving student freedom
description: Drawing on a literature review, the article recommends dialogue-based activities over passive instruction for values-and-policy topics, with dialogue that is structured but not over-structured. "A structured process allows for more efficient and productive exchange of ideas than an unstructured process where students are simply asked for their thoughts or opinions", yet the authors warn that "if there is too much structure, students may rush to reach the \"right answers\"". Scaffolding should promote explanation and argumentation rather than announcement and defense of positions.
requirements: Scaffolding "such as discussion prompts that elicit differences among students and require explanation of different points of view", while also providing "some student freedom" to promote shared knowledge construction.
constraints: Excessive structure risks students rushing to the "right answers"; the article also notes some scholars found student-directed inquiry more effective than instructor-directed activities.
target_learners: Graduate environmental science students
target_learning_goals: Critical, elaborative discourse about values and policy
Empathy for multiple points of view
examples: The curriculum operationalizes this balance: students develop their own discussion prompts as scaffolding for "the culminating activity, a facilitated classroom discussion" following the Toolbox dialogue protocol.
key_sources: Hall Troy E., Piso Zachary, Engebretson Jesse, & O'Rourke Michael. (2018). Evaluating a dialogue-based approach to teaching about values and policy in graduate transdisciplinary environmental science programs. PLoS ONE 13(9): e0202948. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0202948

article_title: The use of low-cost Android tablets to train community health workers in Mukono, Uganda, in the recognition, treatment and prevention of pneumonia in children under five: a pilot randomised controlled trial.
citation: O'Donovan James, Kabali Kenneth, Taylor Celia, Chukhina Margarita, Kading Jacqueline C., Fuld Jonathan, O'Neil Edward. (2018). The use of low-cost Android tablets to train community health workers in Mukono, Uganda, in the recognition, treatment and prevention of pneumonia in children under five: a pilot randomised controlled trial. Human Resources for Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12960-018-0315-7
title: Design mHealth training content with local stakeholders, in the local language, and matched to learners' education and technology experience
description: The authors attribute the cultural appropriateness of their videos to early involvement of CHWs and approval by the Ministry of Health, arguing that "engaging key stakeholders at every level, from CHWs through to the MoH, is vitally important". They also stress that mHealth programs should consider learners' age, education level and prior technology use, and that local-language content contributes to ownership and understanding.
requirements: Videos produced in the local language and reviewed for accuracy by stakeholders such as the Ministry of Health and independent medical doctors
constraints: The authors note mHealth programs must take into consideration the age, level of education and previous technology use of the target learners
target_learners: Community health workers in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Culturally appropriate, comprehensible refresher training on clinical topics such as childhood pneumonia
examples: The study's videos were filmed in Mukono in Luganda with English subtitles, featured local CHWs and a Ugandan physician, and were approved by the Commissioner for Child Health at the MoH
key_sources: O'Donovan James, Kabali Kenneth, Taylor Celia, Chukhina Margarita, Kading Jacqueline C., Fuld Jonathan, O'Neil Edward. (2018). The use of low-cost Android tablets to train community health workers in Mukono, Uganda, in the recognition, treatment and prevention of pneumonia in children under five: a pilot randomised controlled trial. Human Resources for Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12960-018-0315-7

article_title: Disseminating START: training clinical psychologists and admiral nurses as trainers in a psychosocial intervention for carers of people with dementia's depressive and anxiety symptoms.
citation: Lord Kathryn, Rapaport Penny, Cooper Claudia, Livingston Gill. (2017). Disseminating START: training clinical psychologists and admiral nurses as trainers in a psychosocial intervention for carers of people with dementia's depressive and anxiety symptoms. BMJ Open 7(8): e017759. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2017-017759
title: START: a manualised eight-session coping-strategy intervention for family carers of people with dementia
description: START (STrAtegies for RelaTives) "comprises eight manualised sessions delivered to individual carers aimed at supporting them to develop adaptive coping strategies". Sessions cover learning about dementia and carer stress, behavioural management, relaxation, legal and care planning and pleasant activities; carers keep a manual with an individualised plan and a relaxation audio resource. The article disseminated it via free online materials.
requirements: Delivery by supervised graduate or junior psychologists under highly qualified clinical supervision
Fidelity to the START manual, with adherence defined as participating in five or more sessions
constraints: Tested and recommended in an individual, not group-based, therapy format
Eight sessions of therapist time were reported as hard to justify within services under resource pressure
target_learners: family carers of people with dementia
target_learning_goals: adaptive coping strategies
relaxation and managing unhelpful thoughts
behavioural management and communication skills
care and legal planning
examples: In the original RCT, "Carers in the treatment as usual group were seven times more likely to have clinically significant depression than those receiving START at 2 years"
key_sources: Lord Kathryn, Rapaport Penny, Cooper Claudia, Livingston Gill. (2017). Disseminating START: training clinical psychologists and admiral nurses as trainers in a psychosocial intervention for carers of people with dementia's depressive and anxiety symptoms. BMJ Open 7(8): e017759. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2017-017759

article_title: I Can Stand Learning: A Controlled Pilot Intervention Study on the Effects of Increased Standing Time on Cognitive Function in Primary School Children.
citation: Wick Katharina, Faude Oliver, Manes Susanne, Zahner Lukas, Donath Lars. (2018). I Can Stand Learning: A Controlled Pilot Intervention Study on the Effects of Increased Standing Time on Cognitive Function in Primary School Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph15020356
title: Standing desk with balance pad classroom intervention setup (Hüba-Ergofit desk plus unstable floor mat)
description: The intervention equipment consisted of height-adjustable standing desks (Hüba-Ergofit 03.AF.OK.FMH.R, 650 × 650 mm top, fixable between 750 and 1200 mm) each fitted with a foam floor mat (450 × 450 × 60 mm) on which pupils stood, creating an unstable surface. A non-slip layer underneath the mat was applied "To avoid accidents". Children had to maintain standing for at least 10 min once standing, and self-recorded transitions with arrows on a 10-min-unit report sheet covering 775 available minutes per school week.
requirements: Height-adjustable desks and floor mats fitted between the desk legs
A self-report sheet with 10-min units for real-time recording
Teacher reminders to reach the daily standing target
constraints: Standing had to be maintained for at least 10 min per episode
Self-report sheets require discipline and are probably not appropriate for longer periods
target_learners: primary school children aged 10–12 years
target_learning_goals: reduce sedentary classroom time and increase standing during lessons
examples: The intervention class used the desks for 11 weeks from August to December 2014 while the control class received lessons as usual.
key_sources: Wick Katharina, Faude Oliver, Manes Susanne, Zahner Lukas, Donath Lars. (2018). I Can Stand Learning: A Controlled Pilot Intervention Study on the Effects of Increased Standing Time on Cognitive Function in Primary School Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph15020356

article_title: Practicing health promotion in primary care -a reflective enquiry.
citation: Pati S., Chauhan A.S., Mahapatra S., Sinha R., Pati S. (2017). Practicing health promotion in primary care –a reflective enquiry. Journal of Preventive Medicine and Hygiene. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5912790/
title: Incorporate health promotion as a structured module in undergraduate and post-graduate medical curricula
description: The article argues that because the present Indian MBBS curriculum "lacks health promotion component during formative training", physicians enter practice unprepared to deliver health promotion. It recommends "developing and incorporating a structured health promotion module in undergraduate and post-graduate medical curriculum to address the gap", so professionals come to see health promotion as integral to service delivery.
requirements: Curriculum reform at undergraduate and post-graduate medical education levels, with content relevant to the local context
constraints: The article notes an integrated health promotion in mainstream curricula is still missing despite recent postgraduate diploma offerings
target_learners: undergraduate and post-graduate medical students
in-service primary care physicians
target_learning_goals: health promotion knowledge, perception and practice
preventive counseling skills
examples: The study of thirty Odisha physicians documented significant ideal-current gaps that the authors attribute partly to the missing curricular component
key_sources: Pati S., Chauhan A.S., Mahapatra S., Sinha R., Pati S. (2017). Practicing health promotion in primary care –a reflective enquiry. Journal of Preventive Medicine and Hygiene. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5912790/

article_title: What's in a Prerequisite? A Mixed-Methods Approach to Identifying the Impact of a Prerequisite Course.
citation: Sato Brian K., Lee Amanda K., Alam Usman, Dang Jennifer V., Dacanay Samantha J., Morgado Pedro, Pirino Giorgia, Brunner Jo Ellen, Castillo Leanne A., Chan Valerie W., Sandholtz Judith H. (2017). What’s in a Prerequisite? A Mixed-Methods Approach to Identifying the Impact of a Prerequisite Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education 16(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-08-0260
title: Students perceive prerequisites both as sources of background knowledge and future success and as sources of scheduling burden, time-to-degree delay, and cost
description: This pattern captures the dual student view of prerequisites documented through coded interviews. Positively, students cited background knowledge (89.3% of interviews), a safety net (35.7%), and contribution to future success (25.0%); negatively, they cited scheduling (51.7%), wasted time or money (37.9%), and misalignment between prerequisite and later courses (31.0%), noting instructors often re-teach because faculty "aren’t communicating." The article uses these themes to argue prerequisites’ claimed benefits must be demonstrable to students.
requirements: Applicable when assessing or designing prerequisite structures in undergraduate curricula where student perceptions can be solicited.
constraints: Themes derive from 29 interviews in one upper-division microbiology lab context at a single R1 institution.
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate biological sciences majors
target_learning_goals: preparation for subsequent laboratory coursework
examples: Coded interview table listing eight positive attribute categories (e.g., background knowledge at 89.3%) and five negative attribute categories (e.g., scheduling at 51.7%) with representative student quotes.
key_sources: Sato Brian K., Lee Amanda K., Alam Usman, Dang Jennifer V., Dacanay Samantha J., Morgado Pedro, Pirino Giorgia, Brunner Jo Ellen, Castillo Leanne A., Chan Valerie W., Sandholtz Judith H. (2017). What’s in a Prerequisite? A Mixed-Methods Approach to Identifying the Impact of a Prerequisite Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education 16(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-08-0260

article_title: Effectiveness of an individual, online e-learning program about sexually transmitted infections: a prospective cohort study.
citation: Bos-Bonnie Linda H. A., van Bergen Jan E. A. M. J., te Pas Ellen, Kijser Michael A. M., van Dijk Nynke. (2017). Effectiveness of an individual, online e-learning program about sexually transmitted infections: a prospective cohort study. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-017-0625-1
title: E-learning program 'The STI-consultation'
description: An individual, accredited, online CME-program created by the Dutch College of General Practitioners (NHG) with STI Aids Netherlands and the Academic Medical Centre, based on the NHG-guideline 'The STI-consultation' and the CanMEDS competency framework. "Completing the e-learning program 'The STI-consultation' takes about two hours" and it is freely available to all 12,500 Dutch GPs and GP-trainees, with participation voluntary and CME-credits awarded after full completion.
requirements: Freely available online access for GPs and GP-trainees
Full completion required for CME-credits
constraints: Participation is voluntary
Content is specific to the Dutch NHG-guideline 'The STI-consultation'
target_learners: Dutch general practitioners
GP-trainees
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, attitude, and behaviour concerning the STI-consultation, including sexual history taking, additional investigation, and treatment of STI
examples: Didactic methods included the quickscan, short interactive videotaped case-studies, and the CtC-method
key_sources: Bos-Bonnie Linda H. A., van Bergen Jan E. A. M. J., te Pas Ellen, Kijser Michael A. M., van Dijk Nynke. (2017). Effectiveness of an individual, online e-learning program about sexually transmitted infections: a prospective cohort study. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-017-0625-1

article_title: Student perception of group dynamics predicts individual performance: Comfort and equity matter.
citation: Theobald EJ, Eddy SL, Grunspan DZ, Wiggins BL, Crowe AJ. (2017). Student perception of group dynamics predicts individual performance: Comfort and equity matter. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0181336
title: Structure group work to promote positive interdependence, turn-taking, and explicit prompts for explaining reasoning to reduce inequitable group dynamics
description: The article concludes that group activities relying on positive interdependence with turn-taking and explicit prompts help reduce the negative impact of inequitable groups. In the study, the jigsaw activity—where students first independently mastered subtopics, then peer-taught them in new groups with embedded guiding prompts—produced dominator reports that were 67% less likely than in a loosely structured worksheet activity. Improved group function is described as more likely when the task is appropriately complex and requires input from many individuals.
requirements: Tasks must be appropriately complex and require input from many individuals, and group members should experience interdependence rather than independence
constraints: The data do not provide an explanation for why the jigsaw activity resulted in fewer dominators; whether interdependence or the explicit prompts drove the effect is unresolved
The article states that prompts geared toward interdependence should be rigorously tested
target_learners: university students in large-enrollment introductory STEM courses
target_learning_goals: content mastery in biology topics
equitable participation in small-group work
examples: Sections alternated between a single-group worksheet activity and a jigsaw activity in which students worked through one of three worksheet sections independently, conferred with peers who had the same section, then taught their section to a new three-person group.
key_sources: Theobald EJ, Eddy SL, Grunspan DZ, Wiggins BL, Crowe AJ. (2017). Student perception of group dynamics predicts individual performance: Comfort and equity matter. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0181336

article_title: Towards development and validation of an intraoperative assessment tool for robot-assisted radical prostatectomy training: results of a Delphi study.
citation: Morris Christopher, Hoogenes Jen, Shayegan Bobby, Matsumoto Edward D. (2017). Towards development and validation of an intraoperative assessment tool for robot-assisted radical prostatectomy training: results of a Delphi study. International Brazilian Journal of Urology. https://doi.org/10.1590/S1677-5538.IBJU.2016.0420
title: Use a procedure-specific stepwise inventory rather than a single global rating scale to assess trainees across an entire operation
description: The article argues that existing tools are inadequate for whole-procedure assessment: GEARS "is not task-specific; therefore when used, it must be tailored to the task being evaluated", and the generic FRS curriculum "cannot be applied to specific procedures without first tailoring it to the procedure". Because "Metrics for assessing the competency of the entire RARP procedure are lacking", the authors propose rating trainees on each step of the procedure as they progress through the learning curve, citing evidence that a proficiency-based stepwise approach to robotic training is feasible and safe.
requirements: A consensus-derived inventory of the procedure's critical steps and sub-steps
Evaluation metrics built in for each step
constraints: The stepwise tool is procedure-specific; the article notes the RARP inventory may change as feedback accumulates on alternate techniques
target_learners: urology residents (PGY3-5) and fellows in robotic surgery training
target_learning_goals: intraoperative technical competence across the full RARP procedure
examples: The authors state their proposed assessment tool "will allow surgical educators to rate trainees on each step of the RARP procedure as they progress through the learning curve" instead of relying on a single GRS

article_title: A randomised trial of the influence of racial stereotype bias on examiners' scores, feedback and recollections in undergraduate clinical exams.
citation: Yeates Peter, Woolf Katherine, Benbow Emyr, Davies Ben, Boohan Mairhead, Eva Kevin. (2017). A randomised trial of the influence of racial stereotype bias on examiners' scores, feedback and recollections in undergraduate clinical exams. BMC Medicine 15:179. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-017-0943-0
title: Stereotype activation is a separate cognitive process from stereotype application: a stereotype can come to mind during judgement without influencing the decision reached
description: The article distinguishes two cognitive processes: stereotype activation, measured here by faster lexical decision responses to stereotype-related words, and stereotype application, the influence of the stereotype on the judgement itself. As the article puts it, "a stereotype can come to mind during a judgement process without influencing the decision that is reached". The trial's examiners showed activation without application, which the authors attribute to possible motivation to avoid prejudice or to achieve accuracy. This framework organises the study's central null findings.
requirements: A measure of mental activation distinct from judgement outcomes, such as a lexical decision task, is needed to observe activation separately from application
constraints: The article notes it could not definitively claim activation occurred in response to the videos, since there was no control condition without videos
target_learners: OSCE examiners (qualified doctors assessing undergraduate medical students)
target_learning_goals: Fair and unbiased assessment of clinical performance across student ethnicities
examples: Examiners responded faster to stereotype words than neutral words yet assigned identical average scores to Asian and white student performances
key_sources: Yeates Peter, Woolf Katherine, Benbow Emyr, Davies Ben, Boohan Mairhead, Eva Kevin. (2017). A randomised trial of the influence of racial stereotype bias on examiners' scores, feedback and recollections in undergraduate clinical exams. BMC Medicine 15:179. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-017-0943-0

article_title: Assessment of laparoscopic skills of Gynecology and Obstetrics residents after a training program.
citation: Fernandes Carla Ferreira Kikuchi, Ruano José Maria Cordeiro, Kati Lea Mina, Noguti Alberto Sinhiti, Girão Manoel João Batista Castello, Sartori Marair Gracio Ferreira. (2016). Assessment of laparoscopic skills of Gynecology and Obstetrics residents after a training program. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://doi.org/10.1590/S1679-45082016AO3752
title: Teach laparoscopic skills outside the operating room with standardized, reproducible exercises and immediate feedback
description: The article argues that surgical skills for minimally invasive surgery must be acquired outside the operating room, and that "standardization, easy reproducibility of the exercises, immediate feedback after each training session" at acceptable cost bring benefits to teaching laparoscopy. It implements this via a structured box trainer plus animal surgery curriculum with the same preceptors throughout.
requirements: A specialist or experienced preceptor to demonstrate procedures and provide performance feedback for bench models
A training and surgical experimentation center with box trainers and animal facilities
constraints: Animal models are criticized for cost, anatomy, and ethical issues; cadavers for cost, limited availability, and impossibility of simulating complications; virtual simulators for cost, limited tactile feedback, and lack of graphic realism
target_learners: surgical residents in Gynecology and Obstetrics
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic surgical technique and instrument handling skills
examples: The CETEC program gave residents 12 hours of box trainer exercises and 20 hours of pig surgery over eight weeks, with immediate feedback from the same preceptors after each session

Assessment of laparoscopic skills of Gynecology and Obstetrics residents after a training program. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://doi.org/10.1590/S1679-45082016AO3752

article_title: Increasing general practitioners' confidence and self-efficacy in managing obesity: a mixed methods study.
citation: Sturgiss Elizabeth, Haesler Emily, Elmitt Nicholas, van Weel Chris, Douglas Kirsty. (2017). Increasing general practitioners' confidence and self-efficacy in managing obesity: a mixed methods study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2016-014314
title: Build clinicians' professional self-efficacy with a structured toolkit rather than additional training
description: The article recommends supporting clinicians to adopt new practices by supplying a structured management toolkit that enables a performance mastery experience, rather than requiring extra training. GPs "were not offered any training beyond the written handbook" because earlier qualitative work showed they did not want a programme requiring additional training; the structure and support of the materials were identified in interviews as the key reason they felt more confident. The authors conclude that enhancing professional self-efficacy is the first step to improving obesity management in general practice.
requirements: A structured, evidence-based toolkit the clinician can implement directly in their own setting
constraints: Generalisability is limited by the small sample of self-selecting GPs likely to have a particular interest in obesity care
target_learners: general practitioners
primary care clinicians
target_learning_goals: confidence and self-efficacy in managing obesity
adopting new clinical practices
examples: The pilot provided only the written handbook and programme materials; GPs then reported feeling confident enough to discuss obesity with patients outside the research setting
key_sources: Sturgiss Elizabeth, Haesler Emily, Elmitt Nicholas, van Weel Chris, Douglas Kirsty. (2017). Increasing general practitioners' confidence and self-efficacy in managing obesity: a mixed methods study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2016-014314

article_title: Impact of standardized patients on the training of medical students to manage emergencies.
citation: Herbstreit Frank, Merse Stefanie, Schnell Rainer, Noack Marcel, Dirkmann Daniel, Besuch Anna, Peters Jürgen. (2017). Impact of standardized patients on the training of medical students to manage emergencies. Medicine 96(5):e5933. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000005933
title: Adopt standardized-patient training for emergency-medicine teaching only where its small performance benefit justifies the additional resources
description: The article recommends weighing the small, significant OSCE benefit of standardized-patient training against its costs: recruitment and training of actors, moulage, equipment preparation, and instructor and feedback time. It concludes that "teaching management of emergencies using standardized patients can improve medical students' performance in clinical tests" without compromising factual-knowledge learning.
requirements: Availability of trained standardized patients (professional actors recruited and trained by medical faculty) and instructor time for feedback
constraints: The authors state the apparently small benefit "may or may not justify these investments" and that whether the improvement is quantitatively meaningful "must be decided individually" given tight budgets
target_learners: fourth-year (second clinical year) medical students in emergency-medicine courses
target_learning_goals: management of medical emergencies including patient assessment, technical skills, and team interaction
examples: In the trial, 242 students were randomized to three 90-minute standardized-patient sessions or three equal-duration traditional seminars covering acute chest pain, stroke, and acute dyspnea/asthma scenarios
key_sources: Herbstreit Frank, Merse Stefanie, Schnell Rainer, Noack Marcel, Dirkmann Daniel, Besuch Anna, Peters Jürgen. (2017). Impact of standardized patients on the training of medical students to manage emergencies. Medicine 96(5):e5933. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000005933

article_title: Development of a competency-based formative progress test with student-generated MCQs: Results from a multi-centre pilot study.
citation: Wagener S, Möltner A, Tımbıl S, Gornostayeva M, Schultz J-H, Brüstle P, Mohr D, Vander Beken A, Better J, Fries M, Gottschalk M, Günther J, Herrmann L, Kreisel C, Moczko T, Illg C, Jassowicz A, Müller A, Niesert M, Strübing F, Jünger J. (2015). Development of a competency-based formative progress test with student-generated MCQs: Results from a multi-centre pilot study. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 32(4):Doc46. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2015-32/zma000988.shtml
title: Student training programme and dedicated ItemManagementSystem platform for generating and reviewing progress-test MCQs
description: To enable students to develop the progress test, the project ran an intensive training programme of "five 2-day workshops, which occurred between February and October 2013", covering competency-based assessment, CanMEDS roles, the progress test concept, the blueprint, quality criteria for MCQs, group review, and working with the IMS. Students then drafted, group-reviewed, revised and re-reviewed MCQs in workshop and self-organized small-group phases, using a separate IMS platform dedicated solely to this progress test. Group reviews with trainers served as a quality assurance measure, and participants received work-study contracts to ensure long-term cooperation.
requirements: Intensive and comprehensive training of participating students before item writing
Access to a dedicated ItemManagementSystem platform for item generation and review
target_learners: medical students in semesters three to nine from seven German medical schools
target_learning_goals: writing and reviewing quality multiple-choice questions aligned to a competency-based blueprint
examples: A core team of 17 students from five universities emerged from the initial 31 participants and presented the process at the 2013 GMA convention in Graz

article_title: Three methods of delivering clinic-based training on syndromic management of sexually transmitted diseases in South Africa: a pilot study.
citation: Weaver Marcia R, Pillay Erushka, Jed Suzanne L, de Kadt Julia, Galagan Sean, Gilvydis Jennifer, Marumo Eva, Mawandia Shreshth, Naidoo Evasen, Owens Tamara, Prongay Vickery, O'Malley Gabrielle. (2016). Three methods of delivering clinic-based training on syndromic management of sexually transmitted diseases in South Africa: a pilot study. Sex Transm Infect. https://doi.org/10.1136/sextrans-2015-052107
title: Six-module case-based STI training programme deliverable as lecture, computer-based or paper-based formats
description: The STI training programme consists of six modules covering STI introduction and patient history, physical exam and counselling, male urethritis syndrome, vaginal discharge syndrome, genital ulcer syndrome, and lower abdominal pain, with per-module learning objectives such as "Accurately use the NDOH syndromic algorithm for the syndrome or diagnosis". Modules were organised around clinical cases, each designed to be completed in 1 hour, delivered two modules per week for three weeks via trainer-led lecture, computer (with navigation assistance), or printed materials, with all participants receiving the national STI guidelines. Computer-based modules were available online and on compact disc.
requirements: Delivered at clinic level in 2-hour sessions offered twice weekly, with the same frequency and time across all three methods
All participants receive a printed version of the national STI guidelines
constraints: All training materials are in English, which is 1 of 11 official languages of South Africa
target_learners: doctors and nurses assigned to primary healthcare clinics in South Africa
target_learning_goals: syndromic management of sexually transmitted infections per the revised national guidelines
examples: In the pilot, clinics were randomly assigned to one of the three methods or a control arm, and 40 clinics in North West Province participated

article_title: A comprehensive review on learning curve associated problems in endoscopic vein harvesting and the requirement for a standardised training programme.
citation: Krishnamoorthy Bhuvaneswari, Critchley William R., Venkateswaran Rajamiyer V., Barnard James, Caress Ann, Fildes James E., Yonan Nizar. (2016). A comprehensive review on learning curve associated problems in endoscopic vein harvesting and the requirement for a standardised training programme. Journal of Cardiothoracic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13019-016-0442-y
title: Structure EVH training programmes with theoretical knowledge, equipment training and progressive clinical skills, assessed with a validated OSATS
description: The review argues that EVH training should use a surgical skill curriculum training tool that is "structured, reliable and rigorously validated to be incorporated into an objective clinical assessment". It specifies programme elements: theoretical knowledge reinforcing vein integrity preservation, equipment training to improve hand-eye coordination, and gradual introduction to clinical practical skills. Every step should be evaluated using validated Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills (OSATS), which the review states have proven reliability and construct validity for minimally invasive surgical skills.
requirements: Validated OSATS evaluation at every step
Both theoretical and technical knowledge plus performance evaluation in the curriculum
Benchmark criteria to allow progression
constraints: The review notes structured competency-based surgical training tools do not yet exist for EVH and require validation of tasks, experience levels, duration and frequency
target_learners: Novice EVH practitioners in cardiothoracic surgical training
target_learning_goals: Technical operative skill and preservation of vein conduit quality
examples: The review cites competency-based endoscopic curricula in other surgical specialties, and laparoscopic training on video trainers and virtual reality simulators shown to improve performance on real patients
key_sources: Krishnamoorthy Bhuvaneswari, Critchley William R., Venkateswaran Rajamiyer V., Barnard James, Caress Ann, Fildes James E., Yonan Nizar. (2016). Journal of Cardiothoracic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13019-016-0442-y

article_title: Theory in practice instead of theory versus practice--curricular design for task-based learning within a competency oriented curriculum.
citation: Rotthoff T, Schneider M, Ritz-Timme S, Windolf J. (2015). Theory in Practice instead of Theory versus Practice – Curricular design for Task-based Learning within a competency oriented Curriculum. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4330634/
title: Study Guides created by clinical departments to support complaint-based learning
description: Study Guides are discipline-specific learning-support documents developed by Duesseldorf's clinical departments and institutes, accessible via a web-based learning platform by complaint item. "All Study Guides adhere to a conceptual framework: a) learning objectives form the subject's point of view, b) diseases matching the complaints, c) special features in clinical management d) literature recommendations for further reading, e) questions for reflection." The information on special features in clinical management and the reflection questions exceed the contents of textbooks.
requirements: Guides are created by the clinical departments and institutes that have selected a complaint item as course content
constraints: The Guides contain chapters with a selection of complaint items or other reasons for consultation relevant to each specific discipline
target_learners: medical students in workplace-based practice blocks
target_learning_goals: subject-specific understanding of complaint items
clinical management
reflective learning
examples: With the complaint „shortness of breath", students can use a web-based learning platform to find the Study Guides created by departments that selected this complaint item

article_title: Nurses' evaluation of physicians' non-clinical performance in emergency departments: advantages, disadvantages and lessons learned.
citation: Alameddine M, Mufarrij A, Saliba M, Mourad Y, Jabbour R, Hitti E. (2015). Nurses' evaluation of physicians' non-clinical performance in emergency departments: advantages, disadvantages and lessons learned. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-015-0733-3
title: Peer-evaluation and behavioral-change programs should be offered in a staged and incremental manner over a long period with dedicated resources and timely monitoring to achieve sustainable improvement
description: The article's central lesson for sustaining improvements in physicians' non-clinical skills: one-off training and feedback produced gains that were lost by the third evaluation cycle. The authors state that "such programs may need to be offered in a staged and incremental manner over a long period of time with proper dedication of resources and timely monitoring and evaluation of outcomes." This applies to departments using nurse or peer evaluation of physicians' communication, professionalism and leadership.
requirements: Dedicated human and financial resources for repeated evaluation cycles and training programs
Resources and expertise for proper monitoring and evaluation of program outcomes
constraints: The six-month evaluation frequency used between the first two cycles was prohibitive to maintain due to time restrictions and scarcity of human resources
target_learners: Emergency department physicians
Clinical department staff
target_learning_goals: Communication skills
Professionalism
Leadership and system-based practice
examples: After the first evaluation cycle, the ED provided physicians individualized anonymous feedback and hired an external consultant to deliver three four-hour communication training sessions; gains were lost by the third cycle when only feedback was offered
key_sources: Alameddine M, Mufarrij A, Saliba M, Mourad Y, Jabbour R, Hitti E. (2015). Nurses' evaluation of physicians' non-clinical performance in emergency departments: advantages, disadvantages and lessons learned. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-015-0733-3

article_title: The relationship between intelligence and training gains is moderated by training strategy.
citation: Lee Hyunkyu, Boot Walter R., Baniqued Pauline L., Voss Michelle W., Prakash Ruchika Shaurya, Basak Chandramallika, Kramer Arthur F. (2015). The Relationship between Intelligence and Training Gains Is Moderated by Training Strategy. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0123259
title: Use structured strategy training (part-task plus variable priority training) to reduce the limiting influence of individual differences in fluid intelligence
description: The article recommends directed training strategies for learners who would otherwise be limited by lower fluid intelligence. It states that "directed training strategies such as a combination of part-task training and variable priority training may be more useful to overcome the individual differences in fluid intelligence". HVT structures practice by training game components independently and by having learners emphasize different sub-skills across practice blocks, whereas FET leaves learners to find their own methods.
requirements: Training must include part-task training of components and variable priority practice emphasizing different sub-skills within the whole task
constraints: The article notes results from healthy young adults only may not generalize to other populations
target_learners: young adults (ages 18-30) learning complex skills
target_learning_goals: complex task mastery and flexible task coordination
examples: Participants trained with HVT received part-task training in the first five sessions followed by ten sessions of variable priority training, and showed higher training gains with no fluid-intelligence association
key_sources: Lee Hyunkyu, Boot Walter R., Baniqued Pauline L., Voss Michelle W., Prakash Ruchika Shaurya, Basak Chandramallika, Kramer Arthur F. (2015). The Relationship between Intelligence and Training Gains Is Moderated by Training Strategy. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0123259
